meta.title: IELTS Speaking question bank
meta.sampleNote: Sample answers are written by one speaker (a young professional from Sirajganj). Use them for ideas, structure and vocabulary, then answer with your own experience.

questions: Do you work or are you a student?
Why did you choose that job?
What do you like most about your job?
Is there anything you dislike about your work?
Would you like to change your job in the future?

samples.q: Do you work or are you a student?
samples.answer: I'm working at the moment, at an education consultancy, where I [[predominantly]] help students with their applications abroad. It keeps me busy, but seeing someone reach a goal they worked towards is genuinely rewarding, so the effort feels worthwhile.

samples.q: Why did you choose that job?
samples.answer: Mainly because I went through the application process myself as a student and realised how confusing it can be. I wanted to help people [[navigate]] that uncertainty, and this role lets me do exactly that.

samples.q: What do you like most about your job?
samples.answer: Honestly, it's the people. Every student comes with their own hopes and worries, so no two days are identical, and guiding someone through such a [[daunting]] process gives me a real sense of purpose.

samples.q: Is there anything you dislike about your work?
samples.answer: The deadlines can be quite stressful, particularly during the main admission seasons when everything seems to arrive at once. There's a lot of paperwork too, and I'll admit the administrative side can get rather [[tedious]].

samples.q: Would you like to change your job in the future?
samples.answer: Not entirely, but I'd like to grow within the field. Ideally, I'll study abroad myself one day and then come back to a more senior role. For now, though, I'm happy [[honing my skills]] where I am.

questions: What subject did you study?
Why did you choose that subject?
Did you enjoy your time at university?
What was the most useful thing you learned?
Would you like to study something else in the future?

samples.q: What subject did you study?
samples.answer: I studied business administration at university, with a focus on management. It gave me a broad understanding of how organisations actually run, which has proved surprisingly [[invaluable]] in the work I do now.

samples.q: Why did you choose that subject?
samples.answer: Partly because of my father, to be honest. Growing up around his small business, I saw how much planning goes into keeping things running, and I suppose that [[sparked my interest]] in management quite early on.

samples.q: Did you enjoy your time at university?
samples.answer: Very much, on the whole. The coursework was demanding at times, but I made some lifelong friends and took part in a few debating events. Those years really helped me become more [[self-assured]] and independent.

samples.q: What was the most useful thing you learned?
samples.answer: Probably how to communicate clearly in a professional setting. We did a lot of group presentations, which I dreaded at first, but they gradually made me far more [[articulate]], and I rely on that every day at work.

samples.q: Would you like to study something else in the future?
samples.answer: Yes, I'd love to do a master's abroad, possibly in international education or management. I feel it would deepen my understanding of the field and [[open doors]] that aren't really available to me here.

questions: Where is your hometown?
What do you like most about your hometown?
Is your hometown a good place for visitors?
Has your hometown changed much in recent years?
Do you prefer living in a city or the countryside?

samples.q: Where is your hometown?
samples.answer: I'm from Sirajganj, a modest town in the north of Bangladesh, right beside the Jamuna river. It's about four hours from Dhaka by road, and I've lived there most of my life, so it has a certain [[tranquillity]] that feels like home.

samples.q: What do you like most about your hometown?
samples.answer: Without doubt, the river. In the evenings I often walk along the Jamuna embankment, and watching the sun set over the water is incredibly [[soothing]]. The people are warm and welcoming too, which gives it a real sense of community.

samples.q: Is your hometown a good place for visitors?
samples.answer: It's not a major tourist destination, but it has its charms. Sirajganj is known for its handloom weaving, and visitors can take a boat trip on the Jamuna. It suits anyone who enjoys a slower, more [[laid-back]] pace.

samples.q: Has your hometown changed much in recent years?
samples.answer: Quite a lot, actually. There are more shops, better roads and far more traffic than when I was younger. Some of it is welcome progress, but part of me misses how quiet and [[unspoilt]] it used to feel.

samples.q: Do you prefer living in a city or the countryside?
samples.answer: That's a tough one. I enjoy the energy of a city, but I genuinely appreciate the calm of the countryside. Honestly, the [[ideal]] for me would be a quieter town that isn't too far from a city.

questions: Do you live in a house or a flat?
How long have you lived there?
Which room do you spend the most time in?
Is there anything you'd like to change about your home?
What kind of home would you like to live in in the future?

samples.q: Do you live in a house or a flat?
samples.answer: I live in a flat, on the third floor of a building in a quiet residential area. It's a three-bedroom place I share with my family. It suits us well, though I do [[occasionally]] wish we had a bit more open space around us.

samples.q: How long have you lived there?
samples.answer: Well over a decade now, since I was a teenager. Before that we rented a smaller place nearby, so moving there felt like a real step up, and the flat is full of [[fond memories]] for all of us.

samples.q: Which room do you spend the most time in?
samples.answer: Definitely my bedroom, which doubles as my study, so I'm in there for most of the day when I'm home. I've arranged it to be quiet and comfortable, which makes it easy to [[concentrate]].

samples.q: Is there anything you'd like to change about your home?
samples.answer: I'd love a bigger balcony, to be honest. Ours is quite narrow, so there isn't much room for plants or a chair. A bit more outdoor space would make it far more [[inviting]] on pleasant evenings.

samples.q: What kind of home would you like to live in in the future?
samples.answer: Ideally, a small house with a garden, somewhere peaceful but still within reach of the town. I'd like to grow a few vegetables and have space for bookshelves. Nothing grand, just somewhere that feels like a genuine [[sanctuary]].

questions: Can you tell me about your family?
Do you spend much time with your family?
Who are you closest to in your family?
What do you like to do together as a family?
Has your family changed much in recent years?

samples.q: Can you tell me about your family?
samples.answer: It's a fairly typical family. There are five of us: my parents, my two sisters and me, although my elder sister is married now and lives in Dhaka with her husband and children. My father ran a small business until he retired recently, and my mother looks after the home. We're quite [[close-knit]], and those of us at home usually have dinner together every night.

samples.q: Do you spend much time with your family?
samples.answer: Quite a lot, especially in the evenings. Once work is done, we tend to gather in the living room over tea and chat about our day. Those relaxed moments help me [[wind down]] after a long day.

samples.q: Who are you closest to in your family?
samples.answer: Probably my younger sister. She's a student and incredibly hard-working, so we often talk about her studies and plans. I feel quite [[protective]] of her, and she's usually the first person I share news with.

samples.q: What do you like to do together as a family?
samples.answer: We love visiting my grandparents in our ancestral village, which isn't far from Sirajganj. The whole family gathers there, especially during Eid, and those visits have an [[unhurried]] warmth that I really treasure.

samples.q: Has your family changed much in recent years?
samples.answer: Quite a bit, actually. My elder sister got married and moved to Dhaka, and my father has recently retired, so he's at home far more. It was a big [[adjustment]] at first, but it's brought us even closer.

questions: Does your name have any special meaning?
Who chose your name?
Do you have a nickname?
What names are popular in your country?
Would you ever change your name?

samples.q: Does your name have any special meaning?
samples.answer: Yes, it does actually. My name carries a meaning connected to guidance and light, which is fairly common in our culture. I quite like it, because names here are usually chosen with real [[deliberation]] behind them.

samples.q: Who chose your name?
samples.answer: My grandfather did, actually. In our family it's [[customary]] for the eldest relative to suggest a name, and my parents were happy to go along with it. I think that's quite a touching tradition.

samples.q: Do you have a nickname?
samples.answer: Yes, like most people in Bangladesh, I have a short nickname that my family and close friends use. My formal name is really only for official documents, so the nickname feels far more [[affectionate]] and personal.

samples.q: What names are popular in your country?
samples.answer: Names with religious or poetic meanings are very popular here, particularly Arabic and Bengali ones. Recently, though, I've noticed parents choosing shorter, more modern names, which reflects a broader [[generational change]] in taste.

samples.q: Would you ever change your name?
samples.answer: No, I can't imagine doing that. My name connects me to my grandfather and to my family's traditions, so changing it would feel like losing part of my [[heritage]].

questions: What is your typical daily routine?
Do you usually get up early?
Which part of the day do you like most?
Do you prefer having a routine or variety?
Has your routine changed much since you were a student?

samples.q: What is your typical daily routine?
samples.answer: It's fairly structured on weekdays. I get up around seven, have a quick breakfast, and I'm at work by nine. After work I usually study for a couple of hours, then [[unwind]] before bed. Weekends are far more relaxed.

samples.q: Do you usually get up early?
samples.answer: Yes, on weekdays I'm up by seven. I've found I think much more clearly in the mornings, so I make the most of that quiet, [[uninterrupted]] time. On weekends, though, I happily allow myself a lie-in.

samples.q: Which part of the day do you like most?
samples.answer: The early morning, surprisingly. It's quiet, the day hasn't got hectic yet, and I feel clear-headed. A calm start with a cup of tea genuinely sets a [[productive]] tone for everything that follows.

samples.q: Do you prefer having a routine or variety?
samples.answer: A bit of both, ideally. A steady routine keeps me productive, but I'd get bored without some variety. So I like structure on weekdays and something a little more [[spontaneous]] at the weekend.

samples.q: Has your routine changed much since you were a student?
samples.answer: Quite significantly. At university my days were far more flexible, and I'd often stay up late and sleep in. Now that I work full-time, I've had to become much more [[disciplined]], which has honestly been good for me.

questions: Do you know your neighbours well?
How often do you see your neighbours?
Do you ever help your neighbours?
What do you think makes a good neighbour?
Do you think people are as close to their neighbours as they used to be?

samples.q: Do you know your neighbours well?
samples.answer: Reasonably well, yes. In our building people are fairly friendly, so we greet each other and occasionally chat. I wouldn't say we're close, but there's a warm, [[cordial]] relationship, which matters when you live so near people.

samples.q: How often do you see your neighbours?
samples.answer: Almost every day, just in passing, on the stairs or near the entrance, and we usually exchange a quick greeting. During Eid, though, we visit each other properly and share food, which is a [[heartwarming]] custom.

samples.q: Do you ever help your neighbours?
samples.answer: Now and then, yes. There's an elderly man on our floor, so I sometimes carry his shopping upstairs or help with small errands. It's only a small gesture, but I think these acts of [[goodwill]] matter in a community.

samples.q: What do you think makes a good neighbour?
samples.answer: Someone who's respectful and considerate, really. A good neighbour keeps the noise down, says hello and is willing to lend a hand in an emergency, but also respects your privacy and doesn't [[pry]].

samples.q: Do you think people are as close to their neighbours as they used to be?
samples.answer: Not really, especially in bigger cities. When I was younger, neighbours would drop in unannounced for tea. Nowadays people are busier and more private, so those bonds have [[eroded]] somewhat.

questions: Do you have many friends?
How did you meet your closest friends?
Can you describe your best friend?
What do you usually do with your friends?
Do you think it's easy to make friends as an adult?

samples.q: Do you have many friends?
samples.answer: I wouldn't say many, but I have a small circle I really trust. I've always preferred a few close friendships over a wide range of [[acquaintances]]. Those are the people I can be completely myself around.

samples.q: How did you meet your closest friends?
samples.answer: Most of them are from school and university, so we've known each other for years and share a lot of history. A couple are former colleagues too, which shows that friendships can [[blossom]] in unexpected places.

samples.q: Can you describe your best friend?
samples.answer: Sure. He's easygoing, genuinely kind and a great listener, which is probably why we've stayed close for so long. He has this [[reassuring]] way of putting things in perspective whenever I'm stressed.

samples.q: What do you usually do with your friends?
samples.answer: Nothing too elaborate. We usually meet at a local tea stall and chat for hours, or watch a cricket match together. Sometimes we take a walk by the river. It's the easy, [[unpretentious]] company that I value most.

samples.q: Do you think it's easy to make friends as an adult?
samples.answer: Not as easy as it was at school. Adults are busy with work and family, so there are fewer chances to connect naturally. Friendships still form, but they take more time and [[deliberate]] effort.

questions: Where did you grow up?
What did you enjoy doing as a child?
Did you have any hobbies as a child?
Did you have much freedom as a child?
Do you think children today have a better childhood than you had?

samples.q: Where did you grow up?
samples.answer: Mostly in Sirajganj, although I spent many school holidays at my grandparents' home in our village nearby. Both places shaped me, and I still feel a strong sense of [[belonging]] whenever I go back.

samples.q: What did you enjoy doing as a child?
samples.answer: I was quite an outdoorsy kid. I'd spend hours playing cricket with the neighbourhood children until it got dark. Looking back, those were some of the most [[carefree]] times of my life.

samples.q: Did you have any hobbies as a child?
samples.answer: Plenty. I was always outside playing cricket, and I also loved reading comics and adventure stories. Those simple hobbies kept me endlessly [[entertained]], long before phones and screens took over.

samples.q: Did you have much freedom as a child?
samples.answer: Quite a lot, compared to children in big cities today. As long as I was home before dark, my parents were fairly relaxed. Our neighbourhood felt safe, so I could [[roam]] around with friends quite freely.

samples.q: Do you think children today have a better childhood than you had?
samples.answer: In some ways, yes. They have access to far more information and opportunities. However, I think they spend too much time indoors on screens and miss out on the kind of [[unstructured]] outdoor play I enjoyed.

questions: What languages do you speak?
Is English widely spoken in your country?
Would you like to learn another language?
Do you find learning languages difficult?
Do you think children should learn a foreign language at school?

samples.q: What languages do you speak?
samples.answer: I speak Bengali as my mother tongue, and English fairly fluently. I picked up English mostly through school and a lot of self-study, and I use it daily at work, so it's become almost [[instinctive]].

samples.q: Is English widely spoken in your country?
samples.answer: It's widely understood in cities, particularly in business, universities and among younger people. In rural areas, though, Bengali is used for almost everything. English is increasingly seen as a [[gateway]] to better jobs and study opportunities.

samples.q: Would you like to learn another language?
samples.answer: I'd love to learn Arabic, mainly so I can understand the Quran more deeply. I've also considered German, since some students I advise are interested in universities there, so it could give me a [[competitive edge]] at work.

samples.q: Do you find learning languages difficult?
samples.answer: It can be, especially as an adult. Grammar and vocabulary take time, but the real challenge is speaking confidently without fear of mistakes. I think consistent practice and [[immersion]] matter far more than natural talent.

samples.q: Do you think children should learn a foreign language at school?
samples.answer: Absolutely. Children pick up languages far more easily than adults, and early exposure builds confidence. In such an [[interconnected]] world, a second language gives them a real advantage later in life.

questions: What are your plans for the future?
Which country would you most like to study in?
Where would you like to live in the future?
Do you usually plan things carefully?
Do you think your life will be very different in ten years?

samples.q: What are your plans for the future?
samples.answer: In the short term, I'm focused on strengthening my career and possibly studying abroad. Longer term, I'd like to reach a point where my work has real impact and I have the [[stability]] to enjoy life a little more.

samples.q: Which country would you most like to study in?
samples.answer: Probably the UK or Canada. Both have excellent universities and a strong reputation in business and education. Having helped so many students apply there, I understand the process well, which makes the idea far less [[intimidating]].

samples.q: Where would you like to live in the future?
samples.answer: I'd happily spend a few years abroad for study, but eventually I'd like to settle back in Bangladesh, perhaps in Dhaka or near my hometown. My family is here, and I feel deeply [[rooted]] in this place.

samples.q: Do you usually plan things carefully?
samples.answer: For important matters, definitely. I like to set clear goals and break them into manageable steps. That said, I've learned that life rarely goes exactly to plan, so staying [[adaptable]] is just as important.

samples.q: Do you think your life will be very different in ten years?
samples.answer: I imagine so. Hopefully I'll have completed further studies and be in a more senior position. I might have a family of my own by then too, so my priorities will probably [[evolve]] quite a lot.

questions: What do you usually do at the weekend?
Who do you usually spend your weekends with?
Do you prefer weekdays or weekends?
Did you do anything special last weekend?
Are your weekends different now from when you were a child?

samples.q: What do you usually do at the weekend?
samples.answer: I try to keep weekends flexible after a busy week. Usually I catch up on sleep, meet a friend or two, and maybe run some errands. If I'm lucky, I'll fit in a book or a film to properly [[recharge]].

samples.q: Who do you usually spend your weekends with?
samples.answer: Mostly with my family, to be honest. My younger sister and I sometimes go out for snacks, and occasionally we all visit my grandparents in the village. Evenings are usually for friends, so my weekends feel pleasantly [[well-rounded]].

samples.q: Do you prefer weekdays or weekends?
samples.answer: Weekends, without question. Weekdays are productive but tiring, whereas weekends give me space to rest and see people. That balance is what keeps me [[going]] through the week.

samples.q: Did you do anything special last weekend?
samples.answer: Nothing extraordinary. On Friday I went to the mosque for Friday prayers, then spent the afternoon reading. On Saturday I met two old friends for tea, and we ended up chatting for hours, which was [[thoroughly]] enjoyable.

samples.q: Are your weekends different now from when you were a child?
samples.answer: Completely. As a child, weekends meant endless cricket and visits to relatives. Now they're mostly about resting and catching up on things I couldn't do during the week, so they feel less [[adventurous]] but more precious.

questions: How many hours do you usually sleep?
Do you usually sleep well?
Do you take naps during the day?
What do you do when you can't fall asleep?
Do you think people get enough sleep nowadays?

samples.q: How many hours do you usually sleep?
samples.answer: Usually around seven hours on weeknights, which seems to be enough for me. At weekends I sometimes sleep a little longer to [[make up for]] the week, although I try not to overdo it.

samples.q: Do you usually sleep well?
samples.answer: Mostly, yes, though it varies. When my mind is calm I fall asleep quickly, but on stressful days it takes a while to switch off. I've learned that avoiding my phone before bed is [[remarkably]] effective.

samples.q: Do you take naps during the day?
samples.answer: Rarely on workdays, since there simply isn't time. On Fridays, though, I sometimes have a short nap after lunch. Even twenty minutes leaves me feeling [[refreshed]] and noticeably sharper for the rest of the day.

samples.q: What do you do when you can't fall asleep?
samples.answer: I usually get up and read something light for a while rather than lying there frustrated. Sometimes a cup of warm milk helps too. Once my mind settles, I tend to [[drift off]] fairly quickly.

samples.q: Do you think people get enough sleep nowadays?
samples.answer: Not really, particularly young people. Many stay up late on their phones or working, then wake early for work or classes. I think sleep is often treated as a [[luxury]] rather than a necessity these days.

questions: Are you a punctual person?
How do you feel when other people are late?
Are you good at managing your time?
Do you usually wear a watch?
Do you think people are busier today than in the past?

samples.q: Are you a punctual person?
samples.answer: I'd like to think so, yes. I genuinely dislike keeping people waiting, so I usually aim to arrive a little early. To me, being on time is a simple way of showing [[consideration]] for others.

samples.q: How do you feel when other people are late?
samples.answer: It depends on the situation. If it's a friend and only a few minutes, I don't mind at all. But if someone is repeatedly late for professional meetings, I find it quite [[exasperating]], because it wastes everyone's time.

samples.q: Are you good at managing your time?
samples.answer: Mostly, yes. I rely a lot on a simple to-do list, which keeps me on track. I'm not perfect, and things occasionally slip, but planning ahead stops me feeling [[overwhelmed]].

samples.q: Do you usually wear a watch?
samples.answer: Not anymore. I used to wear one my father gave me, but now I just check the time on my phone. I still keep that watch safely in a drawer, though, because it has real [[sentimental value]].

samples.q: Do you think people are busier today than in the past?
samples.answer: I'd say so. With smartphones, we're always reachable, so work often spills into our personal time. Our parents seemed to have clearer boundaries, whereas now life feels far more [[fast-paced]] and demanding.

questions: Who does most of the cooking in your family?
Do you enjoy cooking?
What dishes can you cook?
Do you find cooking relaxing?
Do you think children should learn to cook?

samples.q: Who does most of the cooking in your family?
samples.answer: My mother, without a doubt. She's an excellent cook and takes real pride in it. My younger sister and I help occasionally, but honestly, nobody can [[replicate]] her fish curry, no matter how hard we try.

samples.q: Do you enjoy cooking?
samples.answer: I do, actually, though I only really cook at the weekend. During the week I'm too busy, but on a lazy Saturday I quite enjoy trying a new recipe. I find the whole process rather [[therapeutic]] after a hectic week.

samples.q: What dishes can you cook?
samples.answer: Nothing too ambitious. I can make a decent chicken curry, khichuri and simple fried fish. Lately I've been trying to [[master]] a proper biryani, although my first attempts were fairly disappointing, to put it kindly.

samples.q: Do you find cooking relaxing?
samples.answer: Surprisingly, yes. When I'm not rushed, following a recipe and getting fully [[immersed]] in it takes my mind off everything else. And of course there's the reward of a good meal at the end.

samples.q: Do you think children should learn to cook?
samples.answer: Definitely. Cooking is a basic life skill, and it teaches children about nutrition and independence. If they learn early, they're far less likely to [[fall back on]] fast food when they eventually live on their own.

questions: What do you usually have for breakfast?
What is your favourite meal of the day?
Do you prefer eating at home or in restaurants?
Is there a traditional dish from your country you'd recommend?
Have your eating habits changed in recent years?

samples.q: What do you usually have for breakfast?
samples.answer: Usually something simple, like paratha with egg or a bit of vegetable curry, along with a cup of tea. It's not elaborate, but it's [[wholesome]] and keeps me going until lunch.

samples.q: What is your favourite meal of the day?
samples.answer: Definitely dinner. It's the one meal where the whole family sits down together and actually talks, so it's as much about the company as the food. It's become a small daily [[ritual]] I really value.

samples.q: Do you prefer eating at home or in restaurants?
samples.answer: Mostly at home, to be honest. Home-cooked food is healthier and more comforting. That said, I do enjoy dining out now and then, especially when it's a chance to [[socialise]] with friends over a meal.

samples.q: Is there a traditional dish from your country you'd recommend?
samples.answer: I'd definitely recommend hilsa fish, especially cooked in mustard sauce. It's our national fish, and it has a rich, [[distinctive]] flavour. During Pohela Boishakh, many families eat it with panta bhat.

samples.q: Have your eating habits changed in recent years?
samples.answer: Somewhat, yes. I used to eat a lot of fried street food, but now I try to cut back on oily snacks and eat more vegetables. I haven't given them up completely, but I'm certainly more [[health-conscious]] than before.

questions: Where do you usually go shopping?
Do you enjoy shopping?
Do you prefer shopping alone or with others?
Do you ever buy things on impulse?
Has the way people shop in your country changed?

samples.q: Where do you usually go shopping?
samples.answer: For everyday things, I go to the local market near our home, which is always [[bustling]]. For larger purchases, I'd rather order online or visit one of the bigger shopping centres, where there's more choice.

samples.q: Do you enjoy shopping?
samples.answer: It depends what I'm shopping for, honestly. I like buying books or a bit of tech, but clothes shopping [[drains]] me quickly. These days I do most of it online, which saves me a lot of time.

samples.q: Do you prefer shopping alone or with others?
samples.answer: Alone, usually, because I like to get in and out quickly. When I go with my sister, it turns into an afternoon of [[browsing]] every single shop, which is fun occasionally but exhausting.

samples.q: Do you ever buy things on impulse?
samples.answer: Occasionally, especially books. If I see an interesting title, I find it hard to resist, even if I already have a pile waiting to be read. Otherwise, I'm fairly [[prudent]] with what I spend.

samples.q: Has the way people shop in your country changed?
samples.answer: Dramatically. Not long ago almost everyone shopped at markets, but now online shopping and home delivery are extremely common, especially in cities. Still, traditional markets remain [[resilient]], because people enjoy bargaining and seeing products in person.

questions: What kind of clothes do you like to wear?
Do you wear different clothes at work and at home?
Do you ever wear traditional clothes?
Do you spend a lot on clothes?
Have clothing styles in your country changed much?

samples.q: What kind of clothes do you like to wear?
samples.answer: I tend to keep it simple and comfortable, mostly casual shirts and jeans. I'm not one for chasing trends. As long as something is neat and [[versatile]], I'm perfectly happy with it.

samples.q: Do you wear different clothes at work and at home?
samples.answer: Yes, quite different. At work I wear formal shirts and trousers, since a [[polished]] appearance matters when meeting students and parents. At home, though, I change straight into something loose and comfortable.

samples.q: Do you ever wear traditional clothes?
samples.answer: Yes, mostly on special occasions. For Eid and weddings I always wear a panjabi, which is a long traditional shirt. I really enjoy it, because it feels festive and connects me to our [[cultural roots]].

samples.q: Do you spend a lot on clothes?
samples.answer: Not really. I buy new clothes mainly before Eid or when something wears out. I'd rather invest in a few good-quality items than lots of cheap ones that quickly lose their shape, as it's more [[economical]] in the long run.

samples.q: Have clothing styles in your country changed much?
samples.answer: Considerably, especially among young people. Western styles like jeans and T-shirts are now everyday wear in towns and cities. Even so, traditional clothing remains [[deeply ingrained]], particularly during festivals and family celebrations.

questions: When did you get your first mobile phone?
How often do you use your mobile phone?
What do you mainly use your phone for?
Do you prefer phone calls or text messages?
Do you think young children should have smartphones?

samples.q: When did you get your first mobile phone?
samples.answer: I got my first one when I started college, at around sixteen. It was a basic model that could only make calls and send texts, but I was absolutely [[thrilled]] with it, even though it seems ancient by today's standards.

samples.q: How often do you use your mobile phone?
samples.answer: Far too often, if I'm honest. It's become almost [[indispensable]] for work and staying in touch, so it's rarely out of my hand. Lately I've been trying to set limits, because it's easy to lose track of time.

samples.q: What do you mainly use your phone for?
samples.answer: Mostly for work, to be honest. I reply to students' messages, check emails and join video calls. Outside work, I read the news and keep in touch with my elder sister in Dhaka, so it's become a real [[lifeline]].

samples.q: Do you prefer phone calls or text messages?
samples.answer: For quick things, texting, since it's fast and doesn't interrupt anyone. But for anything important, I much prefer a call. You can hear the tone of someone's voice, which makes the exchange feel far more [[genuine]].

samples.q: Do you think young children should have smartphones?
samples.answer: Not at a very young age. A basic phone for emergencies is sensible, but [[unrestricted]] internet access can be harmful. I think parents should introduce smartphones gradually and keep an eye on how they're used.

questions: What technology do you use most often?
How does technology help you in your work?
Do you think you rely too much on technology?
Is there any piece of technology you'd like to buy?
Do older people in your country find technology difficult?

samples.q: What technology do you use most often?
samples.answer: My laptop, without question. I use it all day at work for applications, emails and research, and in the evenings for studying. My phone is a close second, but the laptop is really the [[backbone]] of my working day.

samples.q: How does technology help you in your work?

questions: Do you watch much television?

samples.q: Do you use streaming services?

samples.q: What kind of programmes do you like?

samples.q: Did you watch much TV when you were a child?

questions: Which social media apps do you use most?

samples.q: Do you often post things online?

samples.q: Do you use social media a lot?
samples.answer: More than I'd like to admit. I use it to stay in touch and follow the news, but I've noticed how easily an hour [[vanishes]]. I'm trying to use it more intentionally rather than out of pure habit.

samples.q: Has social media changed the way people communicate?

questions: What festivals do you celebrate?

samples.q: What festivals do you celebrate?
samples.answer: The two Eids are the biggest for us, along with cultural events like Pohela Boishakh, the Bengali New Year. They're wonderful occasions, full of food, family and colour, and the whole community becomes [[vibrant]].

samples.q: Which festival do you enjoy the most?
samples.answer: Eid-ul-Fitr, without a doubt. After a month of fasting, there's a wonderful sense of relief and joy, and the whole family comes together, often at our village home. The [[jubilant]] mood lasts for days.

samples.q: How do you usually celebrate special occasions?
samples.answer: Usually with family and a large meal, which is really at the heart of any celebration here. We dress up, visit relatives, and the day is loud, lively and warm. Food is always the [[centrepiece]].

samples.q: How did you celebrate festivals when you were a child?
samples.answer: Eid was the highlight of my year. I'd get new clothes, and older relatives would give us salami, a small gift of money. My cousins and I would compare how much we'd collected, which was [[fiercely competitive]].

samples.q: Do you think festivals have changed over the years?
samples.answer: In some ways, yes. People now send greetings online instead of visiting everyone in person, and celebrations have become more [[commercialised]], with lots of shopping. But the core of it, family and food, has stayed exactly the same.

questions: Are there many museums in your hometown?

samples.q: Are there many museums in your hometown?

samples.q: Do you like visiting museums?
samples.answer: Yes, actually. I find them fascinating, especially history museums, because they bring the past to life in a way books can't. I don't go nearly often enough, but each visit is genuinely [[enlightening]].

samples.q: When did you last visit a museum?
samples.answer: About a year ago, I went to the Liberation War Museum in Dhaka while visiting my sister. It was an incredibly moving experience, and some of the personal letters on display were genuinely [[harrowing]] to read.

samples.q: Did you go to museums on school trips?
samples.answer: Only once or twice, as school trips weren't very common where I grew up. I remember being [[captivated]] by the old coins and weapons, though, and asking the guide far too many questions.

samples.q: Do you think museums will still be popular in the future?
samples.answer: I think so, as long as they adapt. Young people expect interactive displays and digital content now, so museums that feel dull and [[static]] may struggle. But seeing real historical objects in person will always have its appeal.

questions: Have you ever been to a concert?

samples.q: Have you ever been to a concert?

samples.q: What kind of events are held in your town?
samples.answer: Mostly local fairs, religious gatherings and cultural programmes on national days. The Baishakhi fair is probably the biggest, with stalls selling handicrafts and snacks, and it draws a [[sizeable]] crowd from the surrounding villages.

samples.q: Do you enjoy going to public events?
samples.answer: I do, in moderation. Cultural fairs and festivals have a wonderful atmosphere, and I like being part of the crowd. Very large, [[chaotic]] events can be a bit much for me, though, so I pick and choose.

samples.answer: Live, if possible, because the atmosphere is half the experience. Watching online is convenient, but it feels a bit [[detached]], as if you're looking in from the outside rather than actually taking part.

samples.q: Is there an event you would love to attend in the future?

questions: What traditions are important in your family?

samples.q: What traditions are important in your family?
samples.answer: Respecting elders is central, so we greet older relatives formally and seek their blessings at Eid. We also make pitha, traditional rice cakes, in winter, which is a [[time-honoured]] ritual my mother learned from my grandmother.

samples.q: Do you think traditional culture is important?
samples.answer: Very much so. It gives people a sense of identity and connects generations. In a fast-changing world, I think [[preserving]] our traditions, our language and festivals especially, matters more than ever.

samples.q: Did your grandparents teach you about traditions?
samples.answer: Very much so, especially my grandmother. She has little formal education, but she's a [[treasure trove]] of folk tales, proverbs and old customs. Listening to her stories as a child gave me a real sense of where I come from.

samples.q: Do you ever wear traditional clothes?
samples.answer: Quite often, actually. I wear a panjabi at Eid, at weddings and on Pohela Boishakh. It's comfortable and elegant, and wearing it gives me a quiet sense of [[belonging]] to something bigger than myself.

samples.q: Do you think young people are losing interest in traditional culture?
samples.answer: To some extent, yes, mainly because of global influences and social media. But I don't think it's [[diminishing]] entirely. Many young people still take great pride in their roots, just alongside a more modern lifestyle.

questions: What is a typical meal in Bangladesh?

samples.q: What is a typical meal in Bangladesh?
samples.answer: Rice is the foundation of almost every meal, usually with fish curry, lentils and some vegetables. There's even a saying that fish and rice make a Bengali, so it's [[deeply rooted]] in our identity.

samples.q: Is food an important part of your culture?
samples.answer: Enormously. In Bangladesh, food is at the centre of almost every gathering. Sharing a meal is how we express [[hospitality]], so it's really far more than just eating.

samples.q: What's your favourite local dish?
samples.answer: Hilsa cooked in mustard sauce, without question. Hilsa is our national fish, and my mother's version is [[unrivalled]] in my opinion. Coming from a river town, fresh fish is something I'd miss terribly if I lived abroad.

samples.q: Can you cook any local dishes?
samples.answer: Only a few basic ones, like dal and a simple egg curry. My mother is an excellent cook, so I've never really had to [[fend for myself]] in the kitchen, which I know will have to change if I study abroad.

samples.q: Has the food in your country changed in recent years?
samples.answer: Quite noticeably. Fast food outlets and cafés have [[mushroomed]] in towns as well as cities, and young people love burgers and pizza. Still, when it comes to family gatherings, traditional home cooking always wins.

questions: Do you follow the news?

samples.q: Do you follow the news?

samples.answer: I rely mostly on my phone's calendar and a simple to-do list. At work I'm handling applications for lots of students with different deadlines, so writing everything down is [[non-negotiable]] for me.

samples.q: Are you more productive in the morning or the evening?
samples.answer: Definitely the morning. My mind is [[sharpest]] then, so I tackle my hardest tasks early. By the evening my focus fades, so I save lighter activities for later in the day.

samples.q: Do you think it's important for students to be organised?

questions: Are you a patient person?

samples.q: Are you a patient person?
samples.answer: Reasonably, yes, though it depends on the situation. I'm quite patient with people, but I can get [[restless]] when I'm stuck waiting, in traffic for instance. It's something I'm consciously working on.

samples.q: Is patience important in your job?
samples.answer: Hugely important. Visa and admission processes can take months, and students naturally get anxious. Part of my role is reassuring them and staying calm and [[composed]], even when they call me for the tenth time about the same thing.

samples.q: Were you patient as a child?
samples.answer: Not in the slightest. I wanted everything immediately, whether it was my food, a new toy or my turn at batting. My parents constantly told me to wait, which I found completely [[infuriating]] at the time.

samples.q: Who is the most patient person you know?
samples.answer: My mother, without question. She looks after our home, helps care for my grandparents and still finds time for everyone. I've never seen her lose her temper, which is honestly [[admirable]] given how much she juggles.

samples.q: Do you think people are less patient nowadays than in the past?
samples.answer: I'd say so. We're used to [[instant gratification]] now, with fast internet, quick deliveries and endless entertainment on our phones. As a result, waiting even a few minutes can feel unbearable to many people.

samples.answer: I really believe they can. Soft blues and greens make a room feel calm, while warm colours tend to be more energising. That's probably why hospitals and offices choose their colour schemes so [[deliberately]].

questions: Do you enjoy giving gifts?

samples.q: What kinds of things make you happy?
samples.answer: Simple things, mostly. Time with people I love, a good book, a quiet evening after a productive day. I've realised over time that lasting [[contentment]] rarely comes from big events, but from small, everyday moments.

samples.q: What made you happy when you were a child?
samples.answer: Very simple pleasures, honestly. Flying kites on the roof, visiting my grandparents in the village and eating mangoes straight from their trees. Life felt [[blissfully]] uncomplicated back then, with no deadlines or responsibilities to worry about.

samples.q: Do you think money can buy happiness?
samples.answer: Only up to a point. Having enough to live comfortably certainly reduces stress, but beyond that, relationships and purpose matter far more. Some of the most cheerful people I know, like my grandmother, live very [[frugally]] indeed.

samples.q: Do you think people are happier now than in the past?
samples.answer: It's hard to say. Life is certainly more comfortable, but people seem more stressed and constantly [[compare themselves]] with others online. My grandparents had far less, yet they seem more at peace than many young people I know.

samples.q: Do you often go to parks?
samples.answer: Not as often as I'd like. There's one decent park about twenty minutes from my flat, and I try to go early on Friday mornings before it fills up. The rest of the week I rarely see anything green.

samples.q: Do you prefer the countryside or the city?
samples.answer: For living, the city - I need the jobs, the internet, the convenience. For a break, the countryside, no question. Two days by a river does more for my head than a month of weekends in town.

samples.q: Did you spend much time outdoors as a child?
samples.answer: All the time. Our neighbourhood was much less built-up then, so there were fields to play in and ponds to swim in. Children today in the same area have a playground the size of a car park.

samples.q: Do you mind noise?
samples.answer: It depends on the kind. Background noise - a café, traffic - I can tune out. What I can't stand is someone's phone speaker on a bus; that gets under my skin instantly.

samples.q: Is your area noisy?
samples.answer: Very. There's construction on two sides of our building and a main road on the third, so the only quiet hour is between four and five in the morning.

samples.q: Do you think cities are noisier than they used to be?
samples.answer: Undoubtedly. My parents talk about hearing birds from their window in the same area where I now hear only horns. More people, more vehicles, more construction - the noise is just the sum of all that.

cueCards.title: Describe a person who has influenced you
cueCards.prompt: Describe a person who has influenced you

sample.answer: I would like to talk about someone very close to home. The person who has influenced me most is my father, who ran a small business in Sirajganj for over thirty years and has only recently retired. Obviously I have known him all my life, but I think I only really started to understand him as a teenager, when I began helping out in his shop after school. Growing up, I watched him deal with setbacks that would have [[discouraged]] most people, yet he always stayed calm and kept going. There were slow seasons, especially during the monsoon, when hardly anyone came in, but he never let his worries spill over into family life. What shaped me was not any single piece of advice, but the quiet example he set day after day. He treated every customer, however difficult, with the same [[integrity]], and he taught me that a good reputation is built slowly and lost quickly. When I was struggling to choose a career, he never pushed me in one direction; instead he encouraged me to be [[self-reliant]] and make my own decisions. Looking back, almost everything I value about hard work and honesty can be traced to him, and I try to bring the same patience to my job at the consultancy, especially with anxious students. His influence has been [[profound]], and I still catch myself asking what he would do in a tricky situation. In many ways he remains my quiet role model, even now that I am an adult, and I suspect he always will be.

followUps.q: Do you still ask your father for advice?
followUps.answer: Yes, quite often, especially about money or big decisions. Since he retired he has more time to talk, so we usually chat over tea in the evening, and his advice is still remarkably [[level-headed]].

followUps.q: Would you like to be like him in the future?
followUps.answer: In many ways, yes. I would love to have his patience and honesty, although I probably will not run a shop. I just hope people eventually see me as someone as trustworthy as he is.

part3Samples.q: Do you think it is important for young people to have role models?
part3Samples.answer: I believe it is absolutely vital for adolescents to have someone to look up to. Role models act as a kind of moral compass, offering guidance on how to navigate life. When a young person admires a professional, they are [[internalising]] the values of hard work and [[perseverance]] that led to that success. Without such figures, young people can feel a little [[unmoored]], lacking any real sense of direction.

part3Samples.q: How have the types of role models changed since your grandparents' time?
part3Samples.answer: There has been a rather dramatic shift, I would say. In my grandparents' era, role models tended to be figures within the immediate community, such as teachers or elders. Today, influence is increasingly [[dominated]] by celebrities and social media personalities, many of whom are famous for very little of substance. I find this shift somewhat concerning, because fame has become almost entirely [[disconnected]] from genuine [[merit]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think people are more influenced by role models in real life or in the media?
part3Samples.answer: That is an interesting question. I would argue that media figures have a wider reach, but real-life role models, like a parent or mentor, have a far deeper and more [[lasting impact]]. The influence of a media personality is often [[superficial]] and [[fleeting]], whereas someone you interact with daily shapes your character in a much more meaningful way.

part3Samples.q: Why do some public figures fail to remain positive role models over time?
part3Samples.answer: I think the main reason is the immense pressure and [[scrutiny]] that come with public life. Constant attention can distort a person's judgement, and some become [[complacent]] once they achieve fame. There is also the temptation of wealth and power, which can gradually [[erode]] the very values that made them admirable in the first place. Sadly, staying grounded under that spotlight is genuinely difficult.

part3Samples.q: In the future, do you think AI or fictional characters could become role models?
part3Samples.answer: It is quite possible, and to some extent it is already happening. Virtual influencers are becoming increasingly [[prevalent]], and young people do form attachments to fictional heroes. However, I would be somewhat [[wary]] of this trend, because a fabricated character lacks the real struggles that make human role models relatable. I think something genuinely [[authentic]] would be lost in that shift.

part3Samples.q: Some believe children should care for their parents in old age. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly agree, at least in principle. In my culture, caring for elderly parents is seen as a moral [[obligation]], a way of repaying the sacrifices they made. That said, I recognise this is not always practical in modern life, so it need not mean living together. What matters is that the elderly are not [[neglected]] and retain their [[dignity]].

cueCards.title: Describe a time when you spent time with a child
cueCards.prompt: Describe a time when you spent time with a child

sample.answer: I would like to describe a lovely afternoon I spent with my nephew. Not long ago, during the winter, my elder sister paid us a surprise visit from Dhaka with her four-year-old son, and I ended up spending a whole afternoon with him. My sister had some errands to run in town with my mother, so I happily volunteered to keep him entertained. I had always found him endearing, but this was the first time we had really had a proper day together, just the two of us. He was remarkably [[inquisitive]] for his age, firing off questions about almost everything, some of which genuinely stumped me, like why the river never runs out of water. We built a fort out of cushions, drew a few clumsy animals, and I read him a couple of stories, putting on silly voices that he found hilarious. Later we walked down to the bank of the Jamuna to watch the boats, which he absolutely loved. What struck me most was how [[perceptive]] children are: he picked up on my mood instantly and kept trying to cheer me up. By evening I was exhausted, but it was the most [[rewarding]] kind of tiredness. It reminded me that spending time with a child forces you to slow down and be fully present, something adults rarely manage. Honestly, that afternoon was [[a welcome escape]] from my usual routine, and I have made a point of seeing him more often since, even if that means a long bus journey to Dhaka.

followUps.q: Do you enjoy spending time with children in general?
followUps.answer: Yes, I do, although I find it quite tiring. Children are so honest and [[unfiltered]] that you cannot pretend around them, and I think that is rather refreshing compared with the adult world.

followUps.q: Would you like to have children of your own one day?
followUps.answer: I think so, but not for a few years. I would like to be settled in my career first, and perhaps finish studying abroad, so that I can give them proper time and attention.

part3Samples.answer: In my view, the most important qualities are patience and [[consistency]]. Children thrive on stability, so a parent who sets clear, fair boundaries helps them feel secure. Equally vital is unconditional love balanced with the willingness to discipline when necessary. part3Samples.q: How is childhood today different from childhood in the past?
part3Samples.answer: Childhood has changed dramatically. In the past, children spent most of their free time playing outdoors and socialising in person. Today, much of that has been [[supplanted]] by screens, which I find rather [[disconcerting]]. Children are also under far more academic pressure now. part3Samples.q: What effect does strict parenting have on children?

On the other, if it is excessively [[authoritarian]], it may [[stifle]] a child's creativity and confidence, or even breed rebellion. part3Samples.answer: The most effective way is by [[modelling]] those values themselves, since children imitate what they see. Beyond that, parents can use everyday situations as [[teaching moments]], discussing honesty or kindness openly. Encouraging empathy, perhaps through community involvement, also helps. part3Samples.q: Some believe children should care for their parents in old age. Do you agree?

part3Samples.q: Do you think family is as important today as it was in the past?
part3Samples.answer: I would say family remains just as important, though its form has changed. The emotional support and sense of [[belonging]] a family provides are timeless human needs. That said, modern life has certainly [[strained]] family bonds, with people moving away for work and spending less time together. So while its importance is [[undiminished]], sustaining it now requires more conscious effort.

part3Samples.q: How are family relationships different now compared to a generation ago?
part3Samples.answer: The biggest difference is probably the shift from large, extended families to smaller, more [[nuclear]] ones. In the past, several generations often lived under one roof, which fostered close bonds. Today, families are more [[dispersed]], and technology has, ironically, both connected and [[distanced]] us. Relationships are more equal now, but arguably less tightly knit.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think many families spend less time together nowadays?
part3Samples.answer: Several factors are at play. The demands of modern careers are [[relentless]], leaving parents exhausted and [[time-poor]]. On top of that, digital devices have become a real distraction, with family members often absorbed in their own screens even when in the same room. This gradual erosion of shared time is genuinely [[detrimental]] to close relationships.

part3Samples.q: How do you think family structures will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I anticipate that families will continue to become smaller and more diverse in form. We will likely see more single-parent households and [[blended families]] becoming [[commonplace]] and widely accepted. Technology may also allow [[far-flung]] relatives to stay connected more easily. Overall, I think the definition of family will grow more flexible and inclusive.

part3Samples.q: What can families do to stay close despite busy modern lives?
part3Samples.answer: I think the key is being [[intentional]] about spending time together. Simple rituals, like sharing at least one meal a day without phones, can make a real difference. Families could also [[prioritise]] occasional trips or activities that create shared memories. Ultimately, closeness does not happen by accident; it has to be actively [[nurtured]] amid the busyness.

part3Samples.q: Some say working hard is more important than having free time. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I respectfully disagree with framing it as either-or. Hard work is certainly important for achievement, and I value [[diligence]]. However, free time is not the opposite of hard work; it is what makes sustained hard work possible by preventing burnout. The two are [[complementary]]. In my view, someone who works intensely but never rests is not admirable but heading towards [[exhaustion]], so balance is wiser.

cueCards.title: Describe a person you admire
cueCards.prompt: Describe a person you admire

sample.answer: Someone I genuinely admire is a former teacher of mine who went far beyond what his job required. I knew him through secondary school in Sirajganj, where he taught mathematics, but his real gift was noticing students who were quietly struggling. I was one of them for a while, because I found algebra completely baffling in my first year with him. In terms of his qualities, he was endlessly [[patient]], staying behind after class to help anyone who asked, and he never made you feel foolish for not understanding. What I admired most was his [[humility]]; despite being extremely knowledgeable, he always spoke to us as equals. He had a way of making difficult ideas feel [[accessible]], often using examples from the local market or cricket scores, and he clearly cared about the person, not just the grade. Years later, I still remember specific things he said that shaped how I think. As for why I admire him, I think what sets people like him apart is that they are motivated by a genuine desire to help rather than any reward. He was never well paid, and he could easily have earned more from private coaching, but he chose to help struggling students for free instead. He left a [[lasting impression]] on hundreds of students, and I count myself lucky to have been one of them. In fact, in my own job I often try to explain things to students the way he once explained things to me.

followUps.q: Are you still in touch with him?
followUps.answer: Not regularly, but I bump into him now and then in town. He is retired now, and he always asks about my work. It is quite touching that he still remembers me after all these years.

followUps.q: Would you ever like to become a teacher?
followUps.answer: Perhaps in some form. My job already involves a lot of guiding and explaining, and I find that side of it deeply [[fulfilling]], but I am not sure I have the patience for a classroom of teenagers.

part3Samples.q: What do you think is the main purpose of education?
part3Samples.answer: In my view, education serves a dual purpose. On a practical level, it equips people with the knowledge and skills needed for employment. But more importantly, I believe its deeper purpose is to [[cultivate]] critical thinking and produce well-rounded, responsible citizens. Education should teach people how to think, not merely what to think. Sadly, many systems overemphasise [[rote learning]] at the expense of this broader [[enrichment]].

part3Samples.q: How is education today different from education in the past?
part3Samples.answer: The differences are considerable. In the past, education was largely teacher-centred, based on memorisation and strict discipline. Today, there is a much greater emphasis on interactive, student-centred learning, and technology has [[revolutionised]] access to information. Learning is now more [[collaborative]] and creative. However, I would argue that academic pressure and competition have also intensified, which is a rather [[double-edged]] development.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think exam results are given so much importance?
part3Samples.answer: I think it stems from the need for a seemingly objective way to measure ability and allocate opportunities. Exams provide a convenient, [[quantifiable]] benchmark for universities and employers. However, this [[overreliance]] on results can be [[counterproductive]], as it encourages students to memorise for tests rather than truly understand. It also fails to capture vital qualities like creativity, which are far harder to quantify.

part3Samples.q: How do you think education will change in the next 20 years?
part3Samples.answer: I anticipate dramatic changes, largely driven by technology. Personalised, AI-assisted learning could [[tailor]] lessons to each student's pace, and online education will make quality teaching far more accessible globally. The traditional classroom may become less central. There will likely also be a stronger focus on [[adaptable]] skills, given that people will need to [[reskill]] repeatedly throughout their careers.

part3Samples.q: How could education systems be improved?
part3Samples.answer: There are several improvements I would suggest. Firstly, systems should place less emphasis on high-stakes exams and more on continuous, practical assessment. Secondly, curricula should be [[modernised]] to include life skills such as financial literacy and emotional intelligence. Finally, investing in teacher training and reducing class sizes would allow for more [[personalised]] learning. The goal should be a more [[holistic]] and flexible model.

part3Samples.q: Some people say governments should promote positive role models. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I partly agree. Governments can certainly [[showcase]] admirable citizens, such as scientists or humanitarians, to counterbalance shallow celebrity culture. However, I am slightly cautious, because state-endorsed role models can easily become [[propaganda]] if handled poorly. So while the intention is commendable, it needs to be done [[transparently]] and without any political agenda.

cueCards.title: Describe an intelligent person you know
cueCards.prompt: Describe an intelligent person you know

sample.answer: I would like to talk about a friend whose mind I have always found slightly intimidating. One of the most intelligent people I know is a close friend from university who studied physics, while I was doing business administration. We met because we lived in the same student hostel, and we have stayed close ever since, even though he now lives in Rajshahi. What sets him apart is not just how much he knows, but how quickly he grasps complicated ideas that leave the rest of us bewildered. He has this [[analytical]] mind that breaks any problem into neat, logical steps. I remember him explaining a statistics concept I had struggled with for weeks in about five minutes, and suddenly it made perfect sense. Yet he is never arrogant about it, which makes his intelligence all the more [[impressive]]. He is also [[intellectually curious]], always reading about subjects far outside his field, from history to economics. I think real intelligence is exactly this combination of sharpness and open-mindedness, rather than simply getting top marks. As for how I feel about him, talking to him is genuinely [[stimulating]], because he challenges your assumptions without ever making you feel small. I will admit that I sometimes feel a little slow beside him, but mostly I just feel grateful. Honestly, I always come away from our conversations having learned something, and that is rare. followUps.q: Do you think intelligence is something people are born with?

followUps.q: Do you often ask him for help?
followUps.answer: Now and then, mostly when I need to make sense of numbers at work. He is always happy to help, although he usually ends up teaching me far more than I actually asked for.

part3Samples.q: What do you think is the best way to learn something new?
part3Samples.answer: In my experience, the most effective way to learn is through active, hands-on practice rather than passive listening. We tend to [[retain]] information far better when we actually apply it. I am a firm believer in [[learning by doing]], and in making mistakes, since they are often the most [[instructive]] experiences. Combining this practical approach with genuine curiosity makes learning both effective and thoroughly engaging.

part3Samples.q: Is it better to learn alone or in a group?
part3Samples.answer: Both have their merits, and the ideal depends on the task. Learning alone allows for focus and lets you progress at your own pace, which suits deep, concentrated study. Group learning, on the other hand, is more [[dynamic]]; you benefit from different perspectives and can clarify doubts through discussion. Personally, I favour a [[blend]] of the two, as they [[complement]] each other nicely.

part3Samples.q: Why do some people find learning easier than others?
part3Samples.answer: There are many contributing factors. Some of it comes down to natural [[aptitude]], but I think motivation and [[mindset]] matter far more. People who are genuinely curious and believe they can improve tend to learn faster. Environment also plays a huge role; a supportive home and good teachers make an enormous difference. So learning ability is really a mix of [[innate]] talent and nurtured habits.

part3Samples.q: Do you think traditional classrooms will disappear in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I doubt they will disappear entirely, but their role will certainly change. Online learning will keep growing, offering flexibility that classrooms cannot match. However, physical classrooms provide something valuable: social interaction, mentorship and a structured environment that many learners need. So rather than [[vanishing]], I expect classrooms to [[evolve]] into more interactive spaces, [[complementing]] rather than being replaced by digital tools.

part3Samples.q: How can people stay motivated when learning independently?
part3Samples.answer: Self-motivation is the biggest challenge in independent learning. I think the key is setting clear, [[achievable]] goals and breaking a large subject into smaller [[milestones]], which gives a regular sense of progress. Establishing a routine helps make studying a habit rather than a struggle. Finding a community of fellow learners online can also provide [[accountability]] and encouragement, which is often what people lack.

part3Samples.q: Some say you are never too old to learn. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I wholeheartedly agree. While learning styles may change with age, the human brain remains capable of acquiring new knowledge and skills throughout life. There are countless inspiring examples of people learning languages, instruments or even new careers late in life. I think the biggest barrier is usually psychological, a [[self-imposed]] belief that it is too late. In reality, curiosity and effort [[transcend]] age entirely, keeping us [[youthful]] in spirit.

cueCards.title: Describe a famous person you would like to meet
cueCards.prompt: Describe a famous person you would like to meet

followUps.q: Would you like to be famous yourself?

followUps.q: Do you think famous people are good role models?

part3Samples.q: Where do you think people get their moral values from?
part3Samples.answer: I believe our moral values come from a combination of sources. Our upbringing and family are hugely influential, [[instilling]] early notions of right and wrong. Culture, religion and society also shape our ethics, as do our own experiences and reflection as we mature. Some argue there is even an innate, universal sense of fairness. So our values are essentially [[absorbed]] from those around us and then [[refined]] through personal reflection over time.

part3Samples.q: Are moral values the same across all cultures?
part3Samples.answer: I think there is a fascinating mix of universal and culturally specific values. Certain core principles, like [[prohibitions]] against murder or valuing honesty and care for others, appear across virtually all cultures, suggesting a shared moral foundation. However, many values, such as attitudes to family, [[individualism]] or specific customs, vary considerably between cultures. So while there are some universal [[moral constants]], ethics are also significantly shaped by cultural context.

part3Samples.q: What happens to a society when it loses its moral values?
part3Samples.answer: A society that loses its shared [[moral compass]] tends to suffer serious consequences. Trust between people erodes, corruption and dishonesty can flourish, and social cohesion breaks down. Without agreed ethical standards, laws alone struggle to maintain order, and self-interest can dominate at the expense of the common good. So a strong shared morality acts as invisible [[social glue]]; its erosion can lead to division, [[distrust]] and dysfunction.

part3Samples.q: How might moral values change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I expect our moral frameworks to be tested and expanded by new challenges. Advances in technology, such as artificial intelligence and genetic engineering, will raise entirely new [[ethical dilemmas]] we have never faced before. Growing awareness may also extend our moral concern further, perhaps towards animals, the environment and future generations. So I anticipate that ethics will continue to [[evolve]], becoming broader in scope as we [[grapple with]] unprecedented moral questions.

part3Samples.q: How can strong moral values be encouraged in young people?
part3Samples.answer: The most powerful way is through example, since children learn ethics primarily by observing the adults around them. Parents and teachers who [[model integrity]], kindness and honesty have a profound influence. Open discussion of ethical issues, encouraging empathy, and involving young people in helping others also help. Rather than simply lecturing, allowing them to [[reason through]] moral situations builds genuine understanding. So values are best [[instilled]] through consistent example and guided reflection.

part3Samples.q: Some say technology is the main cause of modern loneliness. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I partly agree, but I think it is too simplistic to blame technology alone. It is true that excessive screen time can replace real interaction and [[foster]] unhealthy comparison. However, technology can also connect isolated people, such as those far from family. part3: Why do you think loneliness is becoming more common today?

part3Samples.q: Why do you think loneliness is becoming more common today?
part3Samples.answer: I think it is a paradox of modern life. Despite being more digitally connected than ever, many people feel increasingly isolated. Urbanisation has weakened traditional community bonds, and busy, individualistic lifestyles leave little time for genuine connection. Ironically, social media can [[exacerbate]] the problem by replacing deep relationships with [[superficial]] online interaction, leaving a real emotional [[void]].

part3Samples.q: Is loneliness worse in cities or in the countryside?
part3Samples.answer: This is quite counterintuitive. You might assume the countryside, being less populated, would be lonelier, but often the opposite is true. Rural communities tend to be tight-knit, where everyone knows each other. Cities, by contrast, can be profoundly [[alienating]]; you can be surrounded by millions yet feel completely [[anonymous]]. So urban loneliness, born of that anonymity, is arguably the more [[acute]] problem.

part3Samples.q: What effects can long-term loneliness have on a person?
part3Samples.answer: The effects can be genuinely serious. Prolonged loneliness is strongly linked to mental health problems such as depression and anxiety. It can also have physical consequences, as chronic isolation is thought to weaken the immune system and even affect [[longevity]]. Beyond that, it can trap people in a negative cycle, where low mood makes them [[withdraw]] further, deepening the isolation and their sense of [[despair]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think loneliness will become a bigger problem in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I fear it might, if current trends continue. As societies become more individualistic and people increasingly work and socialise remotely, opportunities for spontaneous human contact may [[diminish]]. An ageing population in many countries could also worsen the situation. However, I remain hopeful that growing awareness of the issue will [[prompt]] communities and governments to take [[preventive]] action.

part3Samples.q: What can communities do to reduce loneliness?
part3Samples.answer: Communities can play a powerful role. Creating accessible public spaces and organising local events, from community gardens to social clubs, gives people natural opportunities to connect. Initiatives that specifically reach out to isolated individuals, like [[befriending schemes]] for the elderly, are especially valuable. Ultimately, [[fostering]] a culture where people look out for their neighbours can rebuild the [[social fabric]] that has frayed.

part3Samples.q: Some say building more housing is more important than preserving parks. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I understand the argument given the housing crisis, but I largely disagree with sacrificing parks. While housing is undeniably crucial, green spaces are equally vital for residents' health and wellbeing, and destroying them creates a poorer quality of life. It should not be an either-or choice. With clever planning, cities can build housing on [[brownfield sites]] and increase density elsewhere while preserving parks. So both are essential, and [[pitting them against]] each other is a [[false dilemma]].

part3: Do you think cultural globalisation is a positive development?

part3Samples.q: Do you think cultural globalisation is a positive development?
part3Samples.answer: I see it as a genuinely [[double-edged]] phenomenon. On the positive side, it fosters greater understanding, tolerance and exchange between cultures, and lets us enjoy the best of what the world offers, from food to film. However, there is a real risk that it leads to cultural [[homogenisation]], where dominant cultures [[overwhelm]] local ones. So while I appreciate the connection it brings, I believe we must actively work to preserve cultural diversity alongside it.

part3Samples.q: How has globalisation changed local cultures?
part3Samples.answer: The changes are significant. Local cultures have been enriched by exposure to global ideas, technologies and cuisines. However, they have also been challenged, as global brands, media and the English language spread, sometimes [[eclipsing]] local traditions and languages. The result is often a hybrid culture, blending the local and the global. So globalisation has made cultures more [[interconnected]] and diverse in some ways, yet more [[uniform]] in others.

part3Samples.q: What effect does the spread of English have on other languages?
part3Samples.answer: The spread of English as a global [[lingua franca]] has clear benefits, facilitating international communication, business and science. However, it also poses a threat to [[linguistic diversity]]. As English dominates, some smaller languages are being [[marginalised]] and, in extreme cases, are dying out, taking unique cultural knowledge with them. So while a common language is enormously useful, its dominance risks a loss of the rich linguistic heritage that makes humanity so diverse.

part3Samples.q: Do you think all cultures will eventually become the same?
part3Samples.answer: I do not think so, though they will certainly grow more similar in some respects. While globalisation is a powerful homogenising force, human beings have a deep-seated need for distinct identity and belonging, which tends to make cultures [[resilient]]. We are also seeing movements to actively preserve and revive local traditions. So rather than becoming identical, I expect cultures to blend and influence one another while retaining their [[distinctive]] [[essence]].

part3Samples.q: How can countries protect their cultural identity in a globalised world?
part3Samples.answer: There are several strategies. Governments can support and fund local arts, languages, film and traditions to ensure they thrive. Education that [[instils]] pride in one's heritage is fundamental. Protecting local media and industries from being entirely overwhelmed by [[global giants]] also helps. Crucially, this should be done not by rejecting outside influence, but by celebrating and promoting one's own culture so that it remains [[vibrant]] and valued.

part3Samples.q: Some say the internet has made memorisation unnecessary. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I only partly agree. It is true that we no longer need to memorise facts that we can look up instantly, so pure memorisation is less critical than before. However, I would argue that a solid base of knowledge in your own memory is still essential for [[reasoning]] and creativity, because you cannot connect ideas you do not [[possess]]. So the internet has shifted, rather than [[eliminated]], the value of memory.

part3Samples.q: Why do some people become more ambitious than others?

part3Samples.q: What effect does job dissatisfaction have on people?

part3Samples.q: Are soft skills or hard skills harder to learn?
part3Samples.answer: I would argue soft skills are generally harder to acquire. Hard skills, like using a software program, can be learned through structured courses relatively quickly. Soft skills, however, involve deeply ingrained habits and personality traits, so improving your communication or empathy requires sustained self-awareness and practice over years. They are more [[nuanced]] and [[subtle]], which is precisely why they are so [[prized]] by employers.

part3Samples.q: Why are communication skills so important at work?
part3Samples.answer: Communication is fundamental because it [[underpins]] almost every workplace activity. Clear communication prevents misunderstandings, which can otherwise cause costly errors and conflict. It enables effective teamwork, allows ideas to be shared persuasively, and builds strong relationships with clients and colleagues. Someone who communicates well can influence, lead and collaborate far more effectively. In essence, poor communication can [[derail]] even the most technically [[gifted]] team.

part3Samples.q: Will soft skills become more important as technology advances?
part3Samples.answer: I firmly believe they will. As artificial intelligence automates more technical and analytical tasks, the distinctly human skills, creativity, empathy, leadership and complex communication, will become increasingly valuable. These are precisely the abilities machines struggle to [[replicate]]. So paradoxically, the more technological the world becomes, the more [[premium]] employers are likely to place on these [[irreplaceable]] human qualities.

part3Samples.q: How can people develop their soft skills?
part3Samples.answer: Soft skills are developed mainly through practice and self-reflection. Seeking out situations that stretch you, like leading a project or public speaking, builds confidence and competence. Actively seeking honest feedback and observing people who excel at these skills is invaluable. Reading and formal training can help too. part3Samples.q: Some say peer pressure decreases as people get older. Do you agree?

As people mature, they generally develop a firmer sense of identity and care less about others' approval, making them more [[resilient]] to pressure.
