Disagreements often bring underlying problems to the surface, which allows them to be addressed rather than festering. Healthy conflict can also [[spark]] better ideas and deeper understanding. The key is whether it is managed respectfully; it is unresolved or [[hostile]] conflict that is truly damaging.

part3Samples.q: Is it better to confront a problem directly or avoid it?
part3Samples.answer: In most cases, I believe confronting a problem directly is far healthier. Avoidance may keep the peace temporarily, but the underlying issue tends to [[fester]] and grow worse over time. Addressing it calmly and early usually leads to genuine resolution. part3Samples.q: What are the main causes of conflict between people?
part3Samples.answer: In my experience, most conflict [[stems from]] poor communication and misunderstanding rather than genuine [[malice]]. When people fail to express themselves clearly or make assumptions about others' intentions, friction inevitably arises. Differences in values, competition over resources and simple [[miscommunication]] are also common triggers. Interestingly, many disputes could be avoided entirely with a little more patience and clarity.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will become better at resolving conflicts in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am cautiously optimistic. part3Samples.q: Some say honesty is always the best policy. Do you agree?

However, I think it must be balanced with [[compassion]]; brutal honesty that needlessly wounds someone is not virtuous. So honesty is the best policy, provided it is delivered [[sensitively]].

part3Samples.q: Why do some childhood friendships fade over time?

part3Samples.answer: Consistent effort is really the crucial ingredient. Regular video calls and messages can [[keep a friendship alive]] despite the distance. part3Samples.q: Some say individuals can do little about climate change. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I partly agree but find the statement [[disempowering]]. cueCards.title: Describe a person who is a good parent

followUps.q: Do parents today have an easier job than in the past?
followUps.answer: In some ways yes, with more information and support available. But they also face new pressures, like managing screen time and intense competition in education, which makes parenting quite demanding.

part3Samples.q: What do you think are the most important qualities of a good parent?
part3Samples.answer: In my view, the most important qualities are patience and [[consistency]]. Children thrive on stability, so a parent who sets clear, fair boundaries helps them feel secure. part3Samples.q: How is childhood today different from childhood in the past?
part3Samples.answer: Childhood has changed dramatically. In the past, children spent most of their free time playing outdoors and socialising in person. Today, much of that has been [[supplanted]] by screens, which I find rather [[disconcerting]]. Children are also under far more academic pressure now. So while modern children have more opportunities, they arguably have a less [[carefree]] upbringing.

part3Samples.q: What effect does strict parenting have on children?
part3Samples.answer: It can have mixed effects. On one hand, strict parenting can instil discipline and a strong work ethic. On the other, if it is excessively [[authoritarian]], it may [[stifle]] a child's creativity and confidence, or even breed rebellion. In my opinion, the ideal lies in a balanced approach that is firm but also [[nurturing]] and understanding.

part3Samples.q: How do you think parenting will change in the coming decades?
part3Samples.answer: I expect parenting will become increasingly [[intertwined with]] technology. Parents will likely rely more on apps and online resources for guidance, and managing children's screen time will become an even more [[daunting]] challenge. I also anticipate a move towards more [[egalitarian]] parenting, with responsibilities shared more equally. Hopefully there will also be greater awareness of children's emotional wellbeing.

part3Samples.q: How can parents help children develop good values?
part3Samples.answer: The most effective way is by [[modelling]] those values themselves, since children imitate what they see. Beyond that, parents can use everyday situations as [[teaching moments]], discussing honesty or kindness openly. Encouraging empathy, perhaps through community involvement, also helps. Ultimately, values are [[instilled]] gradually through consistent example rather than through occasional lectures.

part3Samples.q: Some say technology is robbing children of a real childhood. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I partly agree, though I think it is a little [[overstated]]. There is a legitimate concern that excessive screen time is replacing the outdoor play, imagination and face-to-face friendships that define a healthy childhood. However, technology also offers genuine benefits and is simply the reality of the modern world. So rather than [[demonising]] it, I believe the answer lies in [[moderation]], ensuring children still enjoy a rich, balanced upbringing.

cueCards.title: Describe a generous person you know

part3: Where do you think people get their moral values from?

part3Samples.q: Where do you think people get their moral values from?
part3Samples.answer: I believe our moral values come from a combination of sources. Our upbringing and family are hugely influential, [[instilling]] early notions of right and wrong. Culture, religion and society also shape our ethics, as do our own experiences and reflection as we mature. Some argue there is even an innate, universal sense of fairness. So our values are essentially [[absorbed]] from those around us and then [[refined]] through personal reflection over time.

part3Samples.q: Are moral values the same across all cultures?
part3Samples.answer: I think there is a fascinating mix of universal and culturally specific values. Certain core principles, like [[prohibitions]] against murder or valuing honesty and care for others, appear across virtually all cultures, suggesting a shared moral foundation. However, many values, such as attitudes to family, [[individualism]] or specific customs, vary considerably between cultures. So while there are some universal [[moral constants]], ethics are also significantly shaped by cultural context.

part3Samples.q: What happens to a society when it loses its moral values?
part3Samples.answer: A society that loses its shared [[moral compass]] tends to suffer serious consequences. Trust between people erodes, corruption and dishonesty can flourish, and social cohesion breaks down. Without agreed ethical standards, laws alone struggle to maintain order, and self-interest can dominate at the expense of the common good. So a strong shared morality acts as invisible [[social glue]]; its erosion can lead to division, [[distrust]] and dysfunction.

part3Samples.q: How might moral values change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I expect our moral frameworks to be tested and expanded by new challenges. Advances in technology, such as artificial intelligence and genetic engineering, will raise entirely new [[ethical dilemmas]] we have never faced before. Growing awareness may also extend our moral concern further, perhaps towards animals, the environment and future generations. So I anticipate that ethics will continue to [[evolve]], becoming broader in scope as we [[grapple with]] unprecedented moral questions.

part3Samples.q: How can strong moral values be encouraged in young people?
part3Samples.answer: The most powerful way is through example, since children learn ethics primarily by observing the adults around them. Parents and teachers who [[model integrity]], kindness and honesty have a profound influence. Open discussion of ethical issues, encouraging empathy, and involving young people in helping others also help. Rather than simply lecturing, allowing them to [[reason through]] moral situations builds genuine understanding. So values are best [[instilled]] through consistent example and guided reflection.

part3Samples.q: Some say money cannot buy happiness. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I largely agree, though with a [[nuance]]. It is certainly true that beyond meeting our basic needs, more money does not reliably increase happiness, and the richest people are not necessarily the happiest. Lasting happiness comes from relationships and purpose. However, I would add that a lack of money, and the poverty and stress it brings, can definitely cause unhappiness. So money cannot buy happiness, but [[financial security]] can certainly remove a major source of [[misery]] and anxiety.

cueCards.title: Describe a person who has an interesting job
cueCards.prompt: Describe a person who has an interesting job

sample.answer: I would like to talk about a friend whose job I find almost unbelievably exciting. A person with a genuinely interesting job is a friend of mine who works as a wildlife photographer. followUps.q: Do you think interesting jobs are more important than well-paid jobs?

part3Samples.q: What do you think makes people happy at work?
part3Samples.answer: In my opinion, job satisfaction [[stems from]] more than just a good salary. Feeling that your work is meaningful and appreciated is [[paramount]]. A positive relationship with colleagues, opportunities to grow, and a sense of [[autonomy]] all contribute significantly. Ultimately, people are happiest when they feel valued and can see the genuine purpose behind what they do.

part3Samples.q: Is money or a sense of purpose more important for job satisfaction?
part3Samples.answer: While money is obviously necessary, I believe that beyond a certain point, a sense of purpose matters more. A high salary provides comfort, but it does not [[compensate]] for feeling that your work is pointless. People who find meaning in their jobs tend to be far more engaged and resilient. So money is important up to a [[threshold]], but purpose provides the deeper, more lasting [[fulfilment]].

part3Samples.q: What effect does job dissatisfaction have on people?
part3Samples.answer: The effects can be quite serious and far-reaching. Chronic dissatisfaction often leads to stress, low morale and even [[burnout]], which can spill over and harm a person's personal life and health. At work, it results in reduced productivity and higher [[staff turnover]]. Essentially, an unhappy workforce is [[detrimental]] to both the individuals involved and the organisation's overall performance.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will be more or less satisfied with their jobs in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am cautiously optimistic. As automation takes over [[tedious]], repetitive tasks, workers may be freed to focus on more creative and meaningful work, which could boost satisfaction. There is also growing awareness of employee wellbeing. On the other hand, increased job insecurity and the pressure of constant [[connectivity]] could [[undermine]] satisfaction. So the outcome will likely depend on how wisely we manage these changes.

part3Samples.q: What can employers do to make their staff happier?
part3Samples.answer: Employers can do a great deal. Offering fair pay and genuine [[recognition]] for good work is [[fundamental]]. Beyond that, providing opportunities for growth, some flexibility, and a supportive, respectful culture makes an enormous difference. part3Samples.q: Some say humans have no right to interfere with nature. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: This is a nuanced issue. I agree we should minimise harmful interference, such as destroying habitats or exploiting species, as we have caused enormous damage. However, I would argue we now have a responsibility to [[intervene]] positively, through conservation, to repair the damage we have already done. Given our impact, complete non-interference is neither possible nor helpful. So rather than not interfering at all, we should act as responsible [[stewards]], protecting rather than [[plundering]].

cueCards.title: Describe a person from a different culture you know

part3Samples.q: Do you think cultural globalisation is a positive development?
part3Samples.answer: I see it as a genuinely [[double-edged]] phenomenon. On the positive side, it fosters greater understanding, tolerance and exchange between cultures, and lets us enjoy the best of what the world offers, from food to film. However, there is a real risk that it leads to cultural [[homogenisation]], where dominant cultures [[overwhelm]] local ones. So while I appreciate the connection it brings, I believe we must actively work to preserve cultural diversity alongside it.

part3Samples.q: How has globalisation changed local cultures?
part3Samples.answer: The changes are significant. Local cultures have been enriched by exposure to global ideas, technologies and cuisines. However, they have also been challenged, as global brands, media and the English language spread, sometimes [[eclipsing]] local traditions and languages. The result is often a hybrid culture, blending the local and the global. So globalisation has made cultures more [[interconnected]] and diverse in some ways, yet more [[uniform]] in others.

part3Samples.q: What effect does the spread of English have on other languages?
part3Samples.answer: The spread of English as a global [[lingua franca]] has clear benefits, facilitating international communication, business and science. However, it also poses a threat to [[linguistic diversity]]. As English dominates, some smaller languages are being [[marginalised]] and, in extreme cases, are dying out, taking unique cultural knowledge with them. So while a common language is enormously useful, its dominance risks a loss of the rich linguistic heritage that makes humanity so diverse.

part3Samples.q: Do you think all cultures will eventually become the same?
part3Samples.answer: I do not think so, though they will certainly grow more similar in some respects. While globalisation is a powerful homogenising force, human beings have a deep-seated need for distinct identity and belonging, which tends to make cultures [[resilient]]. We are also seeing movements to actively preserve and revive local traditions. So rather than becoming identical, I expect cultures to blend and influence one another while retaining their [[distinctive]] [[essence]].

part3Samples.q: How can countries protect their cultural identity in a globalised world?
part3Samples.answer: There are several strategies. Governments can support and fund local arts, languages, film and traditions to ensure they thrive. Education that [[instils]] pride in one's heritage is fundamental. Protecting local media and industries from being entirely overwhelmed by [[global giants]] also helps. Crucially, this should be done not by rejecting outside influence, but by celebrating and promoting one's own culture so that it remains [[vibrant]] and valued.

part3Samples.q: Some say social media has made friendships shallower. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I largely agree with that sentiment. Social media encourages us to [[accumulate]] hundreds of contacts while investing little in any of them. The constant highlight reels can also breed comparison rather than genuine connection. That said, it depends how you use it; for maintaining existing bonds it is useful. Used as a [[substitute]] for real intimacy, though, it does [[trivialise]] friendship.

cueCards.title: Describe a wise older relative

part3Samples.q: Do you think there is a big generation gap in your country?

part3Samples.q: What are the main differences between the older and younger generations?
part3Samples.answer: The differences are quite [[stark]]. The older generation generally values stability, tradition and hard-earned security, whereas young people tend to prioritise flexibility, self-expression and work-life balance. There is also a huge gap in digital fluency. However, I think these differences are often [[exaggerated]]; at their core, both generations share many of the same fundamental [[aspirations]].

part3Samples.q: Why do older and younger generations sometimes struggle to understand each other?
part3Samples.answer: The root cause is that they have lived through fundamentally different eras. Their formative experiences, technologies and social norms were worlds apart, which shapes how they see everything. This can lead to a failure to [[empathise]], with each side viewing the other's values as [[alien]]. A lack of open, patient communication only [[widens that gulf]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think the generation gap will grow larger in the future?
part3Samples.answer: It is a real possibility, given how quickly technology now [[evolves]]. Each new generation is being shaped by tools the previous one barely understands, which could [[amplify]] the divide. On the other hand, constant connectivity might actually help [[bridge]] it. So the outcome is uncertain, and it may depend on whether we make a deliberate effort to stay connected across ages.

part3Samples.q: What can be done to reduce conflict between generations?
part3Samples.answer: [[Fostering]] genuine dialogue is essential. Creating opportunities for generations to interact meaningfully, whether in families or communities, builds mutual understanding. Both sides need to approach differences with [[humility]] rather than judgement. I also think education plays a role in teaching young people to respect their elders while encouraging older people to remain [[receptive]] to new ideas.

part3Samples.q: Some believe children should care for their parents in old age. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly agree, at least in principle. In my culture, caring for elderly parents is seen as a moral [[obligation]], a way of repaying the sacrifices they made. cueCards.title: Describe a person who solved a problem in a clever way

part3Samples.q: Which soft skills do you think are most valuable in the workplace?
part3Samples.answer: In my view, communication is the single most valuable soft skill, since almost everything at work depends on it. Closely behind it, I would place teamwork and adaptability, as modern workplaces are collaborative and constantly changing. Problem-solving and emotional intelligence are also hugely important. These [[interpersonal]] abilities often distinguish a merely competent employee from a truly [[exceptional]] and [[promotable]] one.

part3Samples.q: Are soft skills or hard skills harder to learn?
part3Samples.answer: I would argue soft skills are generally harder to acquire. Hard skills, like using a software program, can be learned through structured courses relatively quickly. Soft skills, however, involve deeply ingrained habits and personality traits, so improving your communication or empathy requires sustained self-awareness and practice over years. They are more [[nuanced]] and [[subtle]], which is precisely why they are so [[prized]] by employers.

part3Samples.q: Why are communication skills so important at work?
part3Samples.answer: Communication is fundamental because it [[underpins]] almost every workplace activity. Clear communication prevents misunderstandings, which can otherwise cause costly errors and conflict. It enables effective teamwork, allows ideas to be shared persuasively, and builds strong relationships with clients and colleagues. Someone who communicates well can influence, lead and collaborate far more effectively. In essence, poor communication can [[derail]] even the most technically [[gifted]] team.

part3Samples.q: Will soft skills become more important as technology advances?
part3Samples.answer: I firmly believe they will. As artificial intelligence automates more technical and analytical tasks, the distinctly human skills, creativity, empathy, leadership and complex communication, will become increasingly valuable. These are precisely the abilities machines struggle to [[replicate]]. So paradoxically, the more technological the world becomes, the more [[premium]] employers are likely to place on these [[irreplaceable]] human qualities.

part3Samples.q: How can people develop their soft skills?
part3Samples.answer: Soft skills are developed mainly through practice and self-reflection. Seeking out situations that stretch you, like leading a project or public speaking, builds confidence and competence. Actively seeking honest feedback and observing people who excel at these skills is invaluable. Reading and formal training can help too. The key is to treat them as [[learnable]] skills that improve with [[deliberate]] effort, not fixed [[traits]].

part3Samples.q: Some say the internet has made memorisation unnecessary. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I only partly agree. It is true that we no longer need to memorise facts that we can look up instantly, so pure memorisation is less critical than before. However, I would argue that a solid base of knowledge in your own memory is still essential for [[reasoning]] and creativity, because you cannot connect ideas you do not [[possess]]. So the internet has shifted, rather than [[eliminated]], the value of memory.

sample.answer: I would like to talk about the friend whose company I probably enjoy most. A person I always enjoy talking to is a close friend of mine who has a genuinely curious mind. We met at a book club at the local library about four years ago, and since then we have met for tea almost every week, usually at a small café near the river. Our conversations can start with something trivial and end up exploring philosophy, travel or politics, which I find endlessly [[stimulating]]. Last week, for instance, we started talking about a cricket match and somehow ended up debating whether ambition really makes people happy. What makes talking to him so enjoyable is that he actually listens, rather than just waiting for his turn to speak. He is also wonderfully [[open-minded]], so I can share half-formed thoughts without fear of being judged. I think good conversation is a bit of an art, and he is a master of it, although he would never admit that. He knows when to be serious and when to be [[playful]], which keeps things from ever feeling heavy. Honestly, I always come away from our chats feeling energised and having learned something new. In a world where so much communication happens through screens, having someone you can talk to for hours is genuinely [[precious]]. I never take those conversations for granted, and I think they have made me a far better listener and a slightly more thoughtful person as well.

followUps.q: Do you prefer talking face to face or online?
followUps.answer: Face to face, definitely. You can read someone's expressions and tone properly, and the conversation flows more naturally. Online chats are convenient, but they often feel rather [[stilted]] by comparison.

followUps.q: Are you a talkative person?
followUps.answer: It depends on who I am with. With close friends and family I can talk for hours, but in large groups of strangers I tend to be quieter and listen more than I speak.

part3Samples.q: Do you think digital communication is better than face-to-face communication?
part3Samples.answer: I would say it is not better, but rather different, with its own strengths. Digital communication offers [[unmatched]] convenience and lets us stay connected across any distance instantly. However, it lacks the richness of face-to-face interaction, where tone, body language and physical presence convey so much. For deep, emotional conversations, nothing beats being together in person. So digital tools are a wonderful [[supplement]], but not a full [[substitute]] for genuine human contact.

part3Samples.q: How is the way young people communicate different from older generations?
part3Samples.answer: The difference is quite marked. Young people have grown up as [[digital natives]], so they favour instant messaging, voice notes and social media over phone calls, which many find [[intrusive]]. Older generations often prefer calls or in-person conversation. Young people also communicate more through images, emojis and memes, a kind of [[visual shorthand]]. This can lead to occasional misunderstanding between the generations, though both are simply adapting to their era.

part3Samples.q: What effect has instant messaging had on our language?
part3Samples.answer: It has had a noticeable influence. Instant messaging has spawned a whole new informal language of abbreviations, emojis and slang, which allows for quick, expressive communication. Some worry this is [[eroding]] traditional writing skills and grammar, especially among the young. However, I take a more relaxed view; language has always [[evolved]], and people generally understand when to switch between casual and formal [[registers]]. So it is evolution, not decay.

part3Samples.q: How do you think we will communicate in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I imagine communication will become even more immersive and instantaneous. Technologies like virtual reality could allow us to feel genuinely present with distant people, and real-time translation may [[dissolve]] language barriers entirely. We may increasingly communicate through augmented reality overlays too. While exciting, I hope these advances [[enhance]] rather than replace human warmth, and that we do not lose the value of simple, [[unmediated]] face-to-face connection.

part3Samples.q: How can people avoid becoming too dependent on digital communication?
part3Samples.answer: Being intentional is key. Setting aside device-free time, particularly during meals or when with loved ones, helps enormously. Consciously choosing to call or meet someone rather than always texting preserves deeper connection. Turning off unnecessary notifications reduces the [[constant pull]] of our devices. Essentially, we need to treat technology as a tool that serves us, rather than allowing it to [[dominate]] our attention and [[displace]] real interaction.

part3Samples.q: Some say social media has made friendships shallower. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I largely agree with that sentiment. Social media encourages us to [[accumulate]] hundreds of contacts while investing little in any of them. The constant highlight reels can also breed comparison rather than genuine connection. That said, it depends how you use it; for maintaining existing bonds it is useful. Used as a [[substitute]] for real intimacy, though, it does [[trivialise]] friendship.

cueCards.title: Describe a patient person you know
cueCards.prompt: Describe a patient person you know

sample.answer: I would like to talk about someone whose calm I still try to copy. The most patient person I know is a former teacher of mine, whose calm never seemed to break no matter how testing the situation. She taught us Bengali literature at my higher secondary college in Sirajganj, so I was in her class for two years. Teaching a class of restless teenagers is difficult enough, but she handled even the most disruptive students with remarkable [[composure]]. As for how she showed patience, rather than raising her voice, she would pause, take a breath and respond calmly, which was far more effective. I remember one boy who constantly interrupted her lessons; instead of punishing him, she gave him small responsibilities, and by the end of the year he was one of her best students. What I admired was that her patience was not [[passive]]; it came from genuine understanding of why students behaved as they did. She gave people time to learn at their own pace, never making anyone feel rushed or stupid. I think patience like hers is genuinely [[underrated]], because it requires enormous self-control. Watching her, I realised how much damage impatience can do and how much trust patience can build. Honestly, she has made me consciously try to be more [[tolerant]] in my own daily interactions, though I still have a long way to go. At work, when a student asks me the same question for the fifth time, I often think of her.

followUps.q: Are you a patient person?
followUps.answer: Moderately. I am patient with students and older relatives, but I get rather [[irritable]] in traffic or long queues. It is something I am actively working on, with mixed results so far.

followUps.q: Why do you think people are less patient nowadays?
followUps.answer: Mainly because technology has made everything instant. We are used to fast deliveries and immediate replies, so waiting for anything now feels frustrating, even when the delay is perfectly reasonable.

part3Samples.q: Do you think emotional intelligence is more important than academic intelligence?
part3Samples.answer: I would argue they are both important but serve different purposes. Academic intelligence may get you a qualification, but emotional intelligence is often what determines success in life and work, since it [[governs]] how you deal with people. The ability to manage emotions, empathise and communicate is genuinely [[indispensable]]. So while I would not rank one above the other, emotional intelligence is arguably more [[underrated]].

part3Samples.q: Are emotional skills valued more in some professions than others?
part3Samples.answer: Definitely. In [[people-facing]] roles such as teaching, healthcare or management, emotional intelligence is arguably the most important skill of all, as success depends on connecting with others. In more technical or [[solitary]] fields, like programming, it may seem less critical, though even there teamwork requires it. So while its importance varies, I think emotional skills are becoming increasingly valued [[across virtually every sector]].

part3Samples.q: What happens when a person lacks emotional intelligence?
part3Samples.answer: A lack of emotional intelligence can cause real difficulties, both personally and professionally. Such a person may struggle to [[read social cues]], handle criticism, or manage their own reactions, which can damage relationships. They might come across as [[insensitive]] or provoke unnecessary conflict without even realising it. Over time, this can lead to isolation and repeated interpersonal [[friction]].

part3Samples.q: Will emotional intelligence become more important as technology advances?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly believe it will. As machines and AI take over more analytical and routine tasks, the uniquely human skills, like empathy, creativity and emotional connection, will become more valuable, not less. These are precisely the abilities that technology cannot easily [[replicate]]. So [[paradoxically]], in an increasingly automated world, emotional intelligence may become one of our most [[sought-after]] qualities.

part3Samples.q: Can emotional intelligence be taught, and if so, how?
part3Samples.answer: Yes, I firmly believe it can be developed, even if some people are naturally more gifted. Self-awareness can be [[cultivated]] through reflection and honest feedback. Skills like active listening and empathy can be practised deliberately. Schools could help by [[incorporating]] emotional learning into the curriculum from an early age. Like any skill, it improves with [[conscious effort]] and practice, so it is far from fixed.

part3Samples.q: Some say people cannot live without their phones now. Do you agree?

However, phones have become so [[integral]] to how we work, navigate and communicate that living without one would be genuinely inconvenient and isolating in modern society. cueCards.title: Describe a younger person you admire
cueCards.prompt: Describe a younger person you admire

She is also refreshingly [[self-aware]], knowing exactly what she wants and unafraid to pursue it. As for why I admire her, I think her generation faces a lot of pressure, yet she handles it with a calm confidence I did not have at her age. sample.answer: I would like to talk about the person whose food I would choose over any restaurant's. What makes her cooking special is her [[intuitive]] sense of flavour; she seems to know exactly how much of each spice to add without measuring. I think part of what makes her food so good is the care she puts into it; cooking for her is an act of love, not a chore. followUps.answer: I would love to, although perhaps not for work. I would rather travel slowly, spending weeks in one place to properly [[soak up]] the culture, instead of rushing from city to city.

followUps.answer: Probably Canada or the UK, partly because many of my students go there and I would like to see what their lives are like. I am also fascinated by Japan's mix of tradition and technology.

part3Samples.q: What effects does tourism have on local communities?

part3Samples.q: How do you think tourism will change in the future?

cueCards.title: Describe a person who is a good listener
cueCards.prompt: Describe a person who is a good listener
bullets: and how you feel about them

sample.answer: I would like to talk about the person I go to whenever I need to talk something through. The best listener I know is a close friend of mine, and it is a quality I value in her enormously. We met at university, where we were in the same tutorial group, and she now teaches at a school in Sirajganj, so we still meet regularly. In an age when most people are just waiting for their turn to speak, she gives you her complete, [[undivided]] attention. She puts her phone away, makes eye contact and never glances around the room while you are talking. When I talk to her about a problem, she never rushes to offer solutions; instead she lets me express myself fully first, which is surprisingly rare. She asks thoughtful questions that show she has genuinely been paying attention. What makes her such a good listener is her natural [[empathy]]; she seems to feel what you are feeling. As for how I feel about her, I always come away from our conversations feeling lighter, as though a weight has been shared. Last year, when I was unsure whether to apply for a master's degree abroad, she listened to me for an entire evening without once telling me what to do. I think being truly listened to is one of the most [[comforting]] experiences a person can have. Honestly, her ability to listen without judgement is a genuine gift, and it is a big part of why she is so [[treasured]] by everyone who knows her.

followUps.q: Are you a good listener yourself?
followUps.answer: I am getting better. My job has taught me to listen carefully, because students often reveal their real worries only if you give them time. But I still sometimes [[jump in]] too quickly when I get excited.

followUps.q: Why do you think some people are poor listeners?
followUps.answer: Often because they are distracted, particularly by their phones, or because they are more interested in sharing their own opinions. Listening properly takes patience and genuine interest in the other person.

part3Samples.q: Do you think emotional intelligence is more important than academic intelligence?
part3Samples.answer: I would argue they are both important but serve different purposes. Academic intelligence may get you a qualification, but emotional intelligence is often what determines success in life and work, since it [[governs]] how you deal with people. The ability to manage emotions, empathise and communicate is genuinely [[indispensable]]. So while I would not rank one above the other, emotional intelligence is arguably more [[underrated]].

part3Samples.q: Are emotional skills valued more in some professions than others?
part3Samples.answer: Definitely. In [[people-facing]] roles such as teaching, healthcare or management, emotional intelligence is arguably the most important skill of all, as success depends on connecting with others. In more technical or [[solitary]] fields, like programming, it may seem less critical, though even there teamwork requires it. So while its importance varies, I think emotional skills are becoming increasingly valued [[across virtually every sector]].

part3Samples.q: What happens when a person lacks emotional intelligence?
part3Samples.answer: A lack of emotional intelligence can cause real difficulties, both personally and professionally. Such a person may struggle to [[read social cues]], handle criticism, or manage their own reactions, which can damage relationships. They might come across as [[insensitive]] or provoke unnecessary conflict without even realising it. Over time, this can lead to isolation and repeated interpersonal [[friction]].

part3Samples.q: Will emotional intelligence become more important as technology advances?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly believe it will. As machines and AI take over more analytical and routine tasks, the uniquely human skills, like empathy, creativity and emotional connection, will become more valuable, not less. These are precisely the abilities that technology cannot easily [[replicate]]. So [[paradoxically]], in an increasingly automated world, emotional intelligence may become one of our most [[sought-after]] qualities.

part3Samples.q: Can emotional intelligence be taught, and if so, how?
part3Samples.answer: Yes, I firmly believe it can be developed, even if some people are naturally more gifted. Self-awareness can be [[cultivated]] through reflection and honest feedback. Skills like active listening and empathy can be practised deliberately. Schools could help by [[incorporating]] emotional learning into the curriculum from an early age. Like any skill, it improves with [[conscious effort]] and practice, so it is far from fixed.

part3Samples.q: Some say technology is making face-to-face conversation a dying skill. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I think there is a [[kernel of truth]] to this, though I would not go so far as to call it dying. It is certainly true that some young people, accustomed to texting, can feel awkward in direct conversation and may struggle to read social cues. However, humans are inherently social, and the need for real connection persists. So the skill may be underused and in need of [[nurturing]], but I do not believe it will ever become [[obsolete]].

cueCards.title: Describe a city you have visited
cueCards.prompt: Describe a city you have visited
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: I would like to talk about a trip I made to Kolkata, in India, a couple of years ago, which left a lasting impression on me. I went during the winter with two friends from university, and we spent about five days there. It is an old, historic city, and what struck me immediately was its wonderful sense of character. The streets were [[bustling]] with activity, full of markets, trams and street food that smelled incredible. What I loved most was the blend of old and new; grand colonial buildings stood alongside modern shops, creating a genuinely [[atmospheric]] feel. I spent my days exploring museums and wandering through the older neighbourhoods, which felt almost [[timeless]]. We also rode one of the old trams, which rattled along at a wonderfully slow pace. We visited the Victoria Memorial, and I spent a whole afternoon on College Street, which is lined with second-hand bookshops, so as a keen reader I was completely [[in my element]]. The people were remarkably friendly and always happy to point me in the right direction, and since so many of them speak Bengali, I never felt like a complete outsider. Of course, it was crowded and chaotic at times, but that energy was part of its charm. Honestly, I found the whole experience genuinely [[invigorating]], and it gave me a real appreciation for the city's rich cultural heritage. In a way it also felt strangely familiar, because we share so much history, language and food. I would go back without hesitation, ideally for longer next time.

followUps.q: Would you like to go back to Kolkata?
followUps.answer: Yes, definitely. Next time I would like to stay longer and explore some of the smaller neighbourhoods and old cafés. I would also love to go during Durga Puja, when the whole city is beautifully lit up.

followUps.q: Do you prefer visiting cities or the countryside?
followUps.answer: It depends on my mood, really. Cities are exciting for a few days, but I get tired of the noise quite quickly, so for a proper rest I would usually choose the countryside.

cueCards.title: Describe a place near water that you like
cueCards.prompt: Describe a place near water that you like

sample.answer: The place I would like to describe is the riverside near my home in Sirajganj, beside the Jamuna river, which has always been a favourite spot of mine. It is only a short rickshaw ride from our flat, along the embankment on the edge of town. I try to go there two or three times a week, usually in the early evening once I have finished work. There is something deeply [[calming]] about sitting by the water and watching the sun set over it. The gentle sound of the current is wonderfully [[soothing]], and it seems to wash away the stress of daily life. I usually go for a slow walk along the bank, or simply sit with a cup of tea from one of the little stalls and let my mind wander. Sometimes I watch the fishing boats coming in, or children playing near the water's edge. What I love most is how [[tranquil]] it is compared to the noise of the town centre. There is often a cool breeze coming off the water, which is a blessing in the heat, especially in the sticky weeks before the monsoon. Of course, the river has another side too; in the rainy season it swells enormously, and [[riverbank erosion]] has cost many local families their land over the years. Perhaps that is why I respect it as much as I love it. Honestly, being near water has a [[therapeutic]] effect on me that is hard to explain. It is my favourite place to think, and I always leave feeling refreshed.

followUps.q: Do many people go there?
followUps.answer: Yes, quite a lot, especially in the evenings and on holidays. Families come to enjoy the breeze and young people gather to chat, but if you walk a little further along the bank it becomes much quieter.

followUps.q: Has the riverside changed since you were a child?
followUps.answer: Yes, a fair bit. The embankment has been strengthened, and there are more tea stalls and lights now. It is busier than before, but the view across the water is exactly the same.

part3Samples.q: How important are public spaces like parks in a city?
part3Samples.answer: I consider them absolutely essential to a healthy city. Public spaces like parks provide vital areas for recreation, exercise and relaxation, which is crucial for physical and mental wellbeing amid the stress of urban life. They also act as the [[lungs of a city]], improving air quality, and serve as places where the community comes together. So far from being a luxury, well-designed public spaces are fundamental to a [[liveable]] and [[cohesive]] city.

part3Samples.q: Do you think there are enough public spaces in modern cities?
part3Samples.answer: In many rapidly growing cities, unfortunately not. As urban land becomes increasingly valuable, green and public spaces are often sacrificed for commercial or residential development, which I find [[short-sighted]]. Older, well-planned cities tend to have generous parks, whereas newer, denser developments frequently lack them. So while the importance of public space is increasingly recognised, in practice many cities are [[falling short]], prioritising profit over [[liveability]].

part3Samples.q: What effect do green spaces have on people living in cities?
part3Samples.answer: The effects are overwhelmingly positive, in my view. Access to green spaces reduces stress, improves mood and encourages physical activity, benefiting both mental and physical health. They provide a [[peaceful escape]] from the noise and concrete of the city. Socially, they [[foster]] community interaction. Environmentally, they cool cities and clean the air. So green spaces have a genuinely [[restorative]] and beneficial effect on urban wellbeing.

part3Samples.q: Do you think cities will have more or fewer public spaces in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am hopeful there will be more, though it faces real pressure. On one hand, [[intense competition]] for urban land threatens existing spaces. On the other, there is a growing recognition of their importance for wellbeing and sustainability, and many [[forward-thinking]] cities are now actively creating parks, green roofs and pedestrian zones. So the outcome depends on planning priorities, but I am optimistic that the value of public space will increasingly be recognised and [[prioritised]].

part3Samples.q: How can cities create more public spaces despite limited land?
part3Samples.answer: Creativity is key when land is scarce. Cities can [[repurpose]] [[disused]] areas, such as old railway lines turned into elevated parks, or convert rooftops into green spaces and gardens. Pedestrianising streets reclaims space from cars for people. Even small pocket parks on vacant plots make a difference. So even in dense cities, with imaginative planning, it is possible to integrate valuable public and green space into the existing [[urban fabric]].

part3Samples.q: Some say happiness is a choice. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I partly agree, but with important reservations. There is real truth that our attitude, gratitude and how we respond to circumstances significantly influence our happiness, so mindset matters. However, saying happiness is simply a choice can be [[dismissive]] of those facing genuine hardship, mental illness or difficult circumstances beyond their control. So while we have some agency over our happiness, I think it is [[oversimplified]] to call it purely a choice, ignoring the [[structural]] and biological factors involved.

cueCards.title: Describe a quiet place you like to spend time in
cueCards.prompt: Describe a quiet place you like to spend time in

sample.answer: A quiet place I really treasure is a small reading corner in the public library in our town, just a ten-minute walk from our flat. I stumbled upon it by chance a few years ago, when I was looking for somewhere to prepare for my university exams, and I have been going ever since. Tucked away near the back, behind the tall shelves of old newspapers, it is a [[secluded]] little spot that most people seem to overlook. I usually go there to read or study, because the silence helps me concentrate in a way that is impossible at home, where my younger sister is often revising and the television is on in the next room. These days I mostly go on a free afternoon with a novel or a book about business. There is something wonderfully peaceful about being surrounded by books, with only the occasional turning of a page to break the quiet. In our increasingly noisy world, finding somewhere so genuinely [[serene]] feels like a small luxury. I often [[lose track of time]] there, completely [[absorbed]] in whatever I am reading. Honestly, it has become a kind of [[sanctuary]] for me, a place to escape the constant distractions of modern life, and I deliberately leave my phone on silent at the bottom of my bag. I always feel calmer and more focused after spending an afternoon there, and I think everyone deserves a corner like that somewhere in their life.

followUps.q: Do you prefer studying at home or in a library?
followUps.answer: Definitely in a library. At home there are too many distractions, like the television, my phone and family conversations, whereas in a library everyone around me is focused, which makes it much easier to concentrate.

followUps.q: Do many young people in your town use the library?
followUps.answer: Fewer than before, I think. A lot of students now study online or at coaching centres, but during exam season the library still fills up with young people looking for a quiet place to revise.

part3Samples.q: What do you think makes people truly happy?
part3Samples.answer: In my view, lasting happiness comes primarily [[from within]] and from our connections, rather than from external possessions. Strong, loving relationships seem to be the greatest source of happiness. Beyond that, having a sense of purpose, good health, and the freedom to pursue what we find meaningful all contribute enormously. So I believe true happiness is [[rooted in]] connection, purpose and [[gratitude]], not in material wealth.

part3Samples.q: Are people happier now than in the past?
part3Samples.answer: This is a fascinating and debated question. In material terms, we are far better off than previous generations, with more comfort, health and opportunity. Yet, [[curiously]], rates of anxiety and depression seem to be rising, especially among the young. It appears that material progress has not straightforwardly translated into greater happiness. So while we have gained much, I am not convinced we are [[fundamentally]] happier, which suggests happiness depends on more than mere [[prosperity]] and comfort.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think some wealthy people are unhappy?
part3Samples.answer: This reflects the fact that money, beyond meeting basic needs, has [[diminishing returns]] on happiness. Wealthy people may still suffer from poor relationships, a lack of purpose, or the isolation and pressure that wealth can bring. There is also the phenomenon where people constantly adapt and want more, never feeling satisfied. So it demonstrates that happiness is not something money can simply buy; it depends on deeper, [[non-material]] [[fulfilment]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will be happier in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am genuinely uncertain. On one hand, advances in medicine, technology and [[living standards]] could improve wellbeing. There is also growing awareness of mental health and the importance of a balanced life. On the other hand, rising pressures, social media comparison and uncertainty could work against happiness. So I think future happiness will depend less on material progress and more on whether we learn to [[prioritise]] the things that genuinely [[nourish]] human wellbeing.

part3Samples.q: What can societies do to improve people's wellbeing?
part3Samples.answer: Societies can take meaningful steps. Prioritising mental health services and reducing the [[stigma]] around them is crucial. Fostering community, reducing inequality, and ensuring people have access to nature, leisure and a healthy work-life balance all help. Some argue governments should measure national wellbeing, not just economic output. Essentially, by valuing human [[flourishing]] alongside economic growth, societies can create conditions in which more people can genuinely [[thrive]] and feel content.

part3Samples.q: Some say the internet has made memorisation unnecessary. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I only partly agree. It is true that we no longer need to memorise facts that we can look up instantly, so pure memorisation is less critical than before. However, I would argue that a solid base of knowledge in your own memory is still essential for [[reasoning]] and creativity, because you cannot connect ideas you do not [[possess]]. So the internet has shifted, rather than [[eliminated]], the value of memory.

cueCards.title: Describe a historical place you have visited
cueCards.prompt: Describe a historical place you have visited
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: A historical place that genuinely moved me was the Sixty Dome Mosque in Bagerhat, in the south-west of Bangladesh, which I visited during a trip to Khulna about three years ago. It dates back to the fifteenth century, and stepping inside felt like travelling back in time. The architecture was absolutely [[magnificent]], with thick brick walls and long rows of slender stone pillars supporting dozens of small, rounded domes. What struck me most was the sense of history embedded in the walls; you could almost feel the countless generations who had passed through. A local guide explained its [[significance]], telling us that it was built in the time of Khan Jahan Ali and that the whole area is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site, which made the experience far richer than simply looking at old stones. I also wandered around the grounds and the large pond beside it, and I was surprised to learn that the mosque is still used for prayers today, so it is a living place rather than just a monument. I found myself genuinely [[awestruck]] by the craftsmanship of an era without modern machinery. Places like this are an important reminder of our [[heritage]], and I think it is vital that we preserve them, especially as damp and salt are a real threat to old brickwork in that region. Honestly, I came away with a deeper appreciation of the past and how much skill and devotion went into these monuments. It was easily one of the most memorable trips I have taken.

followUps.q: Would you recommend it to foreign visitors?
followUps.answer: Absolutely. It is one of the most important historical sites in Bangladesh, and combining it with a trip to the Sundarbans makes perfect sense, because both are in the same part of the country.

followUps.q: Did you learn about it at school?
followUps.answer: Yes, briefly, in our history lessons, but reading about it in a textbook is nothing compared to standing inside. Seeing it in person made the history feel real rather than just facts to memorise.

part3Samples.q: Do you think traditions are still important in modern society?
part3Samples.answer: I believe they are more important than ever. In a rapidly changing, globalised world, traditions provide a vital sense of identity, continuity and belonging. They connect us to our history and to one another. While some outdated customs deserve to fade, I think the core traditions that [[bind]] a community together are worth [[preserving]]. They give life a certain meaning and rhythm that [[modernity]] alone cannot provide.

part3Samples.q: Are young people less interested in traditions than older generations?
part3Samples.answer: To some extent, yes, though it varies. Young people, being more exposed to global culture and modern lifestyles, sometimes view certain traditions as [[outdated]] or irrelevant. However, I would not say they have abandoned tradition entirely; many still take great pride in their [[cultural roots]], just alongside a more modern outlook. So there is a shift in emphasis, but I think the connection to heritage remains, merely [[reinterpreted]] in a contemporary context.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think some traditions are disappearing?
part3Samples.answer: Several forces are at work. Globalisation and the dominance of Western culture have [[homogenised]] lifestyles, making some local customs seem less relevant. Urbanisation and modern, busy lives also leave less time for elaborate traditional practices. Additionally, as older generations pass away, knowledge and skills are sometimes not passed on. So it is really a combination of cultural [[dilution]] and the practical pressures of modern life [[eroding]] them.

part3Samples.q: Do you think traditions will survive in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am cautiously optimistic. While some traditions will inevitably fade, I believe the most meaningful ones will [[endure]], perhaps in modified forms. There is actually a growing appreciation for heritage as a counterbalance to globalisation, with many people actively seeking to [[revive]] old customs. Technology can also help document and share them. So rather than vanishing, I think traditions will [[evolve]], adapting to remain relevant in a changing world.

part3Samples.q: What can be done to preserve traditional culture?
part3Samples.answer: A [[concerted effort]] is needed. Education is crucial; teaching young people about their heritage in schools fosters pride and understanding. Documenting traditions and supporting the [[artisans]] and elders who hold this knowledge is also vital. Governments and communities can organise festivals and cultural events to keep customs alive and visible. Essentially, making tradition feel relevant and engaging to the young is the key to its [[continuity]].

part3Samples.q: Some say tourism does more harm than good to destinations. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I think it depends entirely on how it is managed. In some over-touristed places, the harm, from environmental damage to cultural erosion and inflated living costs, is undeniable and can indeed outweigh the benefits. However, when managed responsibly and sustainably, tourism can be a tremendous [[force for good]], funding conservation and lifting communities out of poverty. So I would not agree it is inherently harmful; the outcome [[hinges on]] responsible [[stewardship]] and planning.

cueCards.title: Describe a place you would like to visit in the future
cueCards.prompt: Describe a place you would like to visit in the future
bullets: and why you want to go

sample.answer: A place I have long dreamed of visiting is Switzerland, particularly the Alpine region. I first became [[captivated]] by it through photographs and documentaries, which made the scenery look almost unreal, and more recently through my job, because I work at an education consultancy and a few of our students have gone there to study hospitality. When they send photos back, I must admit I feel a little envious. The idea of snow-capped mountains, crystal-clear lakes and charming villages is incredibly [[appealing]] to me, especially as someone who has never actually seen snow. If I ever go, I would love to take the scenic train routes that wind through the mountains, which are said to be breathtaking. I would also like to go hiking beside one of the lakes and perhaps visit a small village where cheese is still made in the traditional way. I imagine the air there is wonderfully fresh, [[a world away from]] the dust and traffic I am used to. What draws me most is the promise of such [[pristine]] natural beauty, which is increasingly rare. I would also love to experience the local culture and food, of course. Honestly, it is at the very top of my [[bucket list]], and I am determined to get there one day, even though it is famously expensive. I think some places are worth saving up for, and this is definitely one of them, so I have quietly started putting a little money aside each month.

followUps.q: Would you prefer to go alone or with others?
followUps.answer: With others, ideally my family or a couple of close friends. Beautiful places are more enjoyable when you can share them, and I think my parents would be amazed to see snow for the first time.

followUps.q: How long would you like to stay there?
followUps.answer: At least two weeks, if I could afford it. I would not want to rush from one place to another; I would rather travel slowly and actually enjoy each place properly.

part3Samples.q: How do you think tourism will change in the future?

part3Samples.q: Some say globalisation mainly benefits wealthy countries. Do you agree?

cueCards.title: Describe a park or garden you like
cueCards.prompt: Describe a park or garden you like

sample.answer: The place I would like to describe is a public park not far from where I live, which is a real green oasis in the middle of our town. It is only about ten minutes' walk from our flat, so it is very easy to reach. I try to visit at least once a week, usually on Friday afternoons, and more often in winter when the weather is pleasant. It is beautifully [[landscaped]], with wide lawns, tall shady trees and a small pond in the middle, surrounded by flower beds that are at their best in early spring. There is also a walking track around the edge and a little play area for children. Sirajganj is getting more built up every year, so having such a [[lush]] green space nearby is genuinely precious. I usually go there to walk, read or simply sit on a bench and [[watch the world go by]]. What I love most is how it brings the community together; families picnic, children play cricket on the grass and elderly men sit chatting for hours. The atmosphere is always [[laid-back]] and cheerful, and nobody seems to be in a hurry. Honestly, spending time surrounded by greenery has a noticeably [[restorative]] effect on me, especially after a stressful week at work. Sometimes I take my four-year-old nephew there when my elder sister visits from Dhaka, and watching him run around is a joy in itself. I think every town needs places like this, and I feel lucky to have one so close.

followUps.q: Do you think your town needs more parks?
followUps.answer: Yes, definitely. The town is growing quickly and new buildings are going up everywhere, so green spaces are shrinking. More parks would give children somewhere safe to play and give everyone a place to breathe.

followUps.q: What do you usually do there at the weekend?
followUps.answer: Mostly I walk a few laps of the track and then sit under a tree with a book. Sometimes I meet a friend there, and we buy roasted peanuts from a vendor and chat for an hour.

cueCards.title: Describe a place where you like to relax
cueCards.prompt: Describe a place where you like to relax
bullets: and why it helps you relax

sample.answer: The place where I relax most completely is actually the rooftop of our building, which offers a surprisingly lovely view over the town. We live on the third floor, so it is just a short climb up the stairs, and on a clear evening you can see the rooftops stretching out towards the river. I go up there most evenings, especially after a long or stressful day at the office. There is something wonderfully [[liberating]] about being up high, away from the noise and crowds below. I usually take a cup of tea, put on some quiet music and simply watch the sky change colour as the sun goes down. Some of our neighbours grow plants in pots up there, so it feels almost like a small garden. The gentle breeze is genuinely [[refreshing]], and it seems to clear my head. What makes it so relaxing is the sense of [[solitude]]; it is my own little escape where no one bothers me. I often do my best thinking there, or sometimes just switch off entirely. During the monsoon I stand under the shelter of the stairwell and watch the rain sweep across the town, which is strangely calming. My job involves a lot of talking and problem-solving, so I need a moment to [[unwind]] before dinner with my family. Honestly, having a spot like this has been [[invaluable]] for my mental wellbeing. It costs nothing, yet it does more for my mood than almost anything else.

followUps.q: Do you ever go up there with other people?
followUps.answer: Occasionally. My younger sister sometimes comes up after she finishes studying, and during Eid the whole family goes up in the evening. Mostly, though, I prefer to keep it as my own quiet time.

followUps.q: Is it easy to find places to relax in your town?
followUps.answer: Not always. Sirajganj is fairly calm compared with Dhaka, but it is still getting busier, and most public places are quite noisy. That is why a private spot like our rooftop is so valuable.

part3Samples.q: What do you think makes people truly happy?
part3Samples.answer: In my view, lasting happiness comes primarily [[from within]] and from our connections, rather than from external possessions. Strong, loving relationships seem to be the greatest source of happiness. Beyond that, having a sense of purpose, good health, and the freedom to pursue what we find meaningful all contribute enormously. So I believe true happiness is [[rooted in]] connection, purpose and [[gratitude]], not in material wealth.

part3Samples.q: Are people happier now than in the past?
part3Samples.answer: This is a fascinating and debated question. In material terms, we are far better off than previous generations, with more comfort, health and opportunity. Yet, [[curiously]], rates of anxiety and depression seem to be rising, especially among the young. It appears that material progress has not straightforwardly translated into greater happiness. So while we have gained much, I am not convinced we are [[fundamentally]] happier, which suggests happiness depends on more than mere [[prosperity]] and comfort.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think some wealthy people are unhappy?
part3Samples.answer: This reflects the fact that money, beyond meeting basic needs, has [[diminishing returns]] on happiness. Wealthy people may still suffer from poor relationships, a lack of purpose, or the isolation and pressure that wealth can bring. There is also the phenomenon where people constantly adapt and want more, never feeling satisfied. So it demonstrates that happiness is not something money can simply buy; it depends on deeper, [[non-material]] [[fulfilment]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will be happier in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am genuinely uncertain. On one hand, advances in medicine, technology and [[living standards]] could improve wellbeing. There is also growing awareness of mental health and the importance of a balanced life. On the other hand, rising pressures, social media comparison and uncertainty could work against happiness. So I think future happiness will depend less on material progress and more on whether we learn to [[prioritise]] the things that genuinely [[nourish]] human wellbeing.

part3Samples.q: What can societies do to improve people's wellbeing?
part3Samples.answer: Societies can take meaningful steps. Prioritising mental health services and reducing the [[stigma]] around them is crucial. Fostering community, reducing inequality, and ensuring people have access to nature, leisure and a healthy work-life balance all help. Some argue governments should measure national wellbeing, not just economic output. Essentially, by valuing human [[flourishing]] alongside economic growth, societies can create conditions in which more people can genuinely [[thrive]] and feel content.

part3Samples.q: Some say working hard is more important than having free time. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I respectfully disagree with framing it as either-or. Hard work is certainly important for achievement, and I value [[diligence]]. However, free time is not the opposite of hard work; it is what makes sustained hard work possible by preventing burnout. The two are [[complementary]]. In my view, someone who works intensely but never rests is not admirable but heading towards [[exhaustion]], so balance is wiser.

cueCards.title: Describe a building you find interesting
cueCards.prompt: Describe a building you find interesting
bullets: and why you find it interesting

sample.answer: A building I find genuinely fascinating is the National Parliament House in Dhaka, known in Bengali as the Jatiya Sangsad Bhaban, which is considered an architectural masterpiece. It stands in the Sher-e-Bangla Nagar area of the capital, surrounded by an artificial lake and wide lawns. Designed by the American architect Louis Kahn, it is unlike anything else in the country. What makes it so striking is its bold, [[geometric]] design, using simple shapes like circles and triangles cut into vast concrete walls. Despite its size, it has a strange sense of lightness and elegance, especially when the whole building is reflected in the still water around it. I find it interesting because it manages to be both [[avant-garde]] and timeless at the same time, even though it was completed in the early 1980s. The way natural light filters through the openings is genuinely [[ingenious]], changing the whole feel of the interior throughout the day. It serves as the seat of our government, so it carries real [[symbolic importance]] too. I have mostly seen the interior in photographs, but I once walked around the grounds while visiting my sister, and the scale of it was quite overwhelming up close. Honestly, every time I see it I notice some new detail I had missed before. I think great architecture like this is a form of art, and it is something the country can [[rightly be proud of]]. I would love to see inside properly one day.

followUps.q: Would you like to see inside it?
followUps.answer: Very much. I have seen photographs of the interior, with light pouring through the huge openings, and I would love to experience that in person if I ever get the chance to go inside.

followUps.q: Do you think modern buildings in Bangladesh are well designed?
followUps.answer: Some are, but many new buildings are rather plain concrete blocks put up in a hurry. I think architects should learn from buildings like this one, which are practical but also genuinely beautiful.

part3Samples.answer: It really depends on one's priorities and stage of life. Cities offer better job opportunities, [[amenities]], healthcare and a vibrant social life, which many find appealing. The countryside, by contrast, offers peace, clean air, space and a stronger sense of community. Personally, I appreciate the convenience of the city for now, but I can see the [[profound appeal]] of a quieter rural life later. So neither is objectively better; each suits different needs and [[temperaments]].

part3Samples.q: How have cities changed over the past few decades?
part3Samples.answer: Cities have transformed dramatically. They have grown enormously in size and population due to rapid urbanisation, becoming denser and often more [[congested]]. Skylines have risen with skyscrapers, and technology has made them smarter. However, this growth has often [[outpaced]] infrastructure, worsening problems like traffic, pollution and housing shortages. So while cities have become more developed and connected, this expansion has brought significant [[growing pains]].

part3Samples.q: Why do so many people move to cities?
part3Samples.answer: The primary driver is economic opportunity. Cities are hubs of employment, offering far more and better-paid jobs than rural areas, which is the biggest [[pull factor]]. They also provide superior access to education, healthcare and services. For many, the appeal of a more exciting, diverse lifestyle is also a draw. So this migration is largely driven by the search for a better standard of living, though it can place enormous [[strain]] on urban [[infrastructure]] and resources.

part3Samples.q: What do you think cities will be like in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I envision cities becoming smarter and, hopefully, greener. Technology will likely manage traffic, energy and services more efficiently through data. There is a strong push towards more sustainable, [[walkable]] cities with more green spaces and cleaner transport. However, they may also become even more crowded. So I am hopeful the cities of the future will be more [[liveable]] and sustainable, provided planning [[prioritises]] people and the environment over pure expansion.

part3Samples.q: How can cities be made better places to live?
part3Samples.answer: Thoughtful [[urban planning]] is the key. Investing in efficient, affordable public transport reduces congestion and pollution. Creating more green spaces and [[pedestrian areas]] improves wellbeing. Ensuring an adequate supply of affordable housing tackles inequality. Designing [[mixed-use]], walkable neighbourhoods fosters community. Essentially, cities become better when they are planned around the needs of people and the environment, rather than simply cars and commerce.

part3Samples.q: Some say art is not as important as science. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I firmly disagree with ranking them this way, as they serve different but equally vital purposes. Science advances our material understanding and improves our lives technologically, which is crucial. But art nourishes our emotional and spiritual lives, fosters empathy, and gives meaning to human existence. A world with science but no art would be efficient yet [[soulless]]. So rather than one being more important, I see them as [[complementary]] pillars of a [[flourishing]] civilisation.

cueCards.title: Describe a place you visited on holiday
cueCards.prompt: Describe a place you visited on holiday
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: I would like to talk about a holiday I took to Cox's Bazar, home to one of the longest natural sea beaches in the world. I went there last winter with a few close friends from university, and it turned out to be one of the most memorable trips of my life. We took an overnight bus from Dhaka, which was tiring, but the excitement kept us going. The beach itself was absolutely [[stunning]], stretching as far as the eye could see. We spent our days swimming, walking along the shore and watching the most spectacular sunsets I have ever seen. One morning we hired a jeep and drove along the Marine Drive towards Inani beach, with green hills on one side and the sea on the other, which was unforgettable. We also stopped at Himchari, where a small waterfall runs down the hillside, although it was only a trickle in the dry season. In the evenings we sampled fresh seafood, which was [[delectable]], especially the grilled fish from the little stalls near the beach. What made it special was the combination of natural beauty and good company, which is a hard thing to beat. We laughed constantly and stayed up late talking, just like in our student days. Being by the sea was genuinely [[rejuvenating]] after months of office life. Honestly, there is something about the vastness of the ocean that puts your everyday worries [[into perspective]]. I came home feeling completely recharged, and it left me with [[cherished]] memories that I still look back on fondly.

followUps.q: Would you go back to Cox's Bazar?
followUps.answer: Yes, without a doubt. Next time I would like to take my parents, because my mother has never seen the sea properly, and I think watching the sunset there together would be very special.

followUps.q: Do you prefer holidays with friends or with family?
followUps.answer: Both have their charms. With friends, trips are more spontaneous and adventurous, while family holidays are calmer and more comfortable. At my age, I probably enjoy the energy of travelling with friends slightly more.

cueCards.title: Describe a place that was full of noise
cueCards.prompt: Describe a place that was full of noise
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: A place I remember as being incredibly noisy was Chawkbazar, a large wholesale market in Old Dhaka. I went there one morning last year, while I was staying with my elder sister, to help my brother-in-law buy things in bulk for a family wedding, and the sheer volume of sound was overwhelming from the moment we stepped out of the rickshaw. The lanes are extremely narrow, and every inch is filled with shops, porters carrying huge loads on their heads and handcarts squeezing past. Traders were shouting out their prices, customers were haggling loudly, and the constant honking of vehicles added to the [[chaos]]. It was genuinely [[deafening]] at times, and I struggled to hear the person next to me. Yet there was an undeniable energy to it all; the noise felt alive rather than unpleasant. I found the whole scene strangely [[exhilarating]], even if I would not want to be there every day. After a couple of hours, though, I was desperate for some quiet, as the constant [[din]] became exhausting, and I had a slight headache by the time we left. Coming from Sirajganj, which is relatively calm, I was amazed that people work in that environment every single day. Honestly, it gave me a real appreciation for peace and quiet, which I usually [[take for granted]]. It was a fascinating, if overwhelming, glimpse of everyday commerce, and I felt I had seen the real heartbeat of the capital.

followUps.q: Do you mind noisy places in general?
followUps.answer: I can tolerate them for a short while, especially if there is a good reason to be there, but I definitely prefer quiet places. After a long day, noise wears me out far more quickly than hard work.

followUps.q: Is your hometown noisy?
followUps.answer: Not really, compared with Dhaka. There is traffic and plenty of rickshaw bells in the town centre, but the residential area where we live is fairly quiet, especially in the evenings.

part3Samples.q: How serious is the problem of pollution in your country?
part3Samples.answer: Unfortunately, pollution is a very serious problem in my country, particularly in the major cities. Air quality often reaches [[hazardous]] levels due to traffic, industry and construction, which [[poses a real threat]] to public health. Water pollution from industrial and domestic waste is also a significant concern. So while there is growing awareness, I would say pollution remains one of our most [[pressing]] environmental and public-health challenges.

part3Samples.q: Which do you think is worse, air pollution or water pollution?
part3Samples.answer: Both are extremely damaging, and it is hard to rank them. Air pollution is perhaps more immediate and [[inescapable]], as we breathe constantly, and it causes widespread respiratory illness. Water pollution, however, is arguably more [[insidious]], contaminating our drinking water and food chain and devastating [[aquatic ecosystems]]. So rather than one being definitively worse, I would say they are both severe problems with different but equally devastating consequences.

part3Samples.q: What are the main causes of pollution in cities?
part3Samples.answer: Urban pollution stems from several sources. Vehicle emissions are a [[primary culprit]], given the sheer density of traffic. Industrial activity and factories release pollutants into the air and water. Construction generates dust, and the burning of fossil fuels for energy contributes heavily. Poor waste management adds to the problem. So it is largely a [[by-product]] of dense population, industry and [[reliance on fossil fuels]] concentrated in a small area.

part3Samples.q: Do you think pollution will get better or worse in the future?

On the other, growing awareness, stricter regulations, and cleaner technologies like electric vehicles and renewable energy offer real solutions. Many developed cities have already reduced pollution significantly. So with sufficient [[political will]] and innovation, I believe we can [[reverse the trend]], but it is not guaranteed.

part3Samples.q: What can be done to reduce pollution?

[[Enforcing]] strict regulations on industrial waste and improving public transport are vital. Better waste management and recycling reduce landfill and litter. On an individual level, reducing consumption and waste helps. Ultimately, a combination of regulation, clean technology and changed behaviour offers the most effective path forward.

part3Samples.q: Some say governments should stop cities from growing too big. Do you agree?
