Skills that were valuable a decade ago can quickly become [[obsolete]], and entirely new fields emerge constantly. To remain employable, workers must continually update their knowledge and [[reskill]]. The old model of one qualification lasting a whole career is no longer viable. In short, adaptability through learning has become a genuine necessity, not a luxury.

part3Samples.q: Do you think lifelong learning will become the norm in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am confident it will, [[out of sheer necessity]]. As careers become less linear and technology evolves ever faster, continuous learning and periodic reskilling will simply be part of working life. I anticipate more flexible, [[bite-sized]] courses and employer-sponsored training becoming [[commonplace]]. Society's whole conception of education will likely shift from a one-off event to an ongoing, lifelong process.

part3Samples.q: What prevents adults from continuing to learn, and how can this be solved?
part3Samples.answer: The main barriers are usually time, cost and lack of confidence. Busy working adults with family commitments struggle to find the time and money for further study. To address this, flexible online and part-time courses are invaluable, as is employer support through funded training. Governments could also offer [[subsidies]] or learning accounts. [[Dismantling]] these obstacles would make lifelong learning genuinely [[attainable]] for everyone.

part3Samples.q: Some say hobbies should be useful, not just for fun. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I respectfully disagree with that as a rule. While hobbies that build skills are certainly valuable, I firmly believe a hobby does not need to be productive to be [[worthwhile]]. The primary purpose of leisure is enjoyment, relaxation and wellbeing, and something that brings pure joy is valuable in itself. Insisting that all free time be useful reflects an overly [[utilitarian]] mindset. Sometimes, doing something simply for pleasure is [[exactly the point]].

cueCards.title: Describe a public place that was recently built or renovated
cueCards.prompt: Describe a public place that was recently built or renovated
bullets: and how you feel about it

sample.answer: A public place that was recently renovated in my town is the riverside walkway along the Jamuna, which has been beautifully transformed over the last couple of years. It runs along the embankment on the edge of Sirajganj, not far from where I live. It used to be quite neglected and run-down, with broken paving, rubbish piling up and hardly any lights, so most people avoided it after dark, and the change has been remarkable. Now it features a wide walking path, proper lighting, rows of young trees and plenty of seating, making it far more [[accessible]] to everyone, including elderly people and families with small children. The whole area feels clean, modern and genuinely [[welcoming]], which it never did before. On any given evening it is now full of people walking, jogging or simply relaxing by the water, and a few tea stalls have opened nearby. What I appreciate most is how the renovation has [[revitalised]] a part of the town that was previously ignored. It has become a real gathering point for the community, and I often bump into neighbours and old classmates there. My parents now walk there most evenings, which is good for my father now that he has retired. Honestly, I think this kind of investment in public spaces is [[commendable]], because it improves everyone's quality of life. My only concern is that it must be properly maintained, or it could [[fall into disrepair]] again. It has quickly become one of my favourite places to unwind, and it shows what good urban planning can achieve.

followUps.q: Do you think more public places should be improved?
followUps.answer: Definitely. There are several parks and fields in our town that are in poor condition, and improving them would benefit everyone, especially children and elderly people who have few other places to go.

followUps.q: Who should pay for improvements like this?
followUps.answer: Mainly the local government, as it is a public space. But I think local businesses could also contribute, because a pleasant area attracts more visitors, which is good for their trade as well.

part3: How important are public spaces like parks in a city?
Do you think there are enough public spaces in modern cities?
What effect do green spaces have on people living in cities?
Do you think cities will have more or fewer public spaces in the future?
How can cities create more public spaces despite limited land?
Some say governments should provide free healthcare for everyone. Do you agree?

part3Samples.q: How important are public spaces like parks in a city?
part3Samples.answer: I consider them absolutely essential to a healthy city. Public spaces like parks provide vital areas for recreation, exercise and relaxation, which is crucial for physical and mental wellbeing amid the stress of urban life. They also act as the [[lungs of a city]], improving air quality, and serve as places where the community comes together. So far from being a luxury, well-designed public spaces are fundamental to a [[liveable]] and [[cohesive]] city.

part3Samples.q: Do you think there are enough public spaces in modern cities?
part3Samples.answer: In many rapidly growing cities, unfortunately not. As urban land becomes increasingly valuable, green and public spaces are often sacrificed for commercial or residential development, which I find [[short-sighted]]. Older, well-planned cities tend to have generous parks, whereas newer, denser developments frequently lack them. So while the importance of public space is increasingly recognised, in practice many cities are [[falling short]], prioritising profit over [[liveability]].

part3Samples.q: What effect do green spaces have on people living in cities?
part3Samples.answer: The effects are overwhelmingly positive, in my view. Access to green spaces reduces stress, improves mood and encourages physical activity, benefiting both mental and physical health. They provide a [[peaceful escape]] from the noise and concrete of the city. Socially, they [[foster]] community interaction. Environmentally, they cool cities and clean the air. So green spaces have a genuinely [[restorative]] and beneficial effect on urban wellbeing.

part3Samples.q: Do you think cities will have more or fewer public spaces in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am hopeful there will be more, though it faces real pressure. On one hand, [[intense competition]] for urban land threatens existing spaces. On the other, there is a growing recognition of their importance for wellbeing and sustainability, and many [[forward-thinking]] cities are now actively creating parks, green roofs and pedestrian zones. So the outcome depends on planning priorities, but I am optimistic that the value of public space will increasingly be recognised and [[prioritised]].

part3Samples.q: How can cities create more public spaces despite limited land?
part3Samples.answer: Creativity is key when land is scarce. Cities can [[repurpose]] [[disused]] areas, such as old railway lines turned into elevated parks, or convert rooftops into green spaces and gardens. Pedestrianising streets reclaims space from cars for people. Even small pocket parks on vacant plots make a difference. So even in dense cities, with imaginative planning, it is possible to integrate valuable public and green space into the existing [[urban fabric]].

part3Samples.q: Some say governments should provide free healthcare for everyone. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly agree with this principle. I believe access to healthcare is a fundamental human right, not a privilege dependent on wealth. Universal healthcare ensures that no one is denied treatment or [[bankrupted]] by illness, which is both humane and promotes a healthier, more productive society. While it is expensive and requires efficient management, the alternative, where people suffer for lack of money, seems deeply [[unjust]]. So I consider free, universal healthcare a worthwhile and [[civilised]] investment.

cueCards.title: Describe a place away from home where you stayed
cueCards.prompt: Describe a place away from home where you stayed
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: A place away from home where I once stayed was a small guesthouse in the hills near Rangamati, during a short break with my family last year. We stayed there because my father had just retired, and we wanted to mark the occasion with a few quiet days somewhere away from the usual tourist crowds. A friend of my father's recommended it, so we booked it without really knowing what to expect. It turned out to be a wonderfully [[charming]] little place, run by a warm local family. The rooms were simple but [[immaculately]] clean, and the view from the balcony, looking out over the hills and the blue water of Kaptai Lake, was [[spectacular]]. What made the stay so memorable was the genuine [[hospitality]] of the hosts, who treated us like old friends and cooked delicious home-style meals, including fresh fish from the lake. In the afternoons we took a boat out on the lake, and in the evenings we sat on the veranda drinking tea and chatting until late. Waking up to birdsong and fresh hill air was a world away from my usual office routine. I felt completely relaxed there in a way that hotels rarely achieve, and it was lovely to see my parents so happy and rested. Honestly, the whole experience was thoroughly [[refreshing]], and it reminded me that the best trips are often about atmosphere rather than luxury. I would happily go back and stay there again.

followUps.q: Do you prefer guesthouses or hotels?
followUps.answer: For a relaxing break, I prefer guesthouses, because they feel more personal and you meet local people. For a work trip, though, a hotel is more practical, as everything is organised and predictable.

followUps.q: Would you recommend the area to others?
followUps.answer: Definitely. Rangamati is beautiful, especially around the lake, and it feels quite different from the rest of Bangladesh. I would just advise people to avoid the peak holiday season, when it gets much busier.

part3: Why do you think people enjoy travelling?
How has travel changed compared to the past?
What effects does tourism have on local communities?
How do you think tourism will change in the future?
How can the negative impacts of tourism be reduced?
Some believe children should care for their parents in old age. Do you agree?

part3Samples.q: Why do you think people enjoy travelling?
part3Samples.answer: People travel for a wonderful variety of reasons. Fundamentally, I think it satisfies a deep human curiosity and desire to escape routine. Experiencing new cultures, landscapes and cuisines is genuinely [[enriching]] and broadens one's perspective. Travel also offers relaxation, adventure and the chance to create lasting memories. For me, the greatest value is how it makes you more [[open-minded]] and [[appreciative]] of the world's incredible diversity.

part3Samples.q: How has travel changed compared to the past?
part3Samples.answer: Travel has been transformed almost beyond recognition. In the past, it was expensive, slow and largely a privilege of the wealthy. Today, [[budget airlines]] and the internet have made it far more accessible and easy to organise, leading to mass tourism. We can now reach distant corners of the globe in hours. While this democratisation is positive, it has also led to [[overcrowding]] at popular sites and a more [[superficial]], hurried style of travel.

part3Samples.q: What effects does tourism have on local communities?
part3Samples.answer: Tourism has profound and mixed effects. Economically, it can bring vital income and jobs, boosting the local economy significantly. However, it can also cause problems: it may [[inflate]] local prices, strain infrastructure, and sometimes lead to the [[commodification]] of culture, where traditions are performed purely for tourists. Environmental damage is another concern. So while tourism offers real economic benefits, it must be managed [[sustainably]] to avoid harming the very communities it supports.

part3Samples.q: How do you think tourism will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I foresee several shifts. Growing environmental awareness will likely make sustainable and [[eco-tourism]] far more popular, as people seek to [[minimise their impact]]. Technology, such as virtual reality, might offer new ways to experience places remotely. There may also be a move towards more meaningful, [[immersive]] travel over mass tourism. So I expect the future of travel to be more conscious, more personalised, and hopefully more responsible.

part3Samples.q: How can the negative impacts of tourism be reduced?
part3Samples.answer: Sustainable tourism practices are the answer. Governments can manage visitor numbers at fragile sites through limits or timed entry to prevent overcrowding. Promoting [[lesser-known]] destinations helps spread the benefits and reduce pressure on [[hotspots]]. Encouraging tourists to respect local cultures and environments, and to support local businesses, is also key. Essentially, prioritising sustainability over sheer volume can [[mitigate]] the harm while preserving the benefits.

part3Samples.q: Some believe children should care for their parents in old age. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly agree, at least in principle. In my culture, caring for elderly parents is seen as a moral [[obligation]], a way of repaying the sacrifices they made. That said, I recognise this is not always practical in modern life, so it need not mean living together. What matters is that the elderly are not [[neglected]] and retain their [[dignity]].

cueCards.title: Describe a market you have visited
cueCards.prompt: Describe a market you have visited
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: A market I find genuinely fascinating is the old bazaar in the centre of Sirajganj, which has been trading for as long as anyone can remember. I love wandering through it whenever I get the chance, usually on a weekend morning. It is a wonderfully [[vibrant]] place, with narrow lanes crammed with stalls selling everything from fresh vegetables, fish and spices to fabrics and handicrafts. Because our district is well known for handloom weaving, there are also shops piled high with colourful saris, lungis and gamchas, many of them made by weavers in nearby villages. The colours, smells and sounds combine to create an atmosphere that is completely [[immersive]]. What I enjoy most is the lively art of haggling, which is expected and almost a game between buyer and seller. I usually go there to buy fresh produce for my mother or small gifts, though half the fun is simply browsing. Before Eid I always buy a new lungi there for my grandfather, because he insists that local cloth is better than anything from Dhaka. The market has a raw, [[authentic]] character that modern shopping malls completely lack. Honestly, there is something special about a place where commerce has happened the same way for generations. Of course, it can be muddy and chaotic during the monsoon, but I have learnt to [[take that in my stride]]. It feels genuinely alive, and I always come away with a small treasure and a real sense of having experienced something [[quintessentially]] local.

followUps.q: Do you think traditional markets will survive?
followUps.answer: I hope so, and I think they will, at least in towns like mine. Many people still prefer fresh food and a personal relationship with sellers, although supermarkets and online shopping are slowly attracting younger customers.

followUps.q: Are you good at bargaining?
followUps.answer: Not as good as my mother, who is an expert. I usually start too high and give in too quickly, so when I need something important, I take her with me.

part3: Do you think people buy more things than they actually need?
How has shopping changed with the rise of the internet?
Why do you think advertising is so influential?
Do you think people will become more conscious consumers in the future?
How can people be encouraged to consume more responsibly?
Some say globalisation is destroying local cultures. Do you agree?

part3Samples.q: Do you think people buy more things than they actually need?
part3Samples.answer: Yes, I think overconsumption is a defining feature of modern society. We are constantly [[bombarded]] with advertising designed to create desires for things we do not truly need. Cheap goods and easy credit make impulsive buying effortless. Many people also shop for emotional reasons, as a form of therapy. So I would say that a great deal of our consumption is driven by [[manufactured]] wants rather than genuine necessity, which is quite [[wasteful]].

part3Samples.q: How has shopping changed with the rise of the internet?
part3Samples.answer: Online shopping has [[revolutionised]] the experience. It offers [[unparalleled]] convenience, allowing people to buy almost anything from home at any hour, with easy price comparison. This has, however, put pressure on traditional physical shops, many of which have struggled. The experience has become more efficient but arguably less social. So while the internet has made shopping far more convenient and accessible, it has also transformed our [[high streets]], not always for the better.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think advertising is so influential?
part3Samples.answer: Advertising is influential because it is sophisticated and [[pervasive]]. It cleverly taps into our emotions, insecurities and aspirations, associating products with happiness, status or belonging rather than mere function. Its sheer ubiquity means we are exposed to it constantly, which [[reinforces]] its messages. Modern targeted advertising is especially potent, as it is tailored precisely to our interests. So it shapes our desires far more than we consciously realise, subtly [[steering]] our behaviour.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will become more conscious consumers in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am cautiously hopeful. There is a growing awareness of the environmental and ethical impact of our purchases, and movements towards [[minimalism]], sustainability and ethical consumption are [[gaining momentum]]. Younger generations in particular seem more [[values-driven]] in their spending. However, the powerful forces of marketing and convenience remain strong. So while I believe conscious consumption will increase, whether it becomes the norm depends on a genuine cultural shift.

part3Samples.q: How can people be encouraged to consume more responsibly?
part3Samples.answer: Education and awareness are key. Helping people understand the true environmental and social cost of their purchases can shift attitudes. Encouraging habits like buying quality over quantity, repairing rather than replacing, and choosing ethical brands makes a difference. Governments can also play a role through regulation and [[incentives]]. Ultimately, [[fostering]] a cultural value of [[sufficiency]] over excess, where we question whether we truly need something, is the most sustainable path.

part3Samples.q: Some say globalisation is destroying local cultures. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I partly agree, as it is a genuine threat. The spread of a dominant global culture can certainly [[overshadow]] and dilute local traditions, languages and customs, leading to a worrying uniformity. However, I would not say it is entirely destructive. Globalisation also allows cultures to share and celebrate their uniqueness on a world stage. So while the risk of [[homogenisation]] is real, cultures can also prove remarkably [[resilient]] and adaptive.

cueCards.title: Describe a place you go to be alone
cueCards.prompt: Describe a place you go to be alone
bullets: and why you go there alone

sample.answer: A place I go to be completely alone is a quiet stretch of the riverbank a short walk from my home, well beyond the busy part of the embankment where people gather in the evenings. To reach it, you follow a narrow path past a few fields and a clump of bamboo, and then the river suddenly opens up in front of you. I tend to go there once or twice a week, and more often whenever I feel overwhelmed and need to clear my head. It is a [[secluded]] spot that few people seem to know about, which is exactly why I love it. I usually just sit on the grass under an old tree, watch the water and let my thoughts settle. Occasionally I bring a book, but more often I do nothing at all, which I rarely get to do these days. There is something deeply [[restorative]] about being alone in nature, with no phone buzzing and no one demanding my attention. I go alone because at home and at work I am constantly surrounded by people, and although I love them, I also need time to [[recharge my batteries]]. I find that a bit of [[solitude]] helps me process my feelings and make sense of whatever is bothering me. Far from feeling lonely, I feel more like myself there than almost anywhere else. Honestly, in a world that never seems to stop, having a private place to simply be is [[a rare luxury]]. I always return home feeling calmer and more centred.

followUps.q: Do you think it is important to spend time alone?
followUps.answer: Yes, I do. Time alone gives you space to reflect and understand your own feelings. Without it, I think people can become stressed and lose touch with what really matters to them.

followUps.q: Does your family know about this place?
followUps.answer: My younger sister does, and she teases me about my secret hideout. My parents know I go for walks by the river, but I do not think they know exactly where I go.

part3: Why do you think loneliness is becoming more common today?
Is loneliness worse in cities or in the countryside?
What effects can long-term loneliness have on a person?
Do you think loneliness will become a bigger problem in the future?
What can communities do to reduce loneliness?
Some say happiness is a choice. Do you agree?

part3Samples.q: Why do you think loneliness is becoming more common today?
part3Samples.answer: I think it is a paradox of modern life. Despite being more digitally connected than ever, many people feel increasingly isolated. Urbanisation has weakened traditional community bonds, and busy, individualistic lifestyles leave little time for genuine connection. Ironically, social media can [[exacerbate]] the problem by replacing deep relationships with [[superficial]] online interaction, leaving a real emotional [[void]].

part3Samples.q: Is loneliness worse in cities or in the countryside?
part3Samples.answer: This is quite counterintuitive. You might assume the countryside, being less populated, would be lonelier, but often the opposite is true. Rural communities tend to be tight-knit, where everyone knows each other. Cities, by contrast, can be profoundly [[alienating]]; you can be surrounded by millions yet feel completely [[anonymous]]. So urban loneliness, born of that anonymity, is arguably the more [[acute]] problem.

part3Samples.q: What effects can long-term loneliness have on a person?
part3Samples.answer: The effects can be genuinely serious. Prolonged loneliness is strongly linked to mental health problems such as depression and anxiety. It can also have physical consequences, as chronic isolation is thought to weaken the immune system and even affect [[longevity]]. Beyond that, it can trap people in a negative cycle, where low mood makes them [[withdraw]] further, deepening the isolation and their sense of [[despair]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think loneliness will become a bigger problem in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I fear it might, if current trends continue. As societies become more individualistic and people increasingly work and socialise remotely, opportunities for spontaneous human contact may [[diminish]]. An ageing population in many countries could also worsen the situation. However, I remain hopeful that growing awareness of the issue will [[prompt]] communities and governments to take [[preventive]] action.

part3Samples.q: What can communities do to reduce loneliness?
part3Samples.answer: Communities can play a powerful role. Creating accessible public spaces and organising local events, from community gardens to social clubs, gives people natural opportunities to connect. Initiatives that specifically reach out to isolated individuals, like [[befriending schemes]] for the elderly, are especially valuable. Ultimately, [[fostering]] a culture where people look out for their neighbours can rebuild the [[social fabric]] that has frayed.

part3Samples.q: Some say happiness is a choice. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I partly agree, but with important reservations. There is real truth that our attitude, gratitude and how we respond to circumstances significantly influence our happiness, so mindset matters. However, saying happiness is simply a choice can be [[dismissive]] of those facing genuine hardship, mental illness or difficult circumstances beyond their control. So while we have some agency over our happiness, I think it is [[oversimplified]] to call it purely a choice, ignoring the [[structural]] and biological factors involved.

cueCards.title: Describe a famous place in your country
cueCards.prompt: Describe a famous place in your country
bullets: and whether you would recommend it

sample.answer: A famous place in my country that I think everyone should see is the National Martyrs' Memorial, which honours those who died in our war of independence in 1971. It is located in Savar, on the outskirts of Dhaka, about an hour's drive from the city centre depending on the traffic. It is a deeply [[poignant]] and symbolic site, and it holds enormous significance for the nation. The memorial itself is architecturally striking, with seven triangular structures of different heights rising towards the sky, and I have read that they represent the key stages of our struggle for independence. It is famous not only for its design but also because every year, on Independence Day and Victory Day, huge crowds come to lay wreaths there, led by the country's leaders. I first visited it on a school trip and went again a few years ago with my younger sister. Visiting it is a genuinely moving experience, as it [[commemorates]] such an important chapter of our history. What makes it so meaningful is that it represents the sacrifice and courage of ordinary people, farmers, students and workers alike. I think it is important for younger generations to visit and understand their [[heritage]]. The surrounding grounds are peaceful and beautifully maintained, with a lake and mass graves nearby, which adds to the [[solemn]] atmosphere. Honestly, I would recommend it to any visitor, ideally early in the morning, because it offers real insight into what shaped our country. It is a place that inspires both reflection and a quiet sense of [[patriotism]].

followUps.q: Do schools in Bangladesh take students there?
followUps.answer: Yes, many schools organise trips there, especially around Victory Day and Independence Day. I think it is a valuable experience, because it helps young people connect emotionally with the history they read about.

followUps.q: Are there other monuments like this in your country?
followUps.answer: Yes, the Central Shaheed Minar in Dhaka commemorates the Language Movement of 1952. On the twenty-first of February, huge numbers of people walk there barefoot at dawn to lay flowers.

part3: Do you think traditions are still important in modern society?
Are young people less interested in traditions than older generations?
Why do you think some traditions are disappearing?
Do you think traditions will survive in the future?
What can be done to preserve traditional culture?
Some say tourism does more harm than good to destinations. Do you agree?

part3Samples.q: Do you think traditions are still important in modern society?
part3Samples.answer: I believe they are more important than ever. In a rapidly changing, globalised world, traditions provide a vital sense of identity, continuity and belonging. They connect us to our history and to one another. While some outdated customs deserve to fade, I think the core traditions that [[bind]] a community together are worth [[preserving]]. They give life a certain meaning and rhythm that [[modernity]] alone cannot provide.

part3Samples.q: Are young people less interested in traditions than older generations?
part3Samples.answer: To some extent, yes, though it varies. Young people, being more exposed to global culture and modern lifestyles, sometimes view certain traditions as [[outdated]] or irrelevant. However, I would not say they have abandoned tradition entirely; many still take great pride in their [[cultural roots]], just alongside a more modern outlook. So there is a shift in emphasis, but I think the connection to heritage remains, merely [[reinterpreted]] in a contemporary context.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think some traditions are disappearing?
part3Samples.answer: Several forces are at work. Globalisation and the dominance of Western culture have [[homogenised]] lifestyles, making some local customs seem less relevant. Urbanisation and modern, busy lives also leave less time for elaborate traditional practices. Additionally, as older generations pass away, knowledge and skills are sometimes not passed on. So it is really a combination of cultural [[dilution]] and the practical pressures of modern life [[eroding]] them.

part3Samples.q: Do you think traditions will survive in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am cautiously optimistic. While some traditions will inevitably fade, I believe the most meaningful ones will [[endure]], perhaps in modified forms. There is actually a growing appreciation for heritage as a counterbalance to globalisation, with many people actively seeking to [[revive]] old customs. Technology can also help document and share them. So rather than vanishing, I think traditions will [[evolve]], adapting to remain relevant in a changing world.

part3Samples.q: What can be done to preserve traditional culture?
part3Samples.answer: A [[concerted effort]] is needed. Education is crucial; teaching young people about their heritage in schools fosters pride and understanding. Documenting traditions and supporting the [[artisans]] and elders who hold this knowledge is also vital. Governments and communities can organise festivals and cultural events to keep customs alive and visible. Essentially, making tradition feel relevant and engaging to the young is the key to its [[continuity]].

part3Samples.q: Some say tourism does more harm than good to destinations. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I think it depends entirely on how it is managed. In some over-touristed places, the harm, from environmental damage to cultural erosion and inflated living costs, is undeniable and can indeed outweigh the benefits. However, when managed responsibly and sustainably, tourism can be a tremendous [[force for good]], funding conservation and lifting communities out of poverty. So I would not agree it is inherently harmful; the outcome [[hinges on]] responsible [[stewardship]] and planning.

cueCards.title: Describe a place you enjoyed visiting as a child
cueCards.prompt: Describe a place you enjoyed visiting as a child

sample.answer: A place I absolutely loved visiting as a child was my grandparents' village home, not far from Sirajganj, where they still live today. Although it is not a long journey, as a small boy it felt like travelling to another world. I went there with my parents and my two sisters, usually during the school holidays and always for Eid, and those visits are among my happiest childhood memories. Often my cousins came too, so the house would be full of noise and laughter. The house was surrounded by open fields and ponds, which felt like a [[boundless]] playground to a small child. I would spend whole days climbing mango trees, fishing with my grandfather and running around barefoot with my cousins. In the monsoon we would jump into the pond from the bank, and my grandmother would scold us and then feed us hot rice and fish. Everything felt wonderfully [[carefree]], far from the rules and routines of school and town life. What made it so special was the sense of freedom and the warmth of the whole extended family gathered together. The pace of life there was so gentle and [[unhurried]]. Honestly, looking back, those visits filled me with a deep sense of [[belonging]] that I still treasure. We still visit often, and my mother helps look after my grandparents, but the village has changed a lot since then, with more concrete houses and fewer open fields. Even so, the memories remain [[vivid]] and precious to me.

followUps.q: Do children today still enjoy visiting villages?
followUps.answer: Some do, but many are so used to screens that they get bored without the internet. My nephew loves it, though, especially chasing the chickens, so I think it depends on how children are introduced to it.

followUps.q: Do you still enjoy going there now?
followUps.answer: Very much, though for different reasons. Now I enjoy sitting with my grandparents, listening to their stories and helping them out, rather than climbing trees. It feels calm and grounding compared with work.

part3: What do you think are the most important qualities of a good parent?
How is childhood today different from childhood in the past?

part3Samples.q: What do you think are the most important qualities of a good parent?
part3Samples.answer: In my view, the most important qualities are patience and [[consistency]]. Children thrive on stability, so a parent who sets clear, fair boundaries helps them feel secure. Equally vital is unconditional love balanced with the willingness to discipline when necessary. A good parent also [[leads by example]], since children tend to [[absorb]] behaviour far more than instructions.

part3Samples.q: How is childhood today different from childhood in the past?
part3Samples.answer: Childhood has changed dramatically. In the past, children spent most of their free time playing outdoors and socialising in person. Today, much of that has been [[supplanted]] by screens, which I find rather [[disconcerting]]. Children are also under far more academic pressure now. So while modern children have more opportunities, they arguably have a less [[carefree]] upbringing.

part3Samples.q: What effect does strict parenting have on children?
part3Samples.answer: It can have mixed effects. On one hand, strict parenting can instil discipline and a strong work ethic. On the other, if it is excessively [[authoritarian]], it may [[stifle]] a child's creativity and confidence, or even breed rebellion. In my opinion, the ideal lies in a balanced approach that is firm but also [[nurturing]] and understanding.

part3Samples.q: How do you think parenting will change in the coming decades?
part3Samples.answer: I expect parenting will become increasingly [[intertwined with]] technology. Parents will likely rely more on apps and online resources for guidance, and managing children's screen time will become an even more [[daunting]] challenge. I also anticipate a move towards more [[egalitarian]] parenting, with responsibilities shared more equally. Hopefully there will also be greater awareness of children's emotional wellbeing.

part3Samples.q: How can parents help children develop good values?
part3Samples.answer: The most effective way is by [[modelling]] those values themselves, since children imitate what they see. Beyond that, parents can use everyday situations as [[teaching moments]], discussing honesty or kindness openly. Encouraging empathy, perhaps through community involvement, also helps. Ultimately, values are [[instilled]] gradually through consistent example rather than through occasional lectures.

part3Samples.q: Some believe children should care for their parents in old age. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly agree, at least in principle. In my culture, caring for elderly parents is seen as a moral [[obligation]], a way of repaying the sacrifices they made. That said, I recognise this is not always practical in modern life, so it need not mean living together. What matters is that the elderly are not [[neglected]] and retain their [[dignity]].

cueCards.title: Describe a sports venue or stadium you have visited
cueCards.prompt: Describe a sports venue or stadium you have visited
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: A sports venue I visited that left a strong impression on me was the Sher-e-Bangla National Cricket Stadium in Mirpur, Dhaka, which is the main home ground of the Bangladesh team. I went there a couple of years ago with my brother-in-law to watch a one-day international, and it was my first time watching live cricket at that level. Cricket is almost a religion in my country, so the atmosphere was electric long before the game even started; people were queuing outside hours in advance, with their faces painted red and green. The stadium was absolutely [[packed to the rafters]], with thousands of fans singing, blowing horns and waving flags. When our team hit a boundary or took a wicket, the roar of the crowd was genuinely [[thunderous]], and I could feel the energy in my chest. What made it so memorable was the incredible sense of [[unity]]; complete strangers were hugging and celebrating together as one. Watching a match on television simply cannot compare to being there in person. The whole experience was thrilling and completely [[immersive]]. We bought snacks from the vendors walking up and down the stands and stayed until the very last ball. Honestly, by the end I had lost my voice from cheering, but I did not care in the slightest, especially as we won comfortably. It was one of the most exciting days of my life, and I would [[jump at the chance]] to go again.

followUps.q: Do you prefer watching sports live or on TV?
followUps.answer: Live, definitely, for the atmosphere, although I watch most matches on television because tickets are hard to get and the stadium is far from Sirajganj. At home, at least, you get the replays and commentary.

followUps.q: Do you play cricket yourself?
followUps.answer: Only casually now. As a boy I played every afternoon with friends in the field near our house, but these days I prefer watching, and I occasionally join a friendly match during the holidays.

part3Samples.q: Why are hobbies important in people's lives?
part3Samples.answer: Hobbies are far more valuable than people often realise. They provide a [[vital outlet]] for relaxation and stress relief, offering a welcome escape from the pressures of work. They also allow for personal growth, creativity and a sense of accomplishment outside our professional identity. Additionally, many hobbies foster social connections. In my view, hobbies are essential for a balanced, fulfilling life, [[nourishing]] parts of ourselves that work often [[neglects]].

part3Samples.q: How do people's leisure activities differ between generations?
part3Samples.answer: There are noticeable differences. Older generations often favour traditional [[pastimes]] like gardening, reading physical books, or socialising in person. Younger people, by contrast, spend much of their leisure time on digital activities, such as gaming, streaming and social media. That said, there is considerable overlap, and interest in older hobbies is [[reviving]] among the young. So the core need for leisure is universal, but the [[medium]] has shifted towards the digital.

part3Samples.q: What are the benefits of having a creative hobby?
part3Samples.answer: Creative hobbies offer numerous benefits. They provide a productive outlet for self-expression and can be deeply [[therapeutic]], reducing stress and improving mental wellbeing. The sense of accomplishment from creating something is genuinely rewarding and boosts confidence. They also keep the mind active and can spark skills that [[enrich]] other areas of life. Essentially, creative pursuits [[nourish the soul]] and offer a fulfilment that passive entertainment simply cannot match.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will have more free time in the future?
part3Samples.answer: This is uncertain. [[Optimistically]], if automation boosts productivity and society chooses to share the gains, people could work less and enjoy more leisure, as concepts like the four-day week suggest. However, there is an opposing risk that [[constant connectivity]] and economic pressure could actually [[erode]] our free time further. So the amount of leisure we have may depend less on technology and more on the choices society makes about priorities.

part3Samples.q: Many people say they have no time for hobbies. What can they do?
part3Samples.answer: It often comes down to priorities rather than an absolute lack of time. People can start by consciously [[carving out]] even small [[pockets of time]], perhaps by reducing passive activities like scrolling on their phones. Scheduling hobby time like any other commitment helps make it happen. Choosing hobbies that fit their lifestyle is also wise. Essentially, treating leisure as essential rather than optional helps people [[reclaim]] time they did not realise they had.

cueCards.title: Describe a place you would like to visit again
cueCards.prompt: Describe a place you would like to visit again
bullets: and why you want to return

sample.answer: A place I would love to visit again is Darjeeling, a small hill town in India, which I went to a few years ago and which completely charmed me. I first went there with two friends from university just after our final exams, crossing the border by land and taking a shared jeep up the winding mountain roads. I only stayed a few days, which was nowhere near long enough to appreciate it fully. The town was wonderfully [[picturesque]], with steep lanes, old colonial buildings and tea gardens clinging to the hillsides, and on clear mornings we could see the snowy Himalayan peaks in the distance. On that first visit I explored the local trails, rode the famous toy train for a short stretch and sampled the regional food, especially the momos, but I feel I only [[scratched the surface]]. What draws me back is the incredibly [[tranquil]] pace of life there, which was a world away from my hectic routine. There is a certain [[magnetic]] quality to some places that stays with you long after you leave, and this town has it. I have often found myself daydreaming about returning and staying longer next time, perhaps in spring when the views are clearer. I would also like to take my parents, because my father loves tea and would enjoy visiting a proper tea estate. Honestly, some destinations simply leave you wanting more, and revisiting it would be a genuine [[delight]]. I hope to make it happen soon.

followUps.q: What would you do differently next time?
followUps.answer: I would stay much longer, at least a week, and go in spring when the views are clearer. I would also like to stay in a small family-run guesthouse rather than a hotel.

followUps.q: Do you prefer visiting new places or returning to familiar ones?
followUps.answer: Generally I prefer new places, because I love discovering something different. But a few special places, like Darjeeling, are worth returning to, because you notice things you missed the first time.

part3: Why do you think people enjoy travelling?
How has travel changed compared to the past?
What effects does tourism have on local communities?
How do you think tourism will change in the future?
How can the negative impacts of tourism be reduced?
Some say globalisation mainly benefits wealthy countries. Do you agree?

part3Samples.q: Why do you think people enjoy travelling?
part3Samples.answer: People travel for a wonderful variety of reasons. Fundamentally, I think it satisfies a deep human curiosity and desire to escape routine. Experiencing new cultures, landscapes and cuisines is genuinely [[enriching]] and broadens one's perspective. Travel also offers relaxation, adventure and the chance to create lasting memories. For me, the greatest value is how it makes you more [[open-minded]] and [[appreciative]] of the world's incredible diversity.

part3Samples.q: How has travel changed compared to the past?
part3Samples.answer: Travel has been transformed almost beyond recognition. In the past, it was expensive, slow and largely a privilege of the wealthy. Today, [[budget airlines]] and the internet have made it far more accessible and easy to organise, leading to mass tourism. We can now reach distant corners of the globe in hours. While this democratisation is positive, it has also led to [[overcrowding]] at popular sites and a more [[superficial]], hurried style of travel.

part3Samples.q: What effects does tourism have on local communities?
part3Samples.answer: Tourism has profound and mixed effects. Economically, it can bring vital income and jobs, boosting the local economy significantly. However, it can also cause problems: it may [[inflate]] local prices, strain infrastructure, and sometimes lead to the [[commodification]] of culture, where traditions are performed purely for tourists. Environmental damage is another concern. So while tourism offers real economic benefits, it must be managed [[sustainably]] to avoid harming the very communities it supports.

part3Samples.q: How do you think tourism will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I foresee several shifts. Growing environmental awareness will likely make sustainable and [[eco-tourism]] far more popular, as people seek to [[minimise their impact]]. Technology, such as virtual reality, might offer new ways to experience places remotely. There may also be a move towards more meaningful, [[immersive]] travel over mass tourism. So I expect the future of travel to be more conscious, more personalised, and hopefully more responsible.

part3Samples.q: How can the negative impacts of tourism be reduced?
part3Samples.answer: Sustainable tourism practices are the answer. Governments can manage visitor numbers at fragile sites through limits or timed entry to prevent overcrowding. Promoting [[lesser-known]] destinations helps spread the benefits and reduce pressure on [[hotspots]]. Encouraging tourists to respect local cultures and environments, and to support local businesses, is also key. Essentially, prioritising sustainability over sheer volume can [[mitigate]] the harm while preserving the benefits.

part3Samples.q: Some say globalisation mainly benefits wealthy countries. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: There is considerable truth to this, though it is not the whole picture. It is often argued that wealthy nations and large corporations reap the greatest rewards, while poorer countries may suffer exploitation and cultural erosion. The benefits are undeniably [[unevenly]] distributed. However, globalisation has arguably also lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty in developing nations. So while the [[playing field]] is far from level, I would not say the benefits are exclusively for the [[privileged]].

cueCards.title: Describe a peaceful place you know
cueCards.prompt: Describe a peaceful place you know

sample.answer: A place I associate with real peace is an old, quiet mosque near my grandparents' home in our ancestral village, which I have known since childhood. It sits at the edge of a pond, shaded by a huge old banyan tree, and it is small, with whitewashed walls and a single dome. I first went there as a little boy, holding my grandfather's hand for Friday prayers, and I still go with him whenever we visit, even though he walks much more slowly now. It is not grand or famous, but it has a wonderfully [[tranquil]] atmosphere that I have never found elsewhere. Whenever I visit, I am struck by the deep sense of calm the moment I step inside. The thick walls seem to [[shut out]] the noise of the world completely, leaving only silence and the occasional sound of birds outside. Inside, the floor is cool and the light is soft, because the windows are small. Even for a few minutes, sitting there is genuinely [[meditative]], and it helps me clear my mind of everyday worries. What makes it so peaceful is not just the quiet, but the sense of [[stillness]] and reflection it encourages, and perhaps also the memories of my grandfather teaching me there. In our fast-paced, noisy lives, such places feel increasingly rare and valuable. Honestly, I always leave feeling lighter and more [[centred]]. I think everyone needs a place like this, somewhere they can retreat to and simply be at peace for a while.

followUps.q: Do you go there often?
followUps.answer: Whenever we visit my grandparents, which is quite often, usually for Friday prayers with my grandfather. Even when I am busy, I try to stop there for a few minutes before we head back to town.

followUps.q: Is it easy to find peaceful places nowadays?
followUps.answer: It is getting harder, especially in towns and cities, where noise and crowds are everywhere. That is why places like this feel so precious, and why I think we should protect them.

part3Samples.q: What do you think makes people truly happy?
part3Samples.answer: In my view, lasting happiness comes primarily [[from within]] and from our connections, rather than from external possessions. Strong, loving relationships seem to be the greatest source of happiness. Beyond that, having a sense of purpose, good health, and the freedom to pursue what we find meaningful all contribute enormously. So I believe true happiness is [[rooted in]] connection, purpose and [[gratitude]], not in material wealth.

part3Samples.q: Are people happier now than in the past?
part3Samples.answer: This is a fascinating and debated question. In material terms, we are far better off than previous generations, with more comfort, health and opportunity. Yet, [[curiously]], rates of anxiety and depression seem to be rising, especially among the young. It appears that material progress has not straightforwardly translated into greater happiness. So while we have gained much, I am not convinced we are [[fundamentally]] happier, which suggests happiness depends on more than mere [[prosperity]] and comfort.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think some wealthy people are unhappy?
part3Samples.answer: This reflects the fact that money, beyond meeting basic needs, has [[diminishing returns]] on happiness. Wealthy people may still suffer from poor relationships, a lack of purpose, or the isolation and pressure that wealth can bring. There is also the phenomenon where people constantly adapt and want more, never feeling satisfied. So it demonstrates that happiness is not something money can simply buy; it depends on deeper, [[non-material]] [[fulfilment]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will be happier in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am genuinely uncertain. On one hand, advances in medicine, technology and [[living standards]] could improve wellbeing. There is also growing awareness of mental health and the importance of a balanced life. On the other hand, rising pressures, social media comparison and uncertainty could work against happiness. So I think future happiness will depend less on material progress and more on whether we learn to [[prioritise]] the things that genuinely [[nourish]] human wellbeing.

part3Samples.q: What can societies do to improve people's wellbeing?
part3Samples.answer: Societies can take meaningful steps. Prioritising mental health services and reducing the [[stigma]] around them is crucial. Fostering community, reducing inequality, and ensuring people have access to nature, leisure and a healthy work-life balance all help. Some argue governments should measure national wellbeing, not just economic output. Essentially, by valuing human [[flourishing]] alongside economic growth, societies can create conditions in which more people can genuinely [[thrive]] and feel content.

part3Samples.q: Some say building more housing is more important than preserving parks. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I understand the argument given the housing crisis, but I largely disagree with sacrificing parks. While housing is undeniably crucial, green spaces are equally vital for residents' health and wellbeing, and destroying them creates a poorer quality of life. It should not be an either-or choice. With clever planning, cities can build housing on [[brownfield sites]] and increase density elsewhere while preserving parks. So both are essential, and [[pitting them against]] each other is a [[false dilemma]].

cueCards.title: Describe a hotel you have stayed in
cueCards.prompt: Describe a hotel you have stayed in
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: A hotel that genuinely exceeded my expectations was a resort in Cox's Bazar where I stayed during a family holiday by the sea, about a year after I started working. It was the first holiday I had helped to pay for, so it felt quite special, and the whole family came, including my elder sister, her husband and their two children. We stayed for four nights in December, when the weather is cool and dry. From the moment we arrived, the service was [[impeccable]], and the staff [[went out of their way]] to make us feel welcome, even arranging a small cake when they found out it was my mother's birthday. The room was spacious and immaculately clean, with a balcony overlooking the ocean, which was [[breathtaking]] at sunrise. What impressed me most was the attention to detail; everything felt thoughtfully designed and genuinely [[luxurious]] without being pretentious. The food was excellent, especially the seafood at dinner, and the whole atmosphere was wonderfully relaxing. I remember spending hours by the pool with my nephew, feeling completely at ease, while my parents walked on the beach. Of course, it was not cheap, but the experience felt [[worth every penny]]. Honestly, a well-run hotel can make or break a holiday, and this one made ours truly special. It set a standard that has been hard to match since. I still remember that stay as one of the most comfortable of my life.

followUps.q: Do you usually stay in hotels when you travel?
followUps.answer: Not usually. On most trips I stay with relatives or in cheaper guesthouses to save money, so that resort was a real treat. It was worth it once, but I could not afford that every time.

followUps.q: What do you think makes a good hotel?
followUps.answer: Friendly, attentive staff most of all, followed by cleanliness and comfort. A beautiful building helps, but if the staff are rude or careless, even the most luxurious hotel will not feel welcoming.

cueCards.title: Describe a place with clean and fresh air
cueCards.prompt: Describe a place with clean and fresh air
bullets: and why the air was so pleasant

sample.answer: A place I associate with wonderfully clean air is a tea estate in the hills near Sylhet, which I visited a couple of years ago during the winter. I had just spent a few days in Dhaka, so the difference in air quality was immediately noticeable and genuinely [[refreshing]]. The moment I stepped off the bus, I could not stop taking deep breaths of the cool, [[crisp]] air. It felt as though my lungs were being cleaned out after days of breathing in the capital's smog and dust. I spent my days walking through the tea gardens and chatting with some of the workers, and in the mornings I climbed a small hill to watch the sunrise over the rows of tea bushes. The fresh air made even simple activities feel [[invigorating]], and I slept better than I had in months. What made it so pleasant was the complete absence of heavy traffic, brick kilns and factories; the environment felt truly [[unpolluted]]. The endless trees and bushes all around must have helped too, and the dew on the leaves in the early morning made everything smell wonderfully green. Honestly, the experience made me realise that clean air is something we [[take for granted]], and how badly urban pollution affects us, especially children and older people like my grandparents. I came away not only feeling healthier but also more conscious of environmental issues, and now I try to walk short distances instead of taking an auto-rickshaw. It is a place I would return to just to breathe properly again.

followUps.q: Is air pollution a problem where you live?
followUps.answer: In Sirajganj it is not as bad as in Dhaka, but it is getting worse, mainly because of dust, traffic and brick kilns in the dry season. During the monsoon the air is much cleaner.

followUps.q: Would you like to live somewhere like that?
followUps.answer: For a while, yes, but perhaps not permanently. The tea gardens are quite remote, and I would miss my family and the convenience of town. A long holiday there every year would be ideal.

part3: How serious is the problem of pollution in your country?

part3Samples.q: How serious is the problem of pollution in your country?
part3Samples.answer: Unfortunately, pollution is a very serious problem in my country, particularly in the major cities. Air quality often reaches [[hazardous]] levels due to traffic, industry and construction, which [[poses a real threat]] to public health. Water pollution from industrial and domestic waste is also a significant concern. So while there is growing awareness, I would say pollution remains one of our most [[pressing]] environmental and public-health challenges.

part3Samples.q: Which do you think is worse, air pollution or water pollution?
part3Samples.answer: Both are extremely damaging, and it is hard to rank them. Air pollution is perhaps more immediate and [[inescapable]], as we breathe constantly, and it causes widespread respiratory illness. Water pollution, however, is arguably more [[insidious]], contaminating our drinking water and food chain and devastating [[aquatic ecosystems]]. So rather than one being definitively worse, I would say they are both severe problems with different but equally devastating consequences.

part3Samples.q: What are the main causes of pollution in cities?
part3Samples.answer: Urban pollution stems from several sources. Vehicle emissions are a [[primary culprit]], given the sheer density of traffic. Industrial activity and factories release pollutants into the air and water. Construction generates dust, and the burning of fossil fuels for energy contributes heavily. Poor waste management adds to the problem. So it is largely a [[by-product]] of dense population, industry and [[reliance on fossil fuels]] concentrated in a small area.

part3Samples.q: Do you think pollution will get better or worse in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am cautiously hopeful it will improve, though it depends on our actions. On one hand, rapid [[industrialisation]] in developing nations could worsen it in the short term. On the other, growing awareness, stricter regulations, and cleaner technologies like electric vehicles and renewable energy offer real solutions. Many developed cities have already reduced pollution significantly. So with sufficient [[political will]] and innovation, I believe we can [[reverse the trend]], but it is not guaranteed.

part3Samples.q: What can be done to reduce pollution?
part3Samples.answer: Tackling pollution requires action [[on multiple fronts]]. Transitioning to renewable energy and electric transport would [[drastically]] cut emissions. [[Enforcing]] strict regulations on industrial waste and improving public transport are vital. Better waste management and recycling reduce landfill and litter. On an individual level, reducing consumption and waste helps. Ultimately, a combination of regulation, clean technology and changed behaviour offers the most effective path forward.

part3Samples.q: Some say individuals can do little about climate change. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I partly agree but find the statement [[disempowering]]. It is true that systemic change by governments and industry is far more impactful than individual action alone, so no one should feel the entire burden rests on them. However, I disagree that individuals are powerless. Collectively, our consumer choices, our voices and, above all, our votes exert real pressure that drives the bigger changes. So individual action is not [[futile]]; it is part of a larger [[momentum]].

cueCards.title: Describe a museum or art gallery you have visited
cueCards.prompt: Describe a museum or art gallery you have visited
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: A museum I found genuinely fascinating was the Bangladesh National Museum in Shahbag, Dhaka, which I first visited on a school trip years ago and again more recently with my younger sister. Although it is quite a long journey from Sirajganj, both visits were well worth the effort. It houses an impressive collection spanning our country's history, from ancient artefacts to modern art, spread over several floors. What I found most [[captivating]] was the section on ancient Bengal, with terracotta plaques, stone sculptures and old coins, some of them more than a thousand years old, beautifully preserved behind glass. Walking through the galleries felt like stepping through different eras, which was genuinely [[enlightening]]. I also spent a long time in the Liberation War gallery, where there are photographs, letters and personal belongings of people who fought in 1971, and that part was very emotional. My sister was particularly interested in the paintings by Zainul Abedin, one of our most celebrated artists. I have always believed that museums are an [[underrated]] way to learn, far more vivid than any textbook. Seeing real historical objects gave me a much deeper appreciation of the past, and it made the stories my grandfather tells feel more real. The building itself was grand and well maintained, adding to the [[sense of occasion]]. Honestly, I could easily have spent an entire day there without getting bored. I think places like this are [[invaluable]], because they keep our history alive for future generations to discover and appreciate.

followUps.q: Do you often go to museums?
followUps.answer: Not as often as I would like, as there are few museums near Sirajganj. Whenever I visit Dhaka for more than a couple of days, though, I try to spend an afternoon in a museum or gallery.

followUps.q: Should museums be free?
followUps.answer: I think entry should be free or very cheap, especially for students, because museums are educational. If people have to think twice about the price, the ones who would benefit most will simply stay away.
