part3Samples.q: Why do you think music is important to people?
part3Samples.answer: Music holds a unique and powerful place in human life. It has an extraordinary ability to [[evoke]] emotion, from joy to sorrow, and to comfort us in a way few other things can. It is also deeply tied to memory and identity, and it brings people together, whether at concerts or festivals. In my view, music is a universal language that [[transcends]] barriers and speaks directly to our emotions, which is why it is so [[cherished]].

part3Samples.q: How has the way people listen to music changed?
part3Samples.answer: It has changed dramatically. In the past, people bought physical records or CDs and often listened to a whole album deliberately. Now, streaming gives us instant access to virtually all recorded music, and we tend to consume it in playlists and individual tracks. This is wonderfully convenient, but some argue it has made listening more [[passive]] and [[fragmented]]. So access has expanded enormously, but our engagement with music may have become more [[cursory]].

part3Samples.q: What effect does learning a musical instrument have on children?
part3Samples.answer: Learning an instrument has remarkably positive effects. Many believe it enhances cognitive development, improving skills like memory, concentration and mathematical ability. It also teaches discipline, patience and perseverance, since [[mastery]] requires consistent practice. Furthermore, it provides a creative outlet and a real sense of accomplishment that boosts confidence. So beyond the joy of making music, it offers profound [[developmental]] and [[character-building]] benefits.

part3Samples.q: Do you think technology will change the arts in the future?
part3Samples.answer: Undoubtedly, and it already is. Technology is providing artists with powerful new tools and mediums, from digital art to AI-generated music, expanding creative possibilities. It has also democratised the arts, allowing anyone to create and share their work globally. However, this raises questions about [[authenticity]] and the role of human creativity. So while technology will transform and [[democratise]] the arts, I hope it will [[augment]] human expression rather than replace it.

part3Samples.q: Arts funding is often cut. How can the arts be better supported?
part3Samples.answer: Supporting the arts requires a [[multi-pronged]] approach. Governments should recognise their cultural and economic value and provide stable funding rather than treating them as [[expendable]]. Encouraging private sponsorship and [[philanthropy]] can supplement this. Integrating arts education properly into schools ensures future generations value them. Making the arts more accessible and affordable to ordinary people also builds public support. Essentially, we must treat the arts as an investment, not a luxury.

part3Samples.q: Some say you are never too old to learn. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I wholeheartedly agree. While learning styles may change with age, the human brain remains capable of acquiring new knowledge and skills throughout life. There are countless inspiring examples of people learning languages, instruments or even new careers late in life. I think the biggest barrier is usually psychological, a [[self-imposed]] belief that it is too late. In reality, curiosity and effort [[transcend]] age entirely, keeping us [[youthful]] in spirit.

cueCards.title: Describe a place that is important to your family
cueCards.prompt: Describe a place that is important to your family
bullets: and how you feel about it

sample.answer: A place that holds deep importance for my family is our ancestral home in the village, not far from Sirajganj, which has been in the family for generations. It is surrounded by rice fields, with a pond at the back and a big courtyard in the middle. Although we now live in a flat in town, this house remains a powerful symbol of our roots. My grandparents still live there, and my mother often goes to help look after them, so we are back and forth all the time. Every major family occasion, from weddings to Eid, seems to bring us all back there, and my elder sister travels from Dhaka with her children for the big celebrations. The house itself is old and simple, with a tin roof and wooden beams, but it is filled with [[sentimental]] value that no amount of money could replace. My father grew up there, and his old wooden school desk is still in one of the rooms. Walking through those rooms fills me with a strong sense of [[continuity]] and belonging. What makes it so important is that it connects the whole extended family across the generations, and my grandfather loves telling stories about the people who lived there before him. In a fast-changing world, having such an [[enduring]] anchor feels genuinely precious. Honestly, I hope we manage to keep it in the family for many years to come, even though some relatives have talked about selling part of the land. It is far more than a building; it is the [[cornerstone]] of our family's identity, and I feel [[deeply attached]] to it.

followUps.q: Do you think your family will keep the house?
followUps.answer: I really hope so. There is some talk about the land, but my father feels strongly that the house should stay in the family, and I think most of us agree with him.

followUps.q: Do young people in Bangladesh still care about their ancestral homes?
followUps.answer: Many do, especially at Eid, when huge numbers of people travel back to their villages. But as more young people settle in cities or abroad, those ties are becoming weaker, which I find a little sad.

part3: Do you think family is as important today as it was in the past?
How are family relationships different now compared to a generation ago?
Why do you think many families spend less time together nowadays?
How do you think family structures will change in the future?
What can families do to stay close despite busy modern lives?
Some say globalisation is destroying local cultures. Do you agree?

part3Samples.q: Do you think family is as important today as it was in the past?
part3Samples.answer: I would say family remains just as important, though its form has changed. The emotional support and sense of [[belonging]] a family provides are timeless human needs. That said, modern life has certainly [[strained]] family bonds, with people moving away for work and spending less time together. So while its importance is [[undiminished]], sustaining it now requires more conscious effort.

part3Samples.q: How are family relationships different now compared to a generation ago?
part3Samples.answer: The biggest difference is probably the shift from large, extended families to smaller, more [[nuclear]] ones. In the past, several generations often lived under one roof, which fostered close bonds. Today, families are more [[dispersed]], and technology has, ironically, both connected and [[distanced]] us. Relationships are more equal now, but arguably less tightly knit.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think many families spend less time together nowadays?
part3Samples.answer: Several factors are at play. The demands of modern careers are [[relentless]], leaving parents exhausted and [[time-poor]]. On top of that, digital devices have become a real distraction, with family members often absorbed in their own screens even when in the same room. This gradual erosion of shared time is genuinely [[detrimental]] to close relationships.

part3Samples.q: How do you think family structures will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I anticipate that families will continue to become smaller and more diverse in form. We will likely see more single-parent households and [[blended families]] becoming [[commonplace]] and widely accepted. Technology may also allow [[far-flung]] relatives to stay connected more easily. Overall, I think the definition of family will grow more flexible and inclusive.

part3Samples.q: What can families do to stay close despite busy modern lives?
part3Samples.answer: I think the key is being [[intentional]] about spending time together. Simple rituals, like sharing at least one meal a day without phones, can make a real difference. Families could also [[prioritise]] occasional trips or activities that create shared memories. Ultimately, closeness does not happen by accident; it has to be actively [[nurtured]] amid the busyness.

part3Samples.q: Some say globalisation is destroying local cultures. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I partly agree, as it is a genuine threat. The spread of a dominant global culture can certainly [[overshadow]] and dilute local traditions, languages and customs, leading to a worrying uniformity. However, I would not say it is entirely destructive. Globalisation also allows cultures to share and celebrate their uniqueness on a world stage. So while the risk of [[homogenisation]] is real, cultures can also prove remarkably [[resilient]] and adaptive.

cueCards.title: Describe a place with interesting architecture
cueCards.prompt: Describe a place with interesting architecture
bullets: and why you find it interesting

sample.answer: A place with genuinely interesting architecture that comes to mind is Ahsan Manzil, an old palace in Old Dhaka, right on the bank of the Buriganga river. It was built in the nineteenth century as the residence of the Nawabs of Dhaka, and today it is a museum, which I visited while staying with my sister last year. People often call it the Pink Palace because of its colour, and it is a striking example of the Indo-Saracenic style, which mixes European and Mughal influences. What fascinated me was the [[craftsmanship]]; the arches, pillars and balconies are full of detail, and a grand staircase at the front leads up to the large dome at the centre of the building. The building is [[ornate]] without feeling excessive, and it blends beauty with clever practical design, such as high ceilings and wide verandas that keep the rooms cool in the heat. I found it remarkable how [[sophisticated]] the design was, considering it was built long before air conditioning. Inside, the rooms display furniture, portraits and household objects from the period, which give you a sense of how the family lived. Standing inside, I felt a real sense of admiration for the skill of the people who created it. Honestly, modern buildings, for all their convenience, rarely have this kind of soul. I think architecture like this tells us a great deal about the culture and values of the past, which is exactly what makes it so [[compelling]] to me. It also reminds me how important it is to [[conserve]] such buildings in a city that is changing so fast.

followUps.q: Do you prefer old or modern buildings?
followUps.answer: For beauty and character, I definitely prefer old buildings. Modern buildings are more comfortable and practical, of course, but they often look the same, whereas old buildings tell you something about the place and its history.

followUps.q: Was it crowded when you visited?
followUps.answer: Yes, fairly crowded, as it is one of the most popular sights in Old Dhaka. There were school groups and families everywhere, but it was still possible to find quieter corners to look around.

part3: Do you think traditions are still important in modern society?
Are young people less interested in traditions than older generations?
Why do you think some traditions are disappearing?
Do you think traditions will survive in the future?
What can be done to preserve traditional culture?
Some say governments should stop cities from growing too big. Do you agree?

part3Samples.q: Do you think traditions are still important in modern society?
part3Samples.answer: I believe they are more important than ever. In a rapidly changing, globalised world, traditions provide a vital sense of identity, continuity and belonging. They connect us to our history and to one another. While some outdated customs deserve to fade, I think the core traditions that [[bind]] a community together are worth [[preserving]]. They give life a certain meaning and rhythm that [[modernity]] alone cannot provide.

part3Samples.q: Are young people less interested in traditions than older generations?
part3Samples.answer: To some extent, yes, though it varies. Young people, being more exposed to global culture and modern lifestyles, sometimes view certain traditions as [[outdated]] or irrelevant. However, I would not say they have abandoned tradition entirely; many still take great pride in their [[cultural roots]], just alongside a more modern outlook. So there is a shift in emphasis, but I think the connection to heritage remains, merely [[reinterpreted]] in a contemporary context.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think some traditions are disappearing?
part3Samples.answer: Several forces are at work. Globalisation and the dominance of Western culture have [[homogenised]] lifestyles, making some local customs seem less relevant. Urbanisation and modern, busy lives also leave less time for elaborate traditional practices. Additionally, as older generations pass away, knowledge and skills are sometimes not passed on. So it is really a combination of cultural [[dilution]] and the practical pressures of modern life [[eroding]] them.

part3Samples.q: Do you think traditions will survive in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am cautiously optimistic. While some traditions will inevitably fade, I believe the most meaningful ones will [[endure]], perhaps in modified forms. There is actually a growing appreciation for heritage as a counterbalance to globalisation, with many people actively seeking to [[revive]] old customs. Technology can also help document and share them. So rather than vanishing, I think traditions will [[evolve]], adapting to remain relevant in a changing world.

part3Samples.q: What can be done to preserve traditional culture?
part3Samples.answer: A [[concerted effort]] is needed. Education is crucial; teaching young people about their heritage in schools fosters pride and understanding. Documenting traditions and supporting the [[artisans]] and elders who hold this knowledge is also vital. Governments and communities can organise festivals and cultural events to keep customs alive and visible. Essentially, making tradition feel relevant and engaging to the young is the key to its [[continuity]].

part3Samples.q: Some say governments should stop cities from growing too big. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I do not think halting growth is realistic or desirable, but managing it is essential. Trying to stop urban growth [[outright]] would be difficult and could stifle economic opportunity. However, I strongly agree that governments should guide this growth intelligently, perhaps by developing smaller [[satellite cities]] and improving rural areas to [[ease the pressure]]. So rather than restricting cities, the focus should be on making growth sustainable and balanced.

cueCards.title: Describe a village or countryside area you have visited
cueCards.prompt: Describe a village or countryside area you have visited
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: A countryside area I visited that I still think about fondly is a small farming village in Bogura district, about two hours from Sirajganj by road. I went there last year during the harvest season to visit a university friend's family, and although I know village life well from my grandparents' home, this place felt even more remote and peaceful. The village was surrounded by endless green paddy fields, and everything moved at a wonderfully [[leisurely]] pace. Most families there grow rice and vegetables, and many keep a few cows and chickens, so the day starts very early. What struck me most was how genuinely [[content]] the people seemed, despite having far fewer material comforts than people in towns and cities. My friend's mother cooked for us on a clay stove, and the food, fresh from their own fields and pond, was some of the best I have ever eaten. We spent our days walking along the narrow paths between the fields, and I even tried my hand at cutting rice, which was far harder than it looked. In the evenings we sat talking under a sky absolutely full of stars. The air was clean and the atmosphere was completely [[unhurried]]. Honestly, the experience gave me a real appreciation for a simpler way of life. It made me question how much of our constant rush is actually necessary. I came away feeling calm and strangely [[rejuvenated]], and I would love to spend more time somewhere like that, [[away from it all]].

followUps.q: Would you like to live in a village like that?
followUps.answer: For a few months, perhaps, but probably not permanently. I love the peace, but my work depends on good internet and being near clients, and I would miss the conveniences of town life.

followUps.q: Are villages in Bangladesh changing?
followUps.answer: Yes, quite rapidly. Most villages now have electricity, mobile phones and better roads, and many young people move away for work. Life is more comfortable, but some of the traditional community spirit is fading.

part3: Do you think living in a city is better than living in the countryside?
How have cities changed over the past few decades?
Why do so many people move to cities?
What do you think cities will be like in the future?
How can cities be made better places to live?
Some say younger generations have life easier than older ones. Do you agree?

part3Samples.q: Do you think living in a city is better than living in the countryside?
part3Samples.answer: It really depends on one's priorities and stage of life. Cities offer better job opportunities, [[amenities]], healthcare and a vibrant social life, which many find appealing. The countryside, by contrast, offers peace, clean air, space and a stronger sense of community. Personally, I appreciate the convenience of the city for now, but I can see the [[profound appeal]] of a quieter rural life later. So neither is objectively better; each suits different needs and [[temperaments]].

part3Samples.q: How have cities changed over the past few decades?
part3Samples.answer: Cities have transformed dramatically. They have grown enormously in size and population due to rapid urbanisation, becoming denser and often more [[congested]]. Skylines have risen with skyscrapers, and technology has made them smarter. However, this growth has often [[outpaced]] infrastructure, worsening problems like traffic, pollution and housing shortages. So while cities have become more developed and connected, this expansion has brought significant [[growing pains]].

part3Samples.q: Why do so many people move to cities?
part3Samples.answer: The primary driver is economic opportunity. Cities are hubs of employment, offering far more and better-paid jobs than rural areas, which is the biggest [[pull factor]]. They also provide superior access to education, healthcare and services. For many, the appeal of a more exciting, diverse lifestyle is also a draw. So this migration is largely driven by the search for a better standard of living, though it can place enormous [[strain]] on urban [[infrastructure]] and resources.

part3Samples.q: What do you think cities will be like in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I envision cities becoming smarter and, hopefully, greener. Technology will likely manage traffic, energy and services more efficiently through data. There is a strong push towards more sustainable, [[walkable]] cities with more green spaces and cleaner transport. However, they may also become even more crowded. So I am hopeful the cities of the future will be more [[liveable]] and sustainable, provided planning [[prioritises]] people and the environment over pure expansion.

part3Samples.q: How can cities be made better places to live?
part3Samples.answer: Thoughtful [[urban planning]] is the key. Investing in efficient, affordable public transport reduces congestion and pollution. Creating more green spaces and [[pedestrian areas]] improves wellbeing. Ensuring an adequate supply of affordable housing tackles inequality. Designing [[mixed-use]], walkable neighbourhoods fosters community. Essentially, cities become better when they are planned around the needs of people and the environment, rather than simply cars and commerce.

part3Samples.q: Some say younger generations have life easier than older ones. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I think it is more [[nuanced]] than that. In material terms, young people today certainly enjoy comforts and technology their grandparents lacked. However, they face their own distinct pressures, such as intense competition, [[job insecurity]] and a constant online spotlight. So I would not say life is simply easier; rather, the [[hardships]] have shifted in nature.

cueCards.title: Describe a place where you like to walk
cueCards.prompt: Describe a place where you like to walk
bullets: and why you like walking there

sample.answer: A place I love to walk is a tree-lined avenue in the park near my home, which runs along one side of the park beneath tall rain trees and a few old mango trees. It is only about ten minutes from our flat, so it is very easy to fit into my day. I try to go there most evenings after work, and on Friday mornings I sometimes go early, before the heat builds up. Usually I go alone, but occasionally I go with a friend, and now that my father has retired he sometimes joins me, which has become a nice chance for us to talk. What makes it perfect for walking is the shade from the mature trees and the wide, well-kept paths. It is far enough from the main roads that the noise fades away, leaving a wonderfully calm atmosphere. I find that walking there is not just good exercise but also genuinely [[meditative]]; it is when I do some of my best thinking. The changing light in the evening, as the sun filters through the leaves, makes the whole place feel [[serene]]. Sometimes I listen to music or a podcast, and other times I simply enjoy the sound of birds settling down for the night. When I walk with my father, he tells me how the town looked when he was young, which I find fascinating. Honestly, this simple daily walk has become one of the most [[rejuvenating]] parts of my routine. It clears my head, [[lifts my spirits]] and gives me a small [[pocket of calm]] in an otherwise busy day.

followUps.q: Do you think walking is a good form of exercise?
followUps.answer: Yes, it is probably the most underrated one. It is free, anyone can do it and it is gentle on the body, yet it still keeps you fit, especially if you walk briskly every day.

followUps.q: Do many people walk there?
followUps.answer: Quite a lot, particularly in the early morning and the evening. You see older people walking for their health, families strolling with children and a few serious joggers who overtake everyone.

part3: How important are public spaces like parks in a city?
Do you think there are enough public spaces in modern cities?
What effect do green spaces have on people living in cities?
Do you think cities will have more or fewer public spaces in the future?
How can cities create more public spaces despite limited land?
Some say happiness is a choice. Do you agree?

part3Samples.q: How important are public spaces like parks in a city?
part3Samples.answer: I consider them absolutely essential to a healthy city. Public spaces like parks provide vital areas for recreation, exercise and relaxation, which is crucial for physical and mental wellbeing amid the stress of urban life. They also act as the [[lungs of a city]], improving air quality, and serve as places where the community comes together. So far from being a luxury, well-designed public spaces are fundamental to a [[liveable]] and [[cohesive]] city.

part3Samples.q: Do you think there are enough public spaces in modern cities?
part3Samples.answer: In many rapidly growing cities, unfortunately not. As urban land becomes increasingly valuable, green and public spaces are often sacrificed for commercial or residential development, which I find [[short-sighted]]. Older, well-planned cities tend to have generous parks, whereas newer, denser developments frequently lack them. So while the importance of public space is increasingly recognised, in practice many cities are [[falling short]], prioritising profit over [[liveability]].

part3Samples.q: What effect do green spaces have on people living in cities?
part3Samples.answer: The effects are overwhelmingly positive, in my view. Access to green spaces reduces stress, improves mood and encourages physical activity, benefiting both mental and physical health. They provide a [[peaceful escape]] from the noise and concrete of the city. Socially, they [[foster]] community interaction. Environmentally, they cool cities and clean the air. So green spaces have a genuinely [[restorative]] and beneficial effect on urban wellbeing.

part3Samples.q: Do you think cities will have more or fewer public spaces in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am hopeful there will be more, though it faces real pressure. On one hand, [[intense competition]] for urban land threatens existing spaces. On the other, there is a growing recognition of their importance for wellbeing and sustainability, and many [[forward-thinking]] cities are now actively creating parks, green roofs and pedestrian zones. So the outcome depends on planning priorities, but I am optimistic that the value of public space will increasingly be recognised and [[prioritised]].

part3Samples.q: How can cities create more public spaces despite limited land?
part3Samples.answer: Creativity is key when land is scarce. Cities can [[repurpose]] [[disused]] areas, such as old railway lines turned into elevated parks, or convert rooftops into green spaces and gardens. Pedestrianising streets reclaims space from cars for people. Even small pocket parks on vacant plots make a difference. So even in dense cities, with imaginative planning, it is possible to integrate valuable public and green space into the existing [[urban fabric]].

part3Samples.q: Some say happiness is a choice. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I partly agree, but with important reservations. There is real truth that our attitude, gratitude and how we respond to circumstances significantly influence our happiness, so mindset matters. However, saying happiness is simply a choice can be [[dismissive]] of those facing genuine hardship, mental illness or difficult circumstances beyond their control. So while we have some agency over our happiness, I think it is [[oversimplified]] to call it purely a choice, ignoring the [[structural]] and biological factors involved.

cueCards.title: Describe your ideal home
cueCards.prompt: Describe your ideal home
bullets: and why it would be ideal for you

sample.answer: If I could design my ideal home, it would be a comfortable two-storey house on the edge of a quiet town, balancing modern convenience with a connection to nature. It would not need to be huge or [[extravagant]]; I value comfort and warmth far more than showing off. I picture large windows that let in plenty of natural light, making the whole space feel open and [[airy]], and a wide veranda where the family could sit together in the evenings with tea. Ideally, it would be somewhere near Sirajganj, perhaps within sight of the Jamuna, so that I could stay close to my parents and grandparents. As for features, a small garden would be essential, somewhere I could grow a few vegetables, plant a mango tree and relax outdoors. Inside, I would want a cosy reading corner with shelves full of books and a proper kitchen, since those are the rooms where I spend most of my time. A spare bedroom would also be important, so that my elder sister and her children could stay whenever they visit from Dhaka. The house would need to be built [[with the monsoon in mind]], raised slightly off the ground so that it never floods. What matters most to me is that it feels genuinely [[welcoming]], both to family and to guests. I would also love it to be in a peaceful area with clean air and friendly neighbours. Honestly, my idea of an ideal home is less about luxury and more about creating a [[sanctuary]] where I can truly relax and feel at peace.

followUps.q: Is your current home similar to your ideal home?
followUps.answer: In some ways. Our flat is comfortable and in a quiet area, but it has no garden and not much natural light. The biggest similarity is that it is full of family, which matters most.

followUps.q: Would you prefer to live in a house or a flat?
followUps.answer: A house, ideally, because of the space and the possibility of having a garden. Flats are more practical and secure in towns, though, so for now I am perfectly happy where I am.

part3: Do you think everyone has the right to affordable housing?
Is it better to rent or to own a home?
Why is housing so expensive in many cities?
How do you think housing will change in the future?
What can be done to make housing more affordable?

part3Samples.q: Do you think everyone has the right to affordable housing?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly believe that access to decent, affordable housing is a [[fundamental human right]], not a privilege. Shelter is a basic need, and stable housing is the foundation upon which people build healthy, productive lives. When housing becomes unaffordable, it drives inequality, homelessness and [[hardship]]. So I think governments have a clear responsibility to ensure that housing is available and affordable to all, treating it as an essential rather than a mere [[commodity]].

part3Samples.q: Is it better to rent or to own a home?
part3Samples.answer: Both have their advantages, depending on circumstances. Owning a home offers stability, security and the chance to build wealth over time, which is why many [[aspire to]] it. Renting, however, offers greater flexibility and freedom from the burdens of maintenance and large [[mortgages]], which suits those who value mobility. So there is no universal answer; it depends on one's financial situation, life stage and how much stability versus flexibility one [[prioritises]].

part3Samples.q: Why is housing so expensive in many cities?
part3Samples.answer: The high cost is driven by a fundamental imbalance between supply and demand. As people [[flock to]] cities for work, demand for housing soars, while the supply of new homes often fails to keep pace due to limited land and slow construction. Property speculation and foreign investment can also inflate prices. So it is largely a matter of high demand meeting [[constrained]] supply, made worse by [[speculation]], pushing prices beyond ordinary people's reach.

part3Samples.q: How do you think housing will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I anticipate several developments. To address shortages and sustainability, we may see more compact, [[high-density]] and eco-friendly housing, along with innovative solutions like modular or [[prefabricated]] homes. Smart-home technology will likely become standard. There may also be a shift towards [[co-living]] arrangements, especially in expensive cities. So future housing may become smaller and denser, but hopefully smarter, greener and more affordable, adapting to modern needs.

part3Samples.q: What can be done to make housing more affordable?
part3Samples.answer: Increasing the supply of housing is fundamental, particularly affordable and social housing built by governments. Reforming planning regulations to allow more construction can help. Measures to [[curb]] speculation, such as taxes on empty properties, may also [[cool prices]]. Rent controls and support for first-time buyers are other options. Essentially, treating housing as a basic need rather than a pure [[investment vehicle]] is key to keeping it accessible and fair.

cueCards.title: Describe a difficult decision you once made
cueCards.prompt: Describe a difficult decision you once made
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about a decision that honestly kept me awake at night for weeks. One of the hardest decisions I have faced was turning down a stable job to pursue something more uncertain but closer to what I actually wanted. This was about two years ago, just after I had been offered a comfortable position with good pay at a bank, only a few months after finishing my BBA. At the same time, a small education consultancy offered me a role helping students apply to study abroad, which paid less but felt far more meaningful. On paper the bank was the sensible choice, which is exactly what made walking away so [[agonising]]. In my town, a bank job is seen as a real achievement, so I knew people would question my judgement. I spent weeks weighing it up, going back and forth, because the secure option felt safe while the other was a genuine [[gamble]]. What ultimately tipped the balance was realising I would probably [[bitterly regret]] not taking the risk far more than any short-term setback. Telling my family was nerve-wracking, since they naturally worried, but they came round once they saw how [[determined]] I was. As for how I felt, I was anxious for a long time, but also strangely [[liberated]]. Looking back, it was a real turning point, and although the following months were rocky, it taught me that the most rewarding paths are rarely the most comfortable. I still feel it was the right call.

followUps.q: Did your family agree with your decision in the end?
followUps.answer: Yes, eventually. My father was the first to support me, probably because he ran his own business for over thirty years and understood taking a chance. My mother took a little longer to feel comfortable.

followUps.q: Do you find it easy to make decisions in general?
followUps.answer: Not really, to be honest. For small things I'm quick, but with big decisions I tend to overthink. These days I try to set myself a deadline so I don't go round in circles forever.

part3: What factors do you think are most important when choosing a career?
Is it better to choose a job you love or a job that pays well?
Why do many people change careers during their lives now?
What kinds of jobs do you think will be most important in the future?
How can young people be helped to make better career decisions?
Some say money is the best measure of success. Do you agree?

part3Samples.q: What factors do you think are most important when choosing a career?
part3Samples.answer: I think the most important factor is genuine interest, because you will spend a huge portion of your life working. A job you are passionate about is far more sustainable than a purely [[lucrative]] one. That said, practical considerations like financial security, job stability and growth opportunities cannot be ignored. Ideally, people should seek a career that [[strikes a healthy balance]] between passion and [[pragmatism]].

part3Samples.q: Is it better to choose a job you love or a job that pays well?
part3Samples.answer: This is the classic dilemma. In an ideal world, you would have both. If forced to choose, I lean towards a job you love, because passion tends to lead to better performance and long-term fulfilment, and money alone rarely brings lasting [[contentment]]. However, this is somewhat a [[privilege]]; those with financial pressures may reasonably [[prioritise]] a stable income first.

part3Samples.q: Why do many people change careers during their lives now?
part3Samples.answer: Several factors drive this. The job market is far more [[volatile]] than in the past, so lifelong employment in one company is increasingly rare. People also have higher expectations of finding meaningful work, and are more willing to [[pursue]] fulfilment. Additionally, rapid technological change means some jobs disappear while new ones emerge, which [[compels]] people to adapt and retrain.

part3Samples.q: What kinds of jobs do you think will be most important in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I believe jobs involving skills that machines cannot easily replicate will be most valuable. This includes creative fields, healthcare, and roles requiring emotional intelligence and complex problem-solving. Careers related to technology, such as AI and data science, will obviously be in high demand, as will jobs focused on [[sustainability]] and renewable energy. Essentially, roles that are [[adaptable]] and distinctly human will [[thrive]].

part3Samples.q: How can young people be helped to make better career decisions?
part3Samples.answer: Better career guidance in schools would make an enormous difference. Too often, students choose paths with little real understanding of what the jobs actually involve. Providing internships and work experience gives them valuable [[exposure]] to different fields. Mentorship from professionals can also offer honest, [[first-hand]] insight. Essentially, we need to help young people make [[informed]] choices rather than blind ones.

part3Samples.q: Some say money is the best measure of success. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly disagree with this narrow view. While money is a tangible and convenient measure, and financial security certainly matters, equating it with success ignores far more important dimensions of a good life. Many wealthy people are deeply unhappy, while many people of [[modest means]] live rich, fulfilling lives. Reducing success to a bank balance seems [[reductive]] and [[misguided]]. True success, in my view, is measured by fulfilment, relationships and character, not currency.

cueCards.title: Describe a time you helped someone
cueCards.prompt: Describe a time you helped someone
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: I'd like to describe a time I helped a new colleague at the education consultancy where I work. A time I clearly remember helping someone was when a younger colleague was struggling badly with a project and close to panicking. It was during our busiest season last year, and he had been asked to prepare several students' university applications with very tight deadlines. He was new and clearly [[overwhelmed]], afraid to admit he was falling behind. I noticed he seemed stressed, so I quietly offered to sit with him after work and go through it together. Over a couple of evenings, we broke the task into manageable steps and slowly untangled the problem. I also showed him the checklist I use for each application and how to deal with the most urgent deadlines first. What I found most [[rewarding]] was watching his confidence gradually return as things started to make sense. He was incredibly grateful, though honestly, helping him did not feel like a chore at all. I think we underestimate how much a small act of [[generosity]] can mean to someone at a low point. It also reminded me of the times people had helped me when I was new and lost. Honestly, that experience left me feeling genuinely [[fulfilled]], and it strengthened our working relationship enormously. These days he is one of the most [[dependable]] people in our office, and I like to think those evenings played a small part in that.

followUps.q: Do you often help your colleagues?
followUps.answer: Fairly often, yes. Our office is quite small, so we depend on each other a lot. If someone is stuck, it is usually quicker for everyone if we pitch in rather than let the problem grow.

followUps.q: Did he ever return the favour?
followUps.answer: He did, actually. A few months later I was buried in visa paperwork before a holiday, and he stayed late to help me finish. It felt good to know the support went both ways.

part3: Where do you think people get their moral values from?
Are moral values the same across all cultures?
What happens to a society when it loses its moral values?
How might moral values change in the future?
How can strong moral values be encouraged in young people?
Some say schools focus too much on academics and not enough on emotional skills. Do you agree?

part3Samples.q: Where do you think people get their moral values from?
part3Samples.answer: I believe our moral values come from a combination of sources. Our upbringing and family are hugely influential, [[instilling]] early notions of right and wrong. Culture, religion and society also shape our ethics, as do our own experiences and reflection as we mature. Some argue there is even an innate, universal sense of fairness. So our values are essentially [[absorbed]] from those around us and then [[refined]] through personal reflection over time.

part3Samples.q: Are moral values the same across all cultures?
part3Samples.answer: I think there is a fascinating mix of universal and culturally specific values. Certain core principles, like [[prohibitions]] against murder or valuing honesty and care for others, appear across virtually all cultures, suggesting a shared moral foundation. However, many values, such as attitudes to family, [[individualism]] or specific customs, vary considerably between cultures. So while there are some universal [[moral constants]], ethics are also significantly shaped by cultural context.

part3Samples.q: What happens to a society when it loses its moral values?
part3Samples.answer: A society that loses its shared [[moral compass]] tends to suffer serious consequences. Trust between people erodes, corruption and dishonesty can flourish, and social cohesion breaks down. Without agreed ethical standards, laws alone struggle to maintain order, and self-interest can dominate at the expense of the common good. So a strong shared morality acts as invisible [[social glue]]; its erosion can lead to division, [[distrust]] and dysfunction.

part3Samples.q: How might moral values change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I expect our moral frameworks to be tested and expanded by new challenges. Advances in technology, such as artificial intelligence and genetic engineering, will raise entirely new [[ethical dilemmas]] we have never faced before. Growing awareness may also extend our moral concern further, perhaps towards animals, the environment and future generations. So I anticipate that ethics will continue to [[evolve]], becoming broader in scope as we [[grapple with]] unprecedented moral questions.

part3Samples.q: How can strong moral values be encouraged in young people?
part3Samples.answer: The most powerful way is through example, since children learn ethics primarily by observing the adults around them. Parents and teachers who [[model integrity]], kindness and honesty have a profound influence. Open discussion of ethical issues, encouraging empathy, and involving young people in helping others also help. Rather than simply lecturing, allowing them to [[reason through]] moral situations builds genuine understanding. So values are best [[instilled]] through consistent example and guided reflection.

part3Samples.q: Some say schools focus too much on academics and not enough on emotional skills. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly agree with this criticism. Traditional education has long [[prioritised]] exam results above all else, often neglecting the emotional and social skills that are equally vital for a fulfilling life. Skills like managing stress, empathising and collaborating are rarely taught explicitly. I think a more [[holistic]] education, one that develops the whole person, would produce far more [[well-rounded]] and capable adults.

cueCards.title: Describe a time when you were very busy
cueCards.prompt: Describe a time when you were very busy
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: The busiest time I can remember was about a year ago, and I still feel slightly tired just thinking about it. A period when I was extraordinarily busy was during the final weeks before a major deadline at work, which happened to coincide with a family event. At the consultancy, it was the peak of the application season, when lots of students were trying to submit their university applications at once, and at the same time my cousin was getting married in our ancestral village. I found myself juggling long working hours with preparations at home, and there simply were not enough hours in the day. My schedule was absolutely [[relentless]]; I would wake early, work through lunch and often continue late into the night. Then at weekends I travelled to the village to help with the arrangements for the wedding. At times it felt genuinely [[overwhelming]], and I worried I might [[drop the ball]] on something important. What got me through was staying organised, making detailed lists and [[prioritising ruthlessly]]. Somehow I managed to meet the deadline and see the family event through successfully. As for how I felt, I was exhausted but also quietly proud. Looking back, it taught me a great deal about managing pressure, and I discovered I was more [[capable]] under stress than I had thought. Honestly, while I would not want to repeat it too often, it was a valuable lesson in resilience and time management.

followUps.q: How do you usually relax after a busy period?
followUps.answer: I like to take a long walk by the Jamuna in the evening, or just sit at home with a cup of tea and a book. After that busy month, I mostly caught up on sleep.

followUps.q: Do you think people are busier now than in the past?
followUps.answer: I think so. My father worked hard, but his work mostly stayed at the shop. Now phones mean work follows us home, so it is much harder to switch off completely.

part3: How important is work-life balance?
Do you think people had a better work-life balance in the past?
What are the consequences of a poor work-life balance?
Do you think work-life balance will improve in the future?
What can people do to achieve a better work-life balance?
Some say happiness is a choice. Do you agree?

part3Samples.q: How important is work-life balance?
part3Samples.answer: I believe it is absolutely essential for long-term wellbeing. Without a healthy balance, people risk burnout, which harms both their health and, ironically, their productivity. Time for family, rest and hobbies is not a luxury; it is what makes us [[resilient]] and effective. In my view, a culture that glorifies overwork is ultimately [[unsustainable]] and [[counterproductive]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think people had a better work-life balance in the past?
part3Samples.answer: In some respects, yes. In the past, work was more clearly confined to the workplace, and once you went home, you were genuinely off duty. Today, smartphones mean we are perpetually [[reachable]], and the boundary between work and personal life has become dangerously [[blurred]]. That said, past generations often worked longer physical hours, so it is not entirely one-sided; the nature of the [[imbalance]] has changed.

part3Samples.q: What are the consequences of a poor work-life balance?
part3Samples.answer: The consequences can be severe. Chronic overwork frequently leads to stress, burnout and serious health problems, both physical and mental. It also strains personal relationships, as work encroaches on time with family and friends. Ironically, it often reduces long-term productivity too. Essentially, neglecting your personal life for work is [[self-defeating]], [[taking a heavy toll]] that eventually [[undermines]] everything.

part3Samples.q: Do you think work-life balance will improve in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am hopeful, though not entirely certain. There is a growing cultural awareness of the importance of wellbeing, and flexible and remote working could, if managed well, improve balance considerably. Concepts like the four-day week are [[gaining traction]]. However, there is a risk that [[constant connectivity]] could make things worse. So improvement is possible, but it will require a [[deliberate cultural shift]] rather than happening automatically.

part3Samples.q: What can people do to achieve a better work-life balance?
part3Samples.answer: On a personal level, setting firm boundaries is crucial, such as not checking work emails after hours. Learning to prioritise and, importantly, to say no to excessive demands helps enormously. Making dedicated time for rest and relationships should be treated as [[non-negotiable]]. However, individuals can [[only do so much]]; employers must also foster a culture that genuinely respects personal time and does not reward [[overwork]].

part3Samples.q: Some say happiness is a choice. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I partly agree, but with important reservations. There is real truth that our attitude, gratitude and how we respond to circumstances significantly influence our happiness, so mindset matters. However, saying happiness is simply a choice can be [[dismissive]] of those facing genuine hardship, mental illness or difficult circumstances beyond their control. So while we have some agency over our happiness, I think it is [[oversimplified]] to call it purely a choice, ignoring the [[structural]] and biological factors involved.

cueCards.title: Describe a time you received good news
cueCards.prompt: Describe a time you received good news
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about the day I found out I had got my current job, because it was a real turning point for me. A moment of wonderful news that I will never forget was when I found out I had been accepted for a position I had desperately wanted. It was a role at an education consultancy, helping students apply to study abroad, which suited both my BBA and my own interest in international education. I had applied weeks earlier and had almost given up hope, so the email from the director caught me completely [[off guard]]. I was actually sitting at a tea stall with a friend when my phone buzzed, and I assumed it was another rejection. I remember reading it several times, hardly able to believe it, feeling utterly [[elated]]. My first instinct was to call my family, who had supported me throughout the stressful application process. My mother answered, and I could hear her telling my father and sister in the background before I had even finished. Their reaction was just as [[overjoyed]] as mine, which made the moment even sweeter. What made the news so meaningful was how hard I had worked and how uncertain the outcome had felt. The relief was almost as strong as the happiness; it was genuinely [[euphoric]]. That evening we celebrated together over my mother's cooking, and I felt an immense sense of [[accomplishment]]. Honestly, it remains one of the happiest days of my life, and it reminded me that persistence really can pay off.

followUps.q: Who is usually the first person you share good news with?
followUps.answer: Usually my mother, because she worries about me the most, so good news means a lot to her. My younger sister is a close second, since she tends to find out everything anyway.

followUps.q: Do you prefer to receive news by phone or in person?
followUps.answer: In person, if possible. You can see someone's face and share the moment properly. That said, for something like a job offer, an email is fine, because you can read it again and again.

part3: How do you define success?
Is success more about hard work or luck?
Why do some people become more ambitious than others?
Do you think the definition of success is changing?
How can society support people to achieve their goals?
Some say happiness is a choice. Do you agree?

part3Samples.q: How do you define success?
part3Samples.answer: I think success is deeply personal and far broader than wealth or status. To me, genuine success means finding [[fulfilment]] in what you do, maintaining good relationships, and feeling that you are growing and contributing something meaningful. While financial security matters, defining success purely by money seems rather [[hollow]]. So I would say true success is a sense of [[contentment]] and purpose, which looks different for every individual.

part3Samples.q: Is success more about hard work or luck?
part3Samples.answer: I believe it is a combination of both, though hard work is the factor within our control. Undeniably, luck plays a role, such as being born into favourable circumstances or being in the right place at the right time. However, hard work, persistence and seizing opportunities are what allow people to [[capitalise on]] that luck. So while luck can open doors, it is usually [[diligence]] and determination that [[sustain]] lasting success.

part3Samples.q: Why do some people become more ambitious than others?
part3Samples.answer: Ambition is shaped by a mix of factors. Upbringing plays a big role; children encouraged to aim high often [[internalise]] that drive. Personal experiences, including hardship, can also fuel a determination to succeed. Individual personality and the influence of role models matter too. Additionally, some are motivated by a fear of failure or a desire for recognition. So ambition usually stems from a blend of [[nurture]], personal circumstance and innate [[temperament]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think the definition of success is changing?
part3Samples.answer: Yes, I believe it is evolving, particularly among younger generations. The traditional [[markers of success]], like a high salary and status, are increasingly being questioned. Many now place greater value on work-life balance, wellbeing, purpose and experiences over pure material wealth. There is a growing recognition that a fulfilling life matters more than a merely impressive one. So the definition of success seems to be shifting towards something more [[holistic]] and meaningful than [[materialistic]].

part3Samples.q: How can society support people to achieve their goals?
part3Samples.answer: Society can do much to help. Ensuring equal access to quality education and opportunities gives everyone a fairer chance, regardless of background. Providing mentorship, resources and support for entrepreneurs and innovators helps too. Creating a culture that values effort and does not [[stigmatise]] failure encourages people to take risks. Essentially, by removing barriers and fostering an [[enabling]] environment, society can help far more people [[fulfil their potential]].

part3Samples.q: Some say happiness is a choice. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I partly agree, but with important reservations. There is real truth that our attitude, gratitude and how we respond to circumstances significantly influence our happiness, so mindset matters. However, saying happiness is simply a choice can be [[dismissive]] of those facing genuine hardship, mental illness or difficult circumstances beyond their control. So while we have some agency over our happiness, I think it is [[oversimplified]] to call it purely a choice, ignoring the [[structural]] and biological factors involved.

cueCards.title: Describe a time you learned a new skill
cueCards.prompt: Describe a time you learned a new skill
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: A skill I taught myself during my university years was cooking, which I had always avoided out of sheer laziness. At home, my mother has always done the cooking, so I never really had to lift a finger in the kitchen. That changed when I moved to Dhaka for my BBA and started sharing a small flat with three other students. Living away from home, I got tired of eating out and decided it was time to become [[self-sufficient]]. I started with simple recipes from online videos, and my early attempts were genuinely disastrous. There was a real [[learning curve]], and I burned more meals than I care to admit, which was quite [[discouraging]] at first. I also rang my mother constantly, asking how much turmeric to add or how long to cook the lentils. But I [[persevered]], and gradually things started to improve. What I found most rewarding was the moment I cooked a proper chicken curry that actually tasted good, and my flatmates asked for more. Beyond the practical benefit, cooking turned out to be surprisingly relaxing, almost [[therapeutic]] after a stressful day. I also realised how much work my mother had been doing for years without a word of complaint. It gave me a real sense of independence and pride. Honestly, learning this skill changed my daily life for the better, and it reminded me that most things become manageable if you are willing to fail a few times first. Now that I am back home, I even cook for the family occasionally.

followUps.q: Do you still cook now?
followUps.answer: Now and then. My mother still rules the kitchen, but on Fridays I sometimes make a simple curry or fried rice for everyone. My younger sister is my harshest critic, which keeps me honest.

followUps.q: What skill would you like to learn next?
followUps.answer: I'd love to learn to play the guitar properly. I listen to a lot of music, and being able to play a few songs for friends and family would be really satisfying.

part3: What do you think is the best way to learn something new?
Is it better to learn alone or in a group?
Why do some people find learning easier than others?
Do you think traditional classrooms will disappear in the future?
How can people stay motivated when learning independently?
Some say you are never too old to learn. Do you agree?

part3Samples.q: What do you think is the best way to learn something new?
part3Samples.answer: In my experience, the most effective way to learn is through active, hands-on practice rather than passive listening. We tend to [[retain]] information far better when we actually apply it. I am a firm believer in [[learning by doing]], and in making mistakes, since they are often the most [[instructive]] experiences. Combining this practical approach with genuine curiosity makes learning both effective and thoroughly engaging.

part3Samples.q: Is it better to learn alone or in a group?
part3Samples.answer: Both have their merits, and the ideal depends on the task. Learning alone allows for focus and lets you progress at your own pace, which suits deep, concentrated study. Group learning, on the other hand, is more [[dynamic]]; you benefit from different perspectives and can clarify doubts through discussion. Personally, I favour a [[blend]] of the two, as they [[complement]] each other nicely.

part3Samples.q: Why do some people find learning easier than others?
part3Samples.answer: There are many contributing factors. Some of it comes down to natural [[aptitude]], but I think motivation and [[mindset]] matter far more. People who are genuinely curious and believe they can improve tend to learn faster. Environment also plays a huge role; a supportive home and good teachers make an enormous difference. So learning ability is really a mix of [[innate]] talent and nurtured habits.

part3Samples.q: Do you think traditional classrooms will disappear in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I doubt they will disappear entirely, but their role will certainly change. Online learning will keep growing, offering flexibility that classrooms cannot match. However, physical classrooms provide something valuable: social interaction, mentorship and a structured environment that many learners need. So rather than [[vanishing]], I expect classrooms to [[evolve]] into more interactive spaces, [[complementing]] rather than being replaced by digital tools.

part3Samples.q: How can people stay motivated when learning independently?
part3Samples.answer: Self-motivation is the biggest challenge in independent learning. I think the key is setting clear, [[achievable]] goals and breaking a large subject into smaller [[milestones]], which gives a regular sense of progress. Establishing a routine helps make studying a habit rather than a struggle. Finding a community of fellow learners online can also provide [[accountability]] and encouragement, which is often what people lack.

part3Samples.q: Some say you are never too old to learn. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I wholeheartedly agree. While learning styles may change with age, the human brain remains capable of acquiring new knowledge and skills throughout life. There are countless inspiring examples of people learning languages, instruments or even new careers late in life. I think the biggest barrier is usually psychological, a [[self-imposed]] belief that it is too late. In reality, curiosity and effort [[transcend]] age entirely, keeping us [[youthful]] in spirit.

cueCards.title: Describe a memorable journey you have taken
cueCards.prompt: Describe a memorable journey you have taken

sample.answer: I'd like to describe a train journey I took a couple of years ago, because my friends and I still talk about it. A journey that stands out vividly in my memory was a long train ride I took through the countryside with a group of close friends. We were travelling from Dhaka to Sylhet to see the tea gardens, but honestly the journey itself turned out to be the highlight. There were four of us, all old university friends, and we had managed to get seats together in the same carriage. We set off early in the morning with bags of snacks and far too much luggage. The train wound slowly through [[picturesque]] landscapes of green paddy fields, rivers and small villages, and later past gentle hills covered in tea. We spent hours chatting, playing cards and simply watching the ever-changing scenery, which was wonderfully [[soothing]]. At almost every station, vendors came on board selling tea and snacks, which only added to the fun. What made it so memorable was not the destination but the shared experience and the sense of freedom. There was something almost [[nostalgic]] about the slow rhythm of train travel, so different from the rush of flying. We laughed until our sides ached and made memories I still treasure. Honestly, that journey taught me that travel is often about the moments in between rather than just arriving. It remains one of my most [[cherished]] trips, precisely because it was so [[unhurried]] and full of good company. By the time we arrived, we were tired, but none of us wanted it to end.

followUps.q: Would you like to make that journey again?
followUps.answer: Definitely. I'd love to do it again, maybe with my younger sister this time, since she has never been to Sylhet. Though I suspect it would not feel quite the same without my friends.

followUps.q: Do you prefer travelling by train or by bus?
followUps.answer: By train, without a doubt. Buses in Bangladesh can be quite cramped and the roads are often jammed, whereas on a train you can stretch your legs and actually enjoy the view.

part3: Why do you think people enjoy travelling?
How has travel changed compared to the past?
What effects does tourism have on local communities?
How do you think tourism will change in the future?
How can the negative impacts of tourism be reduced?
Some say cars should be banned from city centres. Do you agree?

part3Samples.q: Why do you think people enjoy travelling?
part3Samples.answer: People travel for a wonderful variety of reasons. Fundamentally, I think it satisfies a deep human curiosity and desire to escape routine. Experiencing new cultures, landscapes and cuisines is genuinely [[enriching]] and broadens one's perspective. Travel also offers relaxation, adventure and the chance to create lasting memories. For me, the greatest value is how it makes you more [[open-minded]] and [[appreciative]] of the world's incredible diversity.

part3Samples.q: How has travel changed compared to the past?
part3Samples.answer: Travel has been transformed almost beyond recognition. In the past, it was expensive, slow and largely a privilege of the wealthy. Today, [[budget airlines]] and the internet have made it far more accessible and easy to organise, leading to mass tourism. We can now reach distant corners of the globe in hours. While this democratisation is positive, it has also led to [[overcrowding]] at popular sites and a more [[superficial]], hurried style of travel.

part3Samples.q: What effects does tourism have on local communities?
part3Samples.answer: Tourism has profound and mixed effects. Economically, it can bring vital income and jobs, boosting the local economy significantly. However, it can also cause problems: it may [[inflate]] local prices, strain infrastructure, and sometimes lead to the [[commodification]] of culture, where traditions are performed purely for tourists. Environmental damage is another concern. So while tourism offers real economic benefits, it must be managed [[sustainably]] to avoid harming the very communities it supports.

part3Samples.q: How do you think tourism will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I foresee several shifts. Growing environmental awareness will likely make sustainable and [[eco-tourism]] far more popular, as people seek to [[minimise their impact]]. Technology, such as virtual reality, might offer new ways to experience places remotely. There may also be a move towards more meaningful, [[immersive]] travel over mass tourism. So I expect the future of travel to be more conscious, more personalised, and hopefully more responsible.

part3Samples.q: How can the negative impacts of tourism be reduced?
part3Samples.answer: Sustainable tourism practices are the answer. Governments can manage visitor numbers at fragile sites through limits or timed entry to prevent overcrowding. Promoting [[lesser-known]] destinations helps spread the benefits and reduce pressure on [[hotspots]]. Encouraging tourists to respect local cultures and environments, and to support local businesses, is also key. Essentially, prioritising sustainability over sheer volume can [[mitigate]] the harm while preserving the benefits.

part3Samples.q: Some say cars should be banned from city centres. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I broadly agree with this, at least for private cars in the busiest central areas. Many cities that have [[pedestrianised]] their centres seem to have seen reduced pollution, safer streets and more vibrant public life, which is very appealing. However, it must be done carefully, ensuring excellent public transport alternatives and access for deliveries and those with disabilities. So rather than a [[blanket ban]], I support significantly restricting cars to create more [[liveable]], people-friendly centres.

cueCards.title: Describe a time you were late for something
cueCards.prompt: Describe a time you were late for something
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about a morning I would honestly rather forget. A time I was embarrassingly late was for an important job interview a few years ago, just after I had finished university. The interview was in Dhaka, so I stayed the night before at my elder sister's flat, thinking that would give me plenty of time. I had planned everything carefully, but on the day, the traffic was absolutely [[horrendous]] due to an unexpected road closure. I sat helplessly in a CNG auto-rickshaw, watching the minutes tick away, growing more [[jittery]] by the second. I kept checking my watch every thirty seconds, as if that would somehow make the traffic move. I called ahead to apologise, which was [[mortifying]], and eventually arrived nearly half an hour late, [[flustered]] and sweating. To my relief, the interviewers were surprisingly understanding, and the interview went reasonably well despite my terrible start. One of them even joked that being stuck in Dhaka traffic was practically a local tradition, which helped me relax a little. As for how I felt, I was ashamed at first and then hugely relieved. However, the whole experience taught me a valuable lesson about leaving a proper buffer for the unexpected. Since then I have become almost [[obsessive]] about arriving early for anything important. Honestly, the stress of that day was enough to change my habits for good. I now always plan for delays, because I never want to feel that particular kind of panic again. It was a bad day, but I am oddly grateful for it now.

followUps.q: Did you get the job in the end?
followUps.answer: No, I didn't, though I don't think it was only because I was late. Luckily, a few weeks later I was offered my current job at the consultancy, which suits me much better anyway.

followUps.q: Are people in your country usually on time?
followUps.answer: Honestly, not always. Traffic in the cities is so unpredictable that people tend to be quite relaxed about being a little late. For formal things like interviews, though, punctuality really matters.

part3: Do you think public transport should be free?
Is it better to travel by public transport or private car?
What are the effects of traffic congestion on cities?
How do you think transport will change in the future?
How can traffic problems in cities be solved?
Some say governments should stop cities from growing too big. Do you agree?

part3Samples.q: Do you think public transport should be free?
part3Samples.answer: I find the idea appealing, though it is complex. Making public transport free could reduce traffic, cut pollution and help [[lower-income]] people enormously, which are [[compelling]] social benefits. However, it would be extremely expensive to fund and might lead to overcrowding or reduced service quality without careful management. So while I support [[heavily subsidising]] it to keep it affordable, whether it should be entirely free depends on a country's priorities and budget.

part3Samples.q: Is it better to travel by public transport or private car?
part3Samples.answer: Each has its merits, but from a societal viewpoint, public transport is clearly [[preferable]]. It is far more environmentally friendly, reduces congestion, and is cheaper for the user. Private cars, however, offer [[unmatched]] convenience, comfort and flexibility, especially where public transport is poor. So while I personally value the freedom of a car, I believe well-developed public transport is the more sustainable and [[equitable]] option for society as a whole.

part3Samples.q: What are the effects of traffic congestion on cities?
part3Samples.answer: Traffic congestion has serious and costly effects. It wastes an enormous amount of people's time, reducing productivity and quality of life. It significantly worsens air pollution, harming public health and the environment. It also causes frustration and stress for commuters and can [[hamper]] emergency services. Economically, the lost hours and fuel represent a huge [[drain]]. So congestion is far more than an inconvenience; it [[undermines]] a city's efficiency and wellbeing.

part3Samples.q: How do you think transport will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I anticipate significant transformation. Electric vehicles will likely become the norm, drastically cutting emissions, and [[autonomous]], self-driving cars may reshape how we travel. Cities will probably invest more in cycling, walking and clean public transport. Concepts like [[shared mobility]] could reduce car ownership. So the future of transport is likely to be cleaner, smarter and more [[integrated]], hopefully making our cities less polluted and more liveable.

part3Samples.q: How can traffic problems in cities be solved?
part3Samples.answer: A combination of measures is most effective. Investing heavily in reliable, affordable public transport gives people a genuine alternative to driving. Encouraging cycling and walking through better [[infrastructure]] helps too. Some cities use [[congestion charging]] to [[discourage]] car use in busy areas. Better urban planning that reduces the need to travel far is also valuable. Essentially, the solution lies in making sustainable options more attractive than driving, rather than simply widening roads.

part3Samples.q: Some say governments should stop cities from growing too big. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I do not think halting growth is realistic or desirable, but managing it is essential. Trying to stop urban growth [[outright]] would be difficult and could stifle economic opportunity. However, I strongly agree that governments should guide this growth intelligently, perhaps by developing smaller [[satellite cities]] and improving rural areas to [[ease the pressure]]. So rather than restricting cities, the focus should be on making growth sustainable and balanced.

cueCards.title: Describe a time you solved a difficult problem
cueCards.prompt: Describe a time you solved a difficult problem
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about a problem at work that had nothing to do with paperwork and everything to do with people. A difficult problem I once solved involved a serious misunderstanding between two members of a team I was working with at the consultancy. One of them handled students' documents and the other handled visa files, and each felt the other was causing delays. Their disagreement had escalated to the point where it was affecting everyone's work. At first I was reluctant to get involved, because it was not really my responsibility, but I could see the whole office was suffering. Rather than taking sides, I decided to sit down with each of them separately to understand their perspectives. It quickly became clear that the whole conflict stemmed from poor communication rather than any real [[malice]]. I then arranged a calm conversation between them over tea, acting as a neutral [[mediator]]. It was a delicate situation that required a lot of [[tact]], but eventually they [[cleared the air]]. We also agreed on a simple shared checklist, so nobody would be left guessing about who was doing what. What I found most rewarding was seeing them work together productively again afterwards. Honestly, resolving that tension felt like a genuine achievement, and it taught me the value of listening carefully before [[jumping to conclusions]]. part3Samples.q: Is it better to confront a problem directly or avoid it?
part3Samples.answer: In most cases, I believe confronting a problem directly is far healthier. Avoidance may keep the peace temporarily, but the underlying issue tends to [[fester]] and grow worse over time. Addressing it calmly and early usually leads to genuine resolution. That said, direct confrontation should be done [[tactfully]], choosing the right moment, so it does not [[escalate]] into a bigger dispute.

part3Samples.q: What are the main causes of conflict between people?
part3Samples.answer: In my experience, most conflict [[stems from]] poor communication and misunderstanding rather than genuine [[malice]]. When people fail to express themselves clearly or make assumptions about others' intentions, friction inevitably arises. Differences in values, competition over resources and simple [[miscommunication]] are also common triggers. part3Samples.answer: I am cautiously optimistic. It helps to focus on the specific issue rather than attacking the person, and to seek a compromise where possible. In some cases, involving a [[neutral third party]] as a [[mediator]] can be [[invaluable]]. Ultimately, a willingness to see the other's perspective is what unlocks resolution.

part3Samples.q: Some say soft skills should be taught in schools. Do you agree?

part3Samples.q: How do you define success?
part3Samples.answer: I think success is deeply personal and far broader than wealth or status. While financial security matters, defining success purely by money seems rather [[hollow]]. part3Samples.q: Is success more about hard work or luck?
part3Samples.answer: I believe it is a combination of both, though hard work is the factor within our control. Undeniably, luck plays a role, such as being born into favourable circumstances or being in the right place at the right time. However, hard work, persistence and seizing opportunities are what allow people to [[capitalise on]] that luck. So while luck can open doors, it is usually [[diligence]] and determination that [[sustain]] lasting success.

part3Samples.q: Why do some people become more ambitious than others?
part3Samples.answer: Ambition is shaped by a mix of factors. Upbringing plays a big role; children encouraged to aim high often [[internalise]] that drive. Personal experiences, including hardship, can also fuel a determination to succeed. Individual personality and the influence of role models matter too. Additionally, some are motivated by a fear of failure or a desire for recognition. So ambition usually stems from a blend of [[nurture]], personal circumstance and innate [[temperament]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think the definition of success is changing?
part3Samples.answer: Yes, I believe it is evolving, particularly among younger generations. The traditional [[markers of success]], like a high salary and status, are increasingly being questioned. Many now place greater value on work-life balance, wellbeing, purpose and experiences over pure material wealth. There is a growing recognition that a fulfilling life matters more than a merely impressive one. So the definition of success seems to be shifting towards something more [[holistic]] and meaningful than [[materialistic]].

part3Samples.q: Some say you are never too old to learn. Do you agree?

There are countless inspiring examples of people learning languages, instruments or even new careers late in life. part3Samples.q: Which soft skills do you think are most valuable in the workplace?
part3Samples.answer: In my view, communication is the single most valuable soft skill, since almost everything at work depends on it.
