part3Samples.q: Are soft skills or hard skills harder to learn?
part3Samples.answer: I would argue soft skills are generally harder to acquire. Hard skills, like using a software program, can be learned through structured courses relatively quickly. Soft skills, however, involve deeply ingrained habits and personality traits, so improving your communication or empathy requires sustained self-awareness and practice over years. They are more [[nuanced]] and [[subtle]], which is precisely why they are so [[prized]] by employers.

part3Samples.q: Why are communication skills so important at work?
part3Samples.answer: Communication is fundamental because it [[underpins]] almost every workplace activity. Clear communication prevents misunderstandings, which can otherwise cause costly errors and conflict. It enables effective teamwork, allows ideas to be shared persuasively, and builds strong relationships with clients and colleagues. Someone who communicates well can influence, lead and collaborate far more effectively. In essence, poor communication can [[derail]] even the most technically [[gifted]] team.

part3Samples.q: Will soft skills become more important as technology advances?
part3Samples.answer: I firmly believe they will. As artificial intelligence automates more technical and analytical tasks, the distinctly human skills, creativity, empathy, leadership and complex communication, will become increasingly valuable. These are precisely the abilities machines struggle to [[replicate]]. So paradoxically, the more technological the world becomes, the more [[premium]] employers are likely to place on these [[irreplaceable]] human qualities.

part3Samples.q: How can people develop their soft skills?
part3Samples.answer: Soft skills are developed mainly through practice and self-reflection. Seeking out situations that stretch you, like leading a project or public speaking, builds confidence and competence. Actively seeking honest feedback and observing people who excel at these skills is invaluable. Reading and formal training can help too. The key is to treat them as [[learnable]] skills that improve with [[deliberate]] effort, not fixed [[traits]].

part3Samples.q: Some say money is the best measure of success. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly disagree with this narrow view. While money is a tangible and convenient measure, and financial security certainly matters, equating it with success ignores far more important dimensions of a good life. Many wealthy people are deeply unhappy, while many people of [[modest means]] live rich, fulfilling lives. Reducing success to a bank balance seems [[reductive]] and [[misguided]]. True success, in my view, is measured by fulfilment, relationships and character, not currency.

Such a person may struggle to [[read social cues]], handle criticism, or manage their own reactions, which can damage relationships. They might come across as [[insensitive]] or provoke unnecessary conflict without even realising it. Over time, this can lead to isolation and repeated interpersonal [[friction]].

part3Samples.q: Will emotional intelligence become more important as technology advances?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly believe it will. cueCards.title: Describe a time you complained about something

So I would say that a great deal of our consumption is driven by [[manufactured]] wants rather than genuine necessity, which is quite [[wasteful]].

part3Samples.q: How has shopping changed with the rise of the internet?
part3Samples.answer: Online shopping has [[revolutionised]] the experience. It offers [[unparalleled]] convenience, allowing people to buy almost anything from home at any hour, with easy price comparison. This has, however, put pressure on traditional physical shops, many of which have struggled. The experience has become more efficient but arguably less social. So while the internet has made shopping far more convenient and accessible, it has also transformed our [[high streets]], not always for the better.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think advertising is so influential?
part3Samples.answer: Advertising is influential because it is sophisticated and [[pervasive]]. It cleverly taps into our emotions, insecurities and aspirations, associating products with happiness, status or belonging rather than mere function. Its sheer ubiquity means we are exposed to it constantly, which [[reinforces]] its messages. Modern targeted advertising is especially potent, as it is tailored precisely to our interests. So it shapes our desires far more than we consciously realise, subtly [[steering]] our behaviour.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will become more conscious consumers in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am cautiously hopeful. There is a growing awareness of the environmental and ethical impact of our purchases, and movements towards [[minimalism]], sustainability and ethical consumption are [[gaining momentum]]. Younger generations in particular seem more [[values-driven]] in their spending. However, the powerful forces of marketing and convenience remain strong. So while I believe conscious consumption will increase, whether it becomes the norm depends on a genuine cultural shift.

part3Samples.q: How can people be encouraged to consume more responsibly?
part3Samples.answer: Education and awareness are key. Helping people understand the true environmental and social cost of their purchases can shift attitudes. Encouraging habits like buying quality over quantity, repairing rather than replacing, and choosing ethical brands makes a difference. Governments can also play a role through regulation and [[incentives]]. Ultimately, [[fostering]] a cultural value of [[sufficiency]] over excess, where we question whether we truly need something, is the most sustainable path.

cueCards.title: Describe a time you helped a stranger
cueCards.prompt: Describe a time you helped a stranger
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: I'd like to describe a small moment of kindness that happened in the main market in Sirajganj a few months ago. A time I helped a stranger was when I came across an elderly man who had stumbled and dropped his shopping on a busy street. There were vegetables and a bag of rice spread across the road, and rickshaws were [[weaving around]] him. Most people simply walked past, which I found rather [[disheartening]]. I stopped to help him gather his things and made sure he was not hurt. Luckily, apart from a small scrape on his hand, he was fine. He seemed a little shaken, so I stayed with him for a few minutes and offered to walk him to a nearby bench outside a tea stall. He was incredibly grateful, and we ended up having a lovely short chat; it turned out he was a retired schoolteacher who now lived alone, since his children had moved to Dhaka for work. What struck me was how such a small gesture clearly meant a great deal to him. Honestly, it took only a couple of minutes of my time, yet it felt genuinely meaningful. It reminded me that we often overlook small chances to be kind because we are so [[caught up in]] our own lives. That brief encounter left me feeling [[heartened]] for the rest of the day, and it made me more [[attentive]] to people around me who might need help. I still see him in the market sometimes, and he always waves.

followUps.q: Do you think people help strangers less than in the past?
followUps.answer: In big cities, perhaps. Everyone is in a hurry and slightly wary of strangers. In smaller towns like mine, people still tend to stop, although even here I notice it happening less.

followUps.q: Has anyone ever helped you when you were a stranger somewhere?
followUps.answer: Yes, when I got lost in Chattogram once, a shopkeeper drew me a little map and pointed me in the right direction. I have never forgotten how kind he was.

part3: Where do you think people get their moral values from?
Are moral values the same across all cultures?
What happens to a society when it loses its moral values?
How might moral values change in the future?
How can strong moral values be encouraged in young people?
Some say technology is the main cause of modern loneliness. Do you agree?

part3Samples.q: Where do you think people get their moral values from?
part3Samples.answer: I believe our moral values come from a combination of sources. Our upbringing and family are hugely influential, [[instilling]] early notions of right and wrong. Culture, religion and society also shape our ethics, as do our own experiences and reflection as we mature. Some argue there is even an innate, universal sense of fairness. So our values are essentially [[absorbed]] from those around us and then [[refined]] through personal reflection over time.

part3Samples.q: Are moral values the same across all cultures?
part3Samples.answer: I think there is a fascinating mix of universal and culturally specific values. Certain core principles, like [[prohibitions]] against murder or valuing honesty and care for others, appear across virtually all cultures, suggesting a shared moral foundation. However, many values, such as attitudes to family, [[individualism]] or specific customs, vary considerably between cultures. So while there are some universal [[moral constants]], ethics are also significantly shaped by cultural context.

part3Samples.q: What happens to a society when it loses its moral values?
part3Samples.answer: A society that loses its shared [[moral compass]] tends to suffer serious consequences. Trust between people erodes, corruption and dishonesty can flourish, and social cohesion breaks down. Without agreed ethical standards, laws alone struggle to maintain order, and self-interest can dominate at the expense of the common good. So a strong shared morality acts as invisible [[social glue]]; its erosion can lead to division, [[distrust]] and dysfunction.

part3Samples.q: How might moral values change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I expect our moral frameworks to be tested and expanded by new challenges. Advances in technology, such as artificial intelligence and genetic engineering, will raise entirely new [[ethical dilemmas]] we have never faced before. Growing awareness may also extend our moral concern further, perhaps towards animals, the environment and future generations. So I anticipate that ethics will continue to [[evolve]], becoming broader in scope as we [[grapple with]] unprecedented moral questions.

part3Samples.q: How can strong moral values be encouraged in young people?
part3Samples.answer: The most powerful way is through example, since children learn ethics primarily by observing the adults around them. Parents and teachers who [[model integrity]], kindness and honesty have a profound influence. Open discussion of ethical issues, encouraging empathy, and involving young people in helping others also help. Rather than simply lecturing, allowing them to [[reason through]] moral situations builds genuine understanding. So values are best [[instilled]] through consistent example and guided reflection.

part3Samples.q: Some say technology is the main cause of modern loneliness. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I partly agree, but I think it is too simplistic to blame technology alone. It is true that excessive screen time can replace real interaction and [[foster]] unhealthy comparison. However, technology can also connect isolated people, such as those far from family. So the technology itself is [[neutral]]; the real issue is how we use it. The deeper causes lie in broader [[societal]] changes.

cueCards.title: Describe a time you changed your plan
cueCards.prompt: Describe a time you changed your plan
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about a trip that did not go to plan at all, but still turned out well. A time I had to change my plans quite suddenly was when a long-awaited trip with friends fell through at the last minute due to bad weather. The original plan was to spend three days in Cox's Bazar, but a cyclone warning was issued the day before we were due to leave, and our bus was cancelled. I had been looking forward to it for weeks, so the cancellation was initially a [[crushing disappointment]]. Rather than sulking about it, though, we decided to be flexible and [[make the best of]] the situation. We ended up organising a day trip to a char, one of the sandy river islands in the Jamuna, something none of us had planned. We hired a small boat, packed a picnic and spent the afternoon walking on the sandbanks and watching the fishermen bring in their nets. To our surprise, it turned out to be a wonderful day, arguably better than the original plan. What I took from it was that rigidity often leads to frustration, whereas being [[adaptable]] opens up unexpected opportunities. It was a good reminder that plans [[falling apart]] is not always a bad thing. Honestly, some of my best experiences have come from [[spontaneous]] changes like that, and I remember feeling surprisingly content on the boat home as the sun went down. I now try to hold my plans a little more loosely and stay open to whatever comes.

followUps.q: Did you manage to go to Cox's Bazar later?
followUps.answer: Yes, about three months later, once the weather had settled. It was lovely, but funnily enough, when we talk about that year, it is usually the day on the char that we remember.

followUps.q: Do you usually plan your trips carefully?
followUps.answer: I plan the essentials, like transport and where to stay, but I leave the rest fairly open. Too much planning makes a trip feel like work, and the unexpected moments are often the best.

part3: Why do you think people enjoy travelling?
How has travel changed compared to the past?
What effects does tourism have on local communities?
How do you think tourism will change in the future?
How can the negative impacts of tourism be reduced?
Some say hobbies should be useful, not just for fun. Do you agree?

part3Samples.q: Why do you think people enjoy travelling?
part3Samples.answer: People travel for a wonderful variety of reasons. Fundamentally, I think it satisfies a deep human curiosity and desire to escape routine. Experiencing new cultures, landscapes and cuisines is genuinely [[enriching]] and broadens one's perspective. Travel also offers relaxation, adventure and the chance to create lasting memories. For me, the greatest value is how it makes you more [[open-minded]] and [[appreciative]] of the world's incredible diversity.

part3Samples.q: How has travel changed compared to the past?
part3Samples.answer: Travel has been transformed almost beyond recognition. In the past, it was expensive, slow and largely a privilege of the wealthy. Today, [[budget airlines]] and the internet have made it far more accessible and easy to organise, leading to mass tourism. We can now reach distant corners of the globe in hours. While this democratisation is positive, it has also led to [[overcrowding]] at popular sites and a more [[superficial]], hurried style of travel.

part3Samples.q: What effects does tourism have on local communities?
part3Samples.answer: Tourism has profound and mixed effects. Economically, it can bring vital income and jobs, boosting the local economy significantly. However, it can also cause problems: it may [[inflate]] local prices, strain infrastructure, and sometimes lead to the [[commodification]] of culture, where traditions are performed purely for tourists. Environmental damage is another concern. So while tourism offers real economic benefits, it must be managed [[sustainably]] to avoid harming the very communities it supports.

part3Samples.q: How do you think tourism will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I foresee several shifts. Growing environmental awareness will likely make sustainable and [[eco-tourism]] far more popular, as people seek to [[minimise their impact]]. Technology, such as virtual reality, might offer new ways to experience places remotely. There may also be a move towards more meaningful, [[immersive]] travel over mass tourism. So I expect the future of travel to be more conscious, more personalised, and hopefully more responsible.

part3Samples.q: How can the negative impacts of tourism be reduced?
part3Samples.answer: Sustainable tourism practices are the answer. Governments can manage visitor numbers at fragile sites through limits or timed entry to prevent overcrowding. Promoting [[lesser-known]] destinations helps spread the benefits and reduce pressure on [[hotspots]]. Encouraging tourists to respect local cultures and environments, and to support local businesses, is also key. Essentially, prioritising sustainability over sheer volume can [[mitigate]] the harm while preserving the benefits.

part3Samples.q: Some say hobbies should be useful, not just for fun. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I respectfully disagree with that as a rule. While hobbies that build skills are certainly valuable, I firmly believe a hobby does not need to be productive to be [[worthwhile]]. The primary purpose of leisure is enjoyment, relaxation and wellbeing, and something that brings pure joy is valuable in itself. Insisting that all free time be useful reflects an overly [[utilitarian]] mindset. Sometimes, doing something simply for pleasure is [[exactly the point]].

cueCards.title: Describe a time you got lost somewhere
cueCards.prompt: Describe a time you got lost somewhere
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about the time I got lost in Chattogram, a city I had never visited before. It was about three years ago, when I went there with some university friends on a short study tour. A time I got hopelessly lost was during that trip, when I wandered off from my group one afternoon to explore the older part of the city near the port. Before long I realised I had no idea where I was, and to make matters worse, my phone battery had died. I felt a growing sense of [[panic]] as the narrow lanes all started to look the same, and I was completely [[disoriented]]. Rather than making it worse by rushing, I forced myself to [[keep a level head]] and think logically. I asked a friendly shopkeeper for directions, and although his local dialect was quite hard for me to follow, he was very patient and even drew me a little map on a scrap of paper. Eventually I found my way back to a landmark I recognised and reunited with my relieved group, who had been searching for me for nearly an hour. I felt rather [[sheepish]], and my friends teased me about it for the rest of the trip. Looking back, although it was stressful at the time, it turned into a strangely memorable [[escapade]]. It taught me to pay more attention to my surroundings and always memorise a few key landmarks. Honestly, getting lost made me a more careful traveller.

followUps.q: Do you usually rely on your phone for directions?
followUps.answer: Yes, far too much, if I am honest. Since that day, though, I always make sure my phone is charged, and I try to notice a couple of landmarks wherever I go.

followUps.q: Have you been back to Chattogram since then?
followUps.answer: Once, for work, to attend an education fair. This time I stayed close to the venue, but I did recognise the lane where the kind shopkeeper had helped me, which made me smile.

part3Samples.q: Some say people cannot live without their phones now. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I think that is an exaggeration, but it contains an [[uncomfortable truth]]. Obviously, people survived perfectly well before phones, so it is not a literal dependency. However, phones have become so [[integral]] to how we work, navigate and communicate that living without one would be genuinely inconvenient and isolating in modern society. So while we could live without them, our society has become so [[reliant]] on them that it would be a difficult adjustment.

cueCards.title: Describe a time you celebrated a special occasion
cueCards.prompt: Describe a time you celebrated a special occasion
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: I'd like to describe a celebration that my whole family still talks about. A special occasion I celebrated with real joy was my parents' wedding anniversary, which my sisters and I organised as a surprise last year. We had been planning it secretly for weeks, which made the anticipation even more exciting, and keeping it from my mother was not easy, because she notices everything. My elder sister came from Dhaka with her husband and their two children, and my grandparents travelled in from the village. We decorated the house, invited close relatives and arranged all their favourite food, including the biryani my father loves. My younger sister was in charge of the cake, and I handled the guest list. The look of genuine surprise and delight on my parents' faces was absolutely [[priceless]]. It was a wonderfully [[heartwarming]] evening, full of laughter, old stories and a few happy tears. My grandmother even told us how my parents first met, which none of us had heard before. What made it so special was seeing the whole family come together to honour them. In our increasingly busy lives, these gatherings feel [[few and far between]], and so all the more precious. My four-year-old nephew kept trying to blow out the candles before anyone else, which had everyone in fits of laughter. I remember feeling an overwhelming sense of gratitude and love that evening. Honestly, occasions like this remind me of what truly matters. The whole event was thoroughly [[unforgettable]], and I think it meant just as much to us as it did to my parents. It is a night I will always [[treasure]].

followUps.q: Do you often celebrate special occasions with your family?
followUps.answer: Yes, especially Eid, when everyone tries to be together. We are a close-knit family, so even smaller occasions like birthdays usually end with a big dinner at home.

followUps.q: What did your parents say about the surprise?
followUps.answer: My father was lost for words, which is rare for him. My mother cried a little and then immediately started worrying whether there was enough food for everyone, which made us all laugh.

part3: Why do you think festivals are important?
How are festivals celebrated differently now compared to the past?
What effect does commercialisation have on traditional festivals?

How can the true spirit of festivals be preserved?
Some believe children should care for their parents in old age. Do you agree?

part3Samples.q: Why do you think festivals are important?
part3Samples.answer: Festivals serve several important purposes. They provide a much-needed break from routine and an occasion for joy and celebration. More deeply, they reinforce cultural identity and bring communities and families together in shared rituals. They also pass traditions from one generation to the next. In my view, this sense of [[collective]] celebration and [[belonging]] is something people fundamentally need, which is why festivals remain so [[cherished]] across cultures.

part3Samples.q: How are festivals celebrated differently now compared to the past?
part3Samples.answer: The essence remains, but the style has changed. In the past, celebrations were often simpler and more community-focused, with everyone participating directly. Today, festivals have become more [[commercialised]], with an emphasis on spending and consumption. Technology has also changed things; people now share their celebrations on social media. So while festivals are still meaningful, some argue they have lost a degree of [[authenticity]], becoming more about [[consumerism]] than genuine tradition.

part3Samples.q: What effect does commercialisation have on traditional festivals?
part3Samples.answer: The effect is [[double-edged]]. On one hand, commercialisation can boost the economy and [[raise a festival's profile]], making it more widely known. On the other, it can [[dilute]] the festival's original spiritual or cultural meaning, reducing it to a shopping opportunity. The genuine sentiment behind the celebration can get lost amid the advertising and pressure to spend. So it brings visibility, but often at the cost of authenticity and true significance.

part3Samples.q: Do you think traditional festivals will remain popular in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I believe they will, though they will continue to evolve. While the way we celebrate may change, the fundamental human need for community, joy and shared meaning will ensure festivals [[endure]]. There may even be a [[resurgence]] of interest as people seek authenticity in an increasingly digital world. So while some may become more modernised or commercial, I think the core appeal of festivals will [[persist]] and remain relevant for generations.

part3Samples.q: How can the true spirit of festivals be preserved?
part3Samples.answer: Preserving the spirit requires conscious effort. Emphasising the values behind the festival, such as togetherness, gratitude or reflection, rather than just the material aspects, is important. Involving young people in traditional practices and explaining their meaning helps too. Communities can prioritise participation over consumption. Essentially, if we consciously focus on the [[essence]] of a festival rather than its [[commercial trappings]], its true spirit can [[thrive]].

part3Samples.q: Some believe children should care for their parents in old age. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly agree, at least in principle. In my culture, caring for elderly parents is seen as a moral [[obligation]], a way of repaying the sacrifices they made. That said, I recognise this is not always practical in modern life, so it need not mean living together. What matters is that the elderly are not [[neglected]] and retain their [[dignity]].

cueCards.title: Describe a time you had to wait for something
cueCards.prompt: Describe a time you had to wait for something
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about a wait that felt far longer than it really was. A time I had to wait anxiously was for the results of an important exam, which took several weeks to arrive. It was my HSC exam, the final exam at the end of college, and my university plans depended on it. That waiting period was genuinely [[agonising]], because so much depended on the outcome, and there was absolutely nothing I could do to change it. I waited about two months in total. Every day felt longer than the last, and I found myself constantly checking for updates. To distract myself, I tried to stay busy with hobbies and spending time with friends, which helped a little. I read a lot of novels, played cricket in the evenings and took long walks by the river with my father. Still, the [[suspense]] was always there, [[lurking]] in the back of my mind. I remember trying to prepare myself mentally for both possible outcomes, which was difficult. On the day they were published online, my whole family crowded round the computer with me. When the results finally came and turned out to be positive, the relief was [[immense]], and my mother immediately handed out sweets to the neighbours. What that experience taught me was how to cope with uncertainty, which is a genuinely useful skill. Honestly, learning to [[sit with that discomfort]] rather than let it consume me was invaluable. I now handle waiting far better than I used to, knowing that worrying rarely changes the result.

followUps.q: Are you usually a patient person?
followUps.answer: More than I used to be. I can wait calmly for most things now, but I still find traffic jams and slow internet surprisingly hard to tolerate, so there is room for improvement.

followUps.q: What do you usually do while waiting for something?
followUps.answer: I normally read. I always keep a book or an e-book on my phone, so if I am stuck waiting somewhere, the time passes far more pleasantly and I don't feel it is wasted.

part3: What do you think is the main purpose of education?

part3Samples.q: What do you think is the main purpose of education?
part3Samples.answer: In my view, education serves a dual purpose. On a practical level, it equips people with the knowledge and skills needed for employment. But more importantly, I believe its deeper purpose is to [[cultivate]] critical thinking and produce well-rounded, responsible citizens. Education should teach people how to think, not merely what to think. Sadly, many systems overemphasise [[rote learning]] at the expense of this broader [[enrichment]].

part3Samples.q: How is education today different from education in the past?
part3Samples.answer: The differences are considerable. In the past, education was largely teacher-centred, based on memorisation and strict discipline. Today, there is a much greater emphasis on interactive, student-centred learning, and technology has [[revolutionised]] access to information. Learning is now more [[collaborative]] and creative. However, I would argue that academic pressure and competition have also intensified, which is a rather [[double-edged]] development.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think exam results are given so much importance?
part3Samples.answer: I think it stems from the need for a seemingly objective way to measure ability and allocate opportunities. Exams provide a convenient, [[quantifiable]] benchmark for universities and employers. However, this [[overreliance]] on results can be [[counterproductive]], as it encourages students to memorise for tests rather than truly understand. It also fails to capture vital qualities like creativity, which are far harder to quantify.

part3Samples.q: How do you think education will change in the next 20 years?
part3Samples.answer: I anticipate dramatic changes, largely driven by technology. Personalised, AI-assisted learning could [[tailor]] lessons to each student's pace, and online education will make quality teaching far more accessible globally. The traditional classroom may become less central. There will likely also be a stronger focus on [[adaptable]] skills, given that people will need to [[reskill]] repeatedly throughout their careers.

part3Samples.q: How could education systems be improved?
part3Samples.answer: There are several improvements I would suggest. Firstly, systems should place less emphasis on high-stakes exams and more on continuous, practical assessment. Secondly, curricula should be [[modernised]] to include life skills such as financial literacy and emotional intelligence. Finally, investing in teacher training and reducing class sizes would allow for more [[personalised]] learning. The goal should be a more [[holistic]] and flexible model.

part3Samples.q: Some say happiness is a choice. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I partly agree, but with important reservations. There is real truth that our attitude, gratitude and how we respond to circumstances significantly influence our happiness, so mindset matters. However, saying happiness is simply a choice can be [[dismissive]] of those facing genuine hardship, mental illness or difficult circumstances beyond their control. So while we have some agency over our happiness, I think it is [[oversimplified]] to call it purely a choice, ignoring the [[structural]] and biological factors involved.

cueCards.title: Describe a time you made a promise to someone
cueCards.prompt: Describe a time you made a promise to someone
bullets: who you made the promise to
and how you felt about it

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about a promise I made to my younger sister, who means a great deal to me. A promise I made and worked hard to keep was when I assured her I would help her prepare for her exams. It was about a year ago, before her HSC exams, and she was struggling with accounting, which happens to be one of my stronger subjects from my BBA. At the time I was extremely busy at work, so it was a fairly bold commitment. She was quite anxious and had started to lose confidence, which worried all of us. As the weeks went on, keeping that promise became genuinely [[demanding]], because my own workload kept [[piling up]]. There were evenings when I was exhausted and tempted to cancel, but I felt a strong sense of [[obligation]] not to let her down. So I pushed through, spending several evenings a week going over her subjects with her at the dining table after dinner. I also made her a simple timetable so she could see her progress week by week. My mother kept us going with endless cups of tea. When she eventually did well, the pride I felt was [[immense]], and our bond grew even stronger. Keeping that promise meant missing a few cricket matches with friends, but I never regretted it for a moment. What I learned was that keeping a promise, especially an inconvenient one, is a real measure of [[character]]. Honestly, seeing how much my help meant to her made every tiring evening worthwhile. It reinforced my belief that your word should always mean something.

followUps.q: Do you think it is important to keep promises?
followUps.answer: Absolutely. If you break promises often, people stop trusting you, and that trust is very hard to win back. So I try not to promise anything unless I am sure I can deliver.

followUps.q: Does your sister still ask you for help with her studies?
followUps.answer: Sometimes, but less and less. She is at university now and very hard-working, so these days she is more likely to correct my mistakes than ask me to explain anything.

part3Samples.q: Why is honesty important in relationships?
part3Samples.answer: Honesty is really the [[bedrock]] of any healthy relationship. Without it, trust cannot exist, and trust is what allows people to feel safe and secure with one another. Even small lies, once discovered, can [[erode]] that foundation and breed suspicion. In my view, being truthful, even when it is difficult, is what gives a relationship genuine depth and [[resilience]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think people are more or less honest than they were in the past?
part3Samples.answer: That is a difficult question. I do not think human nature has fundamentally changed, but the opportunities for [[deception]] have multiplied with technology, from online scams to fake identities. At the same time, the internet has made it much harder to hide dishonesty, since [[misdeeds]] are quickly exposed. So perhaps we are no less honest, just more [[transparent]].

part3Samples.q: What happens to a society when trust in institutions breaks down?
part3Samples.answer: The consequences are deeply damaging. When people lose faith in institutions like government or the media, it breeds [[cynicism]] and division. Cooperation becomes difficult, conspiracy theories can [[flourish]], and social cohesion begins to unravel. Trust is essentially the glue that holds a society together, so its breakdown can lead to genuine [[instability]] and dysfunction.

part3Samples.q: Do you think it will be harder to trust information in the future?
part3Samples.answer: Unfortunately, I think it will. cueCards.title: Describe a time you were pleasantly surprised

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about a birthday that started badly and ended as one of my favourite days. When I got home in the evening, tired and expecting a quiet dinner, my friends and family jumped out and surprised me with a party. I was completely [[taken aback]]; I genuinely had no idea they had been planning it. It turned out my younger sister had organised the whole thing and had sworn everyone to secrecy. cueCards.title: Describe a time you had a disagreement with someone
cueCards.prompt: Describe a time you had a disagreement with someone

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about a disagreement with one of my closest friends, Rafi, whom I have known since school. A disagreement that I remember clearly was with him over how to handle a shared responsibility during a group trip to Sylhet last year. The two of us were in charge of the money and the plans, but we had quite different ideas about budgeting and planning, and the discussion became rather [[heated]]. We are both quite stubborn, and for a moment it felt as if the whole trip might be spoiled. He wanted to book comfortable hotels and see as much as possible, while I wanted to keep costs down so everyone could afford it. At the time, I felt genuinely frustrated because I was sure my approach was more sensible. However, once we both calmed down, we realised the argument was largely down to poor communication. We sat down and each explained our reasoning properly, which helped enormously. In the end we reached a [[compromise]] that combined the best of both ideas: simple guesthouses, but a couple of special day trips. What I learned was the importance of listening rather than simply trying to win the argument. Honestly, resolving it [[amicably]] actually strengthened our friendship rather than damaging it. It taught me that disagreements are a normal part of any close relationship, and how you handle them matters far more than the disagreement itself. I now try to stay far more [[open-minded]] during such moments, and to [[bite my tongue]] before saying something I might regret.

followUps.answer: Not often, and usually about small things like where to eat or which cricket team is better. Serious disagreements are rare, and when they happen, we try to talk them through calmly.

followUps.q: How did the trip go in the end?
followUps.answer: It went really well. The guesthouses were simple but clean, and the day trip to the tea gardens was the highlight. Rafi even admitted that my budget left us more money for good food.

part3Samples.q: What are the main causes of conflict between people?
part3Samples.answer: In my experience, most conflict [[stems from]] poor communication and misunderstanding rather than genuine [[malice]]. When people fail to express themselves clearly or make assumptions about others' intentions, friction inevitably arises. Differences in values, competition over resources and simple [[miscommunication]] are also common triggers. part3Samples.q: Do you think people will become better at resolving conflicts in the future?

cueCards.title: Describe a time you saw something interesting in the sky
cueCards.prompt: Describe a time you saw something interesting in the sky

sample.answer: I'd like to describe something I saw in the night sky a few years ago, which I still think about. Something genuinely interesting I once saw in the sky was a spectacular meteor shower during a stay at my grandparents' home in our ancestral village. The village is far from any city lights, which made the night sky incredibly clear. My cousin, who follows these things online, told me the shower was expected, so a group of us, including my younger sister, stayed up late and lay on a mat in the courtyard to watch. It was a cool, clear night in December, just after the rice harvest. When the first streaks of light shot across the sky, we were all completely [[mesmerised]]. It was a genuinely [[awe-inspiring]] sight, and the sheer scale of the universe suddenly felt very real. We lay there for over an hour, gasping each time a bright meteor appeared. Even my grandfather came out to join us for a while and told us about the stars he used to navigate by as a young man. What made it so special was the shared sense of wonder among us. Some of the younger cousins fell asleep on the mat, but I stayed awake until the very end. Honestly, in towns and cities we forget how [[magnificent]] the night sky can be. That experience left me feeling small in the best possible way, and it sparked a lasting fascination with astronomy. It is a memory I will always find genuinely [[humbling]], and it made me appreciate the [[unspoilt]] darkness of the countryside.

followUps.q: Do you often look at the stars?
followUps.answer: Not as often as I would like. In Sirajganj there is a bit too much light at night, but whenever we visit the village, I make a point of stepping outside after dinner to look up.

followUps.q: Would you like to learn more about astronomy?
followUps.answer: Yes, I would. I have started reading about it a little, and one day I would love to look through a proper telescope and see the rings of Saturn with my own eyes.

cueCards.title: Describe a time technology helped you solve a problem
cueCards.prompt: Describe a time technology helped you solve a problem

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about a time technology got me out of a tricky situation abroad. part3Samples.q: Why is it important to protect wildlife?
part3Samples.answer: Protecting wildlife is important for several profound reasons. Ecologically, every species plays a role in maintaining the [[delicate balance]] of ecosystems that humans ultimately depend on for clean air, water and food. There is also a strong ethical argument that we have a duty to protect other living creatures. Furthermore, [[biodiversity]] has immense scientific and economic value. So conservation is not merely sentimental; it is essential for [[ecological stability]] and our own survival.

part3Samples.q: Should we prioritise protecting animals or supporting human development?
part3Samples.answer: I reject the idea that these are truly in opposition, though tensions certainly arise. In the short term, development sometimes conflicts with conservation, and people's immediate needs are understandably a priority. However, in the long run, human development depends entirely on a healthy natural world. Destroying nature for short-term gain is ultimately [[self-defeating]]. So rather than choosing one over the other, I believe we must pursue sustainable development that [[reconciles]] both [[imperatives]].

part3Samples.q: What are the main reasons some animal species are becoming extinct?
part3Samples.answer: The primary driver is human activity. Habitat destruction, as forests and wild areas are cleared for agriculture and development, is the biggest threat, leaving animals nowhere to live. Poaching and overfishing directly deplete populations, while pollution and, increasingly, climate change disrupt ecosystems. So extinction is largely a tragic consequence of human [[encroachment]], [[exploitation]] and environmental [[degradation]], rather than natural causes.

part3Samples.q: Are you hopeful about the future of wildlife conservation?
part3Samples.answer: I hold a cautious hope. The threats are severe, and we are losing species at an [[alarming rate]], which is deeply concerning. However, there are genuine success stories where dedicated conservation efforts have brought species [[back from the brink]]. Growing public awareness, international cooperation and new technologies for monitoring wildlife are encouraging. So while the challenge is immense, I believe that with sufficient commitment, we can still preserve much of our [[natural heritage]].

part3Samples.q: What can be done to protect endangered species?
part3Samples.answer: A range of measures is required. Establishing and properly funding protected areas and national parks safeguards vital [[habitats]]. Enforcing strict anti-poaching laws and [[cracking down on]] illegal wildlife trade is crucial. International cooperation and treaties help protect [[migratory]] species. Supporting local communities so they benefit from conservation rather than exploitation is also key. Ultimately, addressing the root causes, like habitat loss and climate change, is essential for lasting protection and recovery.

part3Samples.q: Some say tourism does more harm than good to destinations. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I think it depends entirely on how it is managed. In some over-touristed places, the harm, from environmental damage to cultural erosion and inflated living costs, is undeniable and can indeed outweigh the benefits. However, when managed responsibly and sustainably, tourism can be a tremendous [[force for good]], funding conservation and lifting communities out of poverty. So I would not agree it is inherently harmful; the outcome [[hinges on]] responsible [[stewardship]] and planning.

The focus has shifted, in some cases, from [[togetherness]] to consumerism. That said, this is not universal, and the deeper meaning often survives beneath the commercial surface for those who seek it. So it is a real trend to resist, but not an [[irreversible]] one.

cueCards.title: Describe a time you were proud of a family member
cueCards.prompt: Describe a time you were proud of a family member
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about my younger sister, who is probably the most hard-working person I know. A time I felt enormously proud of a family member was when she finished at the top of her year in her HSC exams and received an award at her college's prize-giving ceremony last year. I had watched her study relentlessly for two years, often sacrificing her social life, so her success felt thoroughly [[well-deserved]]. The whole family went to the ceremony, and my parents were dressed in their best clothes. In our family, education has always been treated as something precious, so this meant a great deal to my parents. Sitting in the audience, I felt [[a lump in my throat]] as her name was called out for the special award. It was a genuinely [[emotional]] moment for the whole family, and my mother could not stop wiping her eyes. What made me so proud was not just the achievement itself, but the [[perseverance]] and discipline she had shown to get there. I remembered all the times she had doubted herself and kept going anyway, sometimes studying until two in the morning. Honestly, seeing her hard work pay off so publicly was one of the most [[uplifting]] experiences I have had. Afterwards, we went out for sweets and tea, and she could not stop smiling. I told her how proud I was, and I meant every word. It was a powerful reminder that dedication truly does pay off in the end, and it made me want to push myself harder too.

followUps.q: Do you and your sister get on well?
followUps.answer: Very well. We tease each other constantly, as siblings do, but she is also the person I talk to when something is bothering me. She gives surprisingly wise advice for her age.

followUps.q: How did your family celebrate her success?
followUps.answer: We had a special dinner at home, and my mother cooked all her favourite dishes. My father also phoned my grandparents in the village, who were absolutely delighted to hear the news.

part3Samples.q: Do you think family is as important today as it was in the past?
part3Samples.answer: I would say family remains just as important, though its form has changed. The emotional support and sense of [[belonging]] a family provides are timeless human needs. That said, modern life has certainly [[strained]] family bonds, with people moving away for work and spending less time together. So while its importance is [[undiminished]], sustaining it now requires more conscious effort.

part3Samples.q: How are family relationships different now compared to a generation ago?
part3Samples.answer: The biggest difference is probably the shift from large, extended families to smaller, more [[nuclear]] ones. In the past, several generations often lived under one roof, which fostered close bonds. Today, families are more [[dispersed]], and technology has, ironically, both connected and [[distanced]] us. Relationships are more equal now, but arguably less tightly knit.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think many families spend less time together nowadays?
part3Samples.answer: Several factors are at play. The demands of modern careers are [[relentless]], leaving parents exhausted and [[time-poor]]. On top of that, digital devices have become a real distraction, with family members often absorbed in their own screens even when in the same room. This gradual erosion of shared time is genuinely [[detrimental]] to close relationships.

part3Samples.q: How do you think family structures will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I anticipate that families will continue to become smaller and more diverse in form. We will likely see more single-parent households and [[blended families]] becoming [[commonplace]] and widely accepted. Technology may also allow [[far-flung]] relatives to stay connected more easily. Overall, I think the definition of family will grow more flexible and inclusive.

part3Samples.q: What can families do to stay close despite busy modern lives?
part3Samples.answer: I think the key is being [[intentional]] about spending time together. Simple rituals, like sharing at least one meal a day without phones, can make a real difference. Families could also [[prioritise]] occasional trips or activities that create shared memories. Ultimately, closeness does not happen by accident; it has to be actively [[nurtured]] amid the busyness.

part3Samples.q: Some say education should be free for everyone. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly agree, at least regarding basic and secondary education. I see education as a fundamental right and a [[public good]], not a privilege for those who can afford it. Free access promotes [[social mobility]] and reduces inequality. For higher education, the picture is more complex due to cost, but I believe it should at least be heavily [[subsidised]] so that talent, not wealth, determines opportunity.

cueCards.title: Describe a time you spent money on something special
cueCards.prompt: Describe a time you spent money on something special
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about the first really expensive thing I ever bought for myself. A time I spent money on something genuinely special was when I bought my first proper laptop with money I had saved myself. It was during my second year at university, and I paid for it with the money I earned from private tuition, teaching two schoolchildren in the evenings. It took me months of careful budgeting, as it was a significant amount for me at the time. I had to be quite [[frugal]], cutting back on unnecessary spending to reach my goal. I kept a small notebook where I wrote down every taka I saved. I stopped eating out, walked instead of taking rickshaws, and said no to a few trips with friends. When I finally had enough and walked into the shop to buy it, the feeling was incredibly [[satisfying]]. It was a mid-range model, nothing fancy, but to me it felt like the most valuable thing in the world. What made it so special was that I had earned it entirely through my own effort and patience, without asking my father for anything. It was not just a purchase; it felt like a genuine [[accomplishment]]. The laptop went on to become essential for my studies and work, so it turned out to be a wise investment too. Honestly, buying something you have saved hard for feels far more rewarding than a casual, [[impulsive]] purchase. That experience taught me the value of patience and [[delayed gratification]], a lesson I still carry with me.

followUps.q: Do you still have that laptop?
followUps.answer: I do, although it is quite slow now. My younger sister used it for her studies for a while, and these days it mostly sits on my desk at home for watching cricket highlights.

followUps.q: Are you good at saving money now?
followUps.answer: Reasonably good, yes. I put a little aside every month, partly because I would like to study abroad one day, and that goal makes it much easier to resist unnecessary spending.

part3: How important is money in life?
Is it better to save money or spend it?

part3Samples.q: How important is money in life?
part3Samples.answer: Money is [[undeniably]] important, but its importance has limits. It is essential for meeting our basic needs, providing security, and giving us freedom and opportunities, so I would never dismiss it. However, beyond a certain point of comfort, its ability to improve our happiness [[diminishes sharply]]. Health, relationships and purpose matter far more. So I see money as a vital tool and [[enabler]], but a poor ultimate goal in itself.

part3Samples.q: Is it better to save money or spend it?
part3Samples.answer: A healthy balance between the two is ideal. Saving is [[prudent]], providing security, peace of mind and the means to achieve future goals or weather emergencies. However, being excessively frugal can mean missing out on valuable experiences and enjoyment in the present. Spending wisely, particularly on experiences and things that genuinely enrich life, is worthwhile. So I favour disciplined saving combined with mindful spending, avoiding both reckless [[extravagance]] and joyless [[hoarding]].

part3Samples.q: What effect does the pursuit of wealth have on people?
part3Samples.answer: The pursuit of wealth has mixed effects. Positively, it can motivate hard work, innovation and achievement, driving both personal and economic progress. However, an excessive obsession with wealth can be corrosive, leading people to become greedy, materialistic, and to neglect relationships, ethics and their own wellbeing. It can foster perpetual dissatisfaction too. So while a healthy desire to prosper is fine, an [[all-consuming]] [[fixation]] on money can genuinely [[distort]] a person's values.

part3Samples.q: Do you think the gap between rich and poor will grow in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am concerned that it might, without deliberate intervention. Trends like automation, which may concentrate wealth among those who own the technology, and globalisation could widen the gap further. However, there is also growing awareness of inequality and political pressure to address it through [[progressive taxation]] and social policy. So the outcome is not [[predetermined]]; whether the gap widens or narrows will depend on the political choices societies make to [[redistribute]] opportunity.

part3Samples.q: What can be done to reduce poverty?
part3Samples.answer: Reducing poverty requires a comprehensive approach. Access to quality education and healthcare is fundamental, as it enables social mobility. Creating decent, well-paid jobs and ensuring fair wages tackles the [[root causes]]. Social [[safety nets]], like unemployment support, protect the most vulnerable. Progressive taxation can fund these efforts. Ultimately, empowering people with opportunities and skills, rather than mere [[handouts]], offers the most sustainable path out of poverty.

part3Samples.q: Some say buying things makes people happy. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I only partly agree. There is undeniably a short-term thrill in acquiring something new, so buying can bring a [[fleeting]] sense of pleasure. However, many people feel this happiness is temporary and superficial, quickly fading in a cycle sometimes called the [[hedonic treadmill]]. Lasting happiness tends to come from experiences and relationships, not possessions. So while shopping offers momentary joy, relying on it for happiness is ultimately [[hollow]] and unfulfilling.

cueCards.title: Describe a time you overcame a fear or challenge
cueCards.prompt: Describe a time you overcame a fear or challenge
bullets: what the fear or challenge was

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about a fear that followed me for most of my life. A significant fear I managed to overcome was my long-standing fear of water, which had followed me since childhood, when I slipped into a pond and swallowed a lot of water before someone pulled me out. Growing up beside the Jamuna, not being able to swim was both limiting and slightly embarrassing. For years I avoided swimming entirely, and I would always find an excuse when my friends went to the river. Eventually, about two years ago, I decided enough was enough, and my cousin in the village, who is a strong swimmer, offered to teach me in the pond behind my grandparents' house. The first few sessions were genuinely [[terrifying]], and I nearly gave up several times. My cousin, however, was incredibly patient and encouraging, which made all the difference. Every weekend we travelled to the village, and he would stand beside me in the water, holding me up until I found my balance. Slowly but surely, my confidence began to grow, and I became less [[petrified]] of deep water. The moment I finally swam from one side of the pond to the other unaided was absolutely [[exhilarating]], and my grandfather clapped from the bank. Overcoming that fear gave me a huge sense of achievement that went far beyond swimming itself. Honestly, it taught me that most fears shrink once you [[confront them head-on]] rather than avoiding them. It was a genuinely [[empowering]] experience, and it made me braver about tackling other things I had been putting off out of fear.

followUps.q: Do you swim regularly now?
followUps.answer: Not regularly, but whenever we visit my grandparents in summer, I go into the pond with my cousins. I am still not a strong swimmer, but I am no longer afraid, which is what matters.

followUps.q: Do you think children should learn to swim?
followUps.answer: Absolutely, especially in a country with so many rivers and ponds like Bangladesh. It is a basic safety skill, and it is much easier to learn as a child than as an adult.

part3: Do you think learning should continue throughout a person's life?

part3Samples.q: Do you think learning should continue throughout a person's life?
part3Samples.answer: Absolutely, I am a firm believer in lifelong learning. The idea that education ends when you leave school is completely [[outdated]], especially in today's fast-changing world. Continuing to learn [[keeps the mind sharp]], opens new opportunities and helps people adapt to change. Beyond practical benefits, I think curiosity and growth are essential to a fulfilling life. Learning should be a [[lifelong pursuit]], not a phase.

part3Samples.q: Is it easier to learn when you are young or when you are older?
part3Samples.answer: There are [[trade-offs]] at each stage. Young people generally absorb new information, especially languages, more easily, and have fewer competing responsibilities. However, adult learners bring focus, motivation and real-world experience that can make their learning more [[purposeful]] and efficient. So while children may have a biological advantage, adults [[compensate]] with discipline and context. Neither is simply easier; it depends on what is being learned.

part3Samples.q: Why is continuous learning becoming more necessary today?
part3Samples.answer: It is primarily because of the [[breakneck pace]] of technological change. Skills that were valuable a decade ago can quickly become [[obsolete]], and entirely new fields emerge constantly. To remain employable, workers must continually update their knowledge and [[reskill]]. The old model of one qualification lasting a whole career is no longer viable. In short, adaptability through learning has become a genuine necessity, not a luxury.

part3Samples.q: Do you think lifelong learning will become the norm in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am confident it will, [[out of sheer necessity]]. As careers become less linear and technology evolves ever faster, continuous learning and periodic reskilling will simply be part of working life. I anticipate more flexible, [[bite-sized]] courses and employer-sponsored training becoming [[commonplace]]. Society's whole conception of education will likely shift from a one-off event to an ongoing, lifelong process.

part3Samples.q: What prevents adults from continuing to learn, and how can this be solved?
part3Samples.answer: The main barriers are usually time, cost and lack of confidence. Busy working adults with family commitments struggle to find the time and money for further study. To address this, flexible online and part-time courses are invaluable, as is employer support through funded training. Governments could also offer [[subsidies]] or learning accounts. [[Dismantling]] these obstacles would make lifelong learning genuinely [[attainable]] for everyone.

part3Samples.q: Some say hobbies should be useful, not just for fun. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I respectfully disagree with that as a rule. While hobbies that build skills are certainly valuable, I firmly believe a hobby does not need to be productive to be [[worthwhile]]. The primary purpose of leisure is enjoyment, relaxation and wellbeing, and something that brings pure joy is valuable in itself. Insisting that all free time be useful reflects an overly [[utilitarian]] mindset. Sometimes, doing something simply for pleasure is [[exactly the point]].

cueCards.title: Describe a time something made you very happy
cueCards.prompt: Describe a time something made you very happy
bullets: and why it made you happy

sample.answer: I'd like to describe a day that made me happier than I had felt in a long time. A moment that filled me with genuine happiness was a spontaneous reunion with old friends I had not seen in years. We had all drifted apart after finishing our BBA, scattered by work and life, some in Dhaka, some in Chattogram and a couple abroad. Then, quite unexpectedly, one of them organised a get-together last winter, and almost everyone managed to come. I was so excited that I took the early morning bus from Sirajganj and arrived far too early. We met at a small restaurant near our old university campus in Dhaka. The moment we all saw each other again was absolutely [[heartwarming]]; it felt as though no time had passed at all. We spent hours [[reminiscing]], laughing about old memories and catching up on each other's lives. We even walked past our old classrooms and the tea stall where we used to spend far too much time. What made it so special was the [[effortless]], genuine warmth between us. In our busy adult lives, such [[carefree]] gatherings have become increasingly rare. I remember feeling completely content, surrounded by people who knew the real me. Honestly, that day reminded me how important old friendships are, and how easily we let them slip away. The whole reunion was thoroughly [[joyful]], and it left me determined to make more effort to stay in touch. We stayed so long that the restaurant staff eventually had to ask us, very politely, to leave. Since then, we have tried to meet at least once a year.

followUps.q: Do you find it hard to stay in touch with old friends?
followUps.answer: Sometimes, yes. Everyone is busy with work and family now. But a quick message or a phone call now and then keeps the connection alive, even if we can't meet often.

followUps.q: What else usually makes you happy?
followUps.answer: Simple things, mostly. A good dinner with my family, a cricket match on television, or a quiet walk by the river in the evening. I don't think happiness needs to be complicated.

part3Samples.q: Do you think it is better to have a few close friends or many acquaintances?
part3Samples.answer: I firmly believe that quality trumps quantity when it comes to friendship. A few close friends who genuinely understand you provide far deeper support than a large circle of [[superficial]] acquaintances. While it is useful to have a wide network for professional reasons, the emotional [[intimacy]] of a true friendship is something that simply cannot be [[replicated]] at scale.

part3Samples.q: How has technology changed the way people make friends?
part3Samples.answer: Technology has transformed it enormously. People now form friendships online with others across the globe, which was [[unimaginable]] a generation ago. This has made connection more [[accessible]], but I would argue these digital friendships can be more [[fragile]]. Meeting through a screen sometimes lacks the depth that comes from sharing real experiences face-to-face.

part3Samples.q: Why do some childhood friendships fade over time?
part3Samples.answer: I think it is largely a natural consequence of people growing and changing. As we mature, our interests, values and circumstances [[diverge]], and friends who once had everything in common may drift apart. Physical distance, when people move for work or study, only [[accelerates]] this. It is sad, but I see it as an almost [[inevitable]] part of life.

part3Samples.q: Do you think online friendships will replace face-to-face ones in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I doubt they will replace them entirely, but they will certainly become more significant. Online friendships are convenient and can be genuinely meaningful. However, humans are [[inherently]] social creatures who crave physical presence, so I believe in-person connection is [[irreplaceable]]. The most likely outcome is a [[hybrid]], where the two forms coexist and complement each other.

part3Samples.q: What can people do to maintain long-distance friendships?
part3Samples.answer: Consistent effort is really the crucial ingredient. Regular video calls and messages can [[keep a friendship alive]] despite the distance. I think it also helps to be [[deliberate]] about planning occasional visits, as nothing quite replaces meeting in person. Ultimately, both parties have to be committed, because a friendship that only one person [[sustains]] rarely lasts.

part3Samples.q: Some say happiness is a choice. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I partly agree, but with important reservations. There is real truth that our attitude, gratitude and how we respond to circumstances significantly influence our happiness, so mindset matters. However, saying happiness is simply a choice can be [[dismissive]] of those facing genuine hardship, mental illness or difficult circumstances beyond their control. So while we have some agency over our happiness, I think it is [[oversimplified]] to call it purely a choice, ignoring the [[structural]] and biological factors involved.

cueCards.title: Describe a time you stayed calm in a difficult situation
cueCards.prompt: Describe a time you stayed calm in a difficult situation
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about a moment when I surprised myself by staying calm. A time I managed to stay calm under real pressure was during a minor emergency at a family gathering, when my grandfather suddenly felt faint. It happened last Eid at my grandparents' village home, where the whole family had gathered for lunch. It was a very hot afternoon, and he had been busy greeting guests all morning. There was an immediate sense of alarm among everyone, and the atmosphere quickly became [[chaotic]], with people shouting advice from every direction. For some reason, I felt a strange sense of clarity and knew someone had to [[take charge]]. I calmly helped him sit down in the shade, brought water, and reassured everyone while we decided whether to call the local doctor. I also asked the children to step back and give him some air. My younger sister ran to fetch a hand fan, which helped a lot. Staying [[composed]] was not easy, because I love him dearly, but I knew that adding to the panic would only make things worse. Thankfully, he recovered within a few minutes, and it turned out he was simply tired and dehydrated. Afterwards, several relatives told me how [[reassuring]] my calmness had been, which surprised me. Honestly, I had not known I was capable of keeping such a level head. That experience taught me that staying [[rational]] in a crisis is a genuinely valuable ability, and it gave me more confidence in myself. My grandmother still mentions it whenever the family gets together.

followUps.q: Is your grandfather well now?
followUps.answer: Yes, thankfully. He is in his eighties but still remarkably sharp and active. Since that day, though, we make sure he rests more and drinks plenty of water, especially during the hot months.

followUps.q: Do you think staying calm can be learned?
followUps.answer: I think so, at least partly. Some people are naturally calmer, but practice and experience help a lot. The more difficult situations you face, the less likely you are to panic.

part3Samples.q: Do you think emotional intelligence is more important than academic intelligence?
part3Samples.answer: I would argue they are both important but serve different purposes. Academic intelligence may get you a qualification, but emotional intelligence is often what determines success in life and work, since it [[governs]] how you deal with people. The ability to manage emotions, empathise and communicate is genuinely [[indispensable]]. So while I would not rank one above the other, emotional intelligence is arguably more [[underrated]].

part3Samples.q: Are emotional skills valued more in some professions than others?
part3Samples.answer: Definitely. In [[people-facing]] roles such as teaching, healthcare or management, emotional intelligence is arguably the most important skill of all, as success depends on connecting with others. In more technical or [[solitary]] fields, like programming, it may seem less critical, though even there teamwork requires it. So while its importance varies, I think emotional skills are becoming increasingly valued [[across virtually every sector]].

part3Samples.q: What happens when a person lacks emotional intelligence?
part3Samples.answer: A lack of emotional intelligence can cause real difficulties, both personally and professionally. Such a person may struggle to [[read social cues]], handle criticism, or manage their own reactions, which can damage relationships. They might come across as [[insensitive]] or provoke unnecessary conflict without even realising it. Over time, this can lead to isolation and repeated interpersonal [[friction]].

part3Samples.q: Will emotional intelligence become more important as technology advances?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly believe it will. As machines and AI take over more analytical and routine tasks, the uniquely human skills, like empathy, creativity and emotional connection, will become more valuable, not less. These are precisely the abilities that technology cannot easily [[replicate]]. So [[paradoxically]], in an increasingly automated world, emotional intelligence may become one of our most [[sought-after]] qualities.

part3Samples.q: Can emotional intelligence be taught, and if so, how?
part3Samples.answer: Yes, I firmly believe it can be developed, even if some people are naturally more gifted. Self-awareness can be [[cultivated]] through reflection and honest feedback. Skills like active listening and empathy can be practised deliberately. Schools could help by [[incorporating]] emotional learning into the curriculum from an early age. Like any skill, it improves with [[conscious effort]] and practice, so it is far from fixed.

part3Samples.q: Some say great leaders are born, not made. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I largely disagree with that idea. While some people may have a natural [[charisma]] or confidence, I firmly believe leadership is a set of skills that can be learned and refined through experience. History is full of leaders who [[grew into the role]]. To claim leaders are simply born [[undermines]] the value of hard work and personal development.

cueCards.title: Describe a time you received help from someone
cueCards.prompt: Describe a time you received help from someone
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about someone who made a big difference to me when I first moved to Dhaka. A time I received invaluable help was when I was moving to the capital to start university and felt completely overwhelmed by everything. I had never lived away from home before, and the size and noise of the city frightened me a little. I remember my mother packing enough food for a week, as if Dhaka had no restaurants. A senior student from my hometown, who was already in his third year, went out of his way to help me settle in. My father had got his number from a family friend, and he met me at the bus station on my very first day. He helped me find accommodation, showed me around, and introduced me to people, which was incredibly [[generous]] of him. He even taught me which buses to take and where to find cheap but decent food near campus. Without his support, those first few weeks would have been far more [[daunting]] and lonely. What struck me was that he expected absolutely nothing in return; his kindness was completely [[selfless]]. I remember feeling deeply [[indebted]] to him, especially since we had barely known each other before. His help made an enormous difference to how quickly I adjusted. Honestly, the experience reminded me how much a small act of kindness can mean to someone in a vulnerable situation. followUps.q: Are you still in contact with him?
followUps.answer: Yes, we still message each other now and then. He works in Dhaka now, and whenever I visit my elder sister there, I try to meet him for a cup of tea.

followUps.q: Do you think people help each other more in small towns or big cities?
followUps.answer: In small towns, I think. People know each other, so helping feels natural. In big cities, people are kind too, but they are often too rushed to notice when someone is struggling.

part3Samples.q: Do you think living in a city is better than living in the countryside?
part3Samples.answer: It really depends on one's priorities and stage of life. Cities offer better job opportunities, [[amenities]], healthcare and a vibrant social life, which many find appealing. The countryside, by contrast, offers peace, clean air, space and a stronger sense of community. Personally, I appreciate the convenience of the city for now, but I can see the [[profound appeal]] of a quieter rural life later. So neither is objectively better; each suits different needs and [[temperaments]].

part3Samples.q: How have cities changed over the past few decades?
part3Samples.answer: Cities have transformed dramatically. They have grown enormously in size and population due to rapid urbanisation, becoming denser and often more [[congested]]. Skylines have risen with skyscrapers, and technology has made them smarter. However, this growth has often [[outpaced]] infrastructure, worsening problems like traffic, pollution and housing shortages. So while cities have become more developed and connected, this expansion has brought significant [[growing pains]].

part3Samples.q: Why do so many people move to cities?
part3Samples.answer: The primary driver is economic opportunity. Cities are hubs of employment, offering far more and better-paid jobs than rural areas, which is the biggest [[pull factor]]. They also provide superior access to education, healthcare and services. For many, the appeal of a more exciting, diverse lifestyle is also a draw. So this migration is largely driven by the search for a better standard of living, though it can place enormous [[strain]] on urban [[infrastructure]] and resources.

part3Samples.q: What do you think cities will be like in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I envision cities becoming smarter and, hopefully, greener. Technology will likely manage traffic, energy and services more efficiently through data. There is a strong push towards more sustainable, [[walkable]] cities with more green spaces and cleaner transport. However, they may also become even more crowded. So I am hopeful the cities of the future will be more [[liveable]] and sustainable, provided planning [[prioritises]] people and the environment over pure expansion.

part3Samples.q: How can cities be made better places to live?
part3Samples.answer: Thoughtful [[urban planning]] is the key. Investing in efficient, affordable public transport reduces congestion and pollution. Creating more green spaces and [[pedestrian areas]] improves wellbeing. Ensuring an adequate supply of affordable housing tackles inequality. Designing [[mixed-use]], walkable neighbourhoods fosters community. Essentially, cities become better when they are planned around the needs of people and the environment, rather than simply cars and commerce.

part3Samples.q: Some say social media has made friendships shallower. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I largely agree with that sentiment. Social media encourages us to [[accumulate]] hundreds of contacts while investing little in any of them. The constant highlight reels can also breed comparison rather than genuine connection. That said, it depends how you use it; for maintaining existing bonds it is useful. Used as a [[substitute]] for real intimacy, though, it does [[trivialise]] friendship.

cueCards.title: Describe a time you taught something to someone
cueCards.prompt: Describe a time you taught something to someone
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about the time I taught my mother to use a smartphone, which was more of a challenge than I expected. cueCards.title: Describe a time you had an interesting conversation
cueCards.prompt: Describe a time you had an interesting conversation

sample.answer: I'd like to describe a conversation with a complete stranger that I still think about. An interesting conversation I remember well was with an elderly man I happened to sit next to during a long train journey from Dhaka back to Sirajganj. It was about a year ago, and the train was delayed, so we had plenty of time. What began as polite small talk gradually turned into a genuinely [[fascinating]] discussion. He was a retired schoolteacher who had lived through decades of enormous change and shared stories that were both moving and eye-opening. He told me how, before the Jamuna bridge was built, crossing the river meant a long and unpredictable ferry journey, sometimes taking half a day. I found his perspective on life incredibly [[insightful]], shaped by experiences so different from my own. Time seemed to fly by as we talked about history, family and how much the world had changed. He was also curious about my work and asked me lots of questions about why so many young people want to study abroad. What made it so [[thought-provoking]] was how open and reflective he was with a complete stranger. By the end of the journey, I felt as though I had learned more than I would from any book. Honestly, that conversation reminded me how much wisdom ordinary people carry, if only we take the time to listen. It was a wonderfully [[enriching]] encounter, and it made me more willing to [[strike up]] conversations with people I do not know.

followUps.answer: More than I used to. On trains and buses I sometimes start a conversation if the other person seems friendly. Not everyone wants to chat, of course, so I try to read the situation first.

followUps.q: Who do you usually enjoy talking to the most?
followUps.answer: My grandfather, probably. He has a story for everything and a very dry sense of humour. Whenever we visit the village, I end up sitting with him for hours.

cueCards.title: Describe a time you took a risk
cueCards.prompt: Describe a time you took a risk
