sample.answer: I'd like to talk about the biggest professional risk I have taken so far. A significant risk I once took was leaving a secure position to join a small, unproven education consultancy that had only just opened. I had been working in the accounts office of a large company for a few months after my BBA, which was safe but, honestly, quite dull. It was a genuinely [[daunting]] decision, because the new company had no guarantee of success and I was giving up stability. Everyone around me thought I was being [[reckless]], which made me doubt myself at times. My mother kept asking whether I was sure, almost every evening at dinner. However, I felt a strong pull towards the opportunity, because I genuinely wanted to help students study abroad, and I decided to trust my instincts. The early months were certainly [[turbulent]]; we had very few clients, and there were moments when I feared I had made a terrible mistake. Gradually, though, the company [[found its feet]], and the experience turned out to be one of the most rewarding of my career so far. What I gained in skills and confidence was [[immeasurable]]. Honestly, taking that leap taught me that calculated risks are sometimes necessary for real growth. It reinforced my belief that playing it safe is not always the wisest choice. followUps.answer: Not really. I am quite careful by nature, and I like to think things through. But I have learned that a well-considered risk can be worth taking, especially when you are young.

part3Samples.q: Why do many people change careers during their lives now?
part3Samples.answer: Several factors drive this. The job market is far more [[volatile]] than in the past, so lifelong employment in one company is increasingly rare. People also have higher expectations of finding meaningful work, and are more willing to [[pursue]] fulfilment. part3Samples.answer: I believe jobs involving skills that machines cannot easily replicate will be most valuable. Many wealthy people are deeply unhappy, while many people of [[modest means]] live rich, fulfilling lives. Reducing success to a bank balance seems [[reductive]] and [[misguided]]. cueCards.title: Describe a time you got up very early
cueCards.prompt: Describe a time you got up very early

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about a morning when I got up far earlier than I ever normally would. A time I got up unusually early was to watch the sunrise from a hilltop during a short trip to Bandarban with friends, about two years ago. We had to wake at around four in the morning, which was genuinely [[brutal]], especially as none of us are naturally early risers. The reason was simple: people had told us that the sunrise over the hills, with clouds drifting below you, was something you had to see at least once. Half asleep, we made the climb in the dark, questioning why we had agreed to it, with only our phone torches to guide us. Our guesthouse owner had kindly woken us with hot tea before we set off. It was surprisingly cold, and I remember wishing I had brought a thicker jacket. But the moment the sun began to rise over the horizon, all the tiredness [[melted away]]. The view was absolutely [[breathtaking]], with the sky shifting through shades of orange and pink, and a sea of clouds stretching out beneath us. It was a genuinely [[serene]] moment, and we stood there in near silence, simply taking it in. What made it so worthwhile was that we had earned that view through real effort. Honestly, that early start turned out to be the [[crowning moment]] of the whole trip. It taught me that sometimes the best moments require sacrificing a bit of comfort, and I would happily do it again.

followUps.q: Are you usually an early riser?
followUps.answer: Not naturally. On working days I get up around seven, which is early enough for me. At the weekend I try to sleep in a little, although the call to prayer usually wakes me anyway.

followUps.q: Do you think getting up early is good for people?
followUps.answer: For many people, yes. The morning is quiet and you can get a lot done before the day becomes busy. But I think it depends on the person, since some people genuinely work better at night.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think people enjoy travelling?
part3Samples.answer: People travel for a wonderful variety of reasons. Fundamentally, I think it satisfies a deep human curiosity and desire to escape routine. Experiencing new cultures, landscapes and cuisines is genuinely [[enriching]] and broadens one's perspective. Travel also offers relaxation, adventure and the chance to create lasting memories. For me, the greatest value is how it makes you more [[open-minded]] and [[appreciative]] of the world's incredible diversity.

part3Samples.q: How has travel changed compared to the past?
part3Samples.answer: Travel has been transformed almost beyond recognition. In the past, it was expensive, slow and largely a privilege of the wealthy. Today, [[budget airlines]] and the internet have made it far more accessible and easy to organise, leading to mass tourism. We can now reach distant corners of the globe in hours. While this democratisation is positive, it has also led to [[overcrowding]] at popular sites and a more [[superficial]], hurried style of travel.

part3Samples.q: What effects does tourism have on local communities?
part3Samples.answer: Tourism has profound and mixed effects. Economically, it can bring vital income and jobs, boosting the local economy significantly. However, it can also cause problems: it may [[inflate]] local prices, strain infrastructure, and sometimes lead to the [[commodification]] of culture, where traditions are performed purely for tourists. Environmental damage is another concern. So while tourism offers real economic benefits, it must be managed [[sustainably]] to avoid harming the very communities it supports.

part3Samples.q: How do you think tourism will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I foresee several shifts. Growing environmental awareness will likely make sustainable and [[eco-tourism]] far more popular, as people seek to [[minimise their impact]]. Technology, such as virtual reality, might offer new ways to experience places remotely. There may also be a move towards more meaningful, [[immersive]] travel over mass tourism. So I expect the future of travel to be more conscious, more personalised, and hopefully more responsible.

part3Samples.q: How can the negative impacts of tourism be reduced?
part3Samples.answer: Sustainable tourism practices are the answer. Governments can manage visitor numbers at fragile sites through limits or timed entry to prevent overcrowding. Promoting [[lesser-known]] destinations helps spread the benefits and reduce pressure on [[hotspots]]. Encouraging tourists to respect local cultures and environments, and to support local businesses, is also key. Essentially, prioritising sustainability over sheer volume can [[mitigate]] the harm while preserving the benefits.

I had done well at college, so I assumed university would be just as easy, and I spent far too much time with friends. I remember phoning my father and struggling to tell him. At first I felt quite [[demoralised]], but after some reflection I realised the failure was entirely my own doing. Rather than dwelling on it, I decided to treat it as a [[wake-up call]]. I completely changed my study habits, becoming far more [[disciplined]] and organised, and I started reviewing my notes every evening instead of cramming at the last minute. The next time around, my results improved dramatically, which proved the lesson had sunk in. Honestly, that early failure was one of the most [[instructive]] experiences of my life. cueCards.title: Describe a special meal you had
cueCards.prompt: Describe a special meal you had

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about a meal that, for me, sums up what Eid is really about. A special meal that stands out in my memory was a large family feast during Eid last year, prepared mostly by my mother and grandmother. We celebrated at my grandparents' home in our ancestral village, and the whole extended family gathered there, which is increasingly rare these days. My elder sister came from Dhaka with her husband and children, and my uncles and cousins came too. My job was to help my grandfather greet the guests and make sure everyone had a seat. The table was [[laden with]] traditional dishes, like beef curry, chicken roast, polao and several kinds of sweets, and the aromas alone were [[mouthwatering]]. What made the meal so special was not just the food, though it was absolutely delicious, but the sense of togetherness. We spent hours eating, talking and laughing, with several generations gathered around one table, from my grandfather in his eighties to my four-year-old nephew. There is something deeply [[comforting]] about a home-cooked meal shared with people you love. In our busy lives, such [[unhurried]] gatherings feel genuinely precious. I remember feeling completely content, surrounded by family and good food. After lunch, the older men sat in the courtyard drinking tea while the children played. Honestly, meals like that are about far more than eating; they are about connection and belonging. It is a [[treasured]] memory, and it reminds me that the best meals are the ones shared with the people who matter most. I am already looking forward to the next Eid.

followUps.q: Can you cook any of those dishes yourself?
followUps.answer: Only a simple chicken curry, I am afraid. The Eid dishes take real skill and a lot of time, so I leave them to my mother and grandmother and happily do the washing up instead.

followUps.q: Do you prefer eating at home or in restaurants?
followUps.answer: At home, definitely. Restaurants are nice for a change, but nothing compares to my mother's cooking, and eating together at home feels far more relaxed and personal.

part3Samples.q: How important is food to a country's culture?
part3Samples.answer: Food is absolutely central to culture, in my view. It is far more than mere [[sustenance]]; it reflects a nation's history, geography, values and social customs. Sharing a meal is a universal expression of hospitality and community. Traditional dishes carry deep [[sentimental]] and cultural significance, passed down through generations. So I would say cuisine is one of the most [[tangible]] and beloved expressions of a country's identity.

part3Samples.q: How have people's eating habits changed over the years?
part3Samples.answer: Eating habits have changed considerably. In the past, people mostly ate home-cooked, seasonal and local food, often together as a family. Today, busy lifestyles have led to more processed food, takeaways and eating [[on the go]], often alone. [[Portion sizes]] have grown, and international cuisine is now widely available. While this offers more variety and convenience, I think it has come at some cost to health and the [[communal]] nature of dining.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think fast food has become so popular?
part3Samples.answer: Its popularity comes down to a few key factors. Firstly, it is convenient and quick, which suits our increasingly busy, time-poor lifestyles. Secondly, it is relatively cheap and consistently tasty, engineered to appeal to our [[cravings]]. Aggressive marketing has also made it [[ubiquitous]] and aspirational. Unfortunately, this convenience comes at a cost, as many argue its popularity has contributed to rising rates of [[obesity]] and related health problems.

part3Samples.q: How do you think the way we eat will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I anticipate significant changes driven by health and sustainability concerns. Plant-based diets and [[alternative proteins]], like lab-grown meat, are likely to become far more [[mainstream]] as we address the environmental impact of food. Technology may also personalise nutrition. Hopefully, there will be a renewed appreciation for healthy, [[sustainable]] eating. So our diets may become more conscious and innovative, balancing convenience with health and the planet.

part3Samples.q: What can be done to encourage people to eat more healthily?
part3Samples.answer: A range of measures could help. Education about nutrition from a young age is fundamental, so people can make informed choices. Making healthy food more affordable and accessible, while perhaps [[taxing unhealthy options]], can shift behaviour. Clear [[food labelling]] and restrictions on junk food advertising, especially to children, would also help. Ultimately, creating an environment where the healthy choice is the easy, [[appealing]] choice is the most effective approach.

part3Samples.q: Some say festivals have become too commercial. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I largely agree with this observation. Many festivals now seem dominated by advertising, sales and pressure to spend, which can [[overshadow]] their original cultural or spiritual meaning. The focus has shifted, in some cases, from [[togetherness]] to consumerism. That said, this is not universal, and the deeper meaning often survives beneath the commercial surface for those who seek it. So it is a real trend to resist, but not an [[irreversible]] one.

cueCards.title: Describe a time you visited a place for the first time
cueCards.prompt: Describe a time you visited a place for the first time

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about my first visit to Dhaka, which made a lasting impression on me. A first visit that I still remember vividly was my trip to the capital when I was about seventeen, which was surprising since it is only a few hours from Sirajganj by road. I went there with my father for a short admission coaching course, and everything about it felt new and slightly [[overwhelming]] at first. The city was enormous, fast-paced and far busier than my quiet hometown, with endless traffic, crowds and noise. We stayed with a relative in Mirpur, and I remember standing on the roof at night, amazed by how many lights there were. Once I got my bearings, though, I found it genuinely [[exhilarating]]. I spent my free time exploring historical sites, markets and museums, soaking it all in, often with a cousin who lived there as my guide. I especially loved the old part of the city, with its narrow lanes, rickshaws and centuries-old buildings. What struck me most was the sheer diversity of people and experiences packed into one place. I found the whole experience thoroughly [[eye-opening]], and it [[broadened my horizons]] considerably. Honestly, visiting somewhere completely unfamiliar reminded me how much there is to discover beyond your own small world. Although it was a little daunting at times, I came away feeling more [[self-assured]] and independent. It made me eager to explore even more new places, and a couple of years later I went back there to study.

followUps.q: How often do you go to Dhaka now?
followUps.answer: Fairly often, maybe once every month or two. My elder sister lives there with her family, and I also go for work sometimes, to attend education fairs or meet university representatives.

followUps.q: Would you prefer to live in Dhaka or in your hometown?
followUps.answer: My hometown, at least for now. Dhaka has more opportunities, but it is exhausting and crowded. In Sirajganj life is calmer, and I can walk by the river whenever I like.

part3: Do you think living in a city is better than living in the countryside?
How have cities changed over the past few decades?

part3Samples.q: Do you think living in a city is better than living in the countryside?
part3Samples.answer: It really depends on one's priorities and stage of life. Cities offer better job opportunities, [[amenities]], healthcare and a vibrant social life, which many find appealing. The countryside, by contrast, offers peace, clean air, space and a stronger sense of community. Personally, I appreciate the convenience of the city for now, but I can see the [[profound appeal]] of a quieter rural life later. So neither is objectively better; each suits different needs and [[temperaments]].

part3Samples.q: How have cities changed over the past few decades?
part3Samples.answer: Cities have transformed dramatically. They have grown enormously in size and population due to rapid urbanisation, becoming denser and often more [[congested]]. Skylines have risen with skyscrapers, and technology has made them smarter. However, this growth has often [[outpaced]] infrastructure, worsening problems like traffic, pollution and housing shortages. So while cities have become more developed and connected, this expansion has brought significant [[growing pains]].

part3Samples.q: Why do so many people move to cities?
part3Samples.answer: The primary driver is economic opportunity. Cities are hubs of employment, offering far more and better-paid jobs than rural areas, which is the biggest [[pull factor]]. They also provide superior access to education, healthcare and services. For many, the appeal of a more exciting, diverse lifestyle is also a draw. So this migration is largely driven by the search for a better standard of living, though it can place enormous [[strain]] on urban [[infrastructure]] and resources.

part3Samples.q: What do you think cities will be like in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I envision cities becoming smarter and, hopefully, greener. Technology will likely manage traffic, energy and services more efficiently through data. There is a strong push towards more sustainable, [[walkable]] cities with more green spaces and cleaner transport. However, they may also become even more crowded. So I am hopeful the cities of the future will be more [[liveable]] and sustainable, provided planning [[prioritises]] people and the environment over pure expansion.

part3Samples.q: How can cities be made better places to live?
part3Samples.answer: Thoughtful [[urban planning]] is the key. Investing in efficient, affordable public transport reduces congestion and pollution. Creating more green spaces and [[pedestrian areas]] improves wellbeing. Ensuring an adequate supply of affordable housing tackles inequality. Designing [[mixed-use]], walkable neighbourhoods fosters community. Essentially, cities become better when they are planned around the needs of people and the environment, rather than simply cars and commerce.

part3Samples.q: Some say tourism does more harm than good to destinations. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I think it depends entirely on how it is managed. In some over-touristed places, the harm, from environmental damage to cultural erosion and inflated living costs, is undeniable and can indeed outweigh the benefits. However, when managed responsibly and sustainably, tourism can be a tremendous [[force for good]], funding conservation and lifting communities out of poverty. So I would not agree it is inherently harmful; the outcome [[hinges on]] responsible [[stewardship]] and planning.

cueCards.title: Describe a time you did something to make someone happy
cueCards.prompt: Describe a time you did something to make someone happy
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about something I did for my father, who has always put his family first. A time I went out of my way to make someone happy was when I organised a small surprise for him on his retirement last year. He had run a small business for over thirty years, often putting the family's needs before his own, so I wanted to do something meaningful. He is quite a modest man, and I knew he would never ask for any kind of celebration himself. With help from my mother and sisters, I secretly gathered old friends, relatives and a few of his long-time customers, and arranged a modest gathering at home to honour him. My mother cooked his favourite dishes, and my younger sister made a small album of old photos from his shop. The look of genuine surprise and joy on his face was absolutely [[priceless]]. He was clearly [[touched]] that so many people had come to celebrate him, and at one point his voice broke as he thanked everyone. What made it so special was seeing someone who rarely asks for anything finally being appreciated. Honestly, the whole thing was as rewarding for me as it was for him. There is a unique kind of happiness that comes from making someone else feel [[valued]]. It reminded me that thoughtful gestures often mean far more than expensive gifts. Seeing him so [[at peace]] that evening is a memory I will always [[treasure]], and it deepened our bond.

followUps.q: How does your father spend his time now that he has retired?
followUps.answer: He reads the newspaper for hours, visits his friends at the local tea stall and spends a lot of time in the village with my grandparents. He seems more relaxed than I have ever seen him.

followUps.q: Do you often do things to make your family happy?
followUps.answer: I try to. Usually it is small things, like bringing home sweets or taking my mother to visit her parents. I think those little gestures matter more than big occasions.

part3: Do you think family is as important today as it was in the past?

part3Samples.q: Do you think family is as important today as it was in the past?
part3Samples.answer: I would say family remains just as important, though its form has changed. The emotional support and sense of [[belonging]] a family provides are timeless human needs. That said, modern life has certainly [[strained]] family bonds, with people moving away for work and spending less time together. So while its importance is [[undiminished]], sustaining it now requires more conscious effort.

part3Samples.q: How are family relationships different now compared to a generation ago?
part3Samples.answer: The biggest difference is probably the shift from large, extended families to smaller, more [[nuclear]] ones. In the past, several generations often lived under one roof, which fostered close bonds. Today, families are more [[dispersed]], and technology has, ironically, both connected and [[distanced]] us. Relationships are more equal now, but arguably less tightly knit.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think many families spend less time together nowadays?
part3Samples.answer: Several factors are at play. The demands of modern careers are [[relentless]], leaving parents exhausted and [[time-poor]]. On top of that, digital devices have become a real distraction, with family members often absorbed in their own screens even when in the same room. This gradual erosion of shared time is genuinely [[detrimental]] to close relationships.

part3Samples.q: How do you think family structures will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I anticipate that families will continue to become smaller and more diverse in form. We will likely see more single-parent households and [[blended families]] becoming [[commonplace]] and widely accepted. Technology may also allow [[far-flung]] relatives to stay connected more easily. Overall, I think the definition of family will grow more flexible and inclusive.

part3Samples.q: What can families do to stay close despite busy modern lives?
part3Samples.answer: I think the key is being [[intentional]] about spending time together. Simple rituals, like sharing at least one meal a day without phones, can make a real difference. Families could also [[prioritise]] occasional trips or activities that create shared memories. Ultimately, closeness does not happen by accident; it has to be actively [[nurtured]] amid the busyness.

part3Samples.q: Some say happiness is a choice. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I partly agree, but with important reservations. There is real truth that our attitude, gratitude and how we respond to circumstances significantly influence our happiness, so mindset matters. However, saying happiness is simply a choice can be [[dismissive]] of those facing genuine hardship, mental illness or difficult circumstances beyond their control. So while we have some agency over our happiness, I think it is [[oversimplified]] to call it purely a choice, ignoring the [[structural]] and biological factors involved.

cueCards.title: Describe a time you reached an agreement after a disagreement
cueCards.prompt: Describe a time you reached an agreement after a disagreement
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about a disagreement during my BBA that ended far better than I expected. A time I reached a hard-won agreement was during a group project when a classmate and I had fundamentally different visions for the final result. We were designing a business plan for a small café, and I wanted to focus on low prices for students, while he wanted a more upmarket place with a stylish design. Initially, neither of us was willing to [[budge]], and the disagreement threatened to [[derail]] the entire project. The tension was uncomfortable, and progress [[ground to a halt]], which was frustrating for the rest of the group. Eventually I suggested we step back and actually listen to each other's reasoning properly, so we met one evening over tea to talk it through. The rest of the group were clearly relieved to see us talking calmly again. Once we did, I realised his idea had genuine merit that I had dismissed too quickly. Through calm discussion, we managed to blend both approaches into something better than either original plan: affordable food in a comfortable, attractive setting. Reaching that [[compromise]] required real humility on both sides, but it was worth it. What I learned was that being stubborn rarely helps, whereas being flexible often leads to a superior outcome. Honestly, the final result was far stronger for having combined our ideas, and I felt relieved and quite proud. It taught me that the best solutions often emerge from disagreement, provided both people are willing to be [[level-headed]] and open-minded.

followUps.q: Are you still friends with that classmate?
followUps.answer: Yes, we actually became good friends after that project. He now works for a bank in Dhaka, and we still joke about our imaginary café whenever we meet up.

followUps.q: Do you find it easy to change your mind?
followUps.answer: Easier than I used to. When someone gives me a good reason, I am happy to change my view. What I find harder is admitting it straight away, but I am working on that.

part3: Do you think conflict between people is always negative?

part3Samples.q: Do you think conflict between people is always negative?
part3Samples.answer: Not necessarily. While conflict is uncomfortable, it can actually be [[constructive]] if handled well. Disagreements often bring underlying problems to the surface, which allows them to be addressed rather than festering. Healthy conflict can also [[spark]] better ideas and deeper understanding. The key is whether it is managed respectfully; it is unresolved or [[hostile]] conflict that is truly damaging.

part3Samples.q: Is it better to confront a problem directly or avoid it?
part3Samples.answer: In most cases, I believe confronting a problem directly is far healthier. Avoidance may keep the peace temporarily, but the underlying issue tends to [[fester]] and grow worse over time. Addressing it calmly and early usually leads to genuine resolution. That said, direct confrontation should be done [[tactfully]], choosing the right moment, so it does not [[escalate]] into a bigger dispute.

part3Samples.q: What are the main causes of conflict between people?
part3Samples.answer: In my experience, most conflict [[stems from]] poor communication and misunderstanding rather than genuine [[malice]]. When people fail to express themselves clearly or make assumptions about others' intentions, friction inevitably arises. Differences in values, competition over resources and simple [[miscommunication]] are also common triggers. Interestingly, many disputes could be avoided entirely with a little more patience and clarity.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will become better at resolving conflicts in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am cautiously optimistic. There is growing awareness of the importance of emotional intelligence and communication skills, which are increasingly taught in schools and workplaces. If this trend continues, future generations may be better [[equipped]] to handle disagreements. On the other hand, online communication can sometimes make people more [[polarised]] and less willing to [[compromise]], so it is not guaranteed.

part3Samples.q: What is the best way to resolve a serious disagreement?
part3Samples.answer: The most effective approach usually involves calm, honest dialogue where both sides genuinely listen to one another. It helps to focus on the specific issue rather than attacking the person, and to seek a compromise where possible. In some cases, involving a [[neutral third party]] as a [[mediator]] can be [[invaluable]]. Ultimately, a willingness to see the other's perspective is what unlocks resolution.

part3Samples.q: Some say soft skills should be taught in schools. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly agree. Given how crucial these skills are for both work and life, it seems a serious oversight that they are rarely taught explicitly. Skills like communication, teamwork and emotional regulation could be [[woven into]] the curriculum from an early age. Equipping young people with these [[competencies]] would make them far more employable and better prepared for life, so it would be a genuinely [[worthwhile]] reform.

cueCards.title: Describe a time you were impressed by something
cueCards.prompt: Describe a time you were impressed by something
bullets: and how you felt about it

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about a performance that completely changed how I think about music. A time I was genuinely impressed was when I went to a large classical music festival in Dhaka with my elder sister and her husband a few years ago. I had always enjoyed music, but I had never experienced anything on that scale in person. The festival ran through the night in a huge open-air venue, with thousands of people sitting on the ground and listening in near silence. We had brought a thin mat and a flask of tea, like most of the people around us. From the moment the performance began, I was completely [[captivated]]. The sheer skill of the musicians, a sitar player and a tabla player responding to each other in perfect harmony, was absolutely [[remarkable]]. What impressed me most was the emotion they managed to convey purely through their instruments, with no words at all. The sound was so rich and powerful that I felt it [[resonate]] in my chest. It was a genuinely [[mesmerising]] experience, quite unlike listening to a recording on my phone. I came away with a whole new appreciation for the years of discipline behind such a performance, since musicians like that often train from childhood. Honestly, it left me feeling deeply [[moved]], and it reminded me of the extraordinary things humans can achieve through dedication. By the time we left, the sun was coming up, and I was tired but completely inspired. I have been eager to attend more live performances ever since.

followUps.q: What kind of music do you usually listen to?
followUps.answer: Mostly Bengali songs, both old classics and some modern bands, and a bit of English pop. I listen while walking by the river in the evening, which is probably my favourite time for music.

followUps.q: Have you ever wanted to learn a musical instrument?
followUps.answer: Yes, the tabla, after that festival. I never actually started, though, because I didn't have the time. Perhaps one day, when life is a little less busy, I will finally give it a try.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think music is important to people?
part3Samples.answer: Music holds a unique and powerful place in human life. It has an extraordinary ability to [[evoke]] emotion, from joy to sorrow, and to comfort us in a way few other things can. It is also deeply tied to memory and identity, and it brings people together, whether at concerts or festivals. In my view, music is a universal language that [[transcends]] barriers and speaks directly to our emotions, which is why it is so [[cherished]].

part3Samples.q: How has the way people listen to music changed?
part3Samples.answer: It has changed dramatically. In the past, people bought physical records or CDs and often listened to a whole album deliberately. Now, streaming gives us instant access to virtually all recorded music, and we tend to consume it in playlists and individual tracks. This is wonderfully convenient, but some argue it has made listening more [[passive]] and [[fragmented]]. So access has expanded enormously, but our engagement with music may have become more [[cursory]].

part3Samples.q: What effect does learning a musical instrument have on children?
part3Samples.answer: Learning an instrument has remarkably positive effects. Many believe it enhances cognitive development, improving skills like memory, concentration and mathematical ability. It also teaches discipline, patience and perseverance, since [[mastery]] requires consistent practice. Furthermore, it provides a creative outlet and a real sense of accomplishment that boosts confidence. So beyond the joy of making music, it offers profound [[developmental]] and [[character-building]] benefits.

part3Samples.q: Do you think technology will change the arts in the future?
part3Samples.answer: Undoubtedly, and it already is. Technology is providing artists with powerful new tools and mediums, from digital art to AI-generated music, expanding creative possibilities. It has also democratised the arts, allowing anyone to create and share their work globally. However, this raises questions about [[authenticity]] and the role of human creativity. So while technology will transform and [[democratise]] the arts, I hope it will [[augment]] human expression rather than replace it.

part3Samples.q: Arts funding is often cut. How can the arts be better supported?
part3Samples.answer: Supporting the arts requires a [[multi-pronged]] approach. Governments should recognise their cultural and economic value and provide stable funding rather than treating them as [[expendable]]. Encouraging private sponsorship and [[philanthropy]] can supplement this. Integrating arts education properly into schools ensures future generations value them. Making the arts more accessible and affordable to ordinary people also builds public support. Essentially, we must treat the arts as an investment, not a luxury.

part3Samples.q: Some say globalisation is destroying local cultures. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I partly agree, as it is a genuine threat. The spread of a dominant global culture can certainly [[overshadow]] and dilute local traditions, languages and customs, leading to a worrying uniformity. However, I would not say it is entirely destructive. Globalisation also allows cultures to share and celebrate their uniqueness on a world stage. So while the risk of [[homogenisation]] is real, cultures can also prove remarkably [[resilient]] and adaptive.

cueCards.title: Describe an adventurous thing you have done
cueCards.prompt: Describe an adventurous thing you have done

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about the most adventurous thing I have ever done, which was a trek in the hills of Bandarban. An adventurous thing I did that pushed me well outside my comfort zone was going on a fairly challenging trek to Keokradong, one of the highest peaks in Bangladesh, with a group of four friends from university. It was about two years ago, in the dry season, when the paths are safer. I am not the most outdoorsy person, so agreeing to it was already a stretch for me. The trail was steep and [[gruelling]] in places, and at several points I genuinely wondered whether I could make it. My legs ached and my lungs burned, but my friends kept [[egging me on]]. We stopped in small villages along the way, where local people offered us water and bananas, which was incredibly kind. We spent the night in a simple guesthouse beside a lake on the way. Reaching the summit after hours of effort was absolutely [[exhilarating]], and the [[panoramic]] view of endless green hills was more than worth it. What made it so rewarding was proving to myself that I was tougher than I had believed. Honestly, I surprised myself with how much I enjoyed the challenge, despite the discomfort. That experience gave me a real taste for adventure and a newfound confidence in my own [[resilience]]. It taught me that stepping outside your comfort zone, while difficult, is often where the most memorable experiences are found. My mother, of course, was relieved to see me home in one piece.

followUps.q: Would you do something like that again?
followUps.answer: Yes, I think so, although I would train a bit beforehand this time. My friends have been talking about a trek in Nepal, and I would love to join them if work allows.

followUps.q: Do you think young people today are adventurous enough?
followUps.answer: Some are very adventurous, but many spend most of their free time on screens. I think a little adventure, even something small, builds confidence in a way that nothing online can.

part3: Why do you think people enjoy travelling?

part3Samples.q: Why do you think people enjoy travelling?
part3Samples.answer: People travel for a wonderful variety of reasons. Fundamentally, I think it satisfies a deep human curiosity and desire to escape routine. Experiencing new cultures, landscapes and cuisines is genuinely [[enriching]] and broadens one's perspective. Travel also offers relaxation, adventure and the chance to create lasting memories. For me, the greatest value is how it makes you more [[open-minded]] and [[appreciative]] of the world's incredible diversity.

part3Samples.q: How has travel changed compared to the past?
part3Samples.answer: Travel has been transformed almost beyond recognition. In the past, it was expensive, slow and largely a privilege of the wealthy. Today, [[budget airlines]] and the internet have made it far more accessible and easy to organise, leading to mass tourism. We can now reach distant corners of the globe in hours. While this democratisation is positive, it has also led to [[overcrowding]] at popular sites and a more [[superficial]], hurried style of travel.

part3Samples.q: What effects does tourism have on local communities?
part3Samples.answer: Tourism has profound and mixed effects. Economically, it can bring vital income and jobs, boosting the local economy significantly. However, it can also cause problems: it may [[inflate]] local prices, strain infrastructure, and sometimes lead to the [[commodification]] of culture, where traditions are performed purely for tourists. Environmental damage is another concern. So while tourism offers real economic benefits, it must be managed [[sustainably]] to avoid harming the very communities it supports.

part3Samples.q: How do you think tourism will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I foresee several shifts. Growing environmental awareness will likely make sustainable and [[eco-tourism]] far more popular, as people seek to [[minimise their impact]]. Technology, such as virtual reality, might offer new ways to experience places remotely. There may also be a move towards more meaningful, [[immersive]] travel over mass tourism. So I expect the future of travel to be more conscious, more personalised, and hopefully more responsible.

part3Samples.q: How can the negative impacts of tourism be reduced?
part3Samples.answer: Sustainable tourism practices are the answer. Governments can manage visitor numbers at fragile sites through limits or timed entry to prevent overcrowding. Promoting [[lesser-known]] destinations helps spread the benefits and reduce pressure on [[hotspots]]. Encouraging tourists to respect local cultures and environments, and to support local businesses, is also key. Essentially, prioritising sustainability over sheer volume can [[mitigate]] the harm while preserving the benefits.

part3Samples.q: Some say hobbies should be useful, not just for fun. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I respectfully disagree with that as a rule. While hobbies that build skills are certainly valuable, I firmly believe a hobby does not need to be productive to be [[worthwhile]]. The primary purpose of leisure is enjoyment, relaxation and wellbeing, and something that brings pure joy is valuable in itself. Insisting that all free time be useful reflects an overly [[utilitarian]] mindset. Sometimes, doing something simply for pleasure is [[exactly the point]].

cueCards.title: Describe a time you kept trying although it was difficult
cueCards.prompt: Describe a time you kept trying although it was difficult
bullets: what you were trying to do
and how you felt about it

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about learning to drive, which tested my patience more than almost anything else. A time I had to keep pushing through real difficulty was while learning to drive about two years ago, which I found far harder than I had expected. I wanted to learn because my father had recently retired and was no longer comfortable driving long distances, so someone in the family needed to take the car to the village. The roads here are full of rickshaws, buses and people crossing without warning, so even a short drive felt stressful. I struggled with confidence behind the wheel and failed my first test, which was genuinely [[disheartening]]. Part of me was tempted to give up entirely and rely on buses and rickshaws instead. However, I knew driving would be a valuable skill, so I forced myself to [[persevere]]. I booked more lessons, practised early in the mornings when the roads were quiet and slowly [[chipped away at]] my nervousness. Progress was frustratingly slow at times, and it required a lot of [[patience]]. When I finally passed on my second attempt, the sense of accomplishment was immense, precisely because it had not come easily. Honestly, that experience taught me the value of [[persistence]] more than almost anything else. It proved that giving up at the first setback would have cost me a skill I now use regularly. My grandparents are always delighted when I drive my parents to visit them, and I have carried that lesson into other challenges ever since.

followUps.q: Do you enjoy driving now?
followUps.answer: On quiet roads, yes, especially the drive to my grandparents' village, which passes through lovely green fields. In busy town traffic, though, I still find it more tiring than enjoyable.

part3Samples.answer: There are [[trade-offs]] at each stage. Young people generally absorb new information, especially languages, more easily, and have fewer competing responsibilities. However, adult learners bring focus, motivation and real-world experience that can make their learning more [[purposeful]] and efficient. So while children may have a biological advantage, adults [[compensate]] with discipline and context. Neither is simply easier; it depends on what is being learned.

part3Samples.q: Why is continuous learning becoming more necessary today?
part3Samples.answer: It is primarily because of the [[breakneck pace]] of technological change. Skills that were valuable a decade ago can quickly become [[obsolete]], and entirely new fields emerge constantly. To remain employable, workers must continually update their knowledge and [[reskill]]. The old model of one qualification lasting a whole career is no longer viable. part3Samples.q: Do you think lifelong learning will become the norm in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am confident it will, [[out of sheer necessity]]. I anticipate more flexible, [[bite-sized]] courses and employer-sponsored training becoming [[commonplace]]. Society's whole conception of education will likely shift from a one-off event to an ongoing, lifelong process.

part3Samples.q: What prevents adults from continuing to learn, and how can this be solved?
part3Samples.answer: The main barriers are usually time, cost and lack of confidence. Busy working adults with family commitments struggle to find the time and money for further study. part3Samples.answer: I broadly agree with this, at least for private cars in the busiest central areas. cueCards.title: Describe a gift you received that was important to you
cueCards.prompt: Describe a gift you received that was important to you

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about something small that I keep on my desk at home. A gift that means a great deal to me is a fountain pen my father gave me when I finished my studies. I remember reading the note twice with a [[lump in my throat]]. What made it so special was the [[thoughtfulness]] behind it, rather than the object itself. My father ran a small business for over thirty years, and I think he knew better than anyone how much a signature can carry. My father is not a man of many words, so this gesture was genuinely [[touching]]. I keep it safely on my desk and use it only on special occasions. In fact, I used it to sign my first employment contract, which felt like keeping a small promise to him. Every time I hold it, I am reminded of his quiet faith in me. Honestly, it is the kind of gift that grows more [[precious]] with time. I think the best presents are those that carry meaning and memory, not just a high price tag. This pen is something I intend to keep for the rest of my life and perhaps pass on one day.

followUps.q: Do you still use the pen?
followUps.answer: Yes, but only for important things, like signing contracts or writing Eid cards. I'm quite careful with it, because refilling a fountain pen and cleaning it properly takes a bit of patience.

followUps.q: Have you ever given your father a gift like that?
followUps.answer: Not quite like that, but when he retired, my sisters and I gave him a good-quality watch. He insisted it was unnecessary, but he has worn it every single day since.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people buy more things than they actually need?
part3Samples.answer: Yes, I think overconsumption is a defining feature of modern society. We are constantly [[bombarded]] with advertising designed to create desires for things we do not truly need. Cheap goods and easy credit make impulsive buying effortless. Many people also shop for emotional reasons, as a form of therapy. So I would say that a great deal of our consumption is driven by [[manufactured]] wants rather than genuine necessity, which is quite [[wasteful]].

part3Samples.q: How has shopping changed with the rise of the internet?
part3Samples.answer: Online shopping has [[revolutionised]] the experience. It offers [[unparalleled]] convenience, allowing people to buy almost anything from home at any hour, with easy price comparison. This has, however, put pressure on traditional physical shops, many of which have struggled. The experience has become more efficient but arguably less social. So while the internet has made shopping far more convenient and accessible, it has also transformed our [[high streets]], not always for the better.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think advertising is so influential?
part3Samples.answer: Advertising is influential because it is sophisticated and [[pervasive]]. It cleverly taps into our emotions, insecurities and aspirations, associating products with happiness, status or belonging rather than mere function. Its sheer ubiquity means we are exposed to it constantly, which [[reinforces]] its messages. Modern targeted advertising is especially potent, as it is tailored precisely to our interests. So it shapes our desires far more than we consciously realise, subtly [[steering]] our behaviour.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will become more conscious consumers in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am cautiously hopeful. There is a growing awareness of the environmental and ethical impact of our purchases, and movements towards [[minimalism]], sustainability and ethical consumption are [[gaining momentum]]. Younger generations in particular seem more [[values-driven]] in their spending. However, the powerful forces of marketing and convenience remain strong. So while I believe conscious consumption will increase, whether it becomes the norm depends on a genuine cultural shift.

part3Samples.q: How can people be encouraged to consume more responsibly?
part3Samples.answer: Education and awareness are key. Helping people understand the true environmental and social cost of their purchases can shift attitudes. Encouraging habits like buying quality over quantity, repairing rather than replacing, and choosing ethical brands makes a difference. Governments can also play a role through regulation and [[incentives]]. Ultimately, [[fostering]] a cultural value of [[sufficiency]] over excess, where we question whether we truly need something, is the most sustainable path.

part3Samples.q: Some believe children should care for their parents in old age. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly agree, at least in principle. In my culture, caring for elderly parents is seen as a moral [[obligation]], a way of repaying the sacrifices they made. That said, I recognise this is not always practical in modern life, so it need not mean living together. What matters is that the elderly are not [[neglected]] and retain their [[dignity]].

cueCards.title: Describe a gift you gave to someone
cueCards.prompt: Describe a gift you gave to someone

sample.answer: I'd like to describe a present I made for someone rather than bought, because it is the one I'm proudest of. A gift I was particularly pleased with was a photo album I put together for my mother's birthday. My mother has spent her whole life looking after all of us, and I felt she deserved something that celebrated that. Rather than buying something generic, I wanted to give her something genuinely [[meaningful]]. I chose an album because I knew she would never ask for anything for herself, and memories matter far more to her than possessions. I spent weeks gathering old family photographs and arranging them chronologically, adding little notes beside each one. Some of them I found in a dusty trunk at my grandparents' village home, including a faded picture of her wedding day, and my elder sister secretly sent me a few from Dhaka as well. It was surprisingly time-consuming, but the effort felt worthwhile. When she opened it, her reaction was absolutely [[priceless]]; she was moved to tears as she flicked through the memories. She kept stopping at certain pages to tell us the story behind each picture, and we ended up sitting around the dining table for hours. What made it so special was that it cost very little money but a great deal of care. She told me it was the most [[heartfelt]] gift she had ever received, which [[meant the world to me]]. Honestly, seeing her so [[delighted]] was far more rewarding than giving an expensive present ever could be. That experience confirmed my belief that the best gifts are personal ones that show you truly know the person. It is something she still treasures and shows to visitors.

followUps.answer: Yes, very much, although it takes me a long time. I like noticing what people mention in passing, so that the gift feels [[personalised]] rather than something picked up at the last minute.

followUps.q: Would you make a homemade gift again?
followUps.answer: Definitely. I'm actually planning one for my grandparents, a small booklet of old family stories and photos, because I think they would value that far more than anything from a shop.

part3Samples.q: Do you think family is as important today as it was in the past?
part3Samples.answer: I would say family remains just as important, though its form has changed. The emotional support and sense of [[belonging]] a family provides are timeless human needs. That said, modern life has certainly [[strained]] family bonds, with people moving away for work and spending less time together. So while its importance is [[undiminished]], sustaining it now requires more conscious effort.

part3Samples.q: How are family relationships different now compared to a generation ago?
part3Samples.answer: The biggest difference is probably the shift from large, extended families to smaller, more [[nuclear]] ones. In the past, several generations often lived under one roof, which fostered close bonds. Today, families are more [[dispersed]], and technology has, ironically, both connected and [[distanced]] us. Relationships are more equal now, but arguably less tightly knit.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think many families spend less time together nowadays?
part3Samples.answer: Several factors are at play. The demands of modern careers are [[relentless]], leaving parents exhausted and [[time-poor]]. On top of that, digital devices have become a real distraction, with family members often absorbed in their own screens even when in the same room. This gradual erosion of shared time is genuinely [[detrimental]] to close relationships.

part3Samples.q: How do you think family structures will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I anticipate that families will continue to become smaller and more diverse in form. We will likely see more single-parent households and [[blended families]] becoming [[commonplace]] and widely accepted. Technology may also allow [[far-flung]] relatives to stay connected more easily. Overall, I think the definition of family will grow more flexible and inclusive.

part3Samples.q: What can families do to stay close despite busy modern lives?
part3Samples.answer: I think the key is being [[intentional]] about spending time together. Simple rituals, like sharing at least one meal a day without phones, can make a real difference. Families could also [[prioritise]] occasional trips or activities that create shared memories. Ultimately, closeness does not happen by accident; it has to be actively [[nurtured]] amid the busyness.

part3Samples.q: Some say buying things makes people happy. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I only partly agree. There is undeniably a short-term thrill in acquiring something new, so buying can bring a [[fleeting]] sense of pleasure. However, many people feel this happiness is temporary and superficial, quickly fading in a cycle sometimes called the [[hedonic treadmill]]. Lasting happiness tends to come from experiences and relationships, not possessions. So while shopping offers momentary joy, relying on it for happiness is ultimately [[hollow]] and unfulfilling.

cueCards.title: Describe a useful object in your home
cueCards.prompt: Describe a useful object in your home

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about something very ordinary that sits on our kitchen counter. A genuinely useful object in my home is my electric kettle, which I honestly could not do without. It is a simple steel one that my younger sister and I bought for the family a couple of years ago. It might sound trivial, but as someone who drinks tea several times a day, it is completely [[indispensable]]. I use it mainly to boil water for tea, but my mother also uses it when she needs hot water for cooking, and my sister makes instant noodles with it during late-night study sessions. I use it first thing in the morning, throughout the day, and last thing at night. On a typical day it must be switched on six or seven times, especially when guests drop by, which happens a lot in our household. What makes it so useful is how quickly and efficiently it boils water, saving me a lot of time. Before I had it, using the stove felt slow and [[cumbersome]] by comparison. It is also wonderfully [[convenient]], with an automatic switch-off that means I never have to watch it. Such a simple [[appliance]] has become woven into my daily routine without my even noticing. Honestly, it is a perfect example of how the most ordinary objects are often the most useful. I think we tend to overlook these everyday items, yet they quietly make life far more [[manageable]]. If it broke tomorrow, I would replace it immediately without a second thought.

followUps.q: Who else in your family uses the kettle?
followUps.answer: Pretty much everyone. My mother uses it while cooking, my younger sister relies on it during late-night study sessions, and my father makes his afternoon tea with it now that he's retired.

followUps.q: Is there anything about it you would improve?
followUps.answer: Perhaps the size. When relatives visit, we have to boil water two or three times for everyone's tea, so a slightly larger one would be more [[practical]] for a household like ours.

cueCards.title: Describe a piece of technology you find useful
cueCards.prompt: Describe a piece of technology you find useful
bullets: how you learned to use it

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about the piece of technology I reach for more often than anything else. A piece of technology I find genuinely useful is my smartphone, which has become an extension of my daily life. I know that is a fairly obvious choice, but its sheer [[versatility]] is remarkable. It functions as my alarm, camera, map, bank and library all in one device. At work, I use it constantly to reply to students' messages, check university deadlines and join video calls with admissions officers abroad. In the evenings, I use it to read e-books, listen to music or video-call my elder sister and her children in Dhaka. I learned to use it intuitively, simply by exploring its features over time. Nobody really taught me; I just experimented, made a few mistakes and occasionally watched a short tutorial when I got stuck. Funnily enough, I've now become the person my parents turn to whenever their own phones misbehave. What makes it so useful is how it [[consolidates]] dozens of tasks that once required separate tools. It has made my life significantly more [[efficient]], allowing me to work, communicate and organise on the move. Of course, I am aware there is a downside; it can be quite [[addictive]] if you are not careful. Still, used sensibly, it is an incredibly powerful tool. Honestly, it is hard to imagine how people managed everyday tasks before smartphones existed. I think it is a perfect example of how technology has become deeply [[embedded]] in modern life, for better or worse, and I would struggle to function without mine.

followUps.q: Do you think you use your smartphone too much?
followUps.answer: Probably, yes, especially in the evenings. I've started leaving it in another room while I read, which helps me [[switch off]] properly and makes that time feel far more restful.

followUps.q: Is there any other technology you find useful?
followUps.answer: My laptop, definitely. For long documents and university applications at work, a phone just isn't enough, so the two complement each other rather well and I use both every day.

part3Samples.q: Do you think smartphones have improved people's lives?
part3Samples.answer: On the whole, I think they have, though not without significant drawbacks. Smartphones have put a world of information, communication and services in our pockets, which is genuinely empowering and convenient. However, they have also introduced constant distraction and a degree of [[dependence]] that can harm our focus and relationships. So I see them as a remarkable tool that has improved life, provided we use them [[consciously]] rather than [[compulsively]].

part3Samples.q: How was life different before smartphones?
part3Samples.answer: Life was noticeably slower and, in some ways, more present. People were less [[contactable]] and more likely to be fully engaged in their [[immediate surroundings]] rather than staring at a screen. Getting lost, being bored or having to memorise information were normal. While we have gained incredible convenience, I think we have lost a certain patience and the ability to simply be [[idle]], which had its own value.

part3Samples.q: What effects does excessive smartphone use have on people?
part3Samples.answer: The effects can be quite detrimental. Excessive use seems to be linked to reduced [[attention spans]], disrupted sleep and increased anxiety, partly due to the constant stream of notifications. It can also erode face-to-face social skills and lead to a [[sedentary]] lifestyle. There is even a recognised phenomenon of phone addiction. So while occasional use is harmless, overuse can genuinely [[impair]] both our mental and physical wellbeing.

part3Samples.q: How do you think mobile technology will develop in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I anticipate devices will become even more integrated into our lives, perhaps evolving beyond the handheld phone into [[wearables]] or augmented reality glasses. Artificial intelligence will make them ever more [[anticipatory]] and personalised. The line between the digital and physical worlds is likely to [[blur]] further. While this promises even greater convenience, I hope it comes with a stronger awareness of the need to remain present and in control.

part3Samples.q: How can people reduce their dependence on their phones?
part3Samples.answer: There are several practical strategies. Turning off non-essential notifications immediately reduces the constant pull to check the phone. [[Designating]] device-free times and zones, such as during meals or in the bedroom, helps re-establish boundaries. Using apps that track and limit screen time can raise awareness of usage. Ultimately, consciously replacing [[mindless scrolling]] with more rewarding activities is the most sustainable way to [[loosen the phone's grip]].

part3Samples.q: Some say the internet makes people less intelligent. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I disagree with that as a [[blanket statement]], though it raises a fair concern. The internet does not make us less intelligent; rather, it changes how we use our intelligence. We may memorise less, relying on it as an external memory, but we have unparalleled access to knowledge. The risk is that passive consumption and short attention spans can weaken deep thinking. So it is a tool that can either [[enrich]] or [[diminish]] the mind, depending on use.

cueCards.title: Describe something you bought that was expensive

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about the most expensive thing I've ever bought for myself. Something expensive I bought after much deliberation was a good-quality laptop for my work and studies. I researched extensively for weeks, comparing models to make sure I was making a [[sensible]] choice. I had saved for it gradually, which made me appreciate its value even more. I [[put aside]] a portion of my salary every month for almost a year, and in the end I paid for it in full, because I didn't want to be paying it off in instalments. When I finally bought it, I felt a mixture of excitement and slight [[apprehension]] at spending so much. However, it quickly proved to be a genuinely [[worthwhile]] investment, as I use it every single day. Its speed and reliability have made my work far more productive. Honestly, although the price was high, the value it has provided over the years has been [[immense]]. It taught me that spending more on something you use constantly is often smarter than buying a cheaper version that disappoints. I have never once regretted the purchase, and I think it was one of my wiser financial decisions.

followUps.q: Have you bought anything expensive since then?
followUps.answer: Nothing on that scale. I tend to be quite careful with money, and I'd rather save towards bigger goals, such as studying abroad, than make [[impulse purchases]] that I might regret later.

followUps.q: Do you prefer to save up or to buy things on credit?
followUps.answer: I definitely prefer to save up first. My father ran his business for over thirty years without borrowing more than he needed, and I suppose I've inherited that cautious attitude.

part3Samples.q: How important is money in life?
part3Samples.answer: Money is [[undeniably]] important, but its importance has limits. However, beyond a certain point of comfort, its ability to improve our happiness [[diminishes sharply]]. Health, relationships and purpose matter far more. So I see money as a vital tool and [[enabler]], but a poor ultimate goal in itself.

part3Samples.q: Is it better to save money or spend it?
part3Samples.answer: A healthy balance between the two is ideal. Saving is [[prudent]], providing security, peace of mind and the means to achieve future goals or weather emergencies. However, being excessively frugal can mean missing out on valuable experiences and enjoyment in the present. Spending wisely, particularly on experiences and things that genuinely enrich life, is worthwhile. So I favour disciplined saving combined with mindful spending, avoiding both reckless [[extravagance]] and joyless [[hoarding]].

part3Samples.q: What effect does the pursuit of wealth have on people?
part3Samples.answer: The pursuit of wealth has mixed effects. Positively, it can motivate hard work, innovation and achievement, driving both personal and economic progress. However, an excessive obsession with wealth can be corrosive, leading people to become greedy, materialistic, and to neglect relationships, ethics and their own wellbeing. It can foster perpetual dissatisfaction too. So while a healthy desire to prosper is fine, an [[all-consuming]] [[fixation]] on money can genuinely [[distort]] a person's values.

However, there is also growing awareness of inequality and political pressure to address it through [[progressive taxation]] and social policy. So the outcome is not [[predetermined]]; whether the gap widens or narrows will depend on the political choices societies make to [[redistribute]] opportunity.

cueCards.title: Describe a photograph you like
cueCards.prompt: Describe a photograph you like

sample.answer: I'd like to describe a photograph that I look at almost every day. A photograph I treasure is one of my entire extended family gathered together at a reunion several years ago. It was taken during Eid in the courtyard of my grandparents' home in the village, with everyone squeezed onto a few plastic chairs and a mat on the ground. My grandparents are sitting in the middle, surrounded by their children and grandchildren, and a couple of neighbours who wandered in at the last minute. It captures a rare moment when everyone, across three generations, was in the same place at the same time. It was taken by my cousin, who had just bought his first proper camera and insisted on setting a timer so he could run into the frame himself. In fact, you can just about see him mid-jump, still trying to reach his spot. What makes it so [[precious]] is that some of the older relatives in it, like my great-uncle, have since passed away. Whenever I look at it, I am filled with a warm sense of [[nostalgia]]. The photo is not technically perfect; it is slightly blurry and someone is looking the wrong way, but that only [[adds to its charm]]. What I love is how it froze a genuinely happy, [[fleeting]] moment forever. It reminds me of the importance of family and how quickly time passes. Honestly, no professionally staged photograph could ever mean as much to me. I keep a printed copy framed on my wall, and it never fails to make me smile. It is a powerful reminder of how [[irreplaceable]] these moments and people are.

followUps.q: Do you take many photographs yourself?
followUps.answer: Quite a few, but mostly on my phone, and I rarely print them. I'd like to change that, because a printed photo somehow feels more permanent than thousands of images [[buried in]] a phone gallery.

followUps.q: Would you like to take a similar photo in the future?

So I think governments have a clear responsibility to ensure that housing is available and affordable to all, treating it as an essential rather than a mere [[commodity]].

part3Samples.answer: Both have their advantages, depending on circumstances. Owning a home offers stability, security and the chance to build wealth over time, which is why many [[aspire to]] it. Renting, however, offers greater flexibility and freedom from the burdens of maintenance and large [[mortgages]], which suits those who value mobility. So there is no universal answer; it depends on one's financial situation, life stage and how much stability versus flexibility one [[prioritises]].

part3Samples.q: Why is housing so expensive in many cities?
part3Samples.answer: The high cost is driven by a fundamental imbalance between supply and demand. As people [[flock to]] cities for work, demand for housing soars, while the supply of new homes often fails to keep pace due to limited land and slow construction. Property speculation and foreign investment can also inflate prices. So it is largely a matter of high demand meeting [[constrained]] supply, made worse by [[speculation]], pushing prices beyond ordinary people's reach.

part3Samples.q: How do you think housing will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I anticipate several developments. To address shortages and sustainability, we may see more compact, [[high-density]] and eco-friendly housing, along with innovative solutions like modular or [[prefabricated]] homes. Smart-home technology will likely become standard. There may also be a shift towards [[co-living]] arrangements, especially in expensive cities. So future housing may become smaller and denser, but hopefully smarter, greener and more affordable, adapting to modern needs.

part3Samples.q: What can be done to make housing more affordable?
part3Samples.answer: Increasing the supply of housing is fundamental, particularly affordable and social housing built by governments. Reforming planning regulations to allow more construction can help. Measures to [[curb]] speculation, such as taxes on empty properties, may also [[cool prices]]. Rent controls and support for first-time buyers are other options. Essentially, treating housing as a basic need rather than a pure [[investment vehicle]] is key to keeping it accessible and fair.

part3Samples.q: Some say money is the best measure of success. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly disagree with this narrow view. While money is a tangible and convenient measure, and financial security certainly matters, equating it with success ignores far more important dimensions of a good life. Many wealthy people are deeply unhappy, while many people of [[modest means]] live rich, fulfilling lives. Reducing success to a bank balance seems [[reductive]] and [[misguided]]. True success, in my view, is measured by fulfilment, relationships and character, not currency.

In my view, music is a universal language that [[transcends]] barriers and speaks directly to our emotions, which is why it is so [[cherished]].

part3Samples.q: How has the way people listen to music changed?
part3Samples.answer: It has changed dramatically. In the past, people bought physical records or CDs and often listened to a whole album deliberately. Now, streaming gives us instant access to virtually all recorded music, and we tend to consume it in playlists and individual tracks. This is wonderfully convenient, but some argue it has made listening more [[passive]] and [[fragmented]]. So access has expanded enormously, but our engagement with music may have become more [[cursory]].

part3Samples.q: What effect does learning a musical instrument have on children?
part3Samples.answer: Learning an instrument has remarkably positive effects. Many believe it enhances cognitive development, improving skills like memory, concentration and mathematical ability. It also teaches discipline, patience and perseverance, since [[mastery]] requires consistent practice. Furthermore, it provides a creative outlet and a real sense of accomplishment that boosts confidence. So beyond the joy of making music, it offers profound [[developmental]] and [[character-building]] benefits.

part3Samples.q: Do you think technology will change the arts in the future?
part3Samples.answer: Undoubtedly, and it already is. Technology is providing artists with powerful new tools and mediums, from digital art to AI-generated music, expanding creative possibilities. part3Samples.q: Arts funding is often cut. How can the arts be better supported?
part3Samples.answer: Supporting the arts requires a [[multi-pronged]] approach. Governments should recognise their cultural and economic value and provide stable funding rather than treating them as [[expendable]]. Encouraging private sponsorship and [[philanthropy]] can supplement this. Integrating arts education properly into schools ensures future generations value them. Making the arts more accessible and affordable to ordinary people also builds public support. Essentially, we must treat the arts as an investment, not a luxury.

part3Samples.q: Some say hobbies should be useful, not just for fun. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I respectfully disagree with that as a rule. While hobbies that build skills are certainly valuable, I firmly believe a hobby does not need to be productive to be [[worthwhile]]. The primary purpose of leisure is enjoyment, relaxation and wellbeing, and something that brings pure joy is valuable in itself. Insisting that all free time be useful reflects an overly [[utilitarian]] mindset. Sometimes, doing something simply for pleasure is [[exactly the point]].

part3: Do you think people buy more things than they actually need?

part3Samples.q: Do you think people buy more things than they actually need?
part3Samples.answer: Yes, I think overconsumption is a defining feature of modern society. We are constantly [[bombarded]] with advertising designed to create desires for things we do not truly need. Cheap goods and easy credit make impulsive buying effortless. Many people also shop for emotional reasons, as a form of therapy. So I would say that a great deal of our consumption is driven by [[manufactured]] wants rather than genuine necessity, which is quite [[wasteful]].

part3Samples.q: How has shopping changed with the rise of the internet?
part3Samples.answer: Online shopping has [[revolutionised]] the experience. It offers [[unparalleled]] convenience, allowing people to buy almost anything from home at any hour, with easy price comparison. This has, however, put pressure on traditional physical shops, many of which have struggled. The experience has become more efficient but arguably less social. So while the internet has made shopping far more convenient and accessible, it has also transformed our [[high streets]], not always for the better.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think advertising is so influential?
part3Samples.answer: Advertising is influential because it is sophisticated and [[pervasive]]. It cleverly taps into our emotions, insecurities and aspirations, associating products with happiness, status or belonging rather than mere function. Its sheer ubiquity means we are exposed to it constantly, which [[reinforces]] its messages. Modern targeted advertising is especially potent, as it is tailored precisely to our interests. So it shapes our desires far more than we consciously realise, subtly [[steering]] our behaviour.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will become more conscious consumers in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am cautiously hopeful. There is a growing awareness of the environmental and ethical impact of our purchases, and movements towards [[minimalism]], sustainability and ethical consumption are [[gaining momentum]]. Younger generations in particular seem more [[values-driven]] in their spending. However, the powerful forces of marketing and convenience remain strong. So while I believe conscious consumption will increase, whether it becomes the norm depends on a genuine cultural shift.

part3Samples.q: How can people be encouraged to consume more responsibly?
part3Samples.answer: Education and awareness are key. Helping people understand the true environmental and social cost of their purchases can shift attitudes. Encouraging habits like buying quality over quantity, repairing rather than replacing, and choosing ethical brands makes a difference. Governments can also play a role through regulation and [[incentives]]. Ultimately, [[fostering]] a cultural value of [[sufficiency]] over excess, where we question whether we truly need something, is the most sustainable path.

part3Samples.q: Some say sustainable products are too expensive for ordinary people. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: There is some truth to this currently, though it is changing. It is true that some sustainable products, like organic food or electric cars, carry a higher [[price tag]], which can put them [[out of reach]] for those on tight budgets. This is a real barrier to [[widespread adoption]]. However, as demand grows and technology improves, prices are steadily falling. So while cost is a genuine obstacle today, I believe sustainability is becoming increasingly affordable and accessible.

followUps.q: Would you prefer an electric car?
followUps.answer: Ideally, yes, because it would be better for the environment. But charging points are still rare outside the big cities here, so for now a fuel-efficient car seems far more realistic.
