part3Samples.q: Do you think public transport should be free?
part3Samples.answer: I find the idea appealing, though it is complex. Making public transport free could reduce traffic, cut pollution and help [[lower-income]] people enormously, which are [[compelling]] social benefits. However, it would be extremely expensive to fund and might lead to overcrowding or reduced service quality without careful management. So while I support [[heavily subsidising]] it to keep it affordable, whether it should be entirely free depends on a country's priorities and budget.

part3Samples.q: Is it better to travel by public transport or private car?
part3Samples.answer: Each has its merits, but from a societal viewpoint, public transport is clearly [[preferable]]. It is far more environmentally friendly, reduces congestion, and is cheaper for the user. Private cars, however, offer [[unmatched]] convenience, comfort and flexibility, especially where public transport is poor. So while I personally value the freedom of a car, I believe well-developed public transport is the more sustainable and [[equitable]] option for society as a whole.

part3Samples.q: What are the effects of traffic congestion on cities?
part3Samples.answer: Traffic congestion has serious and costly effects. It wastes an enormous amount of people's time, reducing productivity and quality of life. It significantly worsens air pollution, harming public health and the environment. It also causes frustration and stress for commuters and can [[hamper]] emergency services. Economically, the lost hours and fuel represent a huge [[drain]]. So congestion is far more than an inconvenience; it [[undermines]] a city's efficiency and wellbeing.

part3Samples.q: How do you think transport will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I anticipate significant transformation. Electric vehicles will likely become the norm, drastically cutting emissions, and [[autonomous]], self-driving cars may reshape how we travel. Cities will probably invest more in cycling, walking and clean public transport. Concepts like [[shared mobility]] could reduce car ownership. So the future of transport is likely to be cleaner, smarter and more [[integrated]], hopefully making our cities less polluted and more liveable.

part3Samples.q: How can traffic problems in cities be solved?
part3Samples.answer: A combination of measures is most effective. Investing heavily in reliable, affordable public transport gives people a genuine alternative to driving. Encouraging cycling and walking through better [[infrastructure]] helps too. Some cities use [[congestion charging]] to [[discourage]] car use in busy areas. Better urban planning that reduces the need to travel far is also valuable. Essentially, the solution lies in making sustainable options more attractive than driving, rather than simply widening roads.

part3Samples.q: Some say factories should be moved away from residential areas. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I largely agree with this as a sensible measure. Locating polluting factories away from where people live can significantly reduce residents' [[direct exposure]] to harmful air and water pollution, protecting public health. However, it is not a complete solution, as pollution still spreads, and it may simply [[shift the burden]] to another community. So while separating industry from homes is beneficial, it must be combined with actually reducing the pollution [[at its source]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think it is better to have a few close friends or many acquaintances?
part3Samples.answer: I firmly believe that quality trumps quantity when it comes to friendship. A few close friends who genuinely understand you provide far deeper support than a large circle of [[superficial]] acquaintances. While it is useful to have a wide network for professional reasons, the emotional [[intimacy]] of a true friendship is something that simply cannot be [[replicated]] at scale.

part3Samples.q: How has technology changed the way people make friends?
part3Samples.answer: Technology has transformed it enormously. People now form friendships online with others across the globe, which was [[unimaginable]] a generation ago. This has made connection more [[accessible]], but I would argue these digital friendships can be more [[fragile]]. Meeting through a screen sometimes lacks the depth that comes from sharing real experiences face-to-face.

part3Samples.q: Why do some childhood friendships fade over time?
part3Samples.answer: I think it is largely a natural consequence of people growing and changing. As we mature, our interests, values and circumstances [[diverge]], and friends who once had everything in common may drift apart. Physical distance, when people move for work or study, only [[accelerates]] this. It is sad, but I see it as an almost [[inevitable]] part of life.

part3Samples.q: Do you think online friendships will replace face-to-face ones in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I doubt they will replace them entirely, but they will certainly become more significant. Online friendships are convenient and can be genuinely meaningful. However, humans are [[inherently]] social creatures who crave physical presence, so I believe in-person connection is [[irreplaceable]]. The most likely outcome is a [[hybrid]], where the two forms coexist and complement each other.

part3Samples.q: What can people do to maintain long-distance friendships?
part3Samples.answer: Consistent effort is really the crucial ingredient. Regular video calls and messages can [[keep a friendship alive]] despite the distance. I think it also helps to be [[deliberate]] about planning occasional visits, as nothing quite replaces meeting in person. Ultimately, both parties have to be committed, because a friendship that only one person [[sustains]] rarely lasts.

part3Samples.q: Some say honesty is always the best policy. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I largely agree, though I would add a small [[caveat]]. As a general principle, honesty builds trust and spares us the burden of maintaining lies, so it is almost always wise. However, I think it must be balanced with [[compassion]]; brutal honesty that needlessly wounds someone is not virtuous. So honesty is the best policy, provided it is delivered [[sensitively]].

part3Samples.q: How are family relationships different now compared to a generation ago?
part3Samples.answer: The biggest difference is probably the shift from large, extended families to smaller, more [[nuclear]] ones. In the past, several generations often lived under one roof, which fostered close bonds. Today, families are more [[dispersed]], and technology has, ironically, both connected and [[distanced]] us. Relationships are more equal now, but arguably less tightly knit.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think many families spend less time together nowadays?
part3Samples.answer: Several factors are at play. The demands of modern careers are [[relentless]], leaving parents exhausted and [[time-poor]]. On top of that, digital devices have become a real distraction, with family members often absorbed in their own screens even when in the same room. This gradual erosion of shared time is genuinely [[detrimental]] to close relationships.

part3Samples.q: How do you think family structures will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I anticipate that families will continue to become smaller and more diverse in form. We will likely see more single-parent households and [[blended families]] becoming [[commonplace]] and widely accepted. part3Samples.q: What can families do to stay close despite busy modern lives?

part3Samples.answer: I partly agree, as it is a genuine threat. The spread of a dominant global culture can certainly [[overshadow]] and dilute local traditions, languages and customs, leading to a worrying uniformity. However, I would not say it is entirely destructive. Globalisation also allows cultures to share and celebrate their uniqueness on a world stage. So while the risk of [[homogenisation]] is real, cultures can also prove remarkably [[resilient]] and adaptive.

It cleverly taps into our emotions, insecurities and aspirations, associating products with happiness, status or belonging rather than mere function. Its sheer ubiquity means we are exposed to it constantly, which [[reinforces]] its messages. Modern targeted advertising is especially potent, as it is tailored precisely to our interests. So it shapes our desires far more than we consciously realise, subtly [[steering]] our behaviour.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will become more conscious consumers in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am cautiously hopeful. There is a growing awareness of the environmental and ethical impact of our purchases, and movements towards [[minimalism]], sustainability and ethical consumption are [[gaining momentum]]. Younger generations in particular seem more [[values-driven]] in their spending. However, the powerful forces of marketing and convenience remain strong. So while I believe conscious consumption will increase, whether it becomes the norm depends on a genuine cultural shift.

part3Samples.q: How can people be encouraged to consume more responsibly?
part3Samples.answer: Education and awareness are key. Helping people understand the true environmental and social cost of their purchases can shift attitudes. Encouraging habits like buying quality over quantity, repairing rather than replacing, and choosing ethical brands makes a difference. Governments can also play a role through regulation and [[incentives]]. Ultimately, [[fostering]] a cultural value of [[sufficiency]] over excess, where we question whether we truly need something, is the most sustainable path.

part3Samples.q: Some say working hard is more important than having free time. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I respectfully disagree with framing it as either-or. Hard work is certainly important for achievement, and I value [[diligence]]. However, free time is not the opposite of hard work; it is what makes sustained hard work possible by preventing burnout. The two are [[complementary]]. In my view, someone who works intensely but never rests is not admirable but heading towards [[exhaustion]], so balance is wiser.

cueCards.title: Describe a magazine or newspaper you like to read
cueCards.prompt: Describe a magazine or newspaper you like to read

What I appreciate most is the depth of its reporting; unlike quick news headlines, it offers thoughtful, [[in-depth]] analysis. It helps me understand the context behind major events, which I find genuinely [[enlightening]]. That is especially useful in my job, because students often ask me about the situation in the countries they hope to study in. The writing is intelligent without being pretentious, which makes even complex topics accessible. Reading it keeps me well [[informed]] about the world in a way that scrolling social media never could. Honestly, in an age of shallow, rapid news consumption, I value having a source that encourages proper reflection. It has also noticeably improved my vocabulary and general knowledge over time. It has become a genuinely enjoyable weekend ritual that leaves me feeling both informed and [[intellectually stimulated]].

followUps.q: Do you ever read local newspapers too?
followUps.answer: Yes, I skim a Bengali daily newspaper most mornings over breakfast, mainly for national news. The magazine is for deeper reading, whereas the newspaper keeps me [[up to date]] with what's happening at home.

followUps.q: Do you prefer reading news in print or online?
followUps.answer: Online, mostly, because it's quicker and more convenient. That said, my father still insists on a printed newspaper every morning, and I do enjoy sharing it with him over tea.

part3: How important is it for people to follow the news?

part3Samples.q: How important is it for people to follow the news?
part3Samples.answer: I believe it is quite important for people to stay reasonably informed, as it is part of being an engaged citizen. Understanding current events helps us make sense of the world and participate in democracy. However, I would add a [[caveat]]; consuming too much news, especially negative or sensational content, can be [[overwhelming]] and [[anxiety-inducing]]. So the ideal is to stay informed through reliable sources without becoming obsessed.

part3Samples.q: How has the way people get news changed over the years?
part3Samples.answer: The change has been revolutionary. In the past, people relied on scheduled TV bulletins and printed newspapers, receiving curated news once or twice a day. Now, news is constant, instant and consumed largely through social media and online sources. This has made news more accessible, but also more [[fragmented]] and harder to verify. The rise of citizen journalism is a benefit, but so too is the spread of [[unverified]], [[sensational]] content.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think fake news spreads so easily?
part3Samples.answer: Several factors are at play. Social media algorithms tend to prioritise engaging content, and false or sensational stories are often more [[provocative]] than the truth. People also share things impulsively without verifying them, especially if they confirm existing beliefs. The lack of traditional editorial gatekeepers online means misinformation can spread [[unchecked]]. Combined with a general decline in media literacy, this creates the perfect conditions for falsehoods to [[proliferate]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think traditional newspapers will survive in the future?
part3Samples.answer: In their printed form, I think they will largely decline, as younger generations consume news almost entirely online. However, I do not believe quality journalism itself will disappear; rather, it will continue its shift to digital platforms and subscription models. The [[reputable]] news organisations behind the papers may well [[endure]], just in a different format. So the printed page may fade, but the institution of journalism should [[persist]].

part3Samples.q: What can be done to combat the spread of misinformation?
part3Samples.answer: Tackling this requires a combined effort. Improving media literacy so people can critically [[evaluate]] sources is perhaps the most important long-term solution. Social media platforms must also take greater responsibility, using fact-checking and adjusting algorithms that reward sensationalism. Supporting quality, independent journalism is equally vital. Ultimately, an informed, [[sceptical]] public is the best defence against the [[tide of misinformation]].

It contains my youthful thoughts, dreams and daily events, which are often [[amusing]] to read back now. There's one entry where I announced very seriously that I would become a famous cricketer, and another describing an argument with my younger sister over the last piece of a mango. I have kept it because it is a genuine [[time capsule]] of who I once was. Whenever I flick through it, I feel a wave of [[nostalgia]] for a simpler time in my life. What makes it so precious is that no amount of money could recreate those honest, [[unfiltered]] memories. It is fascinating, and occasionally [[embarrassing]], to see how much my perspective has changed. Honestly, I think keeping such personal records is genuinely valuable. followUps.q: Do you still keep a diary now?

part3Samples.q: How is childhood today different from childhood in the past?
part3Samples.answer: Childhood has changed dramatically. In the past, children spent most of their free time playing outdoors and socialising in person. Today, much of that has been [[supplanted]] by screens, which I find rather [[disconcerting]]. Children are also under far more academic pressure now. So while modern children have more opportunities, they arguably have a less [[carefree]] upbringing.

part3Samples.q: What effect does strict parenting have on children?
part3Samples.answer: It can have mixed effects. On one hand, strict parenting can instil discipline and a strong work ethic. On the other, if it is excessively [[authoritarian]], it may [[stifle]] a child's creativity and confidence, or even breed rebellion. In my opinion, the ideal lies in a balanced approach that is firm but also [[nurturing]] and understanding.

part3Samples.q: How do you think parenting will change in the coming decades?
part3Samples.answer: I expect parenting will become increasingly [[intertwined with]] technology. Parents will likely rely more on apps and online resources for guidance, and managing children's screen time will become an even more [[daunting]] challenge. I also anticipate a move towards more [[egalitarian]] parenting, with responsibilities shared more equally. Hopefully there will also be greater awareness of children's emotional wellbeing.

part3Samples.q: How can parents help children develop good values?
part3Samples.answer: The most effective way is by [[modelling]] those values themselves, since children imitate what they see. Beyond that, parents can use everyday situations as [[teaching moments]], discussing honesty or kindness openly. Encouraging empathy, perhaps through community involvement, also helps. part3Samples.q: Some say younger generations have life easier than older ones. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I think it is more [[nuanced]] than that. In material terms, young people today certainly enjoy comforts and technology their grandparents lacked. However, they face their own distinct pressures, such as intense competition, [[job insecurity]] and a constant online spotlight. So I would not say life is simply easier; rather, the [[hardships]] have shifted in nature.

cueCards.title: Describe a collection you have or would like to have
cueCards.prompt: Describe a collection you have or would like to have

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about a collection that takes up more and more space in my room every year. A collection I have gradually built up over the years is my collection of books, which has grown into something I am genuinely proud of. part3: Why are hobbies important in people's lives?

part3Samples.q: Why are hobbies important in people's lives?
part3Samples.answer: Hobbies are far more valuable than people often realise. They provide a [[vital outlet]] for relaxation and stress relief, offering a welcome escape from the pressures of work. They also allow for personal growth, creativity and a sense of accomplishment outside our professional identity. Additionally, many hobbies foster social connections. In my view, hobbies are essential for a balanced, fulfilling life, [[nourishing]] parts of ourselves that work often [[neglects]].

part3Samples.q: How do people's leisure activities differ between generations?

Younger people, by contrast, spend much of their leisure time on digital activities, such as gaming, streaming and social media. That said, there is considerable overlap, and interest in older hobbies is [[reviving]] among the young. part3Samples.q: What are the benefits of having a creative hobby?
part3Samples.answer: Creative hobbies offer numerous benefits. They provide a productive outlet for self-expression and can be deeply [[therapeutic]], reducing stress and improving mental wellbeing. The sense of accomplishment from creating something is genuinely rewarding and boosts confidence. They also keep the mind active and can spark skills that [[enrich]] other areas of life. Essentially, creative pursuits [[nourish the soul]] and offer a fulfilment that passive entertainment simply cannot match.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will have more free time in the future?
part3Samples.answer: This is uncertain. [[Optimistically]], if automation boosts productivity and society chooses to share the gains, people could work less and enjoy more leisure, as concepts like the four-day week suggest. People can start by consciously [[carving out]] even small [[pockets of time]], perhaps by reducing passive activities like scrolling on their phones. cueCards.title: Describe a device you would find hard to live without
cueCards.prompt: Describe a device you would find hard to live without

However, they have also introduced constant distraction and a degree of [[dependence]] that can harm our focus and relationships. So I see them as a remarkable tool that has improved life, provided we use them [[consciously]] rather than [[compulsively]].

part3Samples.q: How was life different before smartphones?
part3Samples.answer: Life was noticeably slower and, in some ways, more present. People were less [[contactable]] and more likely to be fully engaged in their [[immediate surroundings]] rather than staring at a screen. Getting lost, being bored or having to memorise information were normal. While we have gained incredible convenience, I think we have lost a certain patience and the ability to simply be [[idle]], which had its own value.

part3Samples.q: What effects does excessive smartphone use have on people?
part3Samples.answer: The effects can be quite detrimental. Excessive use seems to be linked to reduced [[attention spans]], disrupted sleep and increased anxiety, partly due to the constant stream of notifications. It can also erode face-to-face social skills and lead to a [[sedentary]] lifestyle. There is even a recognised phenomenon of phone addiction. part3Samples.q: How do you think mobile technology will develop in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I anticipate devices will become even more integrated into our lives, perhaps evolving beyond the handheld phone into [[wearables]] or augmented reality glasses. part3Samples.q: How can people reduce their dependence on their phones?

part3Samples.q: Some say technology is making face-to-face conversation a dying skill. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I think there is a [[kernel of truth]] to this, though I would not go so far as to call it dying. It is certainly true that some young people, accustomed to texting, can feel awkward in direct conversation and may struggle to read social cues. cueCards.title: Describe an object that is important in your culture
cueCards.prompt: Describe an object that is important in your culture

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about something you can see at almost every celebration in Bangladesh. An object of real cultural importance in my country is the traditional handloom sari, which carries deep significance. It is far more than a piece of clothing; it is a symbol of our heritage and identity. Woven by skilled artisans, each one is a genuine work of [[craftsmanship]], often taking days or even weeks to complete. The finest example is probably the jamdani, a delicate, almost transparent cotton sari whose weaving tradition has been recognised internationally. Women wear handloom saris at weddings, at Eid and especially at Pohela Boishakh, when the streets are full of red and white. They are also given as gifts at important family moments. I have known about it my whole life, having seen the women in my family wear them at every important occasion. My mother keeps a few folded carefully in her cupboard for special days, and since Sirajganj has a long tradition of handloom weaving, I've often seen weavers at work in nearby villages. What makes it so important is that it represents a centuries-old tradition that is sadly [[under threat]] from mass production. Wearing one on special days feels like honouring our [[ancestry]]. The intricate designs are genuinely [[exquisite]], and no two are ever identical. Honestly, I think it is vital that we protect such traditional crafts before they disappear. They connect us to our roots in a tangible way. I feel a real sense of pride whenever I see this beautiful item being worn and celebrated.

followUps.q: Have you ever bought a sari for someone?
followUps.answer: Yes, I bought a handloom sari for my mother last Eid. Choosing one was surprisingly difficult, because there were so many beautiful designs, but she loved the colour I picked.

followUps.q: Do young women in Bangladesh still wear saris?
followUps.answer: Yes, especially on special occasions like Pohela Boishakh and weddings. For everyday life, many prefer the salwar kameez, which is more practical, but the sari is still [[deeply cherished]].

part3Samples.q: Are young people less interested in traditions than older generations?

part3Samples.q: Why do you think some traditions are disappearing?

part3Samples.q: Do you think traditions will survive in the future?

There is actually a growing appreciation for heritage as a counterbalance to globalisation, with many people actively seeking to [[revive]] old customs. part3Samples.q: What can be done to preserve traditional culture?
part3Samples.answer: A [[concerted effort]] is needed. Education is crucial; teaching young people about their heritage in schools fosters pride and understanding. part3Samples.q: Some say globalisation mainly benefits wealthy countries. Do you agree?

It is often argued that wealthy nations and large corporations reap the greatest rewards, while poorer countries may suffer exploitation and cultural erosion. cueCards.title: Describe something you own that you repaired or fixed

What pleased me most was that I had saved money and rescued something from the [[scrap heap]]. Honestly, repairing it myself was far more [[rewarding]] than simply buying a new one. followUps.q: Do you usually repair things or replace them?

part3Samples.q: What does it mean to live sustainably?
part3Samples.answer: To me, living sustainably means meeting our own needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs. In practice, it involves being mindful of our consumption, reducing waste, and using resources efficiently and responsibly. It is about living within the planet's ecological limits rather than [[depleting]] them. Essentially, it is a shift from a throwaway, [[exploitative]] mindset to one of [[stewardship]] and long-term responsibility.

part3Samples.q: Are people more environmentally conscious now than in the past?
part3Samples.answer: Yes, considerably so. Environmental awareness has grown enormously over recent decades, driven by scientific evidence, media coverage and visible impacts like extreme weather. Concepts like recycling, carbon footprints and sustainability are now part of everyday conversation, which was not the case a generation ago. However, I would add that awareness does not always [[translate into action]]. So people are certainly more [[conscious]], even if their behaviour has not fully [[caught up]].

part3Samples.q: Why is it hard for people to change to a more sustainable lifestyle?
part3Samples.answer: Several barriers make it difficult. Sustainable options are sometimes more expensive or less convenient than the alternatives, so cost and habit get in the way. Many people also feel their individual actions are [[insignificant]] against such a vast problem. Additionally, our entire economic system is built around consumption, making unsustainable choices the default. So it is a combination of practical obstacles, [[ingrained habits]] and a sense of [[powerlessness]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think future generations will live more sustainably?
part3Samples.answer: I am hopeful they will, partly [[out of necessity]]. As the impacts of unsustainable living become more severe, future generations will likely be forced to adapt. [[Encouragingly]], young people today already show strong environmental values and are pushing for change. Advances in green technology should also make sustainable living easier and cheaper. So I believe sustainability will increasingly become the norm rather than the exception, driven by both necessity and [[shifting values]].

part3Samples.q: How can governments encourage sustainable behaviour?
part3Samples.answer: Governments have powerful tools [[at their disposal]]. They can use financial incentives, like subsidies for renewable energy or electric cars, and taxes on pollution and waste to [[steer behaviour]]. Investing in sustainable infrastructure, such as public transport and recycling, makes green choices easier. Regulation and clear information, like [[carbon labelling]], also help. Essentially, by making the sustainable choice the easy, affordable and default option, governments can drive widespread change.

part3Samples.q: Some say buying things makes people happy. Do you agree?

cueCards.title: Describe a tradition in your country

Unlike religious festivals, it belongs to every Bengali, which makes it wonderfully [[inclusive]]. In an increasingly globalised world, traditions like this help [[keep our roots alive]]. Honestly, the atmosphere on that day is genuinely [[uplifting]], and it fills people with optimism for the year ahead. Every year I go to the fair with my younger sister, and even though we buy the same sweets and wander past the same stalls, it never loses its charm. I think it is a beautiful example of how a shared tradition can strengthen a whole community's sense of belonging.

It sounds like a cliché, but I think very few people actually live by it. I think this is genuinely important because so many young people are [[paralysed]] by the fear of getting things wrong. In my country especially, exam results are treated as a matter of family honour, so failing can feel like a disaster rather than a lesson. I would give this advice to my younger cousins, who sometimes hesitate to try new things in case they fail. I would also share it with the students I meet at work, many of whom are too scared to apply to good universities in case they are rejected. I would tell them that every successful person has failed countless times, and that setbacks are often the most [[instructive]] experiences of all. The key is to be [[resilient]] and to keep going. A rejection letter or a poor mark is simply information about what to improve next time, not a judgement on who you are. I believe this mindset could help them enormously, freeing them to take risks and pursue their dreams. Honestly, I wish someone had drilled this into me when I was younger, because I wasted opportunities out of fear. I think teaching young people to embrace failure rather than dread it is one of the most [[invaluable]] lessons we can offer them. followUps.q: Who gave you the best advice when you were younger?

I agree with it strongly because it has noticeably improved [[morale]] and reduced unnecessary stress, such as sitting in rush-hour traffic. Honestly, I think it is a genuinely [[progressive]] and sensible approach. It has made me far more loyal to the company, and I think it helps us keep good staff, who might otherwise be tempted by bigger firms in Dhaka. I believe rules like this, which trust employees and prioritise results over [[rigid]] attendance, are the future of work. part3Samples.q: How important is work-life balance?
part3Samples.answer: I believe it is absolutely essential for long-term wellbeing. Without a healthy balance, people risk burnout, which harms both their health and, ironically, their productivity. Time for family, rest and hobbies is not a luxury; it is what makes us [[resilient]] and effective. In my view, a culture that glorifies overwork is ultimately [[unsustainable]] and [[counterproductive]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think people had a better work-life balance in the past?
part3Samples.answer: In some respects, yes. In the past, work was more clearly confined to the workplace, and once you went home, you were genuinely off duty. Today, smartphones mean we are perpetually [[reachable]], and the boundary between work and personal life has become dangerously [[blurred]]. That said, past generations often worked longer physical hours, so it is not entirely one-sided; the nature of the [[imbalance]] has changed.

part3Samples.q: What are the consequences of a poor work-life balance?
part3Samples.answer: The consequences can be severe. Chronic overwork frequently leads to stress, burnout and serious health problems, both physical and mental. It also strains personal relationships, as work encroaches on time with family and friends. Ironically, it often reduces long-term productivity too. Essentially, neglecting your personal life for work is [[self-defeating]], [[taking a heavy toll]] that eventually [[undermines]] everything.

part3Samples.q: Do you think work-life balance will improve in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am hopeful, though not entirely certain. There is a growing cultural awareness of the importance of wellbeing, and flexible and remote working could, if managed well, improve balance considerably. Concepts like the four-day week are [[gaining traction]]. However, there is a risk that [[constant connectivity]] could make things worse. So improvement is possible, but it will require a [[deliberate cultural shift]] rather than happening automatically.

part3Samples.q: What can people do to achieve a better work-life balance?
part3Samples.answer: On a personal level, setting firm boundaries is crucial, such as not checking work emails after hours. Learning to prioritise and, importantly, to say no to excessive demands helps enormously. Making dedicated time for rest and relationships should be treated as [[non-negotiable]]. However, individuals can [[only do so much]]; employers must also foster a culture that genuinely respects personal time and does not reward [[overwork]].

part3Samples.q: Some say people today change jobs too often. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I do not entirely agree that it is a problem. Changing jobs frequently is often a sensible way to gain diverse experience, increase pay and find a better fit, especially in a fast-changing economy. The old model of [[lifelong loyalty]] is somewhat [[outdated]]. That said, changing too often can look unstable to employers and prevent one from developing deep [[expertise]], so a degree of balance is wise.

cueCards.title: Describe a film that made a strong impression on you
cueCards.prompt: Describe a film that made a strong impression on you

sample.answer: A film that made a lasting impression on me was a drama I watched a couple of years ago about a family overcoming hardship. The story followed a father who loses his livelihood and struggles to keep his children in school, while trying to hide his worries from them. On the surface it was a simple story, but it dealt with its themes in a genuinely [[profound]] way. I watched it at home on a quiet evening with my parents, expecting light entertainment, and ended up completely [[absorbed]]. What impressed me most was how realistic and emotionally honest it was; the characters felt like real people rather than actors. The acting was wonderfully [[understated]], with no dramatic speeches, just small looks and silences that said everything. There was one scene where the father quietly skips his own meal so the children can eat, and the whole room went silent. By the end, I was genuinely moved, and I found myself thinking about it for days afterwards. My father, who ran a small business for many years, went unusually quiet, and I think it reminded him of some difficult times of his own. It explored ideas about resilience and family in a way that really [[resonated]] with me. Honestly, I think the mark of a great film is that it stays with you long after the credits roll, and this one certainly did. It was far more than mere entertainment; it offered a real [[insight]] into the human condition. I have recommended it to many friends since, and it remains one of my favourite films.

followUps.q: Do you prefer watching films at home or in the cinema?

part3Samples.q: Do you think online entertainment is better than traditional forms?

However, traditional forms like cinema, live theatre or reading a physical book offer a certain quality and communal experience that online consumption can lack. So I appreciate the convenience, but I do not think it fully replaces the [[richness]] of certain traditional experiences.

part3Samples.q: How is the way people are entertained today different from the past?
part3Samples.answer: The difference is stark. In the past, entertainment was largely communal and scheduled; families gathered to watch a programme at a set time, or went out to the cinema. Today, entertainment is highly individualised and on-demand, consumed alone on personal devices whenever we wish. This offers wonderful freedom, but I think we have lost some of the shared, [[communal]] aspect. Entertainment has become more [[personalised]] yet arguably more [[solitary]].

part3Samples.q: Why has streaming become so popular?
part3Samples.answer: Its popularity comes down to convenience and choice. Streaming offers instant, on-demand access to an enormous library of content that you can watch anywhere, anytime, without adverts. It is also relatively affordable compared to traditional cable. The personalised recommendations keep people engaged, and [[binge-watching]] entire series has become a [[cultural phenomenon]]. Essentially, it perfectly suits the modern desire for flexibility and [[instant gratification]].

part3Samples.q: How do you think entertainment will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I expect entertainment to become far more [[immersive]] and interactive. Virtual and augmented reality could allow us to step inside stories and games rather than merely watching them. Artificial intelligence may create personalised content tailored precisely to individual tastes. The line between passive viewing and active participation will likely blur. part3Samples.q: How can people avoid spending too much time on online entertainment?

part3Samples.q: Some say art is not as important as science. Do you agree?

Science advances our material understanding and improves our lives technologically, which is crucial. But art nourishes our emotional and spiritual lives, fosters empathy, and gives meaning to human existence. A world with science but no art would be efficient yet [[soulless]]. cueCards.title: Describe a song or piece of music that is important to you

sample.answer: A song that holds real significance for me is a particular folk melody that was often played in my home when I was a child. It is a bhatiali song, a traditional kind of boatman's song from our river region, slow and full of longing. I first heard it as a young boy, and it is deeply tied to memories of my grandparents. My grandfather used to hum it while we sat on the veranda of their village home, watching the boats move slowly along the river in the evening. Whenever I hear it now, it instantly transports me back to those [[carefree]] childhood days. What makes it so important is not the song itself but the powerful [[nostalgia]] it evokes. The gentle melody and heartfelt lyrics have a wonderfully [[soothing]] quality that I find comforting. It is amazing how a single piece of music can carry such emotional weight and instantly bring back a whole era of your life. Honestly, I think this is the true power of music; it becomes intertwined with our memories. My grandfather is in his eighties now, and he still hums it sometimes when we visit, which makes it feel even more precious to me. Listening to it now sometimes brings a tear to my eye, in the best possible way. followUps.q: Do young people in your country still listen to folk music?

part3Samples.q: How has the way people listen to music changed?

Now, streaming gives us instant access to virtually all recorded music, and we tend to consume it in playlists and individual tracks. part3Samples.q: What effect does learning a musical instrument have on children?

Governments should recognise their cultural and economic value and provide stable funding rather than treating them as [[expendable]]. Encouraging private sponsorship and [[philanthropy]] can supplement this. Integrating arts education properly into schools ensures future generations value them. part3Samples.q: Some say globalisation is destroying local cultures. Do you agree?

The spread of a dominant global culture can certainly [[overshadow]] and dilute local traditions, languages and customs, leading to a worrying uniformity. cueCards.title: Describe a website or app you find useful

Personally, I favour a [[blend]] of the two, as they [[complement]] each other nicely.

part3Samples.q: Why do some people find learning easier than others?
part3Samples.answer: There are many contributing factors. Some of it comes down to natural [[aptitude]], but I think motivation and [[mindset]] matter far more. part3Samples.q: How do you think work will change in the next few decades?

part3Samples.q: Is working from home better or worse than working in an office?

Personally, I think a [[hybrid]] model captures the best of both, though it requires real [[self-discipline]] to work remotely well.

part3Samples.q: What effects will automation have on employment?
part3Samples.answer: Automation is a genuine [[double-edged sword]]. On one hand, it will [[inevitably]] [[displace]] many workers in routine and manual jobs, which is a serious concern. On the other hand, history shows that technology also creates entirely new industries and roles. The key effect is a shift in the types of jobs available, which means workforces will need to adapt and acquire new skills.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will work fewer hours in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I think it is a real possibility, and one I would welcome. As automation boosts productivity, there is a strong argument that the gains could be shared through shorter working weeks. However, this will not happen automatically; it will require [[deliberate choices]] by businesses and governments to [[prioritise]] wellbeing over pure output.

part3Samples.q: How can workers prepare for a rapidly changing job market?
part3Samples.answer: The single most important thing is to embrace lifelong learning. Workers should continually update their skills and remain [[adaptable]], rather than assuming their current expertise will last forever. part3Samples.q: Some say working hard is more important than having free time. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I respectfully disagree with framing it as either-or. Hard work is certainly important for achievement, and I value [[diligence]]. However, free time is not the opposite of hard work; it is what makes sustained hard work possible by preventing burnout. The two are [[complementary]]. sample.answer: A skill I firmly believe everyone should have is basic cooking. In my view, it is a genuinely essential life skill that far too many people [[neglect]]. sample.answer: A way technology has profoundly changed our lives is in how we communicate with one another. This happened incredibly quickly; within about a decade, cheap smartphones and mobile internet reached almost every corner of Bangladesh, even villages like my grandparents'. My father still remembers queuing at a shop in town to make a short, crackly call to a relative in Dhaka, and letters took over a week to arrive. Today, a video call across continents is effortless and free, which is genuinely [[remarkable]]. I speak to my elder sister in Dhaka almost every day, and my nephew loves showing me his toys on the screen. However, I do have some [[reservations]]; I feel it has sometimes replaced deeper, face-to-face interaction with shallower digital contact. There is a certain irony that we are more connected than ever yet arguably lonelier. At family gatherings, I sometimes notice everyone staring at their phones instead of talking to the people sitting right next to them. Honestly, like most technology, I think it is a [[double-edged sword]]. Used mindfully, it is an incredible tool, but it requires a degree of [[discipline]]. Overall, though, I am grateful for how it has shrunk the world and brought distant people closer.

followUps.answer: My grandfather does, surprisingly well for someone in his eighties. My grandmother prefers ordinary calls, because she finds it strange to see her own face on the screen, which always makes us laugh.

sample.answer: A significant challenge facing young people today is the immense pressure created by social media. The more time we spend scrolling, the more money these companies make, so they have little reason to change. It affects almost all young people, who often feel inadequate when measuring their real lives against these unrealistic highlights. I see it in my younger sister's friends, who worry about how many likes a photo gets, and in some of the students I advise, who compare themselves with classmates who have already gone abroad. I think it can lead to serious anxiety and a distorted sense of self-worth. To tackle it, I believe we need better education about using social media [[mindfully]], along with a cultural shift towards valuing authenticity over appearances. Parents and teachers also need to talk about it openly, rather than simply banning phones. Honestly, I think the platforms themselves should also [[bear some responsibility]] for their design. It is a complex issue without a simple solution. Having grown up alongside this technology, I have felt its effects personally. part3Samples.q: Do you think social media has a positive or negative effect on society?

However, its negative effects are equally significant, from spreading misinformation to fuelling anxiety and comparison. In my view, the platforms themselves are [[neutral]]; the real issue is how we use them. Used [[mindfully]], the benefits can outweigh the drawbacks.

part3Samples.q: How has social media changed the way people communicate?
part3Samples.answer: It has transformed communication dramatically. In the past, staying in touch required letters or calls, whereas now we can share our lives instantly with hundreds of people at once. Communication has become faster and more visual, but arguably more [[superficial]]. We interact more frequently yet often less [[meaningfully]], replacing deep conversations with quick likes and comments. So it has [[widened our reach]] while sometimes shallowing our connections.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think people share so much of their lives online?
part3Samples.answer: I think it stems largely from a deep human desire for validation and connection. Receiving likes and comments triggers a sense of approval that can be quite [[addictive]]. part3Samples.q: How do you think social media will develop in the future?

Artificial intelligence will make content ever more [[personalised]], which raises concerns about [[echo chambers]]. part3Samples.q: What can be done to reduce the harmful effects of social media?

part3Samples.q: Some say peer pressure decreases as people get older. Do you agree?

However, the pressure simply takes on a more [[subtle]] form in adulthood, such as keeping up with colleagues' lifestyles. So it lessens, but it certainly does not [[vanish]].

On one hand, studying abroad would offer invaluable experience and open new doors, but it is expensive and involves leaving my family. My father has recently retired, and my mother often travels to the village to look after my grandparents, so I feel a certain responsibility to be around. On the other hand, staying would mean steady progress but perhaps fewer opportunities for growth. I have a good position at my consultancy, and my manager has hinted that more responsibility may come my way soon. I need to make this decision soon, which makes it feel quite [[pressing]]. Honestly, I keep [[going back and forth]], weighing the potential rewards against the risks and sacrifices. It is a rather [[daunting]] choice, precisely because both paths have real merit. I have been seeking advice from people I trust, including my father and my elder sister, and trying to think about what truly matters to me in the long run. Whatever I decide, I want it to be a well-considered choice rather than an [[impulsive]] one. I am confident I will eventually reach a sensible conclusion, and that I will have no regrets.

followUps.q: How do you usually make big decisions?
followUps.answer: I write down the pros and cons, talk to a few people I trust, and then give myself a few days. Rushing never works for me; I need time for things to [[sink in]].

part3Samples.q: Why do you think so many students want to study abroad?

Studying abroad offers [[cultural immersion]] and independence that home study cannot, and sometimes access to better facilities. However, it is expensive, and studying at home is cheaper, closer to family, and free of the challenge of adapting to a foreign culture. So neither is universally better; it is a matter of [[weighing]] the [[enrichment]] against the cost and difficulty.

part3Samples.q: What challenges do students face when studying in another country?
part3Samples.answer: They face numerous challenges. Culture shock and homesickness are extremely common, especially at first. A language barrier can make both study and daily life difficult and [[isolating]]. There are also practical hurdles, like managing finances and navigating an unfamiliar system alone. part3Samples.q: Do you think studying abroad will become more common in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I think physical study abroad will remain popular but may face competition from online alternatives. Increasingly, students can access foreign universities' courses remotely, offering the academic benefits without the cost of [[relocating]]. However, the cultural and personal growth of actually living abroad is [[irreplaceable]], so demand will [[persist]]. part3Samples.q: Some say job security is more important than job satisfaction. Do you agree?

cueCards.title: Describe a useful habit for managing money
cueCards.prompt: Describe a useful habit for managing money
bullets: and why you would recommend it

sample.answer: A useful habit I have developed for managing money is setting aside a fixed amount of savings every single month, before spending on anything else. I developed this habit a few years ago, after realising I was spending rather [[carelessly]] and never managing to save. When I got my first salary, I spent it on eating out and new gadgets, and by the end of the month there was nothing left. My father, who ran a small business for over thirty years, sat me down and explained how he had always put something aside, even in difficult years. Now, as soon as I receive my salary, I transfer a set portion into a separate savings account. What makes it so effective is that it removes the temptation to spend that money, since it is out of sight. This habit has given me a genuine sense of [[financial security]] and a safety net for emergencies. It is also how I am funding my plans to study abroad, which would be impossible otherwise. Honestly, it has been one of the most [[beneficial]] financial decisions I have ever made. I would strongly recommend it to anyone, because it makes saving automatic rather than an afterthought. The key is to treat savings as a non-negotiable expense, just like any other bill. Over time, even small, consistent amounts add up [[considerably]]. It has taught me the value of discipline and [[delayed gratification]], which are invaluable lessons in life, and I am grateful my father taught me early.

followUps.q: Do young people in your country usually save money?
followUps.answer: Many try, but it is not easy with rising prices and the pressure to keep up with friends. Mobile banking has made saving simpler, though, and I think financial awareness is gradually improving.

followUps.q: Have you taught this habit to anyone else?
followUps.answer: Yes, my younger sister. I encouraged her to save a small part of her pocket money every month, and she was delighted when she could buy her own books without asking our parents.

part3Samples.q: How important is money in life?
part3Samples.answer: Money is [[undeniably]] important, but its importance has limits. It is essential for meeting our basic needs, providing security, and giving us freedom and opportunities, so I would never dismiss it. However, beyond a certain point of comfort, its ability to improve our happiness [[diminishes sharply]]. Health, relationships and purpose matter far more. So I see money as a vital tool and [[enabler]], but a poor ultimate goal in itself.

part3Samples.q: Is it better to save money or spend it?
part3Samples.answer: A healthy balance between the two is ideal. Saving is [[prudent]], providing security, peace of mind and the means to achieve future goals or weather emergencies. However, being excessively frugal can mean missing out on valuable experiences and enjoyment in the present. Spending wisely, particularly on experiences and things that genuinely enrich life, is worthwhile. So I favour disciplined saving combined with mindful spending, avoiding both reckless [[extravagance]] and joyless [[hoarding]].

part3Samples.q: What effect does the pursuit of wealth have on people?
part3Samples.answer: The pursuit of wealth has mixed effects. Positively, it can motivate hard work, innovation and achievement, driving both personal and economic progress. However, an excessive obsession with wealth can be corrosive, leading people to become greedy, materialistic, and to neglect relationships, ethics and their own wellbeing. It can foster perpetual dissatisfaction too. So while a healthy desire to prosper is fine, an [[all-consuming]] [[fixation]] on money can genuinely [[distort]] a person's values.

part3Samples.q: Do you think the gap between rich and poor will grow in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am concerned that it might, without deliberate intervention. Trends like automation, which may concentrate wealth among those who own the technology, and globalisation could widen the gap further. However, there is also growing awareness of inequality and political pressure to address it through [[progressive taxation]] and social policy. So the outcome is not [[predetermined]]; whether the gap widens or narrows will depend on the political choices societies make to [[redistribute]] opportunity.

part3Samples.q: What can be done to reduce poverty?
part3Samples.answer: Reducing poverty requires a comprehensive approach. Access to quality education and healthcare is fundamental, as it enables social mobility. Creating decent, well-paid jobs and ensuring fair wages tackles the [[root causes]]. Social [[safety nets]], like unemployment support, protect the most vulnerable. Progressive taxation can fund these efforts. Ultimately, empowering people with opportunities and skills, rather than mere [[handouts]], offers the most sustainable path out of poverty.

part3Samples.q: Some say buying things makes people happy. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I only partly agree. There is undeniably a short-term thrill in acquiring something new, so buying can bring a [[fleeting]] sense of pleasure. However, many people feel this happiness is temporary and superficial, quickly fading in a cycle sometimes called the [[hedonic treadmill]]. Lasting happiness tends to come from experiences and relationships, not possessions. So while shopping offers momentary joy, relying on it for happiness is ultimately [[hollow]] and unfulfilling.

cueCards.title: Describe a social problem you care about
cueCards.prompt: Describe a social problem you care about
bullets: and what could be done about it

sample.answer: A social problem I care deeply about is the lack of quality education available to children from poorer backgrounds. In my country, a child's future is too often determined by the wealth of their family, which I find genuinely [[unjust]]. Wealthier families can pay for private tutors and good schools, while poorer children often sit in overcrowded classrooms with too few teachers. This matters to me because I believe education is the most powerful tool for breaking the cycle of poverty. I also see it every day in my work, where the students who reach us are usually the lucky ones who had support from the start. It affects millions of talented children who never get the chance to [[fulfil their potential]] simply due to their circumstances. Near my hometown, for example, there are children living on the char lands, the river islands of the Jamuna, who have to cross the river by boat just to reach school, and many simply drop out. I think this is a tragic waste of human potential. To address it, I believe there needs to be far greater investment in public schools and more scholarship opportunities for the [[disadvantaged]]. Better pay for rural teachers would also help attract talented people. Honestly, I think providing equal access to good education is one of the most important things any society can do. It is an issue I feel strongly about, and I try to support relevant charities where I can. I genuinely believe that giving every child a fair start would create a more [[equitable]] and prosperous society for everyone.

followUps.q: Have you ever volunteered to help with this problem?
followUps.answer: A little. During university, I taught basic English to children in my grandparents' village during the holidays. It was only a few weeks, but seeing their enthusiasm was incredibly [[rewarding]].

followUps.q: Do you think the situation is improving?
followUps.answer: Slowly, yes. More girls are in school now than a generation ago, and mobile phones give some access to online lessons. But the gap in quality between rich and poor areas is still very wide.

part3Samples.q: Do you think society treats everyone equally?
part3Samples.answer: Unfortunately, I do not think any society treats everyone truly equally, though many have made real progress. Despite laws promoting equality, discrimination based on factors like gender, ethnicity, class or background still persists, often subtly. People's opportunities are still heavily influenced by the [[circumstances of their birth]]. So while the ideal of equality is widely embraced, in practice significant [[disparities]] and [[injustices]] remain that we must continue to address.

part3Samples.q: Has society become more or less equal over time?
part3Samples.answer: In many respects, society has become considerably more equal. Enormous progress has been made in areas like women's rights, racial equality and the rights of minorities compared to the past. Legal discrimination has been [[dismantled]] in many places. However, economic inequality has actually widened in some countries. So the picture is mixed; we have [[made great strides]] in social and legal equality, while economic disparities remain a [[persistent]] challenge.

part3Samples.q: What are the main causes of inequality in society?
part3Samples.answer: Inequality stems from a [[complex web]] of factors. Unequal access to quality education and healthcare is a major driver, as it limits opportunity from birth. Discrimination based on gender, race or class also plays a role. Economic systems that concentrate wealth, along with the circumstances one is born into, [[perpetuate]] the cycle. So inequality is rarely due to a single cause; it results from [[structural]], historical and social factors that reinforce one another.

part3Samples.q: Do you think full equality is achievable?
part3Samples.answer: I think complete [[equality of outcome]] is probably unrealistic, given natural differences in talent, effort and luck. However, equality of opportunity, where everyone has a genuinely fair chance to succeed, is a [[worthy]] and achievable goal to strive towards. We may never reach a perfectly equal society, but we can continually reduce unfair barriers. So while perfect equality may be an ideal rather than a destination, meaningful progress towards fairness is absolutely [[attainable]].

part3Samples.q: How can governments promote greater equality?
part3Samples.answer: Governments have powerful tools. Ensuring universal access to quality education and healthcare is perhaps the most important, as it [[levels the playing field]]. Progressive taxation and social welfare programmes can reduce economic disparities. Strong anti-discrimination laws protect marginalised groups. Investing in disadvantaged communities helps break cycles of poverty. Essentially, by actively removing barriers and [[redistributing]] opportunity, governments can foster a more [[equitable]] and inclusive society.

part3Samples.q: Some say education should be free for everyone. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly agree, at least regarding basic and secondary education. I see education as a fundamental right and a [[public good]], not a privilege for those who can afford it. Free access promotes [[social mobility]] and reduces inequality. For higher education, the picture is more complex due to cost, but I believe it should at least be heavily [[subsidised]] so that talent, not wealth, determines opportunity.

cueCards.title: Describe an outdoor activity you enjoy
cueCards.prompt: Describe an outdoor activity you enjoy

sample.answer: An outdoor activity I thoroughly enjoy is hiking, particularly in the hill areas of Sylhet and Bandarban. Sirajganj itself is completely flat, so I usually go on a trip once or twice a year, often during the cooler winter months when the trails are dry. I usually go with a small group of close friends from university, which makes it even more enjoyable. We share the planning, travel overnight by bus and stay in simple guesthouses, which is all part of the adventure. What I love about it is the wonderful combination of exercise, fresh air and stunning scenery. After months of office work and busy roads, spending a few days in nature is genuinely [[rejuvenating]]. There is something deeply satisfying about reaching the top of a trail after a challenging climb and being rewarded with a [[breathtaking]] view. In Bandarban, you can sometimes stand above the clouds in the early morning, which I will never forget. Honestly, I find hiking to be both physically and mentally [[restorative]]; it clears my head like nothing else. It is also a great way to bond with friends, away from the distractions of daily life, as the phone signal is often weak anyway. I think spending time in nature is something modern life sorely lacks, and hiking is my favourite way to reconnect with it. Between trips, I make do with long walks along the river at home. I always return home feeling tired but genuinely [[content]]. It is easily one of my favourite ways to spend a holiday, and I am already counting down to our next [[excursion]].

followUps.q: Does your family worry when you go hiking?
followUps.answer: My mother certainly does. She makes me promise to call her every evening and to avoid dangerous trails in the rainy season. It is a small price to pay for her peace of mind.

followUps.q: Would you like to hike in another country?
followUps.answer: Very much. I would love to trek in Nepal one day, perhaps on one of the shorter routes in the Himalayas. The scenery there must be even more [[awe-inspiring]] than anything we have here.

part3Samples.q: Why are hobbies important in people's lives?

In my view, hobbies are essential for a balanced, fulfilling life, [[nourishing]] parts of ourselves that work often [[neglects]].

part3Samples.q: How do people's leisure activities differ between generations?

Younger people, by contrast, spend much of their leisure time on digital activities, such as gaming, streaming and social media. That said, there is considerable overlap, and interest in older hobbies is [[reviving]] among the young. part3Samples.q: What are the benefits of having a creative hobby?
part3Samples.answer: Creative hobbies offer numerous benefits. They provide a productive outlet for self-expression and can be deeply [[therapeutic]], reducing stress and improving mental wellbeing. Essentially, creative pursuits [[nourish the soul]] and offer a fulfilment that passive entertainment simply cannot match.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will have more free time in the future?
part3Samples.answer: This is uncertain. [[Optimistically]], if automation boosts productivity and society chooses to share the gains, people could work less and enjoy more leisure, as concepts like the four-day week suggest. However, there is an opposing risk that [[constant connectivity]] and economic pressure could actually [[erode]] our free time further. So the amount of leisure we have may depend less on technology and more on the choices society makes about priorities.

part3Samples.q: Many people say they have no time for hobbies. What can they do?
part3Samples.answer: It often comes down to priorities rather than an absolute lack of time. part3Samples.q: Some say building more housing is more important than preserving parks. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I understand the argument given the housing crisis, but I largely disagree with sacrificing parks. With clever planning, cities can build housing on [[brownfield sites]] and increase density elsewhere while preserving parks. cueCards.title: Describe a new activity you have started recently

sample.answer: A new activity I have taken up recently is journaling, or writing down my thoughts each day. I bought a simple notebook from a stationery shop near my office, and I write in a mixture of Bengali and English, depending on what feels more natural. Each evening I spend a few minutes reflecting on my day, which has become a calming [[ritual]]. I usually write after dinner, when the house is quiet, sitting at my desk with a cup of tea. Honestly, I have found it far more [[beneficial]] than I expected. It has helped me become more [[self-aware]] and has noticeably reduced my stress. part3Samples.q: What do you think makes people truly happy?

Strong, loving relationships seem to be the greatest source of happiness. Beyond that, having a sense of purpose, good health, and the freedom to pursue what we find meaningful all contribute enormously. So I believe true happiness is [[rooted in]] connection, purpose and [[gratitude]], not in material wealth.

part3Samples.q: Are people happier now than in the past?
part3Samples.answer: This is a fascinating and debated question. In material terms, we are far better off than previous generations, with more comfort, health and opportunity. Yet, [[curiously]], rates of anxiety and depression seem to be rising, especially among the young. It appears that material progress has not straightforwardly translated into greater happiness. So while we have gained much, I am not convinced we are [[fundamentally]] happier, which suggests happiness depends on more than mere [[prosperity]] and comfort.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think some wealthy people are unhappy?
part3Samples.answer: This reflects the fact that money, beyond meeting basic needs, has [[diminishing returns]] on happiness. Wealthy people may still suffer from poor relationships, a lack of purpose, or the isolation and pressure that wealth can bring. There is also the phenomenon where people constantly adapt and want more, never feeling satisfied. So it demonstrates that happiness is not something money can simply buy; it depends on deeper, [[non-material]] [[fulfilment]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will be happier in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am genuinely uncertain. On one hand, advances in medicine, technology and [[living standards]] could improve wellbeing. There is also growing awareness of mental health and the importance of a balanced life. On the other hand, rising pressures, social media comparison and uncertainty could work against happiness. So I think future happiness will depend less on material progress and more on whether we learn to [[prioritise]] the things that genuinely [[nourish]] human wellbeing.

part3Samples.q: What can societies do to improve people's wellbeing?
part3Samples.answer: Societies can take meaningful steps. Prioritising mental health services and reducing the [[stigma]] around them is crucial. Fostering community, reducing inequality, and ensuring people have access to nature, leisure and a healthy work-life balance all help. Some argue governments should measure national wellbeing, not just economic output. Essentially, by valuing human [[flourishing]] alongside economic growth, societies can create conditions in which more people can genuinely [[thrive]] and feel content.

part3Samples.q: Some say hobbies should be useful, not just for fun. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I respectfully disagree with that as a rule. While hobbies that build skills are certainly valuable, I firmly believe a hobby does not need to be productive to be [[worthwhile]]. The primary purpose of leisure is enjoyment, relaxation and wellbeing, and something that brings pure joy is valuable in itself. Insisting that all free time be useful reflects an overly [[utilitarian]] mindset. Sometimes, doing something simply for pleasure is [[exactly the point]].

cueCards.title: Describe how you like to spend your weekends
cueCards.prompt: Describe how you like to spend your weekends

sample.answer: I like to spend my weekends striking a balance between relaxation and being productive. In Bangladesh, the weekend is Friday and Saturday, so it has a slightly different rhythm from the West. After a demanding week, my priority is usually to properly [[unwind]] and recharge. I often start by catching up on sleep, which I sacrifice during the week. On Friday, I go to the mosque with my father for the midday prayer, and afterwards the whole family has a big lunch together, which is the highlight of my week. I then like to meet friends or family, perhaps for a meal or a simple outing, since spending time with loved ones is genuinely [[restorative]]. Once or twice a month, we take the bus to my grandparents' village home, where I sit with my grandfather and listen to his stories. I also try to fit in some of my hobbies, like reading or walking along the Jamuna, which I never have time for during the week. On Saturday evenings, I often meet a couple of old friends at a tea stall near the river. What I enjoy most is the freedom and lack of a rigid schedule; I can be [[spontaneous]] and do whatever I feel like. Honestly, I think weekends are essential for maintaining a healthy work-life balance. Without that break, the weeks would blur into one exhausting stretch. I make a conscious effort not to let work spill into them. A good weekend leaves me feeling refreshed and genuinely [[reinvigorated]], ready to face the week ahead with renewed energy and a clear [[sense of perspective]].

followUps.q: Do you ever work at the weekend?
followUps.answer: Occasionally, when application deadlines are close and students need urgent help. I don't mind now and then, but I try hard not to let it become a habit.

followUps.q: Were your weekends different when you were a child?
followUps.answer: Completely. As a child, I spent weekends playing cricket in the street from morning till evening. Now I value rest and conversation far more, which I suppose is a sign of growing up.

part3Samples.q: How important is work-life balance?
part3Samples.answer: I believe it is absolutely essential for long-term wellbeing. Without a healthy balance, people risk burnout, which harms both their health and, ironically, their productivity. Time for family, rest and hobbies is not a luxury; it is what makes us [[resilient]] and effective. In my view, a culture that glorifies overwork is ultimately [[unsustainable]] and [[counterproductive]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think people had a better work-life balance in the past?
part3Samples.answer: In some respects, yes. In the past, work was more clearly confined to the workplace, and once you went home, you were genuinely off duty. Today, smartphones mean we are perpetually [[reachable]], and the boundary between work and personal life has become dangerously [[blurred]]. That said, past generations often worked longer physical hours, so it is not entirely one-sided; the nature of the [[imbalance]] has changed.

part3Samples.q: What are the consequences of a poor work-life balance?
part3Samples.answer: The consequences can be severe. Chronic overwork frequently leads to stress, burnout and serious health problems, both physical and mental. It also strains personal relationships, as work encroaches on time with family and friends. Ironically, it often reduces long-term productivity too. Essentially, neglecting your personal life for work is [[self-defeating]], [[taking a heavy toll]] that eventually [[undermines]] everything.

part3Samples.q: Do you think work-life balance will improve in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am hopeful, though not entirely certain. There is a growing cultural awareness of the importance of wellbeing, and flexible and remote working could, if managed well, improve balance considerably. Concepts like the four-day week are [[gaining traction]]. However, there is a risk that [[constant connectivity]] could make things worse. So improvement is possible, but it will require a [[deliberate cultural shift]] rather than happening automatically.

part3Samples.q: What can people do to achieve a better work-life balance?
part3Samples.answer: On a personal level, setting firm boundaries is crucial, such as not checking work emails after hours. Learning to prioritise and, importantly, to say no to excessive demands helps enormously. Making dedicated time for rest and relationships should be treated as [[non-negotiable]]. However, individuals can [[only do so much]]; employers must also foster a culture that genuinely respects personal time and does not reward [[overwork]].

part3Samples.q: Some say hobbies should be useful, not just for fun. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I respectfully disagree with that as a rule. While hobbies that build skills are certainly valuable, I firmly believe a hobby does not need to be productive to be [[worthwhile]]. The primary purpose of leisure is enjoyment, relaxation and wellbeing, and something that brings pure joy is valuable in itself. Insisting that all free time be useful reflects an overly [[utilitarian]] mindset. Sometimes, doing something simply for pleasure is [[exactly the point]].

cueCards.title: Describe an important lesson you have learned in life
cueCards.prompt: Describe an important lesson you have learned in life
bullets: and how it has affected you

sample.answer: An important lesson I have learned in life is that failure is not something to be feared, but a valuable teacher. I learned this the hard way, after failing at something I had worked hard for and initially feeling completely [[demoralised]]. After school, I prepared for months for the admission test of a well-known public university, but I missed out on a place by a small margin. For weeks, I barely wanted to leave the house, and I felt I had let my parents down. In time, however, I came to see that the setback taught me far more than easy success ever could. I went on to study business administration at another university, worked hard and discovered a field I truly enjoy. This lesson is important because the fear of failure holds so many people back from even trying. Once I embraced the idea that mistakes are simply part of growth, I became far more [[resilient]] and willing to take risks. Honestly, this shift in mindset has been genuinely [[transformative]]. I now approach challenges with curiosity rather than dread. It has affected every area of my life, from my career to my personal relationships. At work, I now share this story with students who receive rejection letters, and it seems to [[reassure]] them. I think it is one of the most [[liberating]] realisations a person can have. Understanding that failing is part of succeeding has given me the courage to pursue things I once would have avoided entirely, including my plan to study abroad.

followUps.q: How did your parents react when you failed that test?
followUps.answer: Much better than I expected. My father told me he had faced many losses in business and still recovered, and my mother simply cooked my favourite food. Their calm reaction really helped me move on.

followUps.q: Do you think schools should teach this lesson?
followUps.answer: Yes, definitely. Schools here focus so heavily on results that children see failure as shameful. Teachers could [[normalise]] mistakes by showing how every expert once struggled as a beginner.
