part3Samples.q: What do you think are the most important qualities of a good parent?
part3Samples.answer: In my view, the most important qualities are patience and [[consistency]]. Children thrive on stability, so a parent who sets clear, fair boundaries helps them feel secure. Equally vital is unconditional love balanced with the willingness to discipline when necessary. A good parent also [[leads by example]], since children tend to [[absorb]] behaviour far more than instructions.

part3Samples.q: How is childhood today different from childhood in the past?
part3Samples.answer: Childhood has changed dramatically. In the past, children spent most of their free time playing outdoors and socialising in person. Today, much of that has been [[supplanted]] by screens, which I find rather [[disconcerting]]. Children are also under far more academic pressure now. So while modern children have more opportunities, they arguably have a less [[carefree]] upbringing.

part3Samples.q: What effect does strict parenting have on children?
part3Samples.answer: It can have mixed effects. On one hand, strict parenting can instil discipline and a strong work ethic. On the other, if it is excessively [[authoritarian]], it may [[stifle]] a child's creativity and confidence, or even breed rebellion. In my opinion, the ideal lies in a balanced approach that is firm but also [[nurturing]] and understanding.

part3Samples.q: How do you think parenting will change in the coming decades?
part3Samples.answer: I expect parenting will become increasingly [[intertwined with]] technology. Parents will likely rely more on apps and online resources for guidance, and managing children's screen time will become an even more [[daunting]] challenge. I also anticipate a move towards more [[egalitarian]] parenting, with responsibilities shared more equally. Hopefully there will also be greater awareness of children's emotional wellbeing.

part3Samples.q: How can parents help children develop good values?
part3Samples.answer: The most effective way is by [[modelling]] those values themselves, since children imitate what they see. Beyond that, parents can use everyday situations as [[teaching moments]], discussing honesty or kindness openly. Encouraging empathy, perhaps through community involvement, also helps. Ultimately, values are [[instilled]] gradually through consistent example rather than through occasional lectures.

part3Samples.q: Some say education should be free for everyone. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I strongly agree, at least regarding basic and secondary education. I see education as a fundamental right and a [[public good]], not a privilege for those who can afford it. Free access promotes [[social mobility]] and reduces inequality. For higher education, the picture is more complex due to cost, but I believe it should at least be heavily [[subsidised]] so that talent, not wealth, determines opportunity.

cueCards.title: Describe a hobby that is popular in your country
cueCards.prompt: Describe a hobby that is popular in your country
bullets: and how you feel about it

sample.answer: A hobby that is enormously popular in my country is playing and watching cricket. It is genuinely a national passion, cutting across all ages and social backgrounds. You will find children playing it in narrow alleys and open fields all over the country, using whatever equipment they can find. Boys have always dominated, but more and more girls are joining in too, partly inspired by the success of our women's team. Even older men, like my father, follow every ball on television and discuss matches at the tea stall for days afterwards. It is popular partly because it requires very little to get started, making it wonderfully [[accessible]] to everyone. A tennis ball, some tape and a plank of wood are really all you need. I think its popularity also stems from the sense of [[unity]] and pride it brings, especially when the national team performs well. During major matches, the whole country seems to come to a standstill, which is quite [[remarkable]]. Honestly, I think it is a wonderful thing for a nation to share such a common passion. It brings people together in a way few other things can. I am very fond of it myself, mostly as a spectator these days, though I played constantly as a boy. My only slight concern is that cricket [[overshadows]] other sports, like football, which receive far less attention and investment. Still, I believe this shared enthusiasm is a genuinely [[unifying]] force, and it is a lovely part of our national identity.

followUps.q: Is cricket more popular than football in your country?
followUps.answer: Nowadays, yes, although football was once hugely popular too. During the World Cup, people still fly Argentina and Brazil flags from their rooftops, so football hasn't disappeared, it just comes in waves.

followUps.q: Do you think this hobby will stay popular in the future?
followUps.answer: I am fairly sure it will. It is so [[deeply rooted]] in our culture, and every new generation grows up playing it in the street. It is hard to imagine Bangladesh without cricket.

part3Samples.q: Why are hobbies important in people's lives?
part3Samples.answer: Hobbies are far more valuable than people often realise. They provide a [[vital outlet]] for relaxation and stress relief, offering a welcome escape from the pressures of work. They also allow for personal growth, creativity and a sense of accomplishment outside our professional identity. Additionally, many hobbies foster social connections. In my view, hobbies are essential for a balanced, fulfilling life, [[nourishing]] parts of ourselves that work often [[neglects]].

part3Samples.q: How do people's leisure activities differ between generations?
part3Samples.answer: There are noticeable differences. Older generations often favour traditional [[pastimes]] like gardening, reading physical books, or socialising in person. Younger people, by contrast, spend much of their leisure time on digital activities, such as gaming, streaming and social media. That said, there is considerable overlap, and interest in older hobbies is [[reviving]] among the young. So the core need for leisure is universal, but the [[medium]] has shifted towards the digital.

part3Samples.q: What are the benefits of having a creative hobby?
part3Samples.answer: Creative hobbies offer numerous benefits. They provide a productive outlet for self-expression and can be deeply [[therapeutic]], reducing stress and improving mental wellbeing. The sense of accomplishment from creating something is genuinely rewarding and boosts confidence. They also keep the mind active and can spark skills that [[enrich]] other areas of life. Essentially, creative pursuits [[nourish the soul]] and offer a fulfilment that passive entertainment simply cannot match.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will have more free time in the future?
part3Samples.answer: This is uncertain. [[Optimistically]], if automation boosts productivity and society chooses to share the gains, people could work less and enjoy more leisure, as concepts like the four-day week suggest. However, there is an opposing risk that [[constant connectivity]] and economic pressure could actually [[erode]] our free time further. So the amount of leisure we have may depend less on technology and more on the choices society makes about priorities.

part3Samples.q: Many people say they have no time for hobbies. What can they do?
part3Samples.answer: It often comes down to priorities rather than an absolute lack of time. People can start by consciously [[carving out]] even small [[pockets of time]], perhaps by reducing passive activities like scrolling on their phones. Scheduling hobby time like any other commitment helps make it happen. Choosing hobbies that fit their lifestyle is also wise. Essentially, treating leisure as essential rather than optional helps people [[reclaim]] time they did not realise they had.

part3Samples.q: Some people say celebrities are paid too much. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I [[have some sympathy with]] that view. It does seem [[disproportionate]] that an entertainer can earn more in a day than a nurse earns in a year, when the latter arguably contributes more to society. On the other hand, their pay simply reflects the market and the vast revenue they generate. So while it feels [[morally questionable]], it is economically logical.

cueCards.title: Describe a way people can lead a healthier lifestyle
cueCards.prompt: Describe a way people can lead a healthier lifestyle
bullets: and how you feel about it

sample.answer: A simple but effective way people can lead a healthier lifestyle is by incorporating more physical activity into their daily routine, without needing a gym. In my view, small changes like walking instead of driving for short trips, or taking the stairs, can be genuinely [[transformative]] over time. In Bangladesh, for example, many people take a rickshaw even for a five-minute journey, when walking would be just as quick and far healthier. This works because it does not require a huge, intimidating commitment; it simply builds movement into everyday life. You don't need special clothes, money or even extra time, which removes most of the usual excuses. Almost anyone could benefit from this, particularly people with [[sedentary]], desk-based jobs like mine. Older people could benefit too; since my father retired, he has started walking to the market every morning, and he says he feels years younger. I think the reason many people fail to get fit is that they set unrealistic goals and quickly become [[discouraged]]. A gentler, more [[sustainable]] approach is far more likely to stick. Honestly, I feel strongly that health is our most precious asset, yet we [[take it for granted]] until something goes wrong. Combining a little more movement with a balanced diet is a genuinely practical path to better health. It is something I try to practise myself, with my evening walks by the river, and I would encourage everyone to do the same. Small, consistent steps really do add up.

followUps.q: Is it easy to walk in your town?
followUps.answer: In quieter areas, yes, but the main roads can be crowded and there aren't always proper footpaths. The river embankment is ideal, though, which is why it is always busy in the evenings.

followUps.q: Do you think your family lives a healthy lifestyle?
followUps.answer: Mostly, yes. We eat home-cooked food and rarely have takeaways. The weak point is probably our love of sweets and oily snacks, especially during festivals, which is hard to [[resist]].

part3Samples.q: What do you think makes people truly happy?

Beyond that, having a sense of purpose, good health, and the freedom to pursue what we find meaningful all contribute enormously. So I believe true happiness is [[rooted in]] connection, purpose and [[gratitude]], not in material wealth.

part3Samples.q: Are people happier now than in the past?
part3Samples.answer: This is a fascinating and debated question. In material terms, we are far better off than previous generations, with more comfort, health and opportunity. Yet, [[curiously]], rates of anxiety and depression seem to be rising, especially among the young. It appears that material progress has not straightforwardly translated into greater happiness. So while we have gained much, I am not convinced we are [[fundamentally]] happier, which suggests happiness depends on more than mere [[prosperity]] and comfort.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think some wealthy people are unhappy?
part3Samples.answer: This reflects the fact that money, beyond meeting basic needs, has [[diminishing returns]] on happiness. Wealthy people may still suffer from poor relationships, a lack of purpose, or the isolation and pressure that wealth can bring. There is also the phenomenon where people constantly adapt and want more, never feeling satisfied. So it demonstrates that happiness is not something money can simply buy; it depends on deeper, [[non-material]] [[fulfilment]].

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will be happier in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am genuinely uncertain. On one hand, advances in medicine, technology and [[living standards]] could improve wellbeing. There is also growing awareness of mental health and the importance of a balanced life. On the other hand, rising pressures, social media comparison and uncertainty could work against happiness. So I think future happiness will depend less on material progress and more on whether we learn to [[prioritise]] the things that genuinely [[nourish]] human wellbeing.

part3Samples.q: What can societies do to improve people's wellbeing?
part3Samples.answer: Societies can take meaningful steps. Prioritising mental health services and reducing the [[stigma]] around them is crucial. Fostering community, reducing inequality, and ensuring people have access to nature, leisure and a healthy work-life balance all help. Some argue governments should measure national wellbeing, not just economic output. Essentially, by valuing human [[flourishing]] alongside economic growth, societies can create conditions in which more people can genuinely [[thrive]] and feel content.

part3Samples.q: Some say building more housing is more important than preserving parks. Do you agree?

While housing is undeniably crucial, green spaces are equally vital for residents' health and wellbeing, and destroying them creates a poorer quality of life. It should not be an either-or choice. With clever planning, cities can build housing on [[brownfield sites]] and increase density elsewhere while preserving parks. So both are essential, and [[pitting them against]] each other is a [[false dilemma]].

cueCards.prompt: Describe a person who taught you something useful

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about my uncle on my father's side, who taught me how to fix a bicycle puncture when I was about ten. He's a motor mechanic by trade - a big, gruff man who doesn't say much, and to be honest I was slightly scared of him as a child. He had this small workshop at the end of our lane, and I'd sometimes hang around watching him work, mostly because of the smell of rubber glue and engine oil, which I found oddly appealing. One afternoon my bicycle got a flat tyre, and I went to him expecting him to fix it. Instead, he handed me the tools and said, "You do it." He talked me through it step by step - finding the hole by dipping the tube in a bucket of water and watching for bubbles, roughing up the rubber, applying the patch - but he never once touched the bike himself. When I put the tyre back on the wrong way, he just raised an eyebrow and waited until I noticed. It took me nearly an hour to do something he could have done in five minutes. Looking back, the puncture itself wasn't really the lesson. What he actually taught me was that I could figure things out if someone just refused to do them for me. That attitude has been far more useful than the skill - whether it's a broken laptop or a maths problem, my first instinct now is to try before asking for help. So I'd say he gave me a way of thinking rather than just a repair job, and I'm still grateful for it.

part3Samples.q: What do you think is the best way to learn something new?

We tend to [[retain]] information far better when we actually apply it. I am a firm believer in [[learning by doing]], and in making mistakes, since they are often the most [[instructive]] experiences. Combining this practical approach with genuine curiosity makes learning both effective and thoroughly engaging.

part3Samples.q: Is it better to learn alone or in a group?
part3Samples.answer: Both have their merits, and the ideal depends on the task. Learning alone allows for focus and lets you progress at your own pace, which suits deep, concentrated study. Group learning, on the other hand, is more [[dynamic]]; you benefit from different perspectives and can clarify doubts through discussion. Personally, I favour a [[blend]] of the two, as they [[complement]] each other nicely.

part3Samples.q: Why do some people find learning easier than others?
part3Samples.answer: There are many contributing factors. Some of it comes down to natural [[aptitude]], but I think motivation and [[mindset]] matter far more. People who are genuinely curious and believe they can improve tend to learn faster. Environment also plays a huge role; a supportive home and good teachers make an enormous difference. So learning ability is really a mix of [[innate]] talent and nurtured habits.

part3Samples.q: Do you think traditional classrooms will disappear in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I doubt they will disappear entirely, but their role will certainly change. Online learning will keep growing, offering flexibility that classrooms cannot match. However, physical classrooms provide something valuable: social interaction, mentorship and a structured environment that many learners need. So rather than [[vanishing]], I expect classrooms to [[evolve]] into more interactive spaces, [[complementing]] rather than being replaced by digital tools.

part3Samples.q: How can people stay motivated when learning independently?
part3Samples.answer: Self-motivation is the biggest challenge in independent learning. I think the key is setting clear, [[achievable]] goals and breaking a large subject into smaller [[milestones]], which gives a regular sense of progress. Establishing a routine helps make studying a habit rather than a struggle. Finding a community of fellow learners online can also provide [[accountability]] and encouragement, which is often what people lack.

part3Samples.q: Some people think children are given too much freedom today. Do you agree?

A total absence of limits can leave children feeling [[insecure]] rather than free. That said, the opposite extreme is equally harmful, so the goal should be freedom within a [[framework]] of sensible, loving guidance.

cueCards.title: Describe a place you visited that was very different from where you live
cueCards.prompt: Describe a place you visited that was very different from where you live
bullets: and explain how you felt about the difference.

sample.answer: The place I'd like to describe is a small village in the hill districts in the south-east of the country, which I visited last December with three friends from university. We stayed two nights in a wooden house on stilts, owned by a family from one of the indigenous communities there. It was about a two-hour drive up winding roads from the nearest town, and by the time we arrived it was dark and the driver had to use a torch to show us the steps. Almost everything was different from my city life, but the biggest thing was the silence. I'm so used to a constant background of horns and generators that the first night I genuinely couldn't sleep - the quiet felt loud, if that makes sense. Then at five in the morning the roosters started, and that was the alarm clock for the whole village. The houses were all wood and bamboo, raised off the ground, with the kitchen fire in the middle. The food was different too - a lot of bamboo shoot and fresh herbs, very little oil, nothing like the heavy curries I grew up on. And people moved at a completely different pace; nobody was rushing anywhere, because there was nowhere to rush to. How I felt about it changed over the two days. At first I was disoriented, almost anxious - I kept reaching for my phone and there was no signal. By the second day I'd started to feel slightly ashamed of how much noise we city people make, how loudly we talk, how fast we eat. By the time we left I felt calmer than I had in months, and I remember the sound of the first horn when we got back to town like a slap. So it was a small trip, but it made me realise that what I think of as normal is really just one way of living among many.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think people enjoy travelling?
part3Samples.answer: People travel for a wonderful variety of reasons. Fundamentally, I think it satisfies a deep human curiosity and desire to escape routine. Experiencing new cultures, landscapes and cuisines is genuinely [[enriching]] and broadens one's perspective. Travel also offers relaxation, adventure and the chance to create lasting memories. For me, the greatest value is how it makes you more [[open-minded]] and [[appreciative]] of the world's incredible diversity.

part3Samples.q: How has travel changed compared to the past?
part3Samples.answer: Travel has been transformed almost beyond recognition. In the past, it was expensive, slow and largely a privilege of the wealthy. Today, [[budget airlines]] and the internet have made it far more accessible and easy to organise, leading to mass tourism. We can now reach distant corners of the globe in hours. While this democratisation is positive, it has also led to [[overcrowding]] at popular sites and a more [[superficial]], hurried style of travel.

part3Samples.q: What effects does tourism have on local communities?
part3Samples.answer: Tourism has profound and mixed effects. Economically, it can bring vital income and jobs, boosting the local economy significantly. However, it can also cause problems: it may [[inflate]] local prices, strain infrastructure, and sometimes lead to the [[commodification]] of culture, where traditions are performed purely for tourists. Environmental damage is another concern. So while tourism offers real economic benefits, it must be managed [[sustainably]] to avoid harming the very communities it supports.

part3Samples.q: How do you think tourism will change in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I foresee several shifts. Growing environmental awareness will likely make sustainable and [[eco-tourism]] far more popular, as people seek to [[minimise their impact]]. Technology, such as virtual reality, might offer new ways to experience places remotely. There may also be a move towards more meaningful, [[immersive]] travel over mass tourism. So I expect the future of travel to be more conscious, more personalised, and hopefully more responsible.

part3Samples.q: How can the negative impacts of tourism be reduced?
part3Samples.answer: Sustainable tourism practices are the answer. Governments can manage visitor numbers at fragile sites through limits or timed entry to prevent overcrowding. Promoting [[lesser-known]] destinations helps spread the benefits and reduce pressure on [[hotspots]]. Encouraging tourists to respect local cultures and environments, and to support local businesses, is also key. Essentially, prioritising sustainability over sheer volume can [[mitigate]] the harm while preserving the benefits.

part3Samples.q: Some say governments should stop cities from growing too big. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I do not think halting growth is realistic or desirable, but managing it is essential. Trying to stop urban growth [[outright]] would be difficult and could stifle economic opportunity. However, I strongly agree that governments should guide this growth intelligently, perhaps by developing smaller [[satellite cities]] and improving rural areas to [[ease the pressure]]. So rather than restricting cities, the focus should be on making growth sustainable and balanced.

sample.answer: The place I'd like to describe is a particular corner of my university library - the third floor, at the back, by the window that looks out onto a mango tree. The library itself is an old building, and that floor hasn't been renovated, which is exactly why I like it. The desks are heavy wooden ones with initials carved into them by students from decades ago, and each has a green-shaded lamp. It smells of old paper and floor polish. The librarian on that floor is a small, silent woman who enforces the no-talking rule with a glare that could stop traffic, and I'm genuinely a little frightened of her. During term time I go four or five days a week, usually from nine until about one. That corner is popular, so I've learned to arrive early; by ten it's gone. Why it works for me comes down to three things. First - and this was an accident - there's almost no phone signal in that corner, so the biggest distraction in my life simply doesn't function there. Second, the silence is real, not the polite silence of a café where someone's always on a call. And third, being surrounded by other people working creates a kind of pressure I can't generate at home. When the person across from me has been writing for an hour, I feel I can't be the one scrolling. I've tried working at home and in cafés, and my output is maybe half of what it is in that corner. Some of that is the place, some is the routine, but honestly I think a lot of it is the mango tree - looking at something green every few minutes seems to reset my brain. So it's my most productive place, and I'm slightly worried about what happens when I graduate and lose it.

part3Samples.q: What do you think is the best way to learn something new?
part3Samples.answer: In my experience, the most effective way to learn is through active, hands-on practice rather than passive listening. We tend to [[retain]] information far better when we actually apply it. I am a firm believer in [[learning by doing]], and in making mistakes, since they are often the most [[instructive]] experiences. Combining this practical approach with genuine curiosity makes learning both effective and thoroughly engaging.

part3Samples.q: Is it better to learn alone or in a group?
part3Samples.answer: Both have their merits, and the ideal depends on the task. Learning alone allows for focus and lets you progress at your own pace, which suits deep, concentrated study. Group learning, on the other hand, is more [[dynamic]]; you benefit from different perspectives and can clarify doubts through discussion. Personally, I favour a [[blend]] of the two, as they [[complement]] each other nicely.

part3Samples.q: Why do some people find learning easier than others?
part3Samples.answer: There are many contributing factors. Some of it comes down to natural [[aptitude]], but I think motivation and [[mindset]] matter far more. People who are genuinely curious and believe they can improve tend to learn faster. Environment also plays a huge role; a supportive home and good teachers make an enormous difference. So learning ability is really a mix of [[innate]] talent and nurtured habits.

part3Samples.q: Do you think traditional classrooms will disappear in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I doubt they will disappear entirely, but their role will certainly change. Online learning will keep growing, offering flexibility that classrooms cannot match. However, physical classrooms provide something valuable: social interaction, mentorship and a structured environment that many learners need. So rather than [[vanishing]], I expect classrooms to [[evolve]] into more interactive spaces, [[complementing]] rather than being replaced by digital tools.

part3Samples.q: How can people stay motivated when learning independently?
part3Samples.answer: Self-motivation is the biggest challenge in independent learning. I think the key is setting clear, [[achievable]] goals and breaking a large subject into smaller [[milestones]], which gives a regular sense of progress. Establishing a routine helps make studying a habit rather than a struggle. Finding a community of fellow learners online can also provide [[accountability]] and encouragement, which is often what people lack.

part3Samples.q: Some say building more housing is more important than preserving parks. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I understand the argument given the housing crisis, but I largely disagree with sacrificing parks. While housing is undeniably crucial, green spaces are equally vital for residents' health and wellbeing, and destroying them creates a poorer quality of life. It should not be an either-or choice. With clever planning, cities can build housing on [[brownfield sites]] and increase density elsewhere while preserving parks. So both are essential, and [[pitting them against]] each other is a [[false dilemma]].

cueCards.title: Describe something you bought that you were not happy with
cueCards.prompt: Describe something you bought that you were not happy with
bullets: and explain what you did about it.

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about a bag I bought online last year, which turned out to be one of the more embarrassing purchases of my life. I needed a proper bag for job interviews - something that looked professional - and I saw an advert on social media for a leather laptop bag at a very reasonable price, from a page with about fifty thousand followers and glowing reviews. The photos looked great: dark brown, brass fittings, that sort of thing. I ordered it and paid on delivery, about three and a half thousand taka. What arrived was not leather. It was some kind of plastic that had been embossed to look like leather, in a colour closer to orange than brown, and it smelled strongly of chemicals for about a week. I told myself it would be fine. Then, on the second week, on the way to an actual interview, the strap snapped on the stairs of the office building, and my laptop and papers went everywhere in front of the receptionist. I got the job anyway, but I don't think it was because of my entrance. What I did about it was, at first, the sensible thing: I messaged the page, politely, with photos. No reply. I messaged again - six times over two weeks. Eventually they blocked me. There was no phone number, no address, no company name. The fifty thousand followers, I later worked out, were mostly fake. So in the end what I did was learn an expensive lesson. I went to a real shop, touched a real bag, and paid twice as much, and it's still fine two years on. Now if I can't find a physical address for a seller, I don't buy. And I've become the annoying friend who asks "Did you check the page?" before anyone orders anything.

DID: messaged 6 times, blocked; learned lesson; bought from a real shop
+ interview day, strap snapped on the stairs

part3Samples.q: Do you think people buy more things than they actually need?
part3Samples.answer: Yes, I think overconsumption is a defining feature of modern society. We are constantly [[bombarded]] with advertising designed to create desires for things we do not truly need. Cheap goods and easy credit make impulsive buying effortless. Many people also shop for emotional reasons, as a form of therapy. So I would say that a great deal of our consumption is driven by [[manufactured]] wants rather than genuine necessity, which is quite [[wasteful]].

part3Samples.q: How has shopping changed with the rise of the internet?
part3Samples.answer: Online shopping has [[revolutionised]] the experience. It offers [[unparalleled]] convenience, allowing people to buy almost anything from home at any hour, with easy price comparison. This has, however, put pressure on traditional physical shops, many of which have struggled. The experience has become more efficient but arguably less social. So while the internet has made shopping far more convenient and accessible, it has also transformed our [[high streets]], not always for the better.

part3Samples.q: Why do you think advertising is so influential?
part3Samples.answer: Advertising is influential because it is sophisticated and [[pervasive]]. It cleverly taps into our emotions, insecurities and aspirations, associating products with happiness, status or belonging rather than mere function. Its sheer ubiquity means we are exposed to it constantly, which [[reinforces]] its messages. Modern targeted advertising is especially potent, as it is tailored precisely to our interests. So it shapes our desires far more than we consciously realise, subtly [[steering]] our behaviour.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will become more conscious consumers in the future?
part3Samples.answer: I am cautiously hopeful. There is a growing awareness of the environmental and ethical impact of our purchases, and movements towards [[minimalism]], sustainability and ethical consumption are [[gaining momentum]]. Younger generations in particular seem more [[values-driven]] in their spending. However, the powerful forces of marketing and convenience remain strong. So while I believe conscious consumption will increase, whether it becomes the norm depends on a genuine cultural shift.

part3Samples.q: How can people be encouraged to consume more responsibly?
part3Samples.answer: Education and awareness are key. Helping people understand the true environmental and social cost of their purchases can shift attitudes. Encouraging habits like buying quality over quantity, repairing rather than replacing, and choosing ethical brands makes a difference. Governments can also play a role through regulation and [[incentives]]. Ultimately, [[fostering]] a cultural value of [[sufficiency]] over excess, where we question whether we truly need something, is the most sustainable path.

part3Samples.q: Some say money cannot buy happiness. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I largely agree, though with a [[nuance]]. It is certainly true that beyond meeting our basic needs, more money does not reliably increase happiness, and the richest people are not necessarily the happiest. Lasting happiness comes from relationships and purpose. However, I would add that a lack of money, and the poverty and stress it brings, can definitely cause unhappiness. So money cannot buy happiness, but [[financial security]] can certainly remove a major source of [[misery]] and anxiety.

cueCards.title: Describe a sporting event you watched or took part in
cueCards.prompt: Describe a sporting event you watched or took part in
bullets: and explain why you remember it.

sample.answer: The sporting event I'd like to talk about wasn't anything official - it was the final of our neighbourhood cricket tournament, about three years ago, between the team from our lane and the team from the next lane over. It was played on the local school field on a winter afternoon, with a tape-ball - a tennis ball wrapped in electrical tape, which is how most cricket in this country is actually played. The rivalry between the two lanes goes back decades; our fathers played each other. So even though it was, objectively, twenty-two amateurs on a bumpy field, about two hundred people turned up. Kids sat along the boundary wall, old men brought radios and did their own commentary louder than the actual match, and someone's mother sold tea from a flask. The reason I remember it, unfortunately, is that I dropped the catch that decided it. Last over, they needed three runs, the batsman skied one straight to me at mid-off, and I could hear the entire crowd go "ooooh" as it went up. I had time to think. That was the problem. It hit my hands and went through, and they got the two runs, and we lost by two. I expected to be blamed for weeks. What actually happened was the opposite. My teammates were laughing before I'd even picked the ball up; one of them put his arm around me and said something like, "Now you're a real cricketer, you've dropped a final." And then both teams sat together on the field until dark, drinking tea from the same flask, going over every ball. The rivalry, it turned out, was the excuse for the friendship rather than the other way round. So I remember it for the drop, yes, but mostly for what the drop taught me about the people I live among.

WHY: I dropped a catch, we lost by 2 runs, nobody blamed me - the opposite
+ the sound of the whole crowd going "ooooh"; tea after with the other team

part3Samples.q: Why are hobbies important in people's lives?
part3Samples.answer: Hobbies are far more valuable than people often realise. They provide a [[vital outlet]] for relaxation and stress relief, offering a welcome escape from the pressures of work. They also allow for personal growth, creativity and a sense of accomplishment outside our professional identity. Additionally, many hobbies foster social connections. In my view, hobbies are essential for a balanced, fulfilling life, [[nourishing]] parts of ourselves that work often [[neglects]].

part3Samples.q: How do people's leisure activities differ between generations?
part3Samples.answer: There are noticeable differences. Older generations often favour traditional [[pastimes]] like gardening, reading physical books, or socialising in person. Younger people, by contrast, spend much of their leisure time on digital activities, such as gaming, streaming and social media. That said, there is considerable overlap, and interest in older hobbies is [[reviving]] among the young. So the core need for leisure is universal, but the [[medium]] has shifted towards the digital.

part3Samples.q: What are the benefits of having a creative hobby?
part3Samples.answer: Creative hobbies offer numerous benefits. They provide a productive outlet for self-expression and can be deeply [[therapeutic]], reducing stress and improving mental wellbeing. The sense of accomplishment from creating something is genuinely rewarding and boosts confidence. They also keep the mind active and can spark skills that [[enrich]] other areas of life. Essentially, creative pursuits [[nourish the soul]] and offer a fulfilment that passive entertainment simply cannot match.

part3Samples.q: Do you think people will have more free time in the future?
part3Samples.answer: This is uncertain. [[Optimistically]], if automation boosts productivity and society chooses to share the gains, people could work less and enjoy more leisure, as concepts like the four-day week suggest. However, there is an opposing risk that [[constant connectivity]] and economic pressure could actually [[erode]] our free time further. So the amount of leisure we have may depend less on technology and more on the choices society makes about priorities.

part3Samples.q: Many people say they have no time for hobbies. What can they do?
part3Samples.answer: It often comes down to priorities rather than an absolute lack of time. People can start by consciously [[carving out]] even small [[pockets of time]], perhaps by reducing passive activities like scrolling on their phones. Scheduling hobby time like any other commitment helps make it happen. Choosing hobbies that fit their lifestyle is also wise. Essentially, treating leisure as essential rather than optional helps people [[reclaim]] time they did not realise they had.

part3Samples.q: Some people say celebrities are paid too much. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I [[have some sympathy with]] that view. It does seem [[disproportionate]] that an entertainer can earn more in a day than a nurse earns in a year, when the latter arguably contributes more to society. On the other hand, their pay simply reflects the market and the vast revenue they generate. So while it feels [[morally questionable]], it is economically logical.

cueCards.title: Describe a time when the weather changed your plans
cueCards.prompt: Describe a time when the weather changed your plans
bullets: and explain how you felt about the change.

sample.answer: I'd like to talk about a day last summer when a storm cancelled a trip that eight of us had been planning for weeks - and accidentally gave us a better day. The plan was a day trip to a small river island a couple of hours from the city. We'd booked a boat, arranged food, and everyone had taken the day off work, which in my group of friends is a small miracle. We were supposed to leave at seven in the morning. At six, my phone lit up with a storm warning. By eight the sky was completely black - that heavy, greenish dark you get before a real monsoon storm - and the boatman called to say the river was far too rough. Then the rain came, the kind where you can't see the building across the road. The trip was clearly off. What we did instead started as a consolation. Since everyone was already up and dressed and had nothing to do, they all came to my flat. Nine people in a two-bedroom apartment. We cooked a huge pot of khichuri, which is what you're supposed to eat when it rains, and I mean huge - my mother's biggest pot, with eggs and whatever vegetables were in the fridge. Then the power went out, so we played cards by candlelight, shouting over the rain hammering on the tin roof next door. Somebody found an old guitar. It went on until nearly midnight, when the rain finally stopped and they could get home. How I felt went through stages. First, genuinely annoyed - I'd organised the trip, and I felt the whole day had been wasted before it began. By lunchtime I'd stopped thinking about the island. By evening I'd realised that the trip would have been pleasant but this was something else: nobody was taking photos, nobody was checking their phone because the signal had gone, and we just talked, properly, for twelve hours. So the change felt like a loss for about two hours and like a gift ever since. Some of the best plans, it turns out, are cancelled ones.

WEATHER: storm warning at 6am; black sky by 8; river too rough

part3Samples.q: How serious a problem do you think climate change is?

So while some still [[downplay]] it, I believe it is an [[existential]] threat that demands urgent, [[decisive]] action.

part3Samples.q: Do you think richer or poorer countries should do more to fight climate change?
part3Samples.answer: This is a matter of both responsibility and capability. I believe richer, industrialised nations bear a greater responsibility, as they have contributed the most historical emissions and have the financial resources to lead. It seems only fair for them to do more, including helping poorer nations. However, developing countries, some of which are now major emitters, must also participate. So the burden should be shared [[equitably]], with the wealthy [[shouldering]] a [[proportionate]] load.

part3Samples.q: What are the main effects of climate change on people?
part3Samples.answer: The effects on people are wide-ranging and increasingly severe. More intense heatwaves, floods and storms directly threaten lives and homes. Changing weather patterns disrupt agriculture, [[jeopardising]] food security and livelihoods. Rising seas endanger coastal communities, potentially creating large numbers of [[climate refugees]]. There are also serious health impacts. So climate change is not merely an environmental issue; it is a profound [[humanitarian]] one that threatens the stability of entire societies.

part3Samples.q: Do you think we can still prevent the worst effects of climate change?
part3Samples.answer: I believe we still can, but the window is closing rapidly and it will require unprecedented effort. The technology and knowledge to transition to a clean economy largely exist; what is often lacking is the [[political will]] and global cooperation. If we act decisively now, we can still limit the damage, though some impacts are already [[inevitable]]. So I remain hopeful, but only if we treat it with the urgency it truly [[warrants]].

part3Samples.q: What are the most effective ways to tackle climate change?
part3Samples.answer: The most effective solutions involve rapidly [[transitioning away from]] fossil fuels towards renewable energy like solar and wind. Improving energy efficiency and protecting and restoring forests, which absorb carbon, are also crucial. Government policy is key, from [[carbon pricing]] to investment in green technology. Individual lifestyle changes help too. Essentially, it requires a coordinated [[overhaul]] of our energy, transport and consumption systems on a global scale.

part3Samples.q: Some say governments should stop cities from growing too big. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I do not think halting growth is realistic or desirable, but managing it is essential. Trying to stop urban growth [[outright]] would be difficult and could stifle economic opportunity. However, I strongly agree that governments should guide this growth intelligently, perhaps by developing smaller [[satellite cities]] and improving rural areas to [[ease the pressure]]. So rather than restricting cities, the focus should be on making growth sustainable and balanced.

cueCards.title: Describe a job you would like to do in the future
cueCards.prompt: Describe a job you would like to do in the future

sample.answer: The job I'd like to do in the future is urban planning - deciding how a city grows, where the roads and parks and drains go, before the buildings arrive and make it too late. What it involves, as far as I understand it, is a mix of the technical and the political. On the technical side, zoning maps, transport modelling, drainage and flood planning - which in my country is not a minor detail. On the political side, it means sitting in rooms with residents who don't want a road, developers who want three more floors, and officials who want the problem to go away. A planner is the person who has to say "no" to powerful people and "wait" to impatient ones, and back it up with evidence. The skills I'd need are a slightly odd combination: enough maths to model traffic, enough drawing to communicate an idea on paper, and enough diplomacy to survive a public meeting. I'd say I have one of the three - the maths - and I'm working on the drawing. The diplomacy I'll have to learn the hard way. Formally, it means a master's degree in the subject, which is part of why I'm sitting this exam. Why I want it goes back to the town I grew up in. When I was a child there was an open field behind our house where the whole neighbourhood played and, in the monsoon, where the water went. Now it's a car park, and the water goes into people's ground floors instead. Nobody planned that. It just happened, plot by plot, permission by permission, with nobody looking at the whole. My father complains about it every single day. I'd like to be the person whose job is to look at the whole - so that the next field gets kept on purpose rather than lost by accident. It's not a glamorous ambition, and I'll probably lose most of the arguments. But I'd rather lose them than not be in the room.

part3Samples.q: Is it better to choose a job you love or a job that pays well?

If forced to choose, I lean towards a job you love, because passion tends to lead to better performance and long-term fulfilment, and money alone rarely brings lasting [[contentment]]. part3Samples.q: Why do many people change careers during their lives now?
part3Samples.answer: Several factors drive this. The job market is far more [[volatile]] than in the past, so lifelong employment in one company is increasingly rare. People also have higher expectations of finding meaningful work, and are more willing to [[pursue]] fulfilment. part3Samples.q: What kinds of jobs do you think will be most important in the future?

This includes creative fields, healthcare, and roles requiring emotional intelligence and complex problem-solving. Careers related to technology, such as AI and data science, will obviously be in high demand, as will jobs focused on [[sustainability]] and renewable energy. part3Samples.q: How can young people be helped to make better career decisions?

part3Samples.q: Some say machines will eventually do most human jobs. Do you agree?
part3Samples.answer: I think that is something of an exaggeration, at least for the foreseeable future. Machines will certainly automate many tasks, but jobs requiring creativity, empathy, complex judgement and manual [[dexterity]] in unpredictable settings are far harder to replace. Rather than making humans [[redundant]], I believe technology will mostly [[augment]] human work, changing jobs rather than eliminating the need for people entirely.

part3Topics.description: Famous or local figures who inspire others through their actions.

questions.q: Do you think it is important for young people to have role models?
questions.answer: I believe it is absolutely vital for adolescents to have someone to look up to. Role models act as a kind of moral compass, offering guidance on how to navigate life. When a young person admires a professional, they are [[internalising]] the values of hard work and [[perseverance]] that led to that success. Without such figures, young people can feel a little [[unmoored]], lacking any real sense of direction.

questions.q: How have the types of role models changed since your grandparents' time?
questions.answer: There has been a rather dramatic shift, I would say. In my grandparents' era, role models tended to be figures within the immediate community, such as teachers or elders. Today, influence is increasingly [[dominated]] by celebrities and social media personalities, many of whom are famous for very little of substance. I find this shift somewhat concerning, because fame has become almost entirely [[disconnected]] from genuine [[merit]].

questions.q: How do role models affect the way people behave in a society?
questions.answer: They have a profound ripple effect, in my opinion. When influential figures behave ethically, they set a positive standard that others tend to [[emulate]]. Conversely, when role models behave badly, it can [[normalise]] that behaviour, particularly among impressionable young people. So I would argue they play a significant part in shaping a society's [[collective]] values.

questions.q: Why do some public figures fail to remain positive role models over time?
questions.answer: I think the main reason is the immense pressure and [[scrutiny]] that come with public life. Constant attention can distort a person's judgement, and some become [[complacent]] once they achieve fame. There is also the temptation of wealth and power, which can gradually [[erode]] the very values that made them admirable in the first place. Sadly, staying grounded under that spotlight is genuinely difficult.

questions.q: In the future, do you think AI or fictional characters could become role models?
questions.answer: It is quite possible, and to some extent it is already happening. Virtual influencers are becoming increasingly [[prevalent]], and young people do form attachments to fictional heroes. However, I would be somewhat [[wary]] of this trend, because a fabricated character lacks the real struggles that make human role models relatable. I think something genuinely [[authentic]] would be lost in that shift.

questions.q: What can be done to encourage young people to choose positive role models?
questions.answer: Education is key, I believe. Parents and schools should actively help children think [[critically]] about who they admire and why. Rather than simply banning certain influences, which rarely works, we should [[cultivate]] media literacy so young people can distinguish substance from mere celebrity. Highlighting inspiring local figures would also provide more [[attainable]] and grounded examples to follow.

questions.q: Do you think people are more influenced by role models in real life or in the media?
questions.answer: That is an interesting question. I would argue that media figures have a wider reach, but real-life role models, like a parent or mentor, have a far deeper and more [[lasting impact]]. The influence of a media personality is often [[superficial]] and [[fleeting]], whereas someone you interact with daily shapes your character in a much more meaningful way.

questions.q: Some people say governments should promote positive role models. Do you agree?
questions.answer: I partly agree. Governments can certainly [[showcase]] admirable citizens, such as scientists or humanitarians, to counterbalance shallow celebrity culture. However, I am slightly cautious, because state-endorsed role models can easily become [[propaganda]] if handled poorly. So while the intention is commendable, it needs to be done [[transparently]] and without any political agenda.

part3Topics.description: Changing family dynamics and the importance of relationships in modern life.

questions.q: Do you think family is as important today as it was in the past?
questions.answer: I would say family remains just as important, though its form has changed. The emotional support and sense of [[belonging]] a family provides are timeless human needs. That said, modern life has certainly [[strained]] family bonds, with people moving away for work and spending less time together. So while its importance is [[undiminished]], sustaining it now requires more conscious effort.

questions.q: How are family relationships different now compared to a generation ago?
questions.answer: The biggest difference is probably the shift from large, extended families to smaller, more [[nuclear]] ones. In the past, several generations often lived under one roof, which fostered close bonds. Today, families are more [[dispersed]], and technology has, ironically, both connected and [[distanced]] us. Relationships are more equal now, but arguably less tightly knit.

questions.q: Why do you think many families spend less time together nowadays?
questions.answer: Several factors are at play. The demands of modern careers are [[relentless]], leaving parents exhausted and [[time-poor]]. On top of that, digital devices have become a real distraction, with family members often absorbed in their own screens even when in the same room. This gradual erosion of shared time is genuinely [[detrimental]] to close relationships.

questions.q: What role does the extended family play in your culture?
questions.answer: In my culture, the extended family remains absolutely central. Grandparents, uncles and cousins are deeply involved in one another's lives, providing a strong support network. This [[interdependence]] means that responsibilities, from childcare to financial help, are often shared. I think this [[collective]] approach offers a real sense of security, though it can occasionally feel a little [[intrusive]].

questions.q: How do you think family structures will change in the future?
questions.answer: I anticipate that families will continue to become smaller and more diverse in form. We will likely see more single-parent households and [[blended families]] becoming [[commonplace]] and widely accepted. Technology may also allow [[far-flung]] relatives to stay connected more easily. Overall, I think the definition of family will grow more flexible and inclusive.

questions.q: What can families do to stay close despite busy modern lives?
questions.answer: I think the key is being [[intentional]] about spending time together. Simple rituals, like sharing at least one meal a day without phones, can make a real difference. Families could also [[prioritise]] occasional trips or activities that create shared memories. Ultimately, closeness does not happen by accident; it has to be actively [[nurtured]] amid the busyness.

questions.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of living with extended family?
questions.answer: The main advantage is the constant support; there is always someone to help with childcare or during a crisis, which is [[invaluable]]. It also passes down traditions and keeps bonds strong. On the downside, it can mean a lack of privacy and occasional [[friction]] between generations with differing views. So it is really a trade-off between [[solidarity]] and personal independence.

questions.q: Some believe children should care for their parents in old age. Do you agree?
questions.answer: I strongly agree, at least in principle. In my culture, caring for elderly parents is seen as a moral [[obligation]], a way of repaying the sacrifices they made. That said, I recognise this is not always practical in modern life, so it need not mean living together. What matters is that the elderly are not [[neglected]] and retain their [[dignity]].

part3Topics.description: The evolving role of friends and social networks today.

questions.q: Do you think it is better to have a few close friends or many acquaintances?
questions.answer: I firmly believe that quality trumps quantity when it comes to friendship. A few close friends who genuinely understand you provide far deeper support than a large circle of [[superficial]] acquaintances. While it is useful to have a wide network for professional reasons, the emotional [[intimacy]] of a true friendship is something that simply cannot be [[replicated]] at scale.

questions.q: How has technology changed the way people make friends?
questions.answer: Technology has transformed it enormously. People now form friendships online with others across the globe, which was [[unimaginable]] a generation ago. This has made connection more [[accessible]], but I would argue these digital friendships can be more [[fragile]]. Meeting through a screen sometimes lacks the depth that comes from sharing real experiences face-to-face.

questions.q: Why do some childhood friendships fade over time?
questions.answer: I think it is largely a natural consequence of people growing and changing. As we mature, our interests, values and circumstances [[diverge]], and friends who once had everything in common may drift apart. Physical distance, when people move for work or study, only [[accelerates]] this. It is sad, but I see it as an almost [[inevitable]] part of life.

questions.q: How important are friends compared to family in a person's life?
questions.answer: Both are essential, though they serve different roles. Family offers [[unconditional]] support and a sense of roots, whereas friends are people we actively choose, which makes those bonds uniquely [[affirming]]. Friends often understand aspects of our lives that family cannot. I would say a fulfilling life requires a healthy balance of both, as each provides a distinct kind of [[companionship]].

questions.q: Do you think online friendships will replace face-to-face ones in the future?
questions.answer: I doubt they will replace them entirely, but they will certainly become more significant. Online friendships are convenient and can be genuinely meaningful. However, humans are [[inherently]] social creatures who crave physical presence, so I believe in-person connection is [[irreplaceable]]. The most likely outcome is a [[hybrid]], where the two forms coexist and complement each other.

questions.q: What can people do to maintain long-distance friendships?
questions.answer: Consistent effort is really the crucial ingredient. Regular video calls and messages can [[keep a friendship alive]] despite the distance. I think it also helps to be [[deliberate]] about planning occasional visits, as nothing quite replaces meeting in person. Ultimately, both parties have to be committed, because a friendship that only one person [[sustains]] rarely lasts.

questions.q: What are the benefits and drawbacks of having friends from different cultures?
questions.answer: The benefits are considerable. Friends from other cultures [[broaden your perspective]] and challenge your assumptions, which is deeply [[enriching]]. You learn to be more [[tolerant]] and open-minded. The only real drawback might be occasional misunderstandings arising from different customs or communication styles. But in my view, these minor obstacles are easily outweighed by the rewards.

questions.q: Some say social media has made friendships shallower. Do you agree?
questions.answer: I largely agree with that sentiment. Social media encourages us to [[accumulate]] hundreds of contacts while investing little in any of them. The constant highlight reels can also breed comparison rather than genuine connection. That said, it depends how you use it; for maintaining existing bonds it is useful. Used as a [[substitute]] for real intimacy, though, it does [[trivialise]] friendship.

part3Topics.description: Parenting strategies, discipline, and the changing nature of childhood today.

questions.q: What do you think are the most important qualities of a good parent?
questions.answer: In my view, the most important qualities are patience and [[consistency]]. Children thrive on stability, so a parent who sets clear, fair boundaries helps them feel secure. Equally vital is unconditional love balanced with the willingness to discipline when necessary. A good parent also [[leads by example]], since children tend to [[absorb]] behaviour far more than instructions.

questions.q: How is childhood today different from childhood in the past?
questions.answer: Childhood has changed dramatically. In the past, children spent most of their free time playing outdoors and socialising in person. Today, much of that has been [[supplanted]] by screens, which I find rather [[disconcerting]]. Children are also under far more academic pressure now. So while modern children have more opportunities, they arguably have a less [[carefree]] upbringing.

questions.q: What effect does strict parenting have on children?
questions.answer: It can have mixed effects. On one hand, strict parenting can instil discipline and a strong work ethic. On the other, if it is excessively [[authoritarian]], it may [[stifle]] a child's creativity and confidence, or even breed rebellion. In my opinion, the ideal lies in a balanced approach that is firm but also [[nurturing]] and understanding.

questions.q: How does a person's childhood affect them as an adult?
questions.answer: I think childhood is profoundly [[formative]]. The experiences and relationships we have in those early years shape our personality, our self-esteem and how we relate to others. A secure, loving childhood tends to produce confident, well-adjusted adults, whereas a troubled one can leave lasting [[scars]]. In many ways, our childhood [[lays the foundation]] for everything that follows.

questions.q: How do you think parenting will change in the coming decades?
questions.answer: I expect parenting will become increasingly [[intertwined with]] technology. Parents will likely rely more on apps and online resources for guidance, and managing children's screen time will become an even more [[daunting]] challenge. I also anticipate a move towards more [[egalitarian]] parenting, with responsibilities shared more equally. Hopefully there will also be greater awareness of children's emotional wellbeing.

questions.q: How can parents help children develop good values?
questions.answer: The most effective way is by [[modelling]] those values themselves, since children imitate what they see. Beyond that, parents can use everyday situations as [[teaching moments]], discussing honesty or kindness openly. Encouraging empathy, perhaps through community involvement, also helps. Ultimately, values are [[instilled]] gradually through consistent example rather than through occasional lectures.

questions.q: What are the pros and cons of both parents working full time?
questions.answer: The clear advantage is financial; a [[dual income]] provides a higher [[standard of living]] and more opportunities for the children. It can also make both parents positive role models of independence. The downside is that it may leave less time for the children, potentially affecting the parent-child bond. It really [[comes down to]] the quality of the time spent, not just the quantity, and whether adequate childcare is in place.

questions.q: Some people think children are given too much freedom today. Do you agree?
questions.answer: I partly agree. Modern parenting rightly encourages children's independence, but in some cases [[the pendulum has swung]] too far, and children lack clear boundaries. A total absence of limits can leave children feeling [[insecure]] rather than free. That said, the opposite extreme is equally harmful, so the goal should be freedom within a [[framework]] of sensible, loving guidance.

part3Topics.description: Conflicts and similarities between different age groups in society.

questions.q: Do you think there is a big generation gap in your country?
questions.answer: Yes, I think the generation gap in my country is quite [[pronounced]], largely because of the rapid pace of change. Older generations grew up in a very different, more traditional society, while the young have been shaped by technology and global culture. This creates differing values and expectations, which can sometimes lead to [[tension]], though it also brings a healthy [[diversity]] of perspectives.

questions.q: What are the main differences between the older and younger generations?
questions.answer: The differences are quite [[stark]]. The older generation generally values stability, tradition and hard-earned security, whereas young people tend to prioritise flexibility, self-expression and work-life balance. There is also a huge gap in digital fluency. However, I think these differences are often [[exaggerated]]; at their core, both generations share many of the same fundamental [[aspirations]].

questions.q: Why do older and younger generations sometimes struggle to understand each other?
questions.answer: The root cause is that they have lived through fundamentally different eras. Their formative experiences, technologies and social norms were worlds apart, which shapes how they see everything. This can lead to a failure to [[empathise]], with each side viewing the other's values as [[alien]]. A lack of open, patient communication only [[widens that gulf]].

questions.q: How can different generations learn from one another?
questions.answer: There is enormous potential here. Younger people can help older generations navigate technology, while the elderly offer [[invaluable]] wisdom and life experience that no textbook can provide. This kind of exchange, sometimes called reverse mentoring, is [[mutually beneficial]]. When generations genuinely listen to each other, both are [[enriched]], and society as a whole becomes more cohesive.

questions.q: Do you think the generation gap will grow larger in the future?
questions.answer: It is a real possibility, given how quickly technology now [[evolves]]. Each new generation is being shaped by tools the previous one barely understands, which could [[amplify]] the divide. On the other hand, constant connectivity might actually help [[bridge]] it. So the outcome is uncertain, and it may depend on whether we make a deliberate effort to stay connected across ages.

questions.q: What can be done to reduce conflict between generations?
questions.answer: [[Fostering]] genuine dialogue is essential. Creating opportunities for generations to interact meaningfully, whether in families or communities, builds mutual understanding. Both sides need to approach differences with [[humility]] rather than judgement. I also think education plays a role in teaching young people to respect their elders while encouraging older people to remain [[receptive]] to new ideas.

questions.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of a workplace with mixed age groups?
questions.answer: The advantages are significant. A mix of ages brings together the fresh ideas and [[tech-savviness]] of the young with the experience and [[prudence]] of older staff, which is a powerful combination. The potential disadvantage is friction arising from clashing work styles or communication preferences. But with good management, this diversity of thought is far more of an asset than a [[liability]].

questions.q: Some say younger generations have life easier than older ones. Do you agree?
questions.answer: I think it is more [[nuanced]] than that. In material terms, young people today certainly enjoy comforts and technology their grandparents lacked. However, they face their own distinct pressures, such as intense competition, [[job insecurity]] and a constant online spotlight. So I would not say life is simply easier; rather, the [[hardships]] have shifted in nature.

part3Topics.description: The qualities and responsibilities of effective leaders in various fields.

questions.q: What qualities make someone a good leader?
questions.answer: In my opinion, a good leader combines vision with genuine [[integrity]]. They need the ability to inspire and motivate others towards a common goal, but also the humility to listen. Crucially, effective leaders lead by example and take responsibility for failures rather than shifting blame. I think this [[accountability]], paired with genuine [[empathy]], is what earns lasting respect.

questions.q: Is it better for a leader to be respected or feared?
questions.answer: I firmly believe respect is far more effective than fear. A leader who rules through fear may achieve short-term [[compliance]], but this breeds resentment and stifles honest communication. A respected leader, by contrast, inspires genuine loyalty and willing effort. People follow such a leader out of [[conviction]] rather than intimidation, which produces far better and more [[sustainable]] results.

questions.q: What happens to an organisation when it has poor leadership?
questions.answer: The consequences can be severe. Poor leadership often results in low morale, as employees feel [[directionless]] and undervalued. This typically leads to reduced productivity and high staff turnover. Without a clear vision, an organisation can quickly [[stagnate]] or lose its way entirely. In short, weak leadership tends to [[permeate]] every level and undermine the whole enterprise.

questions.q: How important is leadership in bringing about social change?
questions.answer: Leadership is often the decisive factor. Throughout history, major social movements have been galvanised by charismatic leaders who could [[articulate]] a shared vision and mobilise people. A strong leader gives a movement focus and [[momentum]]. That said, I think the best leaders empower others rather than dominate, ensuring the change is [[collective]] rather than dependent on one individual.

questions.q: How do you think leadership styles will change in the future?
questions.answer: I believe we are moving away from the traditional top-down, authoritarian model towards something more [[collaborative]]. Future leaders will likely need to be more emotionally intelligent and adaptable, given how quickly the world changes. There will also be greater emphasis on [[transparency]] and inclusivity. In short, leadership is becoming less about command and more about [[facilitation]].

questions.q: How can society develop better leaders?
questions.answer: I think it starts with education that [[nurtures]] not just intelligence but character and empathy. Providing young people with genuine opportunities to take responsibility, through mentorship or community projects, helps [[cultivate]] leadership skills early. We should also reward ethical leadership rather than [[mere ambition]]. Essentially, good leaders are developed over time, not simply born.

questions.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of a young person becoming a leader?
questions.answer: The advantages include fresh energy, innovative ideas and a willingness to challenge [[outdated conventions]]. Young leaders can be genuinely [[dynamic]]. The main disadvantage is a lack of experience, which may lead to [[impulsive]] decisions or difficulty commanding respect from older colleagues. Ideally, a young leader would be paired with experienced mentors to balance their enthusiasm with wisdom.

questions.q: Some say great leaders are born, not made. Do you agree?
questions.answer: I largely disagree with that idea. While some people may have a natural [[charisma]] or confidence, I firmly believe leadership is a set of skills that can be learned and refined through experience. History is full of leaders who [[grew into the role]]. To claim leaders are simply born [[undermines]] the value of hard work and personal development.

part3Topics.description: The impact of celebrity culture and the pursuit of fame on society.

questions.q: Why do you think so many young people want to be famous?
questions.answer: I think it is largely driven by social media, which has made fame appear both [[glamorous]] and easily attainable. Young people see influencers achieving wealth and adoration seemingly overnight, which is highly [[seductive]]. There is also a deeper human desire for validation and significance. Unfortunately, this often means chasing fame as an end in itself rather than as a [[by-product]] of genuine achievement.

questions.q: How is fame today different from fame in the past?
questions.answer: The nature of fame has changed completely. In the past, fame was usually earned through exceptional talent or accomplishment, and famous people were relatively few. Today, anyone can become famous overnight through a viral video, and fame is often [[fleeting]] and detached from any real skill. Modern celebrity is also far more [[invasive]], with stars under constant [[surveillance]].

questions.q: What effect does celebrity culture have on young people?
questions.answer: The effects are often [[detrimental]], in my view. Constant exposure to celebrities' curated, idealised lives can create unrealistic expectations and [[fuel insecurity]], especially about appearance. It can also promote materialism and a distorted sense of what matters. That said, positive celebrities who [[champion]] good causes can be a genuinely inspiring influence, so it is not entirely negative.

questions.q: Do celebrities have a responsibility to be good role models?
questions.answer: I would argue they do, whether they like it or not. Given the enormous influence they [[wield]] over millions of impressionable fans, celebrities have a certain moral [[obligation]] to behave responsibly. Their actions can genuinely shape public attitudes. However, it is also unfair to expect them to be flawless, since they are human. The key is a basic level of [[accountability]] and awareness.

questions.q: Do you think celebrity culture will become more or less influential in the future?
questions.answer: I suspect it will become even more influential, but also more [[fragmented]]. Rather than a few global superstars, we are likely to see countless niche influencers, each commanding devoted audiences. Technology like virtual influencers may further blur the line between real and fabricated fame. Whether this influence is healthy will depend on whether audiences become more [[discerning]] and [[sceptical]].

questions.q: How can society reduce the negative effects of celebrity obsession?
questions.answer: Media literacy education is crucial here. Teaching young people to critically [[evaluate]] the polished images they see online can lessen the harmful comparisons. Promoting a broader range of admirable figures, such as scientists or activists, would also help [[rebalance]] what we celebrate. Ultimately, encouraging people to derive self-worth from their own lives rather than [[idolising]] others is the real solution.

questions.q: What are the advantages and disadvantages of being famous?
questions.answer: The obvious advantages are wealth, influence and opportunities that most people can only dream of. Fame also provides a platform to promote worthy causes. However, the disadvantages are considerable: a total loss of privacy, relentless [[scrutiny]], and immense pressure that can take a serious toll on mental health. Many celebrities find the constant spotlight genuinely [[suffocating]], so it is far from the [[idyllic]] life it appears.

questions.q: Some people say celebrities are paid too much. Do you agree?
questions.answer: I [[have some sympathy with]] that view. It does seem [[disproportionate]] that an entertainer can earn more in a day than a nurse earns in a year, when the latter arguably contributes more to society. On the other hand, their pay simply reflects the market and the vast revenue they generate. So while it feels [[morally questionable]], it is economically logical.

part3Topics.description: The importance of integrity and trust in personal and public life.

questions.q: Why is honesty important in relationships?
questions.answer: Honesty is really the [[bedrock]] of any healthy relationship. Without it, trust cannot exist, and trust is what allows people to feel safe and secure with one another. Even small lies, once discovered, can [[erode]] that foundation and breed suspicion. In my view, being truthful, even when it is difficult, is what gives a relationship genuine depth and [[resilience]].

questions.q: Do you think people are more or less honest than they were in the past?
questions.answer: That is a difficult question. I do not think human nature has fundamentally changed, but the opportunities for [[deception]] have multiplied with technology, from online scams to fake identities. At the same time, the internet has made it much harder to hide dishonesty, since [[misdeeds]] are quickly exposed. So perhaps we are no less honest, just more [[transparent]].

questions.q: What happens to a society when trust in institutions breaks down?
questions.answer: The consequences are deeply damaging. When people lose faith in institutions like government or the media, it breeds [[cynicism]] and division. Cooperation becomes difficult, conspiracy theories can [[flourish]], and social cohesion begins to unravel. Trust is essentially the glue that holds a society together, so its breakdown can lead to genuine [[instability]] and dysfunction.

questions.q: Is it ever acceptable to tell a lie?
questions.answer: I think there are rare cases where a so-called white lie is justifiable, particularly when the truth would cause needless harm and the lie is genuinely [[benevolent]]. Sparing someone's feelings is a common example. However, this is a [[slippery slope]], because habitual lying, even with good intentions, can [[undermine]] trust. So while not absolute, honesty should be the strong default.

questions.q: Do you think it will be harder to trust information in the future?
questions.answer: Unfortunately, I think it will. With the rise of sophisticated technology like deepfakes and AI-generated content, distinguishing genuine information from [[fabricated]] material will become increasingly difficult. This could make people either dangerously [[gullible]] or excessively cynical. Developing strong critical-thinking skills and reliable verification tools will be absolutely essential to [[navigate]] this new landscape.

questions.q: How can trust be rebuilt once it has been broken?
questions.answer: Rebuilding trust is a slow and difficult process. It requires the person who broke it to take full responsibility and offer a sincere apology, without excuses. More importantly, they must demonstrate changed behaviour [[consistently]] over time, since words alone are not enough. [[The wronged party]], meanwhile, needs to be willing to gradually [[reconcile]]. Essentially, trust is rebuilt through actions, not promises.

questions.q: What are the benefits and risks of being completely honest all the time?
questions.answer: The great benefit of total honesty is that it builds a reputation for [[integrity]], and people know exactly where they stand with you. It fosters deep trust. The risk, however, is that unfiltered honesty can sometimes be hurtful or [[tactless]] if not delivered with care. So I think the ideal is honesty tempered with [[diplomacy]], being truthful but also kind.

questions.q: Some say honesty is always the best policy. Do you agree?
questions.answer: I largely agree, though I would add a small [[caveat]]. As a general principle, honesty builds trust and spares us the burden of maintaining lies, so it is almost always wise. However, I think it must be balanced with [[compassion]]; brutal honesty that needlessly wounds someone is not virtuous. So honesty is the best policy, provided it is delivered [[sensitively]].

part3Topics.description: Peer influence, social conformity, and parental guidance.
