acquaintances.example: I have plenty of acquaintances from university, but only two or three people I would call close friends.

across virtually every sector.meaning: in almost all areas of the economy or all types of industry
across virtually every sector.example: Digital skills are now in demand across virtually every sector, from farming to finance.

on the same page.meaning: sharing the same understanding or agreeing about what to do

on your own schedule.meaning: at times that you choose yourself, without depending on others

once-in-a-lifetime.meaning: very special and unlikely to happen to you again
once-in-a-lifetime.example: Watching the World Cup final live in the stadium would be a once-in-a-lifetime experience.

ongoing public funds.meaning: money from the government that is provided continuously over a long period
ongoing public funds.example: Museums and public libraries usually depend on ongoing public funding to keep their doors open.

only do so much.meaning: there is a limit to what someone is able to achieve alone

open doors.meaning: to create new opportunities for someone

open-minded.meaning: willing to listen to and consider new or different ideas and opinions
open-minded.example: Travelling abroad made me more open-minded about other cultures and ways of life.

oppression.meaning: cruel and unfair treatment of people, especially by limiting their freedom
oppression.example: The 1952 Language Movement was a stand against cultural oppression.

oppressive.meaning: uncomfortably hot and heavy, making you feel tired and uneasy

optimistic.meaning: hopeful and confident that things will turn out well
optimistic.example: I'm fairly optimistic that I'll get a scholarship if I keep improving my IELTS score.

optimistically.meaning: looking at the situation in the most hopeful way
optimistically.example: Optimistically, the new bridge should cut our travel time to Dhaka by at least an hour.

ordeal.meaning: a very unpleasant, difficult or tiring experience
ordeal.example: Getting a new passport used to be a real ordeal, with long queues and endless forms.

original.meaning: new, creative and different from anything done before
original.example: The judges praised her short film for its original story and unusual camera work.

ornate.meaning: decorated with a lot of complicated and detailed patterns
ornate.example: The old zamindar houses near Sirajganj have ornate balconies and carved wooden doors.

out of necessity.meaning: because it is necessary, not because you want to

out of reach.meaning: too expensive or difficult for someone to get or achieve
out of reach.example: For many young people, owning a flat in Dhaka is completely out of reach.

out of sheer necessity.meaning: only because something is completely necessary and there is no other choice
out of sheer necessity.example: Out of sheer necessity, I learnt to cook when I moved away from home for university.

out of sight.meaning: not seen or noticed by others, and so easily forgotten
out of sight.example: Remote workers sometimes worry that being out of sight will mean being overlooked for promotion.

outdated.meaning: old-fashioned and no longer useful or suitable
outdated.example: Some schools still use outdated textbooks that do not reflect modern technology.

outdated conventions.meaning: old customs or rules of behaviour that no longer suit modern life
outdated conventions.example: Young couples today often ignore outdated conventions about who should pay for dinner.

outgrew.meaning: to stop doing or liking something as you become older
outgrew.example: Most children eventually outgrow their fear of the dark.

outlet.meaning: a way of expressing or releasing strong feelings or energy
outlet.example: Writing in a diary has always been a healthy outlet for my worries.

outlet for stress.meaning: an activity that helps you release stress and feel calmer
outlet for stress.example: Playing cricket with friends on Fridays is my main outlet for stress after a busy week.

outmanoeuvre.meaning: to gain an advantage over someone by acting more cleverly or skilfully
outmanoeuvre.example: Smaller companies can sometimes outmanoeuvre big rivals by responding faster to customers' needs.

outpaced.meaning: to develop or grow faster than something else
outpaced.example: Demand for university places has outpaced the number of seats available in public universities.

outright.meaning: completely and immediately, not partly or gradually
outright.example: Rather than banning mobile phones outright, schools could teach students to use them responsibly.

outsourced.meaning: to let someone or something else do a job for you instead of doing it yourself
outsourced.example: Many busy families now outsource cooking and cleaning to paid helpers or delivery apps.

outweigh.meaning: to be greater or more important than something else
outweigh.example: For me, the benefits of studying abroad clearly outweigh the cost and the homesickness.

overbearing.meaning: trying to control other people in an unpleasant way
overbearing.example: An overbearing boss can make even a well-paid job feel unbearable.

overconfident.meaning: too sure of your own abilities, in a way that leads to mistakes
overconfident.example: Overconfident drivers often take risks on the highway that cause serious accidents.

overcrowding.meaning: a situation where too many people are in one place
overcrowding.example: Overcrowding on trains during Eid holidays makes the journey home exhausting.

overemphasis.meaning: giving too much importance or attention to something
overemphasis.example: An overemphasis on exam results can leave students with little time for creativity.

overhaul.meaning: a complete examination and change of a system in order to improve it
overhaul.example: The public transport network in Dhaka needs a complete overhaul, not just a few new buses.

overindulging.meaning: to have too much of something enjoyable, especially food or drink
overindulging.example: It's easy to overindulge on sweets during Eid, when every house you visit offers you something.

overjoyed.meaning: extremely happy and pleased about something that has happened
overjoyed.example: My parents were overjoyed when my younger sister got into a top medical college.

overlooked.meaning: to fail to notice or give proper attention or recognition to someone or something
overlooked.example: Talented employees are sometimes overlooked for promotion simply because they are quiet.

overlooking.meaning: to fail to notice or give proper credit to someone or something
overlooking.example: Employers often overlook older candidates who bring years of practical experience to the job.

overreach.meaning: the use of more power or authority than is proper or allowed
overreach.example: Many citizens worry about government overreach when new surveillance laws are introduced without public debate.

overreliance.meaning: the state of depending too much on one particular thing
overreliance.example: An overreliance on smartphones can weaken our ability to remember simple things like phone numbers.

overrides.meaning: to become more important than everything else, pushing other concerns aside
overrides.example: For many parents, concern for their children's safety overrides every other consideration when choosing a home.

overshadow.meaning: to make something seem less important by being more noticeable or successful
overshadow.example: His brilliant exam results were somewhat overshadowed by his sister's scholarship to a university abroad.

overshadows.meaning: to receive so much attention that something else seems less important
overshadows.example: In many countries one popular sport tends to overshadow others, leaving them with little funding or media attention.

oversimplification.meaning: a description that makes something seem simpler than it really is, ignoring important details
oversimplification.example: Saying that young people are simply lazy is an oversimplification of a complex economic situation.

oversimplified.meaning: to describe something as simpler than it really is, leaving out important facts
oversimplified.example: News reports often oversimplify climate science, which leaves viewers confused about what is actually happening.

overspend.meaning: to spend more money than you intended or can afford
overspend.example: I always make a shopping list before going to the market so that I don't overspend.

overstated.meaning: to describe something as more important or serious than it really is
overstated.example: The benefits of social media for teenagers are sometimes overstated by the companies that run these platforms.

oversupply.meaning: a situation where there is more of something than is needed
oversupply.example: An oversupply of new flats in the city has actually made rents slightly more affordable for young workers.

overthink.meaning: to think about something too much, in a way that causes worry or delay
overthink.example: I tend to overthink small decisions, like what to say in an email to a new client.

overwhelm.meaning: to be so strong or powerful that something else is defeated or swamped
overwhelm.example: Fast food chains can overwhelm small family restaurants that have served local dishes for generations.

overwhelmed.meaning: feeling that you have too much to deal with and cannot cope
overwhelmed.example: During exam season, many students feel overwhelmed by the amount of material they have to revise.

overwhelming.meaning: so great or difficult that it is hard to deal with
overwhelming.example: Moving to a new city alone can be overwhelming at first, but it usually gets easier with time.

overwhelmingly.meaning: in most respects or to a very great degree
overwhelmingly.example: Public opinion was overwhelmingly in favour of building a new bridge across the river.

overwork.meaning: the act of working too hard or for too many hours
overwork.example: Chronic overwork can damage both your health and your relationships with the people you love.

ownership.meaning: a sense of personal responsibility for a task and its results
ownership.example: When students take ownership of their learning, they tend to stay motivated for much longer.

packed to the rafters.meaning: extremely full of people, with no space left
packed to the rafters.example: The wedding hall was packed to the rafters, with relatives arriving from every corner of the country.

panic.meaning: a sudden strong feeling of fear that stops you thinking clearly
panic.example: I felt a moment of panic when I realised I had left my passport at home.

panoramic.meaning: showing or giving a wide view of a large area
panoramic.example: From the top of the hill you get a panoramic view of the river winding through the countryside.

paradox.meaning: a situation that seems strange because it combines two opposite features
paradox.example: It's a paradox that we have more ways to communicate than ever, yet many people feel lonelier.

paradoxically.meaning: in a way that seems surprising because it is the opposite of what you would expect
paradoxically.example: Paradoxically, having too much free time can make people less productive than having a busy schedule.

paralysed.meaning: so affected by a feeling that you are unable to act or decide
paralysed.example: Some graduates are so paralysed by the fear of choosing the wrong career that they delay applying for jobs.

paralysing.meaning: making someone unable to act or make decisions
paralysing.example: For a nervous speaker, the fear of forgetting their words can be absolutely paralysing.

paramount.example: When choosing a school for their children, most parents consider safety and good teaching paramount.

parental controls.meaning: settings on devices or apps that let parents limit what children can see or do
parental controls.example: My elder sister uses parental controls on her tablet so her son only watches cartoons suitable for his age.

passive.meaning: accepting or receiving things without taking an active part
passive.example: Watching television is quite a passive activity compared with playing a sport or learning an instrument.

pastime.meaning: an activity that you do regularly for enjoyment in your free time
pastime.example: Flying kites on rooftops is a popular pastime for children in Bangladesh during the spring.

pastimes.meaning: activities that people do regularly for enjoyment in their free time
pastimes.example: Board games and card games were common pastimes in rural areas long before smartphones arrived.

patch of land.meaning: a small area of ground, often used for growing things
patch of land.example: My grandfather grows chillies and aubergines on a small patch of land behind the village house.

paternalistic.meaning: controlling people supposedly for their own good and limiting their freedom to choose
paternalistic.example: Some people think banning sugary drinks is paternalistic, arguing that adults should decide what they consume.

patience.meaning: the ability to stay calm and not get annoyed when something takes a long time
patience.example: Teaching my grandmother to use a smartphone took a lot of patience, but she can now video call us.

patient.meaning: able to stay calm and understanding without getting annoyed
patient.example: A good teacher needs to be patient with students who take longer to grasp new ideas.

patriotism.meaning: love for your country and a feeling of pride in it
patriotism.example: On Victory Day you can feel a strong sense of patriotism as people wave flags and sing the national anthem.

peace of mind.meaning: a feeling of calm because you are not worried about anything
peace of mind.example: Having some savings in the bank gives me peace of mind in case something unexpected happens.

peaceful escape.meaning: a calm place or activity that lets you get away from stress or noise
peaceful escape.example: For me, a quiet walk along the river is a peaceful escape from the pressures of work.

pedestrian areas.meaning: parts of a town where cars are not allowed so people can walk freely
pedestrian areas.example: More pedestrian areas in the city centre would make shopping far more pleasant and much safer for families.

pedestrianised.meaning: to close a street to traffic so that only people on foot can use it
pedestrianised.example: If the council decided to pedestrianise the main market street, small shops would probably attract more customers.

people-facing.meaning: involving direct contact and communication with other people as a main part of the work
people-facing.example: My job is very people-facing, since I spend most of the day advising students and their parents.

perceptive.meaning: quick to notice and understand things that others might not notice
perceptive.example: My grandmother is remarkably perceptive and always knows when something is bothering me, even before I speak.

perfectly reasonable.meaning: completely fair, sensible and easy to justify
perfectly reasonable.example: It's perfectly reasonable for young people to want some independence once they start earning.

period of adjustment.meaning: a time during which people get used to a new situation
period of adjustment.example: Most international students go through a period of adjustment before they feel at home in a new country.

permanence.meaning: the state of lasting for a very long time or for ever
permanence.example: Many people in my country value the permanence of owning land, since it can be passed down through generations.

permeate.meaning: to spread through every part of something
permeate.example: A positive attitude at work can permeate the whole office and make everyone more cooperative.

perpetual.meaning: never ending, or seeming to continue for ever
perpetual.example: Living in a big city can feel like a perpetual race against traffic, deadlines and noise.

perpetually.meaning: all the time, or in a way that seems never to stop
perpetually.example: My younger sister is perpetually busy with her studies, so we rarely get to watch a film together.

perpetuate.meaning: to make a bad situation or belief continue for a long time
perpetuate.example: Advertisements that show only very thin models can perpetuate unrealistic ideas about beauty.

perseverance.meaning: continued effort to achieve something despite difficulties or slow progress
perseverance.example: Learning a new language as an adult takes a great deal of perseverance, especially when progress feels slow.

persevere.meaning: to keep trying to do something even though it is difficult
persevere.example: If you persevere with daily practice, your speaking fluency will improve more than you might expect.

persevered.meaning: to continue with an activity despite difficulty, rather than giving up
persevered.example: She failed her driving test twice but persevered and finally passed on her third attempt.

persist.meaning: to continue to exist or happen over a long period
persist.example: Although many people now shop online, the tradition of visiting local bazaars before Eid is likely to persist.

persistence.meaning: the quality of continuing to try to achieve something despite difficulty
persistence.example: It took real persistence to get my first job, as I applied to dozens of companies before anyone replied.

persistent.meaning: continuing to exist for a long time and difficult to get rid of
persistent.example: Traffic congestion is a persistent problem in Dhaka, and it seems to get worse every year.

personal touch.meaning: a small detail that makes something feel friendly, individual and special
personal touch.example: A handwritten note adds a personal touch to any gift, however small or inexpensive it is.

personalised.meaning: specially chosen or made for a particular person
personalised.example: Online learning platforms can give students personalised feedback based on their individual strengths and weaknesses.

pervasive.meaning: present everywhere and affecting many parts of life
pervasive.example: Social media has become so pervasive that it's hard to find anyone under thirty without an account.

pessimistic.meaning: expecting bad things to happen or believing the worst about something
pessimistic.example: Some older people are pessimistic about the future, but I think my generation has many reasons for hope.

petrified.meaning: extremely frightened, often so much that you cannot move
petrified.example: I was petrified the first time I had to give a presentation in English in front of the whole class.

phenomenal.meaning: extremely good, impressive or great in size
phenomenal.example: The growth of online learning over the last few years has been phenomenal, especially in developing countries.

philanthropy.meaning: the practice of giving money and help to people in need or to good causes
philanthropy.example: Philanthropy by wealthy business owners has funded many schools and hospitals in rural parts of the country.

phubbing.meaning: ignoring the people you are with by looking at your phone instead
phubbing.example: Phubbing at the dinner table is one habit my family tries hard to avoid, so we keep our phones in another room.

picturesque.meaning: pretty and attractive, especially in a natural or old-fashioned way
picturesque.example: The tea gardens of Sylhet are incredibly picturesque, with neat green rows stretching across the rolling hills.

piling up.meaning: to increase in amount until it becomes difficult to deal with
piling up.example: If I don't reply to emails every day, they soon pile up and I feel completely behind.

pitting them against.meaning: to set two people or things in competition or opposition with each other
pitting them against.example: Pitting science against the arts in schools is pointless, since both develop valuable ways of thinking.

pivotal.meaning: of great importance because other things depend on it
pivotal.example: Finishing university was a pivotal moment in my life, as it gave me the confidence to start working.

placed excessive weight on.meaning: to treat something as much more important than it really should be

playful.meaning: light-hearted and fond of having fun and joking
playful.example: My nephew is so playful that he turns even brushing his teeth into a game.

playing field.meaning: the conditions in which people compete, especially how fair or equal they are
playing field.example: Free online courses help create a more level playing field for students who cannot afford private tuition.

pleasures.meaning: something that gives you a feeling of happiness or enjoyment
pleasures.example: A hot cup of tea on a rainy afternoon is one of my favourite small pleasures.

plundering.meaning: to take or use natural resources in a greedy and damaging way
plundering.example: Large companies should not be allowed to plunder forests for timber without replanting what they cut down.

pocket of calm.meaning: a short, quiet period or small peaceful place within a busy time
pocket of calm.example: My morning cup of tea on the balcony is a pocket of calm before the chaos of the working day.

pockets of time.meaning: small periods of free time available within a busy day
pockets of time.example: I use small pockets of time, like my bus journey to work, to listen to podcasts in English.

poignant.meaning: causing strong feelings of sadness, emotion or regret
poignant.example: Visiting my grandfather's old school was a poignant experience, as he told me stories of friends who had passed away.

polarised.meaning: divided into two groups with completely opposite opinions
polarised.example: Debates about social issues online are often so polarised that people stop listening to each other entirely.

polished.example: Candidates with a polished appearance and confident manner tend to make a stronger first impression at interviews.

political will.meaning: the determination of politicians and governments to take action on something
political will.example: Cleaning up our rivers is possible, but it requires real political will and long-term investment.

pollination.meaning: the transfer of pollen between plants, usually by insects, so they can produce fruit or seeds
pollination.example: Without bees and other insects to carry out pollination, many fruit and vegetable crops would fail.

portion sizes.meaning: the amount of food served to one person at a meal
portion sizes.example: Restaurants in the city have increased their portion sizes, which may be encouraging people to overeat.

poses a real threat.meaning: to be a genuine and serious danger to someone or something
poses a real threat.example: Plastic waste in our rivers poses a real threat to fish and the families who depend on fishing.

possess.meaning: to have or own something, such as a quality, skill or knowledge
possess.example: Good leaders possess the ability to listen carefully before making important decisions.

powerful hold.meaning: strong control or influence over someone's thoughts or behaviour
powerful hold.example: Cricket has a powerful hold on people in my country, and whole streets go quiet during important matches.

powerlessness.meaning: the feeling of being unable to control or change a situation
powerlessness.example: Watching floods destroy villages on the news can create a sense of powerlessness among ordinary citizens.

practical.meaning: suitable and useful for a particular purpose or situation
practical.example: A small motorbike is more practical than a car in crowded towns, where parking is almost impossible.

pragmatism.meaning: dealing with things in a sensible, realistic way rather than following ideals
pragmatism.example: Choosing a university often involves some pragmatism, such as considering job prospects as well as personal interests.

precarious.meaning: not safe or secure, and likely to go wrong
precarious.example: Many freelance workers live in a precarious financial situation, never knowing how much they will earn next month.

precariousness.meaning: the state of being uncertain, insecure and likely to change for the worse
precariousness.example: The precariousness of short-term contracts makes it difficult for young workers to plan their futures.

precious.meaning: very valuable and important to you, often for emotional reasons
precious.example: Old family photos have become precious to me since my grandparents started getting older.

predetermined.meaning: decided or fixed in advance so that it cannot be changed
predetermined.example: I don't believe a child's future is predetermined by their family background, although it certainly matters.

predominantly.meaning: mostly, mainly or for the most part
predominantly.example: My hometown is predominantly agricultural, although small factories have opened on the outskirts recently.

prefabricated.meaning: built from parts made in a factory and quickly put together on site
prefabricated.example: Prefabricated homes can be built in weeks, which could help families who lose their houses in floods.

preferable.meaning: better or more suitable than something else
preferable.example: For long journeys, I find the train preferable to the bus because I can read comfortably.

premature deaths.meaning: death that happens much earlier than normal, often from a preventable cause
premature deaths.example: Smoking remains one of the leading causes of premature death, which is why many governments tax cigarettes heavily.

premium.meaning: great value or importance given to something, as in placing a premium on it
premium.example: Many companies now place a premium on teamwork and communication skills when hiring graduates.

preserve.meaning: to keep something safe and prevent it from being lost or damaged
preserve.example: It's important to preserve traditional crafts like pottery so younger generations can still learn them.

preserving.meaning: to keep a memory or moment so that it is not forgotten
preserving.example: Writing a diary is a lovely way of preserving memories that might otherwise fade over the years.

pressing.meaning: needing to be dealt with immediately; urgent
pressing.example: With the application deadline only a week away, finishing my personal statement is my most pressing task.

pressing issue.meaning: a serious problem that needs attention immediately
pressing issue.example: Air pollution has become a pressing issue in Dhaka, affecting the health of millions of residents.

prestige.meaning: respect and admiration given to something because of its success or high status
prestige.example: Some students choose a university for its prestige rather than for the quality of the course they want.

prestigious.meaning: respected and admired as being very important or of high quality
prestigious.example: Getting a scholarship to a prestigious university abroad is the dream of many students I work with.

prevalent.meaning: existing very commonly among a group of people or at a particular time
prevalent.example: Online shopping has become increasingly prevalent in Bangladesh, even in smaller towns.

prevention.meaning: action taken to stop something bad, such as crime, from happening
prevention.example: Crime prevention programmes for young people are often cheaper and more effective than building new prisons.

preventive.meaning: intended to stop something harmful before it happens
preventive.example: Regular health check-ups are a simple preventive measure that can catch problems early.

price tag.meaning: the cost of something, especially when it is high
price tag.example: Studying abroad comes with a hefty price tag, so many families take out loans to cover the fees.

priceless.meaning: so valuable, especially emotionally, that no price could be put on it
priceless.example: The letters my grandfather wrote to my grandmother are priceless to our whole family.

primary culprit.meaning: the main cause of a problem or of something bad
primary culprit.example: Plastic bags are often seen as the primary culprit behind blocked drains during the monsoon.

prioritise.meaning: to decide that something is more important than other things and deal with it first
prioritise.example: During exam season, my sister has to prioritise revision over seeing her friends.

prioritised.meaning: to treat something as more important and give it more attention or resources
prioritised.example: I hope that cycle lanes will be prioritised in future city planning, as roads are getting more dangerous.

prioritises.meaning: to put one thing before others because it is considered more important
prioritises.example: A good manager prioritises the wellbeing of the team as well as the company's targets.

prioritising ruthlessly.meaning: to focus firmly on the most important tasks and drop less important ones
prioritising ruthlessly.example: When you have too many deadlines at once, you have to prioritise ruthlessly and ignore anything non-essential.

pristine.meaning: in its original condition, completely clean and unspoilt
pristine.example: Parts of the Sundarbans remain pristine, with dense mangrove forest stretching as far as the eye can see.

privacy paradox.meaning: the gap between people saying they value privacy and still sharing personal data freely
privacy paradox.example: The privacy paradox explains why people complain about data collection yet happily accept every app's terms and conditions.

privilege.meaning: a special honour or opportunity that makes you feel lucky
privilege.example: It was a real privilege to meet my favourite author at a book fair in Dhaka last year.

privileged.meaning: having special advantages because of wealth or social position
privileged.example: Private tutoring is often available only to privileged families, which widens the gap between rich and poor students.

prized.meaning: highly valued and wanted by many people
prized.example: Fluent English and digital skills are highly prized by employers in almost every industry today.

procrastinate.meaning: to delay doing something you should do, usually because it is boring or unpleasant
procrastinate.example: I used to procrastinate before exams, but now I set small daily goals to stay on track.

productive.meaning: achieving a lot or leading to good, useful results
productive.example: I find I'm most productive early in the morning, before the office gets noisy.

productive citizens.meaning: a member of society who works and contributes positively to the community
productive citizens.example: Good vocational training helps young people become productive citizens who can support themselves and their families.

proficient.meaning: skilled and experienced at doing something
proficient.example: Most office jobs nowadays require you to be proficient in basic computer programs like spreadsheets.

profitable.meaning: bringing financial gain or other benefit
profitable.example: Many farmers have switched to growing vegetables because they are more profitable than rice.

profound.meaning: very great, deep or intense in its effect
profound.example: Moving to a new country can have a profound effect on the way you see your own culture.

profound appeal.meaning: a deep and strong attraction that something has for someone
profound appeal.example: For many city workers, simple village life holds a profound appeal, with its fresh air and slower pace.

profound influence.meaning: a very strong and lasting effect on someone or something
profound influence.example: My grandfather has had a profound influence on my values, especially honesty and hard work.

progression.meaning: a gradual move or development from one stage to the next
progression.example: Moving from assistant to team leader felt like a natural progression after three years in the same company.

progressive.meaning: supporting new, modern ideas and methods
progressive.example: Our school had a progressive headteacher who encouraged debates and group projects instead of pure memorisation.

progressive taxation.meaning: a tax system in which people who earn more pay a higher rate of tax
progressive taxation.example: Supporters of progressive taxation argue that it funds public services fairly by asking more from the wealthy.

prohibitions.meaning: a rule or law that forbids something
prohibitions.example: Most religions share prohibitions against lying and stealing, which suggests some values are universal.

proliferate.meaning: to increase rapidly in number or spread quickly
proliferate.example: Coffee shops have started to proliferate in Dhaka, especially in areas popular with students.

promising.meaning: showing signs of being successful or good in the future
promising.example: Early signs are promising, and the new metro rail seems to be reducing travel times for commuters.

promotable.meaning: likely or suitable to be given a higher position at work
promotable.example: Showing initiative and helping colleagues are qualities that make an employee genuinely promotable.

prompt.meaning: to cause someone to take action or make a decision
prompt.example: The floods last year prompted the local council to repair the river embankment.

prone.meaning: likely to suffer from something or be affected by it
prone.example: Elderly people living alone are more prone to loneliness, especially if their children have moved away.

pronounced.example: The difference between city and village lifestyles is quite pronounced in Bangladesh, especially in terms of technology.

propaganda.meaning: biased or misleading information used to promote a political cause or point of view
propaganda.example: During wartime, governments often use films and posters as propaganda to shape public opinion.

proponents.meaning: a person who supports an idea or course of action
proponents.example: Proponents of online learning say it gives rural students access to teachers they would never otherwise meet.

proportionate.meaning: in the correct relationship in size or amount to something else
proportionate.example: Punishments should be proportionate to the crime, so minor offences shouldn't lead to long prison sentences.

prosperity.meaning: the state of being successful and comfortable, especially financially
prosperity.example: Better roads and bridges have brought new prosperity to many towns along the Jamuna.

protective.meaning: wanting to keep someone you care about safe from harm
protective.example: My father is very protective of my younger sister and always asks who she's going out with.

provocative.meaning: intended to cause a strong reaction, especially anger or excitement
provocative.example: Some news websites use provocative headlines simply to attract clicks and shares.

provoke thought.meaning: to make people think seriously and carefully about something
provoke thought.example: A good documentary should not only entertain but also provoke thought about important social issues.

prudence.meaning: careful good judgement that avoids unnecessary risks
prudence.example: My father's financial prudence meant our family always had savings for emergencies.

prudent.meaning: careful and sensible, especially when making decisions about money
prudent.example: It's prudent to compare prices at a few shops before buying an expensive phone.

pry.meaning: to try too hard to find out private details about someone's life
pry.example: My neighbours are friendly, but they never pry into our family matters, which I really appreciate.

public good.meaning: something that benefits everyone in society and should be available to all
public good.example: Clean air is a public good, so governments have a duty to protect it for everyone.

pull factor.meaning: something that attracts people to move to a particular place
pull factor.example: Better healthcare is a major pull factor that draws families from villages to district towns.

purposeful.meaning: having a clear aim and a sense of meaning
purposeful.example: Volunteering at weekends makes my free time feel more purposeful than just scrolling on my phone.

purposefully.meaning: with a clear aim, in a deliberate and considered way
purposefully.example: When technology is used purposefully in classrooms, it can make lessons much more engaging.

pursue.meaning: to try to achieve or follow something over a period of time
pursue.example: I hope to pursue a master's degree abroad once I have saved enough money.

pursuit.meaning: the act of trying to achieve or obtain something
pursuit.example: The pursuit of wealth alone rarely makes people happy in the long term.

put aside.meaning: to save an amount of money regularly for a particular purpose
put aside.example: I try to put aside a little money each month to help with my sister's university fees.

put me at ease.meaning: to make someone feel relaxed and comfortable in a situation
put me at ease.example: A good interviewer tries to put candidates at ease with some friendly small talk at the start.

quaint.meaning: attractive and charming in an unusual or old-fashioned way
quaint.example: The village has a quaint little tea stall where old men gather every afternoon to chat.

quantifiable.meaning: able to be measured or expressed as a number

quiet dignity.meaning: a calm, serious and respectable quality that does not seek attention

quintessentially.meaning: in a way that is a perfect, typical example of something

raise a festival's profile.meaning: to make something more widely known and noticed by the public

rally round.meaning: to come together to help and support someone who is in difficulty

rarity.meaning: something that is unusual and does not happen often

rational.meaning: based on clear thinking and reason rather than emotion

reachable.meaning: able to be contacted, for example by phone or message

reactive.meaning: responding to problems after they happen rather than preventing them

read social cues.meaning: to understand how others are feeling from their behaviour, expressions and tone

readily.example: Most people readily accept cookies on websites without reading what information is being collected.

real-world play.meaning: children playing physically with objects and people rather than on screens

reaps.meaning: to get something good as a result of your own efforts or investment

reason through.meaning: to think about something carefully and logically in order to reach a conclusion

reasoning.meaning: the process of thinking logically about something to form a judgement
reasoning.example: Maths develops logical reasoning, which is useful in everyday decisions like planning a monthly budget.

reassure.meaning: to say or do something to make someone feel less worried

reassuring.meaning: making you feel less worried or anxious
reassuring.example: It's reassuring to know that my family will always support me, whatever I decide to do.

rebalance.meaning: to change something so that its different parts are more equal or fair
rebalance.example: Many young professionals are trying to rebalance their lives by spending less time at work and more with family.

receptive.meaning: willing to listen to and accept new ideas or suggestions
receptive.example: My father was surprisingly receptive when I suggested he try online banking.

recharge.meaning: to rest and relax in order to regain your energy

recharge my batteries.meaning: to rest and relax so that you feel full of energy again

reckless.meaning: acting without thinking about the possible dangers or consequences
reckless.example: Driving fast on the highway during heavy rain is reckless and puts other people in danger too.

reclaim.meaning: to get back something that was lost or taken away
reclaim.example: Turning off work notifications at weekends has helped me reclaim time for my family and hobbies.

recognition.meaning: praise and appreciation for someone's work or achievements
recognition.example: Teachers often work long hours without much recognition, which can make them feel undervalued.

reconcile.meaning: to become friendly with someone again after a disagreement
reconcile.example: After months of not speaking, the two brothers finally reconciled at their father's birthday dinner.

reconciles.meaning: to find a way for two opposing needs or ideas to exist together
reconciles.example: Good city planning reconciles the need for new housing with the need to protect green spaces.

redistribute.meaning: to share something out in a different way, usually so it is fairer
redistribute.example: Some economists believe governments should redistribute wealth by investing more in schools in poorer regions.

redistributing.meaning: to move resources to different people or places so they are shared more fairly
redistributing.example: Redistributing funding towards rural hospitals could greatly improve healthcare for people far from big cities.

redistribution.meaning: the act of spreading something across different people or places in a new way
redistribution.example: The growth of remote work may lead to a redistribution of jobs from capital cities to smaller towns.

redress.meaning: to correct something that is wrong or unfair
redress.example: Scholarships for students from poor families help redress the imbalance in access to higher education.

reductive.meaning: making something complex seem much simpler than it really is
reductive.example: Judging a school only by its exam results is reductive, as it ignores sport, arts and character.

redundant.meaning: no longer needed, especially of workers whose jobs are replaced by machines
redundant.example: Some bank clerks have become redundant as more customers manage their accounts through mobile apps.

refined.meaning: to improve an idea or belief by making small changes over time
refined.example: Travelling and meeting new people has helped me refine my views on what really matters in life.

reflection.meaning: careful, quiet thought about something, especially your own life or experiences
reflection.example: Walking alone by the river gives me time for reflection after a stressful week.

reflective.meaning: thinking deeply and carefully about things
reflective.example: Reading novels encourages a more reflective attitude, helping people understand lives very different from their own.

refreshed.meaning: feeling less tired and more energetic than before

refreshing.meaning: making you feel more energetic and less tired or hot

registers.meaning: a style of language suited to a particular situation, such as formal or informal
registers.example: IELTS candidates need to use an appropriate register and avoid slang when writing formal letters.

regulation.meaning: official rules or control over an activity, usually by a government
regulation.example: Stricter regulation of street food vendors could reduce illnesses caused by poor hygiene.

rehabilitation.meaning: helping offenders change their behaviour and return to normal life in society
rehabilitation.example: Education and job training in prisons are key to rehabilitation, giving offenders a real chance to change.

reinforces.meaning: to make an idea, belief or feeling stronger
reinforces.example: Parents who read regularly reinforce the message that books are enjoyable, not just something for school.

reintegration.meaning: the process of returning to society and becoming accepted in it again
reintegration.example: Community support is vital for the reintegration of former prisoners, who often struggle to find work.

reinterpreted.meaning: to present or understand something in a new or different way
reinterpreted.example: Young designers often reinterpret traditional sarees with modern colours and patterns.

reinvigorated.meaning: full of new energy and enthusiasm

rejuvenate.meaning: to make someone feel fresher, healthier and more energetic

rejuvenated.meaning: feeling fresh, healthy and full of energy again

rejuvenating.meaning: making you feel fresh, healthy and full of energy
rejuvenating.example: Swimming in the early morning is a rejuvenating way to start the day.

relentless.meaning: continuing without stopping or becoming less intense
relentless.example: The relentless noise of car horns in Dhaka can be exhausting if you're not used to it.

reliable.meaning: able to be trusted to do what is expected or promised
reliable.example: A reliable friend is someone who turns up when they say they will, even when it's inconvenient.

reliance on fossil fuels.meaning: depending heavily on coal, oil and gas for energy
reliance on fossil fuels.example: Reducing our reliance on fossil fuels will require major investment in solar and wind power.

reliant.meaning: needing something or someone in order to function or succeed

relic.meaning: an old object kept because of its historical or emotional value

relieve pressure.meaning: to reduce the demands or strain on a system, place or person

religiously.meaning: regularly and carefully, without ever failing to do it

relocating.meaning: to move to a new place to live or work

reluctantly.meaning: in a way that shows you do not really want to do something

relying solely on.meaning: to depend on only one thing without using anything else

remarkable.meaning: unusual or surprising in a way that deserves attention
remarkable.example: The speed at which mobile banking spread across rural Bangladesh has been truly remarkable.

remarkably.meaning: to an unusual or surprising degree
remarkably.example: The new metro is remarkably clean and punctual, which has made my commute much easier.

remarkably adaptable.meaning: surprisingly able to change and adjust to new situations
remarkably adaptable.example: Children are remarkably adaptable and often settle into new schools faster than their parents expect.

reminisce.meaning: to talk or think about pleasant experiences from the past
reminisce.example: Whenever my uncles visit, they love to reminisce about their childhood in the village.

reminiscing.meaning: to talk together about pleasant shared memories from the past

remote.meaning: far away from towns, cities and other people

render efforts ineffective.meaning: to cause actions or attempts to fail to produce the intended result

renewal.meaning: a feeling of new life, energy and a fresh start

repairable.meaning: able to be fixed when broken or damaged

repairing.meaning: to improve a relationship or situation that has been damaged
repairing.example: It took several honest conversations to repair my friendship with a colleague after a silly argument.

repatriating.meaning: to bring people, money or skills back to their home country
repatriating.example: Some governments offer tax incentives to repatriate talented scientists who have been working overseas.

repercussions.meaning: an effect, usually a bad one, that happens as a result of an action

repetitive.meaning: saying or doing the same thing too many times, so it becomes boring

replicate.meaning: to do or make something again in exactly the same way

replicated.meaning: to repeat or copy something so that it happens again elsewhere or on a larger scale

repurpose.meaning: to change something so that it can be used for a different purpose

reputable.meaning: having a good reputation and trusted by people

resentment.meaning: a feeling of anger because you think you have been treated unfairly

reservations.meaning: a feeling of doubt about whether something is good or right
reservations.example: I have some reservations about online degrees, as students may miss out on campus life.

reserved.meaning: quiet and slow to show feelings or opinions to other people

resilience.meaning: the ability to recover quickly and keep going after difficulties

resilient.meaning: able to survive difficult conditions and remain strong
resilient.example: Small family businesses in my town proved resilient during the pandemic, adapting by delivering goods to homes.

resist.meaning: to stop yourself from doing or having something that you want

reskill.meaning: to learn new skills so that you can do a different job
reskill.example: Workers whose jobs are automated will need support to reskill for roles in growing industries.

resolved.example: After failing the exam once, she was resolved to pass it the second time, whatever it took.

resonate.meaning: to produce a deep, full sound that continues and vibrates
resonate.example: The call to prayer seemed to resonate through the quiet streets early in the morning.

resonated.meaning: to seem meaningful to someone because it matches their own experiences or feelings
resonated.example: The film's story about a family leaving their village really resonated with my parents.

resource depletion.meaning: the using up of natural resources such as water or forests faster than they can be replaced

resourceful.meaning: good at finding clever ways to solve problems with what is available
resourceful.example: My mother is incredibly resourceful and can make a delicious meal from whatever is left in the kitchen.

responsibility.meaning: a duty or task that you are expected to do

rest on your achievements.meaning: to stop making an effort because you are satisfied with what you have already achieved

restless.meaning: unable to stay still or relaxed because you are bored, impatient or anxious
restless.example: After a week at home during the holidays, I started to feel restless and wanted to travel somewhere.

restorative.meaning: making you feel healthier, calmer and full of energy again
restorative.example: A quiet weekend in my grandparents' village is always restorative after a busy month at work.

resurface.meaning: to appear again after being hidden or forgotten for some time
resurface.example: Old habits often resurface when people are under pressure, even after years of trying to change.

resurgence.meaning: a situation in which something becomes popular or active again after a period of decline
resurgence.example: There has been a resurgence in vinyl records among young music fans who enjoy the warmer sound.

retain.meaning: to keep information in your memory

retreat.meaning: a quiet, private place where you go to relax and escape from daily pressures
retreat.example: The small balcony of our flat is my retreat on hot evenings, with a cup of tea and a book.

reupholstered.meaning: to put new padding and a new fabric cover on a chair or sofa

reverence.meaning: a feeling of deep respect and admiration for something
reverence.example: Visitors speak in whispers inside the old mosque, out of reverence for the place.

reverse the trend.meaning: to change a pattern of development so that it starts moving in the opposite direction

revitalised.meaning: to give new life, energy and activity to a place

revitalising.meaning: to bring new economic activity and life to an area or community
revitalising.example: Local festivals can play a big role in revitalising small towns that young people have left.

revive.meaning: to make an old custom or tradition popular or active again

reviving.meaning: to become popular or active again after a period of decline
reviving.example: Interest in board games seems to be reviving as families look for ways to spend time away from screens.

revolutionary.meaning: involving a completely new idea that causes a great change

revolutionise.meaning: to completely change something in a way that greatly improves it

revolutionised.meaning: to completely change the way something is done, usually for the better

revolutionising.meaning: to change the way something is done completely and in a positive way

rewarding.meaning: giving you satisfaction and pleasure because it feels useful or worthwhile

richness.meaning: the quality of being full of interesting variety, depth and meaning
richness.example: Travelling helped me appreciate the richness of cultures very different from my own.

rightly be proud of.meaning: to have good reason to feel pleased and satisfied about something

rigid.meaning: strict and not able to be changed or adapted to different situations

rise to the occasion.meaning: to deal successfully with a difficult situation by doing better than expected

ritual.meaning: something you do regularly in the same way, often because it gives you pleasure
ritual.example: Drinking tea with my father after Friday prayers has become a little family ritual.

riverbank erosion.meaning: the gradual wearing away of land at the edge of a river by moving water

roam.meaning: to walk or travel around freely without a fixed plan

root causes.meaning: the basic, underlying reason why a problem exists

rooted.meaning: feeling a strong sense of belonging to a particular place or community

rooted in.meaning: based on or coming from something as its origin

rote learning.meaning: learning by repeating things until you remember them, without really understanding them
rote learning.example: Rote learning might help students pass exams, but it rarely teaches them to think critically.

rounded.meaning: balanced and complete, with a good variety of experiences or qualities
rounded.example: Sports and hobbies help children become more rounded individuals, not just good exam takers.

rudimentary.meaning: very basic and not well developed

rule of law.meaning: the principle that everyone, including leaders, must obey the same laws

ruthless.meaning: determined to get what you want without caring if you hurt others

ruthlessly.meaning: in a very firm and determined way, without letting less important things distract you

safeguard.meaning: to protect something carefully so that it is not lost or harmed
safeguard.example: I try to safeguard my evenings for family time, even when work gets busy.

safeguarding.meaning: to protect people or things from harm or danger
safeguarding.example: Schools have an important role in safeguarding children's wellbeing, both online and offline.

safety nets.meaning: government help that protects people from falling into extreme poverty

sanctuary.meaning: a peaceful place where you feel safe and can escape from stress
sanctuary.example: For me, the riverside path near my home is a sanctuary from noise and deadlines.

satellite cities.meaning: a smaller city built near a large one to reduce pressure on it

satisfaction.meaning: a pleasant feeling you get when you achieve something or get what you wanted
satisfaction.example: There is real satisfaction in finishing a long novel you almost gave up on.

satisfying.meaning: giving you a feeling of pleasure because you have achieved something

scale of influence.meaning: how widely and powerfully someone can affect people or events

scars.meaning: lasting emotional damage caused by an unpleasant experience

sceptical.meaning: tending to doubt whether something is true until there is good evidence
sceptical.example: I am always sceptical of adverts that promise you can learn a language in two weeks.

scrambling.meaning: to rush to do something quickly and in a disorganised way
scrambling.example: I hate scrambling to pack my bag on the morning of a trip, so I prepare the night before.

scrap heap.meaning: a place where things that are no longer wanted are thrown away
scrap heap.example: My old bicycle was heading for the scrap heap until my father repaired it.

scratched the surface.meaning: to deal with only a very small part of a subject or experience
scratched the surface.example: I spent three days in Chittagong, but I felt I had only scratched the surface of the city.

screen-bound.meaning: spending most of the time using screens such as phones, computers or TVs

scribble.meaning: to write something quickly and carelessly

scrolling.meaning: moving continuously through content on a phone or computer screen
scrolling.example: I set a timer on my phone to stop endless scrolling before bed.

scrutinise.meaning: to examine something very carefully to find mistakes or check it is true
scrutinise.example: I always scrutinise university websites carefully before recommending a course to a student.

scrutiny.meaning: careful and critical attention from other people
scrutiny.example: Politicians face intense public scrutiny, so every comment they make is analysed.

seamless.meaning: happening smoothly without any problems or interruptions

seamlessly.meaning: smoothly and naturally, without any obvious join or difficulty
seamlessly.example: Good teachers seamlessly combine humour and discipline in the classroom.

seasonal employment.meaning: work that is available only at certain times of the year
seasonal employment.example: The rice harvest provides seasonal employment for many labourers in rural Bangladesh.

secluded.meaning: quiet, private and hidden away from other people
secluded.example: We found a secluded spot by the river where we could chat without any noise.

second-hand.meaning: previously owned or used by someone else
second-hand.example: Most of my textbooks at university were second-hand, which saved me a lot of money.

sedentary.meaning: involving a lot of sitting and very little physical activity
sedentary.example: Because my job is so sedentary, I make a point of walking by the river every evening.

sedentary lifestyle.meaning: a way of living that involves a lot of sitting and little exercise
sedentary lifestyle.example: Office workers can counter a sedentary lifestyle by taking short walks during their breaks.

seductive.meaning: very attractive and tempting, making you want something
seductive.example: The idea of becoming rich overnight through online trading is seductive but usually unrealistic.

seeing it through.meaning: to continue with a difficult task until it is finished
seeing it through.example: Writing my final project was exhausting, but I was determined to see it through.

seemingly endless.meaning: appearing to continue for ever, with no end in sight
seemingly endless.example: In the monsoon, there are seemingly endless days of rain when the streets turn into streams.

selective.meaning: careful about what you choose, only accepting things that are good for you
selective.example: I have become more selective about the news I read, focusing on reliable sources.

self-assurance.meaning: confidence in yourself and your abilities
self-assurance.example: Giving presentations at university gave me a self-assurance I never had at school.

self-assured.meaning: confident in your own abilities and calm in how you behave
self-assured.example: My younger sister has become much more self-assured since she started giving presentations in class.

self-aware.meaning: having a clear understanding of your own feelings, strengths and weaknesses
self-aware.example: Keeping a journal has made me more self-aware about what triggers my stress.

self-censor.meaning: to avoid saying or writing what you think because you fear criticism or punishment
self-censor.example: Many people self-censor on social media because they worry their employer might see their posts.

self-control.meaning: the ability to control your emotions and desires
self-control.example: It takes real self-control to leave your phone in another room while studying.

self-defeating.meaning: causing more problems and preventing you from achieving what you want
self-defeating.example: Skipping sleep to study more is self-defeating, because a tired brain cannot learn properly.

self-directed.meaning: able to organise and manage your own learning or work without supervision
self-directed.example: Online courses suit self-directed learners who can set their own goals and deadlines.

self-discipline.meaning: the ability to make yourself do things you should do, even when it is difficult
self-discipline.example: Learning a language on your own requires a great deal of self-discipline and patience.

self-expression.meaning: the showing of your personality, feelings or ideas through art, clothes or activities
self-expression.example: For many young people, music is an important form of self-expression.

self-imposed.meaning: created by yourself rather than by others
self-imposed.example: Many of the limits we feel are self-imposed, such as believing we are too old to learn.

self-interest.meaning: concern only for your own advantage rather than for others
self-interest.example: Countries often act out of self-interest rather than cooperating on global problems.

self-reliant.meaning: able to do things and make decisions without needing help from others
self-reliant.example: Living in a hostel taught me to be more self-reliant, from managing money to cooking.

self-sufficient.meaning: able to provide what you need yourself without relying on others
self-sufficient.example: My grandparents are almost self-sufficient in vegetables because they grow most of what they eat.

self-taught.meaning: having learned a skill by yourself rather than from a teacher
self-taught.example: My cousin is a self-taught guitarist who learned entirely from online videos.

selfless.meaning: caring more about other people's needs than your own
selfless.example: Nurses often show selfless dedication, working long shifts to care for strangers.

seniority.meaning: a higher position or rank gained by working somewhere for a long time
seniority.example: In many companies, promotions still depend more on seniority than on actual performance.

sensational.meaning: presented in a shocking way to attract attention rather than to inform
sensational.example: Some news websites use sensational headlines just to get more clicks.

sensationalism.meaning: reporting news in a shocking or exaggerated way to attract attention
sensationalism.example: Responsible journalists avoid sensationalism, even when it would attract a bigger audience.

sense of loss.meaning: a feeling of sadness because something or someone important is no longer there
sense of loss.example: When my best friend moved abroad, I felt a deep sense of loss for months.

sense of occasion.meaning: a feeling that an event is special and important

sense of ownership.meaning: a feeling of responsibility for something because you helped to create or manage it
sense of ownership.example: Letting students choose their own projects gives them a stronger sense of ownership over their learning.

sense of perspective.meaning: the ability to judge how important things really are, without exaggerating problems
sense of perspective.example: Spending time with my grandparents always gives me a sense of perspective about my own worries.

sense of self.meaning: your understanding of who you are and what makes you unique
sense of self.example: Moving to a new country can challenge your sense of self in unexpected ways.

sensible.meaning: reasonable and based on good judgement
sensible.example: Saving part of your salary each month is a sensible habit to start early.

sensible compromise.meaning: a reasonable solution in which each side accepts less than it originally wanted
